Part 1: Key decisions and facts

Go/no-go gates. NO at an early gate costs the least.

# Question Threshold Evidence If NO
1 Are signed pilot partner commitments in hand (at least 3 adult ESL programs and 2 technical/safety-training organizations, with enrolment guarantees) and at least 3 publisher letters of interest, with baseline dropout evidence no worse than 35%? Signed commitments from at least 3 ESL programs and 2 technical organizations by Month 3, plus at least 3 non-binding publisher letters; baseline-study dropout not above 35%; guarantees covering at least 320 expected completers by Month 6. Signed MOUs and enrolment guarantees at Month 3; publisher letters at Month 3; baseline dropout analysis at Month 3 (run in a form that ethics review permits); guarantee audit at Month 6. Delay Phase 2 launch and re-recruit from standby sites; if guarantees cover fewer than 320 expected completers by Month 6, cancel Phase 2 or pivot the wedge before further spend (premortem FM3).
2 Can safety-critical glossary and labeling pilots proceed under counsel and insurer advice without formal regulatory approval and without disproportionate premiums? Written counsel advice and informal regulator input that no formal approval is required for glossary/labeling scope; insurance cover available at no more than $50K per year (estimate); legal/liability spend within $150K-$200K (estimate). Counsel retained by Month 2; liability strategy, broker quotes and regulator written input at Month 4 (other documents say Month 6 or 8; align to Month 4). Cancel or defer the technical/safety cohort and proceed ESL-only. This changes the 4-arm, 320-completer design, so the gate population and validity conditions must be re-registered before Phase 2. Do not run live-procedure pilots.
3 Can raters score pronunciation consistency reliably on the locked ordinal reading and single accent anchor, and does the ordinal converter stay unambiguous? Inter-rater kappa at least 0.70 floor (target 0.75) at the Month 10 dry run, with at least 3 raters at 0.75 on pre-screening by Month 4; no more than 5% ambiguous conversions (proposed threshold) in the Month 4 conversion test; marker symbol and spoken form fixed in writing. Pre-screening Month 4; micro-calibration on 100-200 words Month 6; dry run and kappa check Month 10; converter test on 200-300 real documents Month 4. Retrain and retest; then 4-week Phase 1 extension (about $85K, estimate) or synthetic baseline plus human verification. If kappa is still below 0.70, the board drops pronunciation consistency as a primary metric or pivots. If ambiguity exceeds 5% after one redesign, withdraw the ordinal rule from the gate. No Phase 2 launch on unreliable scoring.
4 Is Phase 1 exit met: rules locked, four metrics and thresholds pre-registered with a power analysis confirming 80 completers per arm, 5,000 entries with usable audio, and enrolment forecast to deliver at least 320 completers within the $175K pre-gate draw cap? Pre-registration on OSF by Month 11 with psychometrician sign-off; rules locked Month 12; lexicon coverage at least 85%; ethics approval in hand; forecast completers at least 320 (enrolment at least 460 at no more than 30% dropout) at the enrolment audit; cumulative pre-gate draws not above $175K. Power analysis Month 5; validity study Months 10-11; pre-registration Month 11; Phase 1 exit review Month 12; enrolment audit Month 12-13 (one agreed month); earned-value report. Delay Phase 2 start only by board vote with a power check; activate contingency incentives ($20K-$30K, estimate) or resize enrolment to 123-146 per arm if baseline dropout is 35-45%. If forecast draws exceed $175K with no funded plan for 80 completers per arm, halt Phase 2 and descope or cancel (premortem FM1 stop rule).
5 Do the Month 24 pilot results show GO: all four pre-registered metrics pass on valid data? Ordinal error down at least 25%; comprehension no more than 10% slower than control; pronunciation consistency at least 15% above control and statistically significant; 30-day retention at least 70% of post-test and not below control; validity: at least 80 completers per arm, follow-up at least 70%, kappa at least 0.70. Data lock including 30-day follow-up Month 22; analysis and gate dossier Months 22-24; board decision Month 24. Valid data with any metric failing is NO-GO: close the project and return up to $1.2M (less draws and wind-down). Invalid or inconclusive data leads to a board-decided 3-6 month extension (about $300K-$600K, estimate), whose funding source must be decided in advance.
6 Is a written steward commitment signed for post-v1.0 maintenance, as the precondition for the v1.0 release? Signed MOU with a steward showing a funding source for $150K-$250K per year (estimate); at least 2 written letters of interest by Month 24; funding commitments at least 50% of $150K per year at Month 30. Candidate brief at Month 12; letters of interest by Month 24; MOU negotiation Months 27-30; signed MOU at Month 30 (Month 33 is only the latest point at which a delayed release can still be triggered). Do not release v1.0; go to the board for a scaled stewardship model or a funder consortium. If nothing is signed by Month 33, cancel the public release and close with archived materials, unless a funded deferral beyond Month 36 is explicitly decided.

What you need to decide, and by when.

5 open decisions: 4 high and 1 medium severity. The safety-cohort fallback (Month 4 = 2027-02-13) and baseline study form (Month 1 = 2026-11-13) are the most urgent, since they shape the Month 3 (2027-01-13) partner gate and the 4-arm design. The reserve waterfall should be settled by Month 6 (2027-04-13), and the steward fallback and steward funding before Month 27 (2029-01-13). Until then the plan can proceed on canonical values: Phase 1 rule drafting, lexicon, board setup and counsel retention.

1. Reserve waterfall (🔴 High)

Decision: How is the $0.35M reserve ranked and released across pre-gate protection, a Phase 2 extension after inconclusive data, Phase 3 top-up and Phase 2.5?

Why it is open: Canonical rule caps pre-gate draws at $175K and releases the balance only after a Month 24 (2028-10-13) GO. Reviews charge a $300K-$600K extension and Phase 2.5 to the 'entire reserve', which an inconclusive result cannot release.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Board may release a defined part of the post-gate balance for a validated extension without a GO. Extension of up to about $175K becomes fundable; still below a 3-month extension ($300K) unless Phase 3 underspend adds. Weakens the gate-protection of funds. reserve_draw_rule; gate_funds_at_risk; Reviews 1, 2, 4, 5, 10.
B. Cap any extension at what the $175K pre-gate cap and Phase 3 underspend can cover. Extension limited to a shorter period than 3-6 months; the reserve order is fixed and no Phase 2.5 is funded. phase2_extension_fallback; free_reserve_after_fallbacks.
C. Treat extension as unfunded; require descoping or termination. Keeps the reserve rule intact; inconclusive data leads to descope or wind-down, with up to $1.2M returnable. phase2_go_no_go_rule wording; extension text in reviews.
  • If nobody decides: Canonical rule applies: no post-gate release without a GO, so an extension is unfunded.
  • Owner: Project Sponsor and Funding Authority, on Steering Committee recommendation
  • Decide by: Month 6 (2027-04-13), before the pre-registration and enrolment commitments that set Phase 2 exposure.
  • Blocks: Phase 1 exit (Month 12 = 2027-10-13) and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) inconclusive-data branch.

2. Safety-cohort fallback (🔴 High)

Decision: If safety-critical pilots cannot proceed, does the gate become an ESL-only 2-arm design, or is the technical cohort deferred to a Phase 2.5?

Why it is open: Canonical design is 4 arms and 320 completers. Reviews defer the cohort after 4 or 6 months and date regulator advice at Month 4, 6 or 8 (2027-02-13, 2027-04-13, 2027-06-13).

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. ESL-only 2-arm gate (160 completers), technical cohort non-gating. Keeps Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate timing; narrows evidence to ESL; re-register validity conditions; lowers enrolment and participant costs. pilot_design; pilot_min_completers; pilot_enrolment_and_dropout; pitch claims.
B. Defer the technical cohort to a Phase 2.5 after Month 24 (2028-10-13). Needs funding outside the current budget; the gate rests on ESL arms; safety benefit claims remain unvalidated at gate. pilot_design; phase3_budget; adoption_wedge.
C. Hold the 4-arm gate and delay the gate until approval is secured. Pilot window shrinks or the gate slips past Month 24 (2028-10-13); extension cost of $85K-$170K per 4-8 weeks (estimate). pilot_schedule; safety_limits; budget.
  • If nobody decides: At Month 4 (2027-02-13) with no written counsel and regulator advice, the technical cohort is cancelled or deferred and ESL-only runs, with unregistered validity conditions.
  • Owner: Steering Committee with Compliance & Risk Management Committee; Sponsor if budget changes
  • Decide by: Month 4 (2027-02-13) (liability strategy and written regulator advice), before Phase 2 design is registered.
  • Blocks: Phase 1 exit gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-13) and pre-registration (Month 11 = 2027-09-13).

Why it is open: FM4 cancels at Month 33 (2029-07-13). Reviews 5, 6, 9, 14 and Self-audit 20 allow deferral to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or later, outside the funded program.

4. Steward funding from project budget (🔴 High)

Decision: Does the steward receive any project money (reserve or Phase 3 underspend), or is stewardship funded entirely externally?

Why it is open: Pitch states the steward receives the $0.35M reserve plus pro-rata Phase 3 funding. The plan treats $150K-$250K per year (estimate) as unfunded; the reserve is also claimed elsewhere.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Steward receives nothing from the project budget. Reserve remains for the gate and extension; steward must find $150K-$250K per year (estimate) externally, raising the Month 30 (2029-04-13) MOU risk. Pitch Collaboration Opportunities.
B. Fixed capped seed from unspent Phase 3 or reserve, ranked after gate protection and extension. Improves MOU odds; only available after a GO; needs a stated cap. reserve_draw_rule; stewardship_funding_gap; pitch.
C. Funding entirely external (consortium or funder). Project funds untouched; adds funder outreach work before Month 24 (2028-10-13). stewardship_funding_gap; outreach plan.
  • If nobody decides: The pitch transfer is removed; stewardship stays an unfunded gap.
  • Owner: Project Sponsor and Funding Authority
  • Decide by: Month 12 (2027-10-13), so candidate stewards see terms in the candidate brief.
  • Blocks: Steward MOU (Month 30 = 2029-04-13) and v1.0 release.

Why it is open: The study (20-30 learners, Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) precedes ethics approval (Month 6 = 2027-04-13), consent forms and partner signatures (Month 3 = 2027-01-13), and cannot observe 30-day or 12-month dropout.

free_reserve_after_fallbacks Free reserve after a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K draw) = $265K ($350K - $85K); remaining pre-gate headroom under the $175K cap = $90K; a following 3-month Phase 2 extension ($300K) would leave a $35K shortfall (estimate) estimate Added to avoid counting the same $350K reserve twice: $85K + $300K = $385K exceeds $350K by $35K, so the two fallbacks cannot both be fully funded; a psychometric do-over ($200K-$300K in Risk 3) also exceeds the $175K pre-gate cap and needs a board decision.

overrun_exposure $300K overrun scenario = 8.6% of budget (estimate); exceeds the $175K pre-gate draw cap by $125K estimate 300/3,500 = 8.6%; 300 - 175 = 125; the shortfall must come from scope cuts outside the pilot arms or a new board decision to lift the cap (still within the $350K reserve if no other draws have been made).
phase1_exit_gate Month 12 (2027-10-13) Phase 1 exit: rules locked, draft standard comment window closed, 4 metrics pre-registered, 5,000 entries with usable audio, lexicon coverage >=85%, inter-rater kappa >=0.70 floor (target 0.75), partner commitments signed, ethics approval in hand proposed threshold Distinct from the Phase 2 outcome gate: Phase 1 tests readiness and rule/instrument quality, not learner outcomes; kappa floor aligned to 0.70 (the extension trigger and Phase 2 validity condition) with 0.75 as target, so the exit gate does not contradict the fallback rule.
phase2_go_no_go_rule Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go: GO only if all four metrics meet their pre-registered thresholds AND validity conditions hold (>=80 completers per arm, follow-up completion >=70%, kappa >=0.70); valid data with any metric failing = NO-GO; invalid/inconclusive data = board-decided extension proposed threshold Brief requires a go/no-go after Phase 2 on four metrics; the review asked for pre-registered numeric rules, so a conjunctive rule with a separate 'inconclusive' branch is set.
gate_ordinal_error >=25% relative reduction in ordinal error rate vs. standard-English control (proposed threshold, finalized in pre-registration) proposed threshold Review example 25% and pre-assessment 20% are both illustrative; 25% chosen because the ordinal rule is mechanical and fully taught, so a 20% bar risks a false-positive.
gate_comprehension_speed Clear English reading/comprehension time no more than 10% slower than standard-English control (proposed threshold) proposed threshold Pre-assessment example value, adopted as the proposal because recognizability is the key adoption risk; to be confirmed by the psychometrician.
gate_pronunciation_consistency Pronunciation consistency score >=15% above control with statistically significant difference (proposed threshold, calibrate at pre-registration); scoring reliability kappa >=0.75 target, floor 0.70 proposed threshold No documents give an outcome magnitude, so 15% is a placeholder to be calibrated; kappa 0.75/0.70 come from the risk register and assumptions.
gate_retention_30day 30-day retention: >=70% of immediate post-test performance retained at 30 days and not below control (proposed threshold) proposed threshold 70% appears in the pre-assessment as both 'learner continuation' and the recruit-retention goal; the knowledge-retention metric is defined separately from participant dropout (<=30%).
intelligibility_target Average adult comprehension of Clear English text reaches >=90% of standard-English control accuracy within 2 weeks of exposure (90% is a proposed threshold) user constraint The 2-week intelligibility window is the user's constraint; the 90% operationalisation is an added proposal.
pilot_min_completers At least 80 completers per arm (estimate, to be confirmed by power analysis); 320 completers across 4 arms estimate Documents give 50-100 per condition; 80 is the pre-assessment/review figure for ~80% power at alpha 0.05 and is not yet validated; 80 x 4 = 320.
pilot_enrolment_and_dropout Enrol >=115 per arm (80 / 0.70 = 114.3, rounded up) = 460 total across 4 arms; tolerated dropout <=30%; all enrolment complete by Month 13 (2027-11-13) estimate The '15% over-recruitment' (92 per arm) would only retain 80 completers at ~13% dropout (80/92 = 87%), contradicting the 30% dropout tolerance, so enrolment is sized from 30% dropout instead; 115 x 4 = 460, and 460 x 0.70 = 322 >= 320 completers.
pilot_design 2 cohorts (adult ESL; native-speaker technical/safety-glossary) x 2 conditions (Clear English vs standard-English control) = 4 arms decision Brief names both cohorts; the control group is required by the purpose-built, control-calibrated metric design.
pilot_partner_commitments Signed commitments by Month 3 (2027-01-13): >=3 adult ESL programs (target 3-4) and >=2 technical/safety-training organizations (target 2-3), plus non-binding publisher letters of interest proposed threshold Risk 2 and pre-assessment give 3-4 / 2-3; the lower bounds are set as the go threshold, escalation to the board if missed. pilot_schedule Enrolment complete Month 13 (2027-11-13); midpoint check Month 18 (2028-04-13); extra validation (if needed) by Month 21 (2028-07-13); data lock incl. 30-day follow-up by Month 22 (2028-08-13); analysis and gate dossier Months 22-24 (2028-08-13 to 2028-10-13) decision Pre-assessment ran sessions through Month 24 (2028-10-13), which leaves no time to analyse before the gate; data lock at Month 22 (2028-08-13) makes the Month 24 (2028-10-13) decision feasible.
ordinal_rule Option A: numeric ordinals with one invariant prefix marker on every digit string; fixed spoken reading published; legacy 1st/2nd/3rd forms accepted and mechanically convertible; marker symbol and spoken form fixed by Month 10 (2027-08-13) decision Scenario 'Pragmatic Foundation' (fit 9/10); spelled forms like 'oneth' and the suffix-only variant rejected for native-reader rejection risk and legacy-suffix clashes.
g2p_approach Standard spellings unchanged; pronunciation delivered as an optional software-generated overlay (ruby-style in digital, printed key in print); no respelling in v1.0 decision Overlay chosen over respelling (Pioneer's Gambit) to protect recognizability and publisher compatibility; adoption over linguistic purity.
morphology_threshold Retain all irregular forms within the top 1,000 lexicon words by frequency; regularize only lower-frequency irregulars with low recognition penalty; cap at 25% of irregular verbs/plurals changed (all proposed); go/went is retained proposed threshold Frequency-band option chosen for recognizability; the cutoff and cap are arbitrary until pilot error data exist; dual-form pilots rejected because retiring a form later causes churn.
homograph_policy Disambiguation marker mandatory only in safety-critical/procedural documents for a published list of <=50 high-impact pairs (proposed cap); optional elsewhere; no authoring plugin funded in v1.0 decision Option 1 keeps the list manageable and avoids tooling dependency the $3.5M budget cannot maintain; examples lead/lead and read/read are from the brief.
lexicon 5,000-word core lexicon: 4,500 frequency-led general words + 500-word (10%) reserved technical/safety block; coverage of pilot running text >=85% (audit Month 8 = 2027-06-13; expansion fix by Month 10 = 2027-08-13) proposed threshold 5,000 words is the user constraint; 85% from assumptions (risk register range 85-90%); 4,500 + 500 = 5,000 and 500/5,000 = 10%; the block serves the technical cohort without letting the list change mid-pilot.
audio_production Single-accent recording of all 5,000 entries (about 10,000 files at 2 takes), Months 6-11 (2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13), budget $80K-$120K (estimate); if cost exceeds $20 per entry ($100K total), switch to synthetic baseline plus human verification of the highest-friction subset; recording only 3,000-4,000 words violates the 5,000-word user constraint and is not an in-scope fallback estimate Pre-assessment $80K-$120K and $20/entry trigger; $80K-$120K / 5,000 = $16-$24 per entry, so the upper $100K-$120K part of the range lies above the $20 trigger and would activate the synthetic-baseline switch; 5,000 x 2 takes = 10,000 files (upper end of 7,500-10,000). The review's 3,000-4,000-word fallback needs an explicit user/board scope-change decision (merged here from the former separate fallback fact).
accent_anchor One reference accent chosen and justified by Month 3 (2027-01-13); mapping of other accents documented by Month 12 (2027-10-13); additional accents deferred to post-v1.0 (optional 200-300 word proof-of-concept sample, $10K-$15K, estimate) decision Single anchor keeps the pronunciation score auditable; full multi-accent coverage would add $50K-$100K (estimate) and is declined.
adoption_wedge ESL-first: Clear English offered as a supplementary module beside standard English; technical glossary cohort is secondary decision Pragmatic Foundation wedge; satisfies 'optimize for adoption' and the no-replacement constraint.
safety_limits Safety-critical pilots limited to glossary and labeling exercises, no live operational procedures before Month 24 (2028-10-13); legal counsel retained by Month 2 (2026-12-13); liability strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13); legal/liability spend capped at $150K-$200K (estimate); all materials disclaimed and human-reviewed decision Low-likelihood/high-severity risk is bounded by deferring live use; if liability insurance is unavailable or above $50K per year (estimate), safety-critical use stays glossary-only after the gate too.

Focus and Context

Clear English is a parallel English variant for adult ESL learners and technical writers, tested through rigorous pilots with pre-registered metrics and gated at Month 24 (2028-10-13) on defensible evidence before any public release. If pilots meet thresholds (ordinal error ≥25% reduction, comprehension ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control with a statistically significant difference, 30-day retention ≥70% of post-test performance and not below control), the standard advances; GO requires all four metrics to pass and validity to hold (≥80 completers per arm, follow-up ≥70%, kappa ≥0.70); valid data with any metric failing is NO-GO, with up to $1.2M returnable (less draws and wind-down) and the project closing; invalid or inconclusive data leads to a board-decided extension. The core tension: lightweight rules and supplementary positioning maximize adoption, but weak evidence risks credibility loss and abandonment post-launch.

Purpose and Goals

Design, pilot, and conditionally publish Clear English Standard v1.0 within 36 months and $3.5M (fixed envelope), using an ESL-first adoption wedge and a defensible Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate. Success means ≥3 licensed third-party adopters (at least 1 ESL publisher) and a written stewardship commitment for post-v1.0 maintenance ($150K–$250K/year, estimate), confirmed before v1.0 release at Month 30 (2029-04-13).

Key Deliverables and Outcomes

Phase 1 (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 exit): rules locked; 5,000-word lexicon with single-accent audio; pre-registered metrics on Open Science Framework; ethics approval; ≥3 ESL and ≥2 technical-training partner commitments. Phase 2 (Month 24 = 2028-10-13 gate): ≥80 completers per arm on four pre-registered metrics; defensible go/no-go dossier. Phase 3 (Month 36 = 2029-10-13): v1.0 published; ≥3 adopters licensed; stewardship MOU signed and transitioned; 5-year roadmap published.

Timeline and Budget

36 months: Phase 1 Months 0–12 (2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13) ($1.1M rules + corpus), Phase 2 Months 12–24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13) ($1.2M pilots), Phase 3 Months 24–36 (2028-10-13 to 2029-10-13) ($0.85M release + adoption), $0.35M reserve (capped pre-gate draws $175K, 5% of budget). Critical path: Month 2 (2026-12-13) psychometrician hire; Month 3 (2027-01-13) pilot partner commitments; Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-analysis plan registration; Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate; Month 30 (2029-04-13) v1.0 release conditional on stewardship MOU.

Risks and Mitigations

Risk 1 (High likelihood, high impact): Pilot recruitment/retention shortfall (actual dropout 35–45% vs. plan 30%) reduces completers to 63–75 per arm (6–21% below 80-per-arm minimum) from the 115-per-arm (460 total) enrolment, risking statistical power. Mitigation: conduct baseline recruitment study Months 1–2 (2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13); hire cohort manager by Month 6 (2027-04-13) (acceleration to Month 4 = 2027-02-13 is a proposal, with cost to be assessed); activate contingency incentives ($20K–$30K, estimate) if enrollment lags. Risk 2 (Medium likelihood, high impact): Pre-registered thresholds not locked or disputed at Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate. Mitigation: hire psychometrician Month 2 (2026-12-13); deliver power analysis Month 5 (2027-03-13); pre-register Month 11 (2027-09-13); publish on OSF with board sign-off. Risk 3 (High likelihood, medium impact): Stewardship unfunded post-Month 36 (2029-10-13) causes standard atrophy within 12–24 months (Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13). Mitigation: begin steward search Month 12 (2027-10-13); secure MOU by Month 30 (2029-04-13) before v1.0 release.

Audience Tailoring

Audience is project leadership, editorial board, and funders evaluating a 36-month, $3.5M language-standardization initiative. Tone is pragmatic and evidence-focused, emphasizing adoption over linguistic purity and gating rigor over timeline compression. Details are operationalized (Month N deadlines, signed commitments, pre-registered metrics) to support go/no-go decisions at key gates (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 rules lock, Month 24 = 2028-10-13 pilot gate, Month 36 = 2029-10-13 stewardship handoff).

Action Orientation

Immediate actions (by Month 2 = 2026-12-13): (1) Hire independent psychometrician with signed contract specifying power analysis and pre-analysis plan deliverables. (2) Retain legal counsel (product liability + data protection). (3) Engage Institutional Review Board for ethics approval. By Month 1 (2026-11-13): (4) Publish Editorial Board Charter with voting rules and tiebreak arbiter provisions. By Month 3 (2027-01-13): (5) Secure signed pilot partner commitments (≥3 ESL, ≥2 technical orgs). By Month 5 (2027-03-13): (6) Agree the tiebreak arbiter. By Month 6 (2027-04-13): (7) Hire Phase 2 Cohort Manager (1.0 FTE) with retention KPIs. All actions have 2-week slip escalation triggers to the board.

Overall Takeaway

Clear English Standard can succeed if three critical conditions are met: (1) pre-registered, empirically justified gate thresholds locked by Month 11 (2027-09-13) and defensible through independent review; (2) pilot sample size ≥80 per arm with dropout ≤30% achieved through early baseline validation and dedicated cohort management; (3) stewardship commitment secured by Month 30 (2029-04-13) as a precondition for v1.0 release. Without these, the project risks a scientifically disputable gate, underpowered pilots (invalid data, which leads to a board-decided extension of 3–6 months rather than a NO-GO), and post-launch standard atrophy—outcomes that put up to $1.2M of Phase 3 and reserve funding at risk and leave $1.5M–$2.5M of stewardship value unfunded. The evidence-gated, adoption-first positioning is the project's core strength; protecting that credibility requires rigor at every gate and early transparency on stewardship risk.

Feedback

Five areas for strengthening the plan: (1) Commission power analysis by Month 5 (2027-03-13) specifying effect-size benchmarks and confirming 80 per arm is adequate; publish sensitivity analyses in pre-analysis plan (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) to foreclose post-hoc disputes. (2) Conduct baseline recruitment study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) with N=20–30 learners to validate dropout assumptions and reallocate Phase 2 participant budget ($78K–$161K) if baseline confirms >30% attrition. (3) Establish monthly earned-value budget tracking (by Month 1 = 2026-11-13) with >10% variance thresholds to catch cost overruns before consuming the $175K pre-gate draw cap ($35K–$90K headroom estimate). (4) Begin steward identification (Month 12 = 2027-10-13) with formal capability audits and letters of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13); make stewardship MOU a v1.0 release precondition to avoid post-launch orphaning. (5) Publish KPI dashboard (enrollment, dropout, budget, pre-analysis plan registration) updated monthly for board transparency; tie release decisions to explicit, pre-registered metrics to defend against stakeholder claims of goalpost-moving or political bias.

Unoptimized waterfall. Parallel work not modelled here.

Part 2: Supporting analysis

Persuasive elevator pitch.

Clear English Standard: A Parallel English Variant for Adult ESL Learners and Technical Writers

Project Overview

Imagine a pathway for adult learners to finally read English with confidence—without replacing the English they know.

Clear English Standard is a parallel English variant designed for adult ESL learners and technical writers who lose critical information to spelling irregularities, unpredictable ordinals, and ambiguous words. Over 36 months and $3.5M, this project will deliver a public standard with regularized ordinals, pronunciation guidance, and homograph disambiguation—validated through rigorous pilots at Month 24 (2028-10-13), optionally adopted by ESL publishers and safety-critical sectors, and stewarded for long-term stability.

This is not a replacement. Clear English sits alongside standard English as a supplementary module and optional overlay. Learners and organizations choose it. The standard is built on defensible evidence: four pre-registered gate metrics (ordinal error reduction ≥25%, comprehension speed within 10% of control, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control with a statistically significant difference, 30-day retention ≥70% of post-test and not below control), independently reviewed assessments, and a 5,000-word reference lexicon validated in real classrooms and technical settings.

Clear English matters because inconsistency costs learners time and errors cost lives. A native speaker absorbs "read (present)" vs. "read (past)" through years of exposure; an ESL learner sees contradiction. A technical glossary resolves that gap—saving seconds on every procedure and potentially preventing miscommunication in safety-critical work.

This project is evidence-gated, not ideologically driven. GO requires all four pre-registered metrics to meet their thresholds and validity to hold (≥80 completers per arm, follow-up ≥70%, kappa ≥0.70). Valid data with any metric failing is a NO-GO: the project stops before public release and up to $1.2M is returnable, less draws and wind-down costs. Invalid or inconclusive data leads to a board-decided extension. If the gate is passed, Clear English becomes a certified, openly licensed resource that any publisher or standards body can adopt on transparent terms, without mandates or takeover of K-12 education.

Target Audience

  • Primary: Adult ESL program leaders and ESL publishers seeking a proven, evidence-backed curriculum innovation; technical and safety-training organizations evaluating ways to reduce documentation errors.
  • Secondary: Editorial boards, standards bodies (TESOL, IATEFL, ASD-STE100 maintainers) and academic linguistics researchers interested in language-planning and constructed-variant precedent.
  • Tertiary: Potential steward organizations and language-policy advocates in non-profit sectors.
  • Not: K-12 educators, policymakers seeking mandates, or general public audiences.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

Educator and publisher pushback

Risk: Teachers resist a "non-standard" variant or publishers see it as a competitor.

Mitigation: Position as supplementary, not replacement; co-design protocols with teachers from Month 1 (2026-11-13); engage TESOL/IATEFL early; fund an educator liaison.

Pilot recruitment shortfall

Risk: Enrollments fall below 80 completers per arm, invalidating gate metrics.

Mitigation: Sign commitments by Month 3 (2027-01-13); over-recruit to ≥115 per arm; use incentives ($50–$150 stipends) and a dedicated cohort manager by Month 6 (2027-04-13).

Assessment validity

Risk: Pronunciation raters disagree (kappa <0.70), making the go/no-go gate disputable.

Mitigation: Pre-register thresholds by Month 11 (2027-09-13); run a validity study by Month 10 (2027-08-13); retrain raters; extend Phase 1 by 4 weeks if needed.

Safety-critical liability

Risk: Misreading in operational procedures causing harm.

Mitigation: Limit pilots to glossary and labeling only; retain legal counsel by Month 2 (2026-12-13); disclaim all materials; human-review every entry.

Metrics for Success

Gate metrics (Month 24 = 2028-10-13)

  • Ordinal error reduction ≥25% vs. standard-English control
  • Comprehension speed ≤10% slower than control
  • Pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control with a statistically significant difference (kappa ≥0.75 target, floor 0.70, as a separate validity condition)
  • 30-day retention ≥70% of post-test performance and not below control

Operational metrics (Phase 1 exit, Month 12 = 2027-10-13)

  • Rules locked; 5,000 entries with usable audio
  • Inter-rater kappa ≥0.70
  • Ethics approval in hand
  • ≥3 ESL and ≥2 technical-training partner commitments

Adoption metrics (Month 36 = 2029-10-13)

  • ≥3 licensed third-party adopters (at least 1 ESL publisher)
  • Written steward commitment signed by Month 30 (2029-04-13), as the condition for the v1.0 release
  • Conformance checklists passed by ≥2 published materials

Fidelity and risk metrics

  • No rule changes during pilots
  • Zero safety incidents in pilot glossaries
  • Stranding of <$175K pre-gate reserve before Month 24 (2028-10-13) no-go fallback

Stakeholder Benefits

ESL programs and learners

A defensible, certified supplementary curriculum module with validated gains in ordinal recognition, pronunciation consistency and 30-day retention; optional overlay that does not disrupt standard English teaching.

Technical and safety-training organizations

A 500-word safety-critical glossary with mandatory homograph markers in procedures, reducing ambiguity-driven errors without the cost of full controlled-language training.

ESL publishers

License-to-use the reference lexicon, style guide and assessment items on permissive terms; gain competitive advantage by offering Clear English modules certified against a public checklist.

Standards bodies (TESOL, IATEFL)

A precedent for evidence-gated language innovation; no institutional turf conflict (independent non-profit steward).

Linguistics and language-policy researchers

A real-world test case of constructed-variant adoption, governance and fragmentation control.

Ethical Considerations

Transparency and evidence

All pilot data, decision logs and assessment instruments made public (with participant consent); pre-registered metrics and thresholds locked before pilots start to prevent p-hacking and selective reporting.

Inclusivity and accent bias

Reference accent chosen by Month 3 (2027-01-13) with documented mapping of other major English varieties; pronunciation consistency score scored on shared phonemic contrasts to avoid privileging one region; additional accents proposed as optional post-v1.0 (not funded in this phase).

Informed consent and data protection

Ethics approval by Month 6 (2027-04-13); encrypted audio storage with GDPR compliance; participants compensated fairly ($50–$150 stipends); right to withdraw.

Liability and safety

Safety-critical pilots limited to glossary and labeling, no live procedures; legal counsel retained; all materials disclaimed; human review of every homograph marker.

Equity

Free, open-licensed standard with no paywall; certification mark is non-profit and awards based on a published conformance checklist, not gatekeeping; no mandates or K-12 replacement claims.

Collaboration Opportunities

ESL program partnerships

Co-develop pilot curriculum, recruit and support learner cohorts (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13); receive published curriculum materials and conformance training.

Technical-writing and safety-training organizations

Co-design the 500-word safety-critical glossary; pilot homograph-marking protocols; receive validated glossary with licensing rights.

ESL publishers

License reference lexicon, dictionary and style guide; adopt Clear English as a supplementary module; use public conformance checklist for certification.

Linguistics and applied-language research

Commission or collaborate on pronunciation-rater calibration, morphology-error analysis and adoption-barrier research; access anonymized pilot data for secondary analysis (after Month 24 = 2028-10-13 gate).

Standards bodies (ASD-STE100, ICAO, plain-language networks)

Validate one-way mapping table from existing standards; co-author compatibility guidance; refer members to Clear English resources (no formal liaison funded).

Post-v1.0 steward organization

Assume governance, change-control and archive roles; receive $0.35M reserve release post-gate plus pro-rata Phase 3 funding if a written commitment is signed by Month 30 (2029-04-13); Month 33 (2029-07-13) is only the latest point at which a delayed release can still be triggered.

Long-term Vision

Institutional sustainability

Clear English Standard is transferred to a committed, non-profit steward organization by Month 36 (2029-10-13) with a published 10-year governance roadmap, change-control calendar and annual budget ($150K–$250K per year, estimate). The steward enforces the certification mark, approves third-party adopters against a public checklist and coordinates maintenance without centralized control.

Adoption pathway

By Month 36 (2029-10-13), ≥3 third-party adopters (at least 1 ESL publisher) integrate Clear English into courseware and glossaries, reaching an estimated 10,000–50,000 learners within 5 years; safety-critical sectors adopt the 500-word glossary in procedure manuals and training, reducing ambiguity-driven errors.

Evolution and resilience

v1.0 is frozen for 12 months post-release; v2.0 consolidates pilot feedback and post-launch usage data by Month 42 (2030-04-13). Fragmentation is controlled by the certification mark and the requirement that variants beyond 10% of rules adopt a distinct name.

Knowledge and precedent

Clear English becomes a documented case study in evidence-gated language planning, governance and constructed-variant adoption, contributing to applied linguistics research and informing future language-standardization initiatives.

Call to Action

ESL program leaders and technical-training organizations

Express interest in pilot partnership by Month 3 (2027-01-13). Sign a Memorandum of Understanding committing to ≥115 learner enrollments and onsite assessment sessions; we provide curriculum, incentives ($50–$150 per participant) and expert facilitation.

ESL publishers and standards bodies

Review the draft standard at Month 11 (2027-09-13) during the 30-day public comment window; submit conformance letters of interest by Month 12 (2027-10-13).

Potential steward organizations

Contact the project lead to discuss post-v1.0 governance roles and funding partnerships by Month 24 (2028-10-13).

Goal Statement: Design, pilot and publish Clear English Standard v1.0, a parallel (not replacement) English variant with regularized ordinals, spelling-to-sound guidance, capped morphology changes and homograph disambiguation, within 36 months and $3.5M (user constraint), led by an ESL-first adoption wedge.

SMART Criteria

  • Specific: Deliver a public Clear English Standard v1.0 with rule set and rationale, 5,000-word reference dictionary, style guide, pilot curriculum with assessments and open licensing policy, for adult ESL, technical writing and safety-critical glossary use, without mandates or K-12 replacement.
  • Measurable: Success is a Month 24 (2028-10-13) GO on four pre-registered metrics: ordinal error reduction >=25% (proposed threshold), comprehension speed within 10% of control, pronunciation consistency >=15% above control with a statistically significant difference (scoring kappa target 0.75, floor 0.70 as a separate validity condition), 30-day retention >=70% of post-test and not below control. Also >=3 licensed third-party adopters by Month 36 (2029-10-13) (proposed).
  • Achievable: Feasible through a gated three-phase plan, light-touch rules (standard spellings kept, prefix ordinals coexisting with legacy forms) and a $3.5M budget with a $0.35M reserve. Limits: scarce psychometric skills, pilot attrition, and unfunded post-Month-36 stewardship.
  • Relevant: Gives ESL learners and technical writers a consistent, optional standard that reduces high-friction inconsistencies and ambiguity, with evidence-based adoption by publishers and standards bodies rather than mandates.
  • Time-bound: 36 months from Month 0 (2026-10-13): Phase 1 Months 0-12 (2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13) rules and corpus; Phase 2 Months 12-24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13) pilots with go/no-go at Month 24 (2028-10-13); Phase 3 Months 24-36 (2028-10-13 to 2029-10-13) release and limited adoption, v1.0 by Month 30 (2029-04-13) (proposed).

Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

Key Risks

  • Educator, publisher and standards-body rejection or pushback reducing adoption and pilot engagement
  • Pilot recruitment shortfall or dropout above 30% invalidating gate metrics
  • Weak or disputable assessment validity and rater reliability (kappa below 0.70)
  • Editorial board deadlock or rule ambiguity delaying the Month 12 (2027-10-13) rules lock
  • Safety-critical liability exposure from misreading of Clear English text

Diverse Risks

  • Budget overrun (a $300K overrun is 8.6% of budget, estimate) exceeding the $175K pre-gate reserve cap
  • Phase 1 slippage compressing the pilot window, with Phase 2 extension costing up to $300K for 3 months (estimate)
  • Fragmentation and unofficial variants after release
  • Pilot audio privacy and ethics approval delays
  • Unfunded stewardship after Month 36 (2029-10-13) ($150K-$250K per year, estimate)

Mitigation Plans

  • Position as supplementary ESL module; co-design protocols with teachers, engage TESOL/IATEFL and publishers from Months 1-3 (2026-11-13 to 2027-01-13), fund an educator liaison
  • Sign enrolment commitments by Month 3 (2027-01-13), over-recruit to >=115 per arm (estimate), use incentives and a cohort manager by Month 6 (2027-04-13)
  • Pre-register thresholds by Month 11 (2027-09-13), run validity study and dry run at Month 10 (2027-08-13), retrain raters, and extend Phase 1 by 4 weeks if kappa stays below 0.70
  • Publish board charter by Month 1 (2026-11-13), resolve disputes by Month 10 (2027-08-13), use external arbiter, freeze rules during pilots
  • Limit pilots to glossary and labeling, retain legal counsel by Month 2 (2026-12-13), disclaim and human-review all materials, use monthly budget tracking and critical-path reviews, certification mark and early steward search

  • Ethics/IRB approval for pilot research with human participants
  • Data-sharing and consent agreements with pilot partner institutions
  • Trademark or certification-mark registration for the 'Clear English' name
  • Open license for text and dictionary

Compliance Standards

  • GDPR and US state data-protection laws for pilot audio and scores
  • Research ethics and informed-consent standards
  • Product liability and disclaimer practice for safety-critical materials
  • Accessibility and fair-use norms for published curricula

Regulatory Bodies

  • Institutional Review Board or research ethics committee
  • Data-protection authorities (ICO, US state regulators)
  • Education authorities and accreditation bodies in pilot jurisdictions
  • Workplace safety regulators (OSHA, HSE) for safety-critical contexts

Compliance Actions

  • Engage ethics review at Months 1-2 (2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) and obtain approval by Month 6 (2027-04-13)
  • Secure encrypted audio storage by Month 6 (2027-04-13) and audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13)
  • Publish privacy policy and consent forms by Month 12 (2027-10-13)
  • Retain legal counsel by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and set liability strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13)
  • Decide licensing and certification model by Month 6 (2027-04-13) and publish by Month 12 (2027-10-13)

Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The five Critical levers (Ordinal Marker Architecture, Grapheme-to-Phoneme Depth, Adoption Wedge, Outcome Metric Battery, Phase Budget) cover the main tensions: rule ambition versus recognizability and adoption, evidence rigor versus a fixed budget, and breadth versus depth of market entry. High levers refine content and governance. No distinct lever addresses risk and liability management for safety-critical pilots, or educator-outreach and training capacity.

Decision 1: Ordinal Marker Architecture

Lever ID: 1a9e4740-06a2-43cd-9ac0-fb5ab53fb48e

The Core Decision: Sets the single rule that replaces 1st/2nd/3rd, 11th–13th and 21st/31st patterns, and thereby the most visible, testable feature of the standard. Scope covers written form, a fixed spoken reading and machine conversion of legacy forms. Success metrics: ordinal error rate in pilots, native-reader acceptance, reading speed, and ease of automatic conversion in dates, lists and procedures.

Why It Matters: Choosing between a numeric form with one invariant marker (A) and fully spelled ordinals with regular endings (B) decides how many learners can use the rule on day one. Numeric forms are shorter and match how ordinals already appear in dates, lists and procedures, but they leave the spoken form unresolved. Spelled forms fix speech and writing together but add new unfamiliar words such as 'oneth' that native readers may reject.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Adopt numeric ordinals with one invariant suffix on every digit string, so 1, 2, 3, 11, 21 all take the same marker, and publish a fixed spoken reading for that suffix.
  2. Adopt numeric ordinals with an invariant prefix marker placed before the digits, avoiding clashes with the legacy 1st/2nd/3rd suffixes and letting software convert both forms mechanically.
  3. Adopt fully spelled ordinals with a single regular -th ending, retain digits only in tables and codes, and justify the choice through pilot reading-speed comparisons.

Trade-Off / Risk: Option A is cheaper to teach and machine-convert, but it leaves pronunciation open; option B resolves speech yet risks native-reader rejection of forms like 'oneth', so the choice should be tested rather than argued.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Outcome Metric Battery Design, since ordinal error rate is a go/no-go metric, and strengthens Adoption Wedge and Sequencing by giving safety-critical procedures and numbered steps an immediately usable, low-cost rule.

Conflict: Pulls against Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth: a spelled-out ordinal form implies respelling, while a numeric marker leaves spoken form to the pronunciation layer. Also strains Reference Accent Anchor when fixing the spoken reading.

Justification: Critical, Sets the most visible, testable rule of the standard and feeds the ordinal error rate gate metric. Connects to Outcome Metric Battery, Adoption Wedge, G2P Depth and Accent Anchor, and controls the numeric-versus-spelled trade-off between native-reader acceptance and spoken-form resolution.

Decision 2: Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth

Lever ID: f2c8fd84-4f48-425c-87f3-17d8bb34c18b

The Core Decision: Determines whether Clear English changes spelling itself or only layers guidance on top of it, which sets conversion cost, tooling needs and educator acceptance. Scope is the 5,000-word lexicon and its respelling key or overlay. Success metrics: pronunciation consistency score, recognition distance of changed forms, compatibility with search and dictionary tools, and publisher willingness to adopt.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how far the standard departs from conventional spelling. Leaving spellings intact and adding a pronunciation layer protects recognizability and publisher buy-in, but learners still face irregular spelling. Respelling words directly fixes the sound mapping but breaks compatibility with existing text, search tools and dictionaries, and raises the risk of fragmentation.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Keep standard spellings unchanged and add a consistent pronunciation-guidance layer to the 5,000-word lexicon, using one minimal respelling key in dictionaries and teaching materials.
  2. Respell only a ranked shortlist of the highest-friction spelling patterns in the core lexicon, keeping every changed form within easy recognition distance of its standard spelling.
  3. Render pronunciation as an optional software-generated overlay, such as ruby-style annotations in digital materials, so printed text stays standard while learners see the regularized mapping on demand.

Trade-Off / Risk: A guidance layer is the safest route to adoption, but it does not truly fix spelling-to-sound inconsistency; deeper respelling delivers that fix while multiplying conversion costs and the risk that educators reject the variant.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Reference Accent Anchor, which supplies the sound targets the mapping encodes, and with Core Lexicon Selection Basis, which defines which words get guidance first. A light-touch layer also eases Licensing and Name Stewardship.

Conflict: Deeper respelling conflicts with Change-Control and Release Cadence, because each respelling change forces reprints and invalidates materials, and with Adoption Wedge and Sequencing, where publishers and educators resist incompatible text.

Justification: Critical, Controls the core trade-off between fixing spelling-to-sound and preserving compatibility and publisher buy-in. Hub linking Accent Anchor, Core Lexicon, Change-Control, Adoption Wedge, Licensing and Homograph markers; deeper respelling directly raises fragmentation and rejection risk against the adoption priority.

Decision 3: Adoption Wedge and Sequencing

Lever ID: 3a239b73-ec97-45dc-9dbd-d3e4250b89a3

The Core Decision: Chooses which user group meets Clear English first and therefore which evidence, partners and liability exposure the program builds. The choice shapes pilot recruitment, the form of materials and the credibility story for the Phase 2 go/no-go. Success metrics: pilot cohort enrollment, partner commitments, time to first real-world use and absence of stalled approvals.

Why It Matters: The first market chosen shapes the evidence, the partners and the risk exposure of the program. Safety-critical documentation offers clear measurable benefits but brings liability concerns and slow organizational approval. ESL publishers move faster and supply learners for pilots, but they may demand full curricula and treat the variant as a competitor to standard English teaching.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Lead with adult ESL programs and publishers, offering Clear English as a supplementary module that sits alongside standard English curricula rather than replacing them.
  2. Lead with a technical glossary for safety-critical documentation, co-developed with one or two industry or standards-body partners and tested in real working procedures.
  3. Lead with a free, standalone reference site and browser extension that lets any reader toggle between standard and Clear English forms, building a user base before institutional partnerships.

Trade-Off / Risk: Each wedge builds a different evidence base, so choosing one early narrows the others; the risk is that a safety-critical pilot gets stalled by liability review while the ESL track starves for rules.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Sets priorities for Outcome Metric Battery Design and Core Lexicon Selection Basis, because the chosen wedge determines which metrics and which glossary vocabulary are collected first, and supports Licensing and Name Stewardship through early partner agreements.

Conflict: Competes with Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve: pursuing one wedge deeply starves the others, and a safety-critical lead raises liability and slow approvals that clash with Change-Control and Release Cadence.

Justification: Critical, The central hub: determines which partners, evidence, liability exposure and glossary vocabulary the program builds first. Synergies run to metrics, lexicon, licensing and homograph policy; conflicts with budget and change-control. Directly serves the plan's 'optimize for adoption' directive.

Decision 4: Outcome Metric Battery Design

Lever ID: 8066426e-2101-40b0-a31b-2c802373d134

The Core Decision: Defines the instruments, scoring rules and sampling that turn the four gate metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) into decision-grade evidence. Scope includes control-group design, inter-rater reliability for pronunciation scoring, and pre-registered pass/fail thresholds fixed before Month 12 (2027-10-13). Success means the Phase 2 go/no-go cannot be disputed as measurement artefact by educators or standards bodies.

Why It Matters: This lever decides how comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency and 30-day retention are actually measured in the pilots. Instrument choices determine whether the Phase 2 go/no-go decision rests on defensible evidence or on noisy proxies. Richer instruments need more psychometric expertise and more supervised sessions, which draws on pilot budget and learner time.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Adopt validated off-the-shelf reading, listening and recall instruments and adapt them minimally, accepting less precision on Clear English-specific features in exchange for external credibility.
  2. Develop a purpose-built assessment set for each of the four metrics, calibrated against a standard-English control group, and have an independent psychometrician review item validity before the pilots begin.
  3. Embed measurement in normal course work through passive digital logging of response times and error patterns, supplemented by a small supervised audio-capture sample for pronunciation scoring.

Trade-Off / Risk: Purpose-built instruments fit the four gate metrics but are untested and costly to validate; borrowed instruments are credible yet may miss exactly the ordinal and pronunciation effects the standard is meant to change.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve, because credible metrics justify staged release of funds. Also amplifies Adoption Wedge and Sequencing by giving partner organizations defensible evidence that Clear English works in their setting.

Conflict: Competes with Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve, since purpose-built instruments and psychometric review consume pilot money. Also clashes with Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth and Reference Accent Anchor if rules shift mid-pilot, invalidating calibrated items.

Justification: Critical, Converts the four gate metrics into decision-grade evidence for the Phase 2 go/no-go. Pulls together ordinal, morphology, accent and G2P choices and competes with budget; weak instruments make the gate disputable and undermine partner confidence.

Decision 5: Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve

Lever ID: 093258bc-f4c3-4775-bec5-b125346fcf20

The Core Decision: Allocates the fixed $3.5M across rule specification, pilots and public release, and sets the size and release conditions of any contingency reserve. The split determines how many pilot sites, assessment sessions and print runs are affordable, and whether a no-go at the Phase 2 gate returns funds or strands them. Success means each gate is adequately funded without overspending before evidence exists.

Why It Matters: This lever splits the fixed $3.5M across rule specification, pilots and public release, and decides how much is held back as a reserve. Front-loading Phase 1 gives sturdier rules but squeezes pilots, where the evidence for the go/no-go gate is generated. A larger reserve protects against rework after Phase 2 but reduces what can be spent on outreach and curriculum quality.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Weight spending toward Phase 2 pilots and assessments, keeping Phase 1 lean through a small expert team and a deliberately narrow first rule set that can be piloted quickly.
  2. Spread spending roughly evenly across the three phases, with a modest unallocated reserve released by the editorial board only after the go/no-go decision.
  3. Hold a large contingent tranche that is released in stages against evidence milestones, so that a no-go outcome at Phase 2 returns unspent funds rather than financing a weak launch.

Trade-Off / Risk: Weighting toward pilots strengthens the evidence base, but a thin Phase 1 risks piloting flawed rules; a large staged reserve disciplines spending yet can leave teams under-resourced during the work that must come first.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Outcome Metric Battery Design by funding the supervised sessions and psychometric review the gate depends on. Also supports Adoption Wedge and Sequencing by reserving money for Phase 3 outreach once the evidence is in.

Conflict: Constrains Outcome Metric Battery Design and Core Lexicon Selection Basis, since a lean Phase 1 or a large held reserve limits corpus work and instrument validation. Staged release also slows Editorial Board Seat Allocation's capacity to commission early work.

Justification: Critical, Fixed $3.5M envelope governs every other lever's feasibility: metric validation, multi-accent audio, tooling, outreach and licensing administration all compete for it. Controls the evidence-versus-lean-rules trade-off and whether a no-go returns funds.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold

Lever ID: 440edab7-8f36-408e-81ab-03bd984e89ac

The Core Decision: Defines the cutoff that decides which irregular verbs and plurals are regularized and which are retained, protecting recognizability while still removing real learning friction. The rule must be publishable, explainable and reproducible by third parties. Success metrics: share of the defined subset changed, misread rate on regularized forms, native-speaker acceptance, and learner retention after 30 days.

Why It Matters: The retention rule determines which irregular verbs and plurals are regularized and which are left alone. A frequency-based threshold keeps the most common forms, such as go/went, intact because learners already meet them constantly, and regularizes rarer ones where relearning cost is low. A looser threshold raises regularity but erodes the recognizability constraint and invites native-speaker resistance.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Retain every irregular form that falls within a high-frequency band of the core lexicon and regularize only lower-frequency irregulars, publishing the cutoff and the resulting list openly.
  2. Select forms for regularization using error data from ESL learner corpora, regularizing only those irregulars that learners most often get wrong and that have a low recognition penalty.
  3. Accept both regularized and legacy irregular forms during the pilot, then retire whichever form pilot readers resolve more slowly or misread more often before locking v1.0.

Trade-Off / Risk: A frequency cutoff protects intelligibility, but the cutoff value itself is arbitrary until pilot data exists, and the plan's own example go/went would probably be retained rather than regularized.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Draws directly on Core Lexicon Selection Basis, whose frequency data defines the high-frequency band, and relies on Outcome Metric Battery Design to supply error and reading-speed data for tuning the cutoff before v1.0 lock.

Conflict: Trades off against Change-Control and Release Cadence: accepting dual forms during the pilot means later retiring one, creating churn. Aggressive regularization also strains Editorial Board Seat Allocation when native-speaker members resist.

Justification: High, Governs the recognizability-versus-regularity trade-off for verbs and plurals, drawing on lexicon frequency and metric data and straining board consensus. Strong interactions, but a bounded rule subset with a likely conservative cutoff limits systemic reach.

Decision 7: Homograph Disambiguation Policy

Lever ID: 79d385f2-41b8-499f-9ae8-c2c2a22cf147

The Core Decision: Specifies when a homograph or homophone pair needs a marker, a rewrite or nothing, and how that obligation is enforced in different document types. Scope is a short, published high-impact pair list such as lead/lead and read/read. Success metrics: misreading rate in safety-critical test passages, authoring burden per page, compliance consistency and list size kept manageable.

Why It Matters: This lever decides when a marker, a rewrite, or nothing at all is required for pairs such as lead/lead or read/read. Mandatory markers in safety-critical text reduce misreading risk but add visual clutter and authoring burden. Optional markers are easier to adopt but produce inconsistent practice that undermines the standard's value for safety documents.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require a disambiguation marker only in safety-critical and procedural documents for a short, published list of high-impact pairs, and leave it optional elsewhere.
  2. Replace markers with controlled-language writing rules that require authors to rephrase sentences so context resolves each homograph, as in simplified technical writing standards.
  3. Insert markers automatically through an authoring-tool plugin that flags ambiguous words and proposes the marked form, so authors approve rather than memorize the pair list.

Trade-Off / Risk: Tool-assisted marking lowers authoring burden, but it adds software development cost and a dependency on tooling that the $3.5M budget and small team may not sustain beyond the pilot.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Controlled-Language Alignment Posture, since rewrite rules and marker rules can share one authoring checklist, and strengthens Adoption Wedge and Sequencing when the safety-critical track needs a concrete, measurable risk reduction.

Conflict: Constrains Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve if tool-assisted marking is chosen, since plugin development and maintenance compete with pilot and outreach funds. Mandatory markers also conflict with Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth by adding visual clutter.

Justification: High, Delivers the concrete, measurable risk reduction that makes the safety-critical track credible. Links to controlled-language rules, lexicon, G2P clutter and budget if tooling is chosen; scope is a short pair list, so influence is narrower than the critical levers.

Decision 8: Reference Accent Anchor

Lever ID: d12e1659-c616-44f6-95e8-5eb35c1e2615

The Core Decision: Chooses which pronunciation model underpins the grapheme-to-phoneme rules, audio recordings, dictionary guidance and pilot scoring. Beyond measurement convenience, it determines which learner populations see the biggest gains and whether adoption is perceived as regional. Success metrics: pronunciation consistency score reliability across raters, share of core-lexicon entries with usable audio by Month 12 (2027-10-13), and no significant accent-based drop in pilot comprehension or retention.

Why It Matters: The accent chosen for pronunciation guidance and audio models decides which vowel and consonant contrasts the grapheme-to-phoneme rules treat as fixed and which learners gain the most. A single anchor makes the pronunciation consistency score straightforward to measure, but it can alienate speakers of other major varieties and narrow adoption outside the anchor region.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Anchor all pronunciation guidance, recordings and pilot scoring to one widely taught reference accent, and document how other accents map onto it.
  2. Specify only the phoneme contrasts shared across major English varieties, leave other vowel realizations deliberately unspecified, and score pilot pronunciation consistency on the shared contrasts alone.
  3. Record every core-lexicon entry in several regional accents, let publishers and learners select an accent profile, and keep the written form identical across all profiles.

Trade-Off / Risk: A single anchor accent keeps measurement clean but quietly privileges one speaker population, while a multi-accent design widens appeal at the cost of recording effort and a muddier pronunciation consistency metric for the go/no-go gate.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth, since a fixed anchor decides which contrasts the mapping must encode. It also strengthens Outcome Metric Battery Design by giving the pronunciation consistency score a clean, auditable reference.

Conflict: Trades off against Core Lexicon Selection Basis and Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve: multi-accent recording multiplies per-word audio effort across 5,000 entries, while a single anchor narrows appeal beyond one region.

Justification: Medium, Supplies the sound targets for G2P rules and a clean pronunciation score, but is largely a supporting input to the G2P depth decision. Main tension is recording effort versus regional appeal, which is an optimization within budget.

Decision 9: Core Lexicon Selection Basis

Lever ID: 533fda13-50d1-49c7-98aa-d1c490efbbd9

The Core Decision: Sets the selection principle for the 5,000-word core lexicon, which is the unit the dictionary, pronunciation guidance and pilot curriculum all operate on. The choice defines first beneficiaries (general ESL learners versus safety-critical readers) and how quickly pilot cohorts perceive value. Success metrics: coverage of running text in pilot glossaries, share of entries needing rule exceptions, and auditability of the list's provenance.

Why It Matters: The principle used to pick the 5,000 core words determines whom the dictionary serves first and how quickly pilot cohorts see practical value. A frequency-led list maximizes general coverage, while a domain-led list improves safety-critical usefulness but may omit everyday words learners need to read the surrounding text.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build the 5,000-word list from general-English frequency corpora, then add a small reserved block of technical and safety terms to cover pilot glossaries.
  2. Seed the list with safety-critical and technical glossary terms first, then fill the remaining slots with the highest-frequency general words needed to read those documents.
  3. Derive the list from incident reports, near-miss records and procedure manuals where ambiguous wording caused confusion, then fill gaps from ESL syllabus word lists.

Trade-Off / Risk: Frequency lists are defensible and easy to audit but generic; incident-driven selection is persuasive to safety stakeholders yet depends on access to sensitive records that organizations may be unwilling or slow to share.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Homograph Disambiguation Policy and Adoption Wedge and Sequencing: an incident-informed or domain-seeded list surfaces the high-impact ambiguous pairs and gives the safety-critical wedge a concrete, credible vocabulary to start with.

Conflict: Conflicts with Controlled-Language Alignment Posture, which may impose an existing controlled vocabulary, and with Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold, since frequency-led lists contain the most entrenched irregular forms that resist regularization.

Justification: High, Defines the 5,000-word unit on which dictionary, pronunciation guidance and curriculum operate. Enables homograph identification and the safety-critical wedge, and conflicts with morphology retention and controlled-language vocabulary. Important, but largely downstream of the wedge choice.

Decision 10: Change-Control and Release Cadence

Lever ID: c310f188-a76c-47fb-ab70-544c06a4980f

The Core Decision: Governs how the standard changes after v1.0: freeze periods, errata handling, scheduled revisions or a candidate-and-comment path. It is the mechanism that converts pilot findings into rule fixes without destabilizing printed materials already in circulation. Success metrics: time from change proposal to ruling, number of concurrent live versions, publisher confidence in stability, and the count of unofficial forks.

Why It Matters: The rules for amending the standard after v1.0 determine whether publishers and teachers can trust it as stable or see it as a moving target. Frequent revision answers pilot feedback quickly but multiplies version confusion, while a hard freeze protects materials yet locks in any rule errors the pilots expose.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Freeze v1.0 for a fixed period after publication, accepting only errata, and collect change proposals for a single consolidated v2.0 review.
  2. Issue scheduled minor revisions at fixed intervals, each with a published deprecation notice and a conversion table from the previous release.
  3. Release v1.0 as a candidate standard with an open public-comment window and a sandbox for registered experimental forks before ratifying the final rule set.

Trade-Off / Risk: Stability and responsiveness pull in opposite directions; the board must choose which failure it can better absorb, and an unclear cadence invites the fragmentation the risk register already flags.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Reinforces Licensing and Name Stewardship by giving certification or share-alike terms a defined version baseline to test conformance against. It also supports Editorial Board Seat Allocation with a predictable decision calendar.

Conflict: Constrains Outcome Metric Battery Design and Ordinal Marker Architecture: a hard freeze locks in any rule errors the Phase 2 pilots expose, while rapid revisions undermine comparability of pilot data and printed curricula.

Justification: Medium, Matters for post-v1.0 stability and fragmentation control, reinforcing licensing and board decisions. Operates mostly after the Phase 2 gate, so it is less central to the near-term strategic outcome than rule and evidence choices.

Decision 11: Licensing and Name Stewardship

Lever ID: e6d5785e-6fe6-4aaa-bc8d-121c6c4eaa77

The Core Decision: Determines the legal and brand terms under which the standard, dictionary and the 'Clear English' name circulate. It balances low-friction uptake by ESL publishers and standards bodies against protection from diluted or non-conforming material using the name. Success metrics: number of third-party adopters licensed, share of labelled materials passing a conformance check, and absence of confusing look-alike variants by Month 36 (2029-10-13).

Why It Matters: How the standard, dictionary and the name 'Clear English' are licensed shapes both third-party uptake and the project's ability to prevent diluted or divergent versions. Permissive terms lower adoption friction, but without some name control any publisher can label non-conforming material as Clear English.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Release all deliverables under a fully permissive open license with no restrictions on the name, relying on the editorial board's reputation to signal the authoritative version.
  2. License the text and dictionary openly, but reserve the name as a certification mark awarded to materials that pass a published conformance checklist.
  3. Use a share-alike license that requires derivative works to declare which rules they diverge from and to adopt a distinct name once they diverge.

Trade-Off / Risk: Open terms and quality control conflict: certification marks protect integrity but add an administrative burden and a gatekeeper image that may deter the ESL publishers and standards bodies whose adoption the project needs.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Adoption Wedge and Sequencing by letting early adopters reuse materials with clear terms, and works with Change-Control and Release Cadence, where versioned conformance checklists make name stewardship enforceable.

Conflict: Tensions with Controlled-Language Alignment Posture and Editorial Board Seat Allocation: certification gatekeeping can deter standards bodies and publishers, and it demands board capacity and administrative budget that Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve must absorb.

Justification: High, Controls the open-uptake versus anti-fragmentation trade-off central to third-party adoption by publishers and standards bodies. Connects to wedge, change-control and board capacity, but its impact materializes mainly in Phase 3 after the evidence exists.

Decision 12: Controlled-Language Alignment Posture

Lever ID: 8fb6c1ea-42bc-4ded-8e9d-ae685aa0f1f3

The Core Decision: Defines how Clear English relates to existing controlled languages such as ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English and plain-language guidance, which technical writers already follow. The choice sets the effort for safety-critical adopters, whether one or two rule sets must be run, and how much design freedom the project retains. Success metrics: share of pilot technical documents passing both rule sets, and writer conversion effort.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how Clear English relates to existing controlled languages such as Simplified Technical English and plain-language guidance already used in safety-critical writing. Tight alignment lowers the barrier for technical writers who already follow a controlled vocabulary, but it ties the standard to another body's conventions. A distant posture preserves design freedom but forces safety-critical adopters to run two rule sets.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build Clear English as a compatible overlay that reuses the vocabulary and sentence-writing constraints of an existing controlled language, adding only the orthographic and ordinal rules on top.
  2. Design Clear English as an independent standard with its own rules, and publish a one-way mapping table so technical writers can translate from existing controlled-language documents.
  3. Co-develop the safety-critical glossary jointly with a controlled-language maintainer, so one shared term list is validated under both rule sets and each side can cite the other.

Trade-Off / Risk: Alignment speeds acceptance among technical writers, yet it imports another standard's limits and politics, and the claimed compatibility is hard to verify until pilot documents are actually run through both rule sets.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Adoption Wedge and Sequencing by giving technical writers a familiar on-ramp, and supports Core Lexicon Selection Basis when a shared safety-critical term list is validated under both rule sets.

Conflict: Constrains Homograph Disambiguation Policy and Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth, since an overlay inherits another body's vocabulary and conventions, limiting orthographic freedom and requiring coordination with an external maintainer's schedule.

Justification: Medium, Offers a familiar on-ramp for technical writers and shared glossary validation, but mainly serves the safety-critical wedge and overlaps with homograph and lexicon choices. Useful positioning optimization, with external-maintainer dependence limiting leverage.

Decision 13: Editorial Board Seat Allocation

Lever ID: cc0df26c-1351-481b-8450-753f7da0225e

The Core Decision: Sets who holds voting and veto authority over rule decisions, and how linguistic review, practitioners and learners are represented. Beyond composition, it fixes decision procedures, term lengths and conflict-of-interest rules that determine perceived legitimacy among educators, publishers and standards bodies. Success shows in rule-decision turnaround, retained seats, and endorsement by named partner institutions rather than linguistic elegance.

Why It Matters: This lever determines who sits on the editorial board and linguistic review panel and who holds decision authority over rule changes. A board weighted toward linguists favors internal consistency, while one weighted toward ESL teachers, technical writers and standards-body staff favors usability and adoption. The balance also shapes whether educators treat the standard as their own or as something imposed from outside.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Seat a linguist-majority board with advisory seats for practitioners, giving rule decisions a rigorous basis while risking the perception that the standard is academic and detached from classrooms.
  2. Seat a practitioner-majority board of ESL instructors, technical writers and safety trainers, with linguists holding a formal review-and-veto role limited to rule-conflict and ambiguity findings.
  3. Rotate board seats on fixed terms and add a standing learner panel whose pilot feedback must be formally answered in the published rationale for each rule.

Trade-Off / Risk: Practitioner weighting aligns with the adoption priority, but without strong linguistic review, rule ambiguity and drift can creep in; rotating seats add legitimacy at the cost of institutional memory and decision speed.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Adoption Wedge and Sequencing and Controlled-Language Alignment Posture, since practitioner and standards-body seats open partner channels. Also strengthens Change-Control and Release Cadence by giving revisions a legitimate, accountable decision body.

Conflict: Tension with Change-Control and Release Cadence, because rotating or large boards slow decisions and dilute institutional memory. Also trades off against Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold and Homograph Disambiguation Policy, where linguist-weighted consistency pulls against practitioner usability preferences.

Justification: High, Fixes who holds rule authority and whether educators and standards bodies see the standard as legitimate. Opens partner channels for wedge and controlled-language alignment and sets the usability-versus-consistency balance in morphology and homograph decisions.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Moderately ambitious, institution-scale standards initiative: a parallel (not replacement) English variant with a 5,000-word core lexicon, a $3.5M (user constraint) budget and a 3-year, 3-phase timeline. Targets niche but high-value audiences (adult ESL, technical and safety-critical writing) and explicitly rejects mandates, K-12 replacement and universal-adoption claims.

Risk and Novelty: Novel and unproven: constructed-variant standardization with unknown native-reader acceptance. Main risks are educator pushback, rule ambiguity, fragmentation and liability in safety-critical use. The plan manages these through gating (go/no-go at Month 24 = 2028-10-13), optional markers and a capped change threshold, so the posture is moderate risk with evidence-first discipline.

Complexity and Constraints: Moderate-to-high operational complexity: rule specification, reference corpus, pronunciation guidance, print and digital curriculum, four gate metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention), governance, licensing and outreach. Fixed budget, fixed 12-month phases, physical pilot sites with in-person assessment, and a pre-registered metrics requirement before Month 12 (2027-10-13).

Domain and Tone: Public-interest language standardization and education; business purpose without profit motive. Tone is pragmatic, evidence-driven and adoption-first ('optimize for user adoption, not linguistic purity'; 'don't pick the most aggressive scenario').

Holistic Profile: A cautious-but-credible, adoption-first standards program: modest linguistic intervention that coexists with standard English, ESL-led pilots, defensible gate evidence at Month 24 (2028-10-13) and balanced funding across three phases. It seeks real third-party uptake rather than maximal linguistic fix or minimal spend.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Pragmatic Foundation

Strategic Logic: Build credible evidence with moderate-risk choices: an invariant ordinal prefix that coexists with legacy forms and converts mechanically, an on-demand pronunciation overlay that leaves printed text standard, and an ESL-first supplementary wedge that fits the pilot cohorts. Purpose-built, independently reviewed assessments give the go/no-go gate defensible data on the ordinal and pronunciation effects, while an even budget spread and a modest board-controlled reserve keep Phase 1 adequately resourced. This is the path best aligned with the brief's adoption-first, no-mandate stance.
