Fit Score: 9/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Prefix ordinals coexisting with legacy forms, an optional overlay leaving print standard, an ESL-first supplementary wedge, purpose-built validated gate metrics and an even budget align closely with the adoption-first, no-mandate, evidence-gated brief.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Ordinal Marker Architecture: Adopt numeric ordinals with an invariant prefix marker placed before the digits, avoiding clashes with the legacy 1st/2nd/3rd suffixes and letting software convert both forms mechanically.
  • Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth: Render pronunciation as an optional software-generated overlay, such as ruby-style annotations in digital materials, so printed text stays standard while learners see the regularized mapping on demand.
  • Adoption Wedge and Sequencing: Lead with adult ESL programs and publishers, offering Clear English as a supplementary module that sits alongside standard English curricula rather than replacing them.
  • Outcome Metric Battery Design: Develop a purpose-built assessment set for each of the four metrics, calibrated against a standard-English control group, and have an independent psychometrician review item validity before the pilots begin.
  • Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve: Spread spending roughly evenly across the three phases, with a modest unallocated reserve released by the editorial board only after the go/no-go decision.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Fits adoption-first, no-mandate stance: an invariant ordinal prefix coexists with legacy 1st/2nd/3rd forms and converts mechanically, while an optional overlay leaves printed text standard, so educators and publishers are not forced to switch.
  • Fits the gate: purpose-built, independently reviewed assessments cover the four Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go metrics, notably ordinal error rate and pronunciation consistency.
  • Fits the budget: an even phase split and a modest board-controlled reserve keep Phase 1 rules and the 5,000-word lexicon properly resourced.
  • Pioneer's Gambit rejected: respelling, 'oneth'-style ordinals and a consumer-toggle wedge are the aggressive path the brief excludes, with a thin Phase 1 and fragmentation risk.
  • Prudent Consolidator less suitable: off-the-shelf instruments may miss Clear English-specific effects, and a large held reserve can starve early work.
  • Caveat: print materials still need the pronunciation key printed.

Alternative Paths

The Pioneer's Gambit

Strategic Logic: Pursue the deepest functional fix and the fastest user-base growth: fully spelled regular ordinals, respelling of the highest-friction patterns, and a free reader-facing toggle that builds usage before institutions commit. Spending is front-loaded to pilots and passive measurement at scale to generate evidence quickly, accepting the risks of native-reader rejection, fragmentation and a thin Phase 1. It is shown as the upper bound of ambition; given the brief's instruction to avoid the most aggressive scenario and to optimize for adoption over linguistic purity, it is not the recommended path.

Fit Score: 3/10

Assessment of this Path: Respelling, spelled-out ordinals such as 'oneth', a consumer toggle-first wedge and a thin Phase 1 are the aggressive path the brief rules out; they heighten native-reader rejection and fragmentation and favor linguistic fix over adoption.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Ordinal Marker Architecture: Adopt fully spelled ordinals with a single regular -th ending, retain digits only in tables and codes, and justify the choice through pilot reading-speed comparisons.
  • Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth: Respell only a ranked shortlist of the highest-friction spelling patterns in the core lexicon, keeping every changed form within easy recognition distance of its standard spelling.
  • Adoption Wedge and Sequencing: Lead with a free, standalone reference site and browser extension that lets any reader toggle between standard and Clear English forms, building a user base before institutional partnerships.
  • Outcome Metric Battery Design: Embed measurement in normal course work through passive digital logging of response times and error patterns, supplemented by a small supervised audio-capture sample for pronunciation scoring.
  • Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve: Weight spending toward Phase 2 pilots and assessments, keeping Phase 1 lean through a small expert team and a deliberately narrow first rule set that can be piloted quickly.

The Prudent Consolidator

Strategic Logic: Minimize conversion cost, educator pushback and financial exposure: keep standard spellings intact, add a single pronunciation-guidance layer, use the cheapest-to-teach ordinal scheme, and measure with validated external instruments for maximum credibility. A large contingent tranche is released only against evidence milestones, so a no-go at Month 24 (2028-10-13) returns unspent funds rather than financing a weak launch. The trade-off is that the fix to spelling-to-sound inconsistency is shallow and less precise on Clear English-specific effects.

Fit Score: 6/10

Assessment of this Path: Low-risk and credible, but off-the-shelf instruments may miss ordinal and pronunciation effects that drive the go/no-go gate, and a large held reserve can under-resource Phase 1 rules and corpus work; the spelling-to-sound fix is shallow.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • Ordinal Marker Architecture: Adopt numeric ordinals with one invariant suffix on every digit string, so 1, 2, 3, 11, 21 all take the same marker, and publish a fixed spoken reading for that suffix.
  • Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth: Keep standard spellings unchanged and add a consistent pronunciation-guidance layer to the 5,000-word lexicon, using one minimal respelling key in dictionaries and teaching materials.
  • Adoption Wedge and Sequencing: Lead with adult ESL programs and publishers, offering Clear English as a supplementary module that sits alongside standard English curricula rather than replacing them.
  • Outcome Metric Battery Design: Adopt validated off-the-shelf reading, listening and recall instruments and adapt them minimally, accepting less precision on Clear English-specific features in exchange for external credibility.
  • Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve: Hold a large contingent tranche that is released in stages against evidence milestones, so that a no-go outcome at Phase 2 returns unspent funds rather than financing a weak launch.

Purpose

Purpose: business

Purpose Detailed: Three-year, gated, $3.5M language-standardization program (rule specification and reference corpus, pilot learning materials and usability testing, public standard release with limited-scope adoption) for education, ESL, technical writing and safety-critical documentation. Deliverables are a public standard, reference dictionary, style guide, pilot curriculum and an open licensing policy, with editorial-board governance, a risk register, outreach to academic partners, ESL publishers and standards organizations, and a go/no-go decision after Phase 2. This is a standards and public-interest language initiative aimed at wide adoption, not a profit-seeking venture.

Topic: Design and launch of "Clear English", a standardized parallel variant of English with regularized ordinals, spelling-to-sound mapping, morphology and homograph disambiguation

Domain

Primary domain: Language Standardization

Secondary domains: Applied Linguistics, ESL Pedagogy, Orthography Design

Rationale: Language Standardization is the only outcome candidate that owns the project's overall success criterion: a governed, versioned standard variant of English. Lexicography is a component deliverable, Orthography Design and Applied Linguistics are methods, and ESL Pedagogy and Standards Development are adoption or process support.

Disciplines this project involves:

Domain Importance Specificity Role Reason
Language Standardization 5 5 outcome Core deliverable is a formal standardized English variant with rules, lexicon, and governance.
Orthography Design 5 5 method Grapheme-to-phoneme mapping, ordinal notation, and minimal diacritics are the core rule-design mechanism.
Applied Linguistics 5 4 method Phonology, morphology, and orthography design underpin grapheme-to-phoneme mapping and regularization rules.
Controlled Language Authoring 4 5 market Safety-critical and technical documentation, comparable to Simplified Technical English, is a target adoption market.
ESL Pedagogy 4 4 market Adult ESL learners are pilot cohort and primary adoption audience for curriculum.
Lexicography 4 4 outcome The 5,000-word reference dictionary with pronunciation guidance and mappings is a core deliverable.
Standards Development 4 4 stakeholder Editorial board governance, versioned standard, licensing, and standards-organization outreach require formal standards practice.
Instructional Design 4 4 method Print and digital pilot curriculum with assessments must be designed for adult learners.
Educational Psychometrics 4 4 method Go/no-go depends on valid comprehension, error-rate, and retention measurement from pilots.

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: The plan is a three-year, $3.5M program to design and launch "Clear English", a standardized variant of English. It is not executable purely online with zero benefit from physical presence or resources, so it is classified as physical. The physical requirements are:

  • Pilot cohorts: adult ESL learners and native speakers working with a safety-critical or technical glossary. Recruiting, enrolling and running them involves in-person classes, sessions or workshops at real sites (adult education centers, ESL programs, industrial or safety-training settings). Usability testing and comprehension assessments (comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) benefit from, and in practice require, in-person administration and supervised audio capture of pronunciation.
  • Print curriculum: the pilot curriculum is explicitly "print + digital". Printing, producing, distributing and handing out physical learner materials is a physical activity and resource requirement.
  • Team and governance: an editorial board, linguistic reviewers, researchers and curriculum designers need workspaces, equipment, and in-person board meetings and review sessions. Staffing and office or co-working space are real-world resources funded by the budget.
  • Outreach: engaging academic partners, ESL publishers and standards organizations involves in-person meetings, conferences and workshops, with associated travel.
  • Pronunciation and phonology work: building the grapheme-to-phoneme mapping and pronunciation guidance for 5,000 words benefits from recording and testing with real speakers (studio or field recordings), which is physical.
  • Safety-critical documentation adoption: limited-scope adoption in technical or safety-critical settings requires testing documents in real operating environments with real workers.

Although the deliverables (standard, dictionary, style guide, licensing policy) are largely documents, the plan depends on human participants, physical materials, travel and facilities. Under the "if in doubt, physical" rule, the plan is physical.

Physical Locations

This plan does not imply any physical location.

Requirements for physical locations

  • Access to adult ESL learners (community colleges, adult education centers, language schools) for in-person pilot cohorts
  • Access to native speakers in technical or safety-critical training settings
  • Proximity to universities with applied linguistics and psychometric expertise
  • Office or co-working space for editorial board, linguists and curriculum designers
  • Quiet room or studio capacity for supervised audio capture of pronunciation
  • Good transport links for outreach to publishers and standards organizations
  • Moderate cost of living and labor to fit a $3.5M total budget (user constraint)
  • English-speaking environment so that reference accent and native-reader testing are practical

Location 1

United Kingdom

Cambridge / Oxford area, England

University-adjacent offices near Cambridge or Oxford; partner language schools and ESL publishers (e.g., Cambridge, Oxford)

Rationale: Dense cluster of ESL publishers, assessment bodies, applied linguists and psychometric expertise. Strong access to adult ESL schools and standards-oriented organizations. Supports the ESL-first wedge and credible pilot measurement. Office costs are higher than in smaller cities.

Location 2

United States

Washington, D.C. metro area (including Arlington and Northern Virginia)

Co-working or university-affiliated office space near Georgetown University / Center for Applied Linguistics-type organizations; partner adult ESL programs in the metro area

Rationale: Large, diverse adult ESL population and many adult education programs. Proximity to standards bodies, federal safety and technical-writing communities and applied linguistics departments. Good air and rail links for outreach. Cost is higher but offset by access to partners and pilot participants.

Location 3

United States

Austin, Texas or similar mid-cost metro

Co-working space near University of Texas at Austin; adult ESL centers, community colleges and industrial or energy-sector training sites in the region

Rationale: Lower cost than coastal hubs, with a large adult ESL population, a university linguistics base and nearby industrial and energy safety-training settings for the technical-glossary cohort. Fits the budget limit while serving both pilot cohorts.

Location Summary

The plan names no site, but it is physical: in-person pilot cohorts, print curriculum, board meetings, audio capture and outreach all need real sites. Three options are suggested. Cambridge/Oxford offers publisher and assessment expertise. Washington, D.C. offers diverse ESL cohorts plus standards and safety communities. Austin offers lower cost with ESL and industrial training access. Final choice should weigh partner commitments and budget fit.

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • USD: Primary currency for the $3.5M budget constraint specified by the user. All budget splits across three phases, staff salaries, pilot assessments, print curriculum production and outreach travel will be denominated in USD for consolidated reporting.
  • GBP: Relevant for Location 1 (Cambridge/Oxford area, England). If the editorial board, linguistic review, or any portion of pilot cohorts are situated in the UK, local spending on office space, ESL school partnerships, publisher meetings and assessment administration will occur in GBP.
  • EUR: Relevant if outreach expands to European standards bodies, ESL publishers or applied linguistics networks. Safety-critical documentation adoption may involve coordination with European regulatory bodies or technical-writing organizations where EUR transactions occur.

Primary currency: USD

Currency strategy: All budgeting and financial reporting will be conducted in USD, aligning with the fixed $3.5M constraint. Phase splits and milestone payments will be tracked in USD. For operations in the UK (Location 1 option), GBP exchange rates should be locked at contract signature to avoid variance in office, partner and pilot costs; a modest contingency (2–3% of UK-based spending) is recommended to absorb currency fluctuation. If outreach to European standards bodies or ESL publishers occurs in Phase 3, EUR spending should be pre-approved and capped as a percentage of outreach budget. No hedging instruments are necessary given the modest scale and the administrative burden they impose on a small team; instead, fixed-rate agreements with vendors and partners will be prioritized to minimize exchange-rate surprise.

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Regulatory & Standards Adoption

Educational and standards bodies (ESL publishers, national curricula authorities, standards-setting organizations) may reject Clear English as a non-standard variant or threat to unified English instruction, delaying or blocking third-party adoption. Regulatory bodies in jurisdictions requiring alignment with national language standards may refuse to permit use in accredited programs. The standard's legal standing and protection against dilution or divergent forks remain undefined until licensing is finalized.

Impact: Rejection by key adopter groups could reduce pilot enrollment and Phase 3 adoption to near zero, effectively ending the initiative despite completion of rule specification. Regulatory delays of 4–8 months could push pilot timeline into Month 28–32 (2029-02-13 to 2029-06-13) and jeopardize the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate. Uncontrolled fragmentation and unofficial variants could emerge within 18–24 months of public release, damaging credibility and undermining adoption claims.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Engage national language-curriculum authorities and standards bodies (e.g., Common European Framework, TESOL leadership) in advisory roles from Month 1 (2026-11-13) to gauge regulatory appetite and identify formal approval pathways. Prepare formal submissions to relevant standards bodies by Month 15 (2028-01-13). Establish a licensing and name-stewardship framework by Month 12 (2027-10-13) that reserves the 'Clear English' mark for conforming materials and includes a public conformance checklist. Create a formal dispute-resolution procedure within the editorial board for handling divergent forks.

Risk 2 - Pilot Recruitment & Participant Retention

Recruiting and retaining sufficient adult ESL and native-speaker cohorts for statistically valid gate metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) may prove difficult if partnership institutions lack capacity, funding or learner availability. The plan requires in-person supervised sessions, audio capture and 30-day follow-up, imposing high participant burden. High dropout rates could render pilot data inconclusive at the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate.

Impact: Insufficient cohort size (fewer than 50–100 learners per condition) may make the four gate metrics statistically unreliable, forcing either extension of Phase 2 by 3–6 months or a disputed no-go decision. Dropout rates above 30% could reduce effective sample sizes further. A failed or inconclusive gate decision could strand Phase 3 funding ($800K–$1.2M, estimated) and delay market entry to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or beyond. Recruitment delays alone could consume 4–8 weeks of the 12-month Phase 2 window.

Likelihood: High

Severity: High

Action: Secure commitments from at least 3–4 adult ESL programs and 2–3 technical/safety-training organizations by Month 3 (2027-01-13), including written enrollment guarantees and contact-hour or per-learner payment terms. Offer learner incentives (certificates, small stipends, discounted course fees) to reduce dropout. Design assessments to fit existing course schedules to minimize added burden. Hire a dedicated Phase 2 project manager focused on cohort administration and retention by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Build a 10–15% contingency into projected cohort size to absorb attrition.

Risk 3 - Technical & Assessment Validity

Purpose-built gate metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) must be validated and pre-registered before Month 12 (2027-10-13) to ensure credibility for the Phase 2 go/no-go decision. Developing psychometrically sound instruments tailored to Clear English-specific effects requires expert effort and pilot testing that may exceed initial timeline or budget. If instruments are weak or inconsistently applied, the go/no-go decision will be scientifically disputable and lose partner confidence.

Impact: Instrument validation failures could delay metrics pre-registration by 2–4 months, compressing the Phase 2 pilot window to 8 months or fewer. Weak or disputed metrics could make the Phase 2 gate non-credible, forcing either a do-over at additional cost ($200K–$300K, estimated) or a gate decision that partners reject, stalling Phase 3 planning. Inconsistent scoring of pronunciation consistency across raters could inflate measurement noise, obscuring true effects and leading to a false-negative go/no-go outcome.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Hire an independent psychometrician or applied measurement specialist by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and budget $150K–$200K (estimated) for instrument design, validation and inter-rater reliability studies. Pre-register the metric design, pass/fail thresholds and primary analysis plan on an open repository (e.g., OSF) by Month 11 (2027-09-13), 30 days before the Month 12 (2027-10-13) deadline. Conduct a small pilot validity study (N=20–30) in Month 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) to confirm instruments discriminate between Clear English and standard English conditions before Phase 2 enrollment begins.

Risk 4 - Rule Ambiguity & Editorial Board Consensus

The morphology retention threshold, homograph disambiguation policy and ordinal marker pronunciation require editorial board consensus before Phase 1 rules can be finalized at Month 12 (2027-10-13). If board members (linguists, practitioners, learners) hold conflicting preferences—e.g., linguists favoring consistency versus teachers favoring recognizability—rule specifications may remain ambiguous, vague or internally contradictory. Unresolved conflicts delay rule publication and weaken the rule set's credibility for pilots.

Impact: Unresolved editorial disputes could push rule finalization by 4–12 weeks into Phase 2, compressing the pilot window. Ambiguous or internally inconsistent rules (e.g., unclear morphology exceptions or conflicting ordinal-marker guidance) could force rule clarifications or errata mid-pilot, invalidating earlier assessments and inflating measurement noise. A visibly divided editorial board could undermine educator and publisher confidence in the standard before pilots begin.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish editorial board composition and decision procedures by Month 1 (2026-11-13), including clear voting rules, conflict-of-interest management and a formal 'decision logging' process that documents disagreements and the rationale for each ruling. Conduct a first editorial board meeting by Month 2 (2026-12-13) to surface rule tensions and assign rule-specification workstreams to board subcommittees. Set a hard rule-finalization deadline of Month 11 (2027-09-13), requiring all rule ambiguities to be resolved in writing and published as a draft standard by Month 11 (2027-09-13) for a 30-day public-comment window before finalization.

Risk 5 - Financial & Budget Overrun

The fixed $3.5M budget must be split across three 12-month phases, including rule specification, 5,000-word core lexicon with pronunciation recordings, reference corpus, purpose-built pilot assessments, print and digital curriculum design, pilot administration and outreach. Any of several line items could overrun: audio recording (multi-accent recordings at scale), psychometric validation (more expensive than estimated), pilot incentives and cohort management (retention costs), or unforeseen operational expenses (office space inflation, staff turnover requiring recruitment costs, technology licensing). A $200K–$500K overrun could force budget cuts mid-project.

Impact: A $300K overrun (8.6% of budget) during Phase 1–2 could force either reductions in pilot scope (fewer cohorts, smaller assessment battery), curriculum quality (less refined pilot materials) or postponement of outreach. Cutting Phase 2 pilot scope would undermine the go/no-go gate evidence. Cost overruns discovered in Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) leave limited time to recover and no clear contingency plan. If contingency reserve is depleted before Phase 2 ends, a no-go decision would leave no unspent funds to return.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Implement a detailed Phase-wise budget with monthly tracking and rolling 6-month forecasts beginning Month 1 (2026-11-13). Establish a spending review gate at Month 9 (2027-07-13) to assess Phase 1 expenses against budget and adjust Phase 2 allocations if needed. Allocate a clear contingency reserve of $175K–$250K (5–7% of budget) controlled by the editorial board and released only for pre-approved, evidence-backed needs (e.g., additional psychometric validation if Phase 1 pilot signals a tight gate). Negotiate fixed-rate contracts with curriculum vendors and audio studios by Month 3 (2027-01-13) to lock recording and design costs.

Risk 6 - Pronunciation Consistency Measurement & Accent Selection

The pronunciation consistency score, a key go/no-go gate metric, depends on a chosen reference accent (e.g., Received Pronunciation, General American) and reliable inter-rater scoring. If raters disagree on whether learner pronunciation matches the reference, the metric becomes noisy and unreliable. Choosing a single reference accent alienates speakers of other major varieties (Australian, Indian, South African English), narrowing adoption perception. Audio capture, storage and scoring infrastructure must be secured and tested before Phase 2 pilots begin.

Impact: Poor inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa <0.70) on pronunciation scoring would inflate measurement error, obscuring true Clear English effects and risking a false-negative gate outcome, delaying or killing Phase 3. Accent selection disputes (e.g., objections to British or American bias) could trigger criticism from standards bodies or ESL organizations, damaging the standard's perceived neutrality. Audio infrastructure failures (missing recordings, inaudible files, storage loss) could make pronunciations impossible to score, invalidating the metric.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Anchor the reference accent selection by Month 3 (2027-01-13), with explicit written justification and documentation of how other major accents map to the anchor. Conduct inter-rater training and a calibration study (N=30–50 recordings) in Month 11 (2027-09-13), targeting Cohen's kappa ≥0.75 and publishing the scoring rubric openly. Secure audio storage infrastructure and backup protocols by Month 6 (2027-04-13); conduct a dry-run with a small pilot cohort (N=5–10) in Month 10 (2027-08-13) to test recording, storage and scoring workflows. If inter-rater reliability falls below 0.70 at Month 11 (2027-09-13), extend Phase 1 by 4 weeks to conduct additional rater training rather than proceeding to Phase 2 with weak measurement.

Risk 7 - Safety-Critical Adoption & Liability

If the project pursues a safety-critical adoption wedge (technical glossaries, procedures, incident reports), it assumes responsibility for the safety and clarity of documents using Clear English. Misreading or ambiguity in safety-critical text (e.g., a procedure or hazard label) caused by Clear English rules or gaps could result in injury, regulatory investigation or litigation. Liability exposure increases if Clear English forms are adopted in real working environments (factories, laboratories, medical settings) during Phase 2 pilots or Phase 3 early adoption. Insurance, legal review and risk-approval processes may be costly and slow.

Impact: A serious incident linked to Clear English documentation could result in litigation, regulatory action (e.g., from OSHA, EPA or equivalent bodies), and immediate pause or withdrawal of the standard, ending the initiative. Legal review and liability insurance could cost $100K–$300K (estimated) and delay safety-critical partner engagement by 2–4 months. Regulatory approval or safety-case review for safety-critical use could stretch to 6–12 months, pushing pilot enrollment into Month 30–36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13). Any incident, even if not fatal or injurious, would trigger media scrutiny and credibility loss.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: If pursuing the safety-critical adoption wedge, secure legal counsel specializing in product liability and regulatory compliance by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and develop a risk-mitigation and liability-insurance strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13), with costs capped at $150K–$200K. Conduct a formal safety-case review with partner organizations (e.g., industry standards bodies) before any safety-critical pilot material is used in real working environments. Require all safety-critical pilot documents to carry explicit disclaimers and to be reviewed by qualified human experts (not Clear English alone) before deployment. Establish an incident-reporting protocol and a rapid-response team to address any misreading or clarity issues discovered during pilots. Consider capping safety-critical pilots to non-life-critical procedures or glossaries (e.g., warnings, labeling) rather than core operational procedures until post-Phase-2 evidence is strong.

Risk 8 - Educator Pushback & Teacher Training

Teachers, curriculum designers and ESL instructors may resist Clear English adoption for multiple reasons: perceived threat to standard English teaching, unfamiliarity with the rules, skepticism about evidence claims, or concern that learners will be confused by a non-standard variant. Without active teacher buy-in and training, pilots will fail. Educator pushback could manifest as low engagement, non-compliance with pilot protocols, or vocal criticism that damages public credibility. Training teacher cohorts on Clear English rules and pedagogy is a significant operational burden not fully budgeted in the plan.

Impact: Low educator engagement or non-compliance could reduce pilot quality and statistical power, making gate metrics unreliable or inconclusive. Public criticism from respected teachers or professional organizations (TESOL, IATEFL) could trigger negative media coverage, damaging credibility before the go/no-go gate decision. Inadequate teacher training could lead to rule misapplication in pilot materials, invalidating assessment results. Educator resistance could reduce Phase 3 adoption by 30–50% even if the gate decision is positive.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Engage ESL teacher professional organizations (TESOL, IATEFL, national equivalents) as advisory partners by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and co-design pilot protocols with practicing teachers to increase buy-in. Develop a comprehensive teacher training program (online and in-person) by Month 10 (2027-08-13) covering Clear English rules, rationale, pilot administration and learner communication. Recruit and hire a dedicated educator-liaison person (0.5–1.0 FTE, estimated $50K–$70K for Phase 2) responsible for teacher engagement, training delivery and feedback loops. Offer continuing education credits or stipends to pilot teachers (estimated $20K–$40K across Phase 2) to incentivize active participation.

Risk 9 - Fragmentation & Unofficial Variants

Once the Clear English standard is published, third parties may create divergent variants or forks—e.g., a 'Simplified Clear English' for children, a 'Medical Clear English' with specialized terminology, or non-conforming materials labeled as Clear English but not adhering to the official rule set. Licensing and name-stewardship controls are planned but may be weak or unenforceable, especially against offshore publishers or open-source projects. Fragmentation undermines the standard's value for consistent communication and creates confusion for learners and users.

Impact: Uncontrolled fragmentation could emerge within 12–24 months of Phase 3 public release, reducing the perceived value of the standard and making adoption claims (e.g., 'Clear English is widely used for safety documentation') false. Certification and dispute-resolution overhead could consume 5–10% of ongoing governance budget ($50K–$100K annually post-Phase 3, not budgeted). Confusion over which variant is 'official' could depress adoption if educators and publishers perceive the standard as unstable or political.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Finalize the Licensing and Name Stewardship decision (Decision 11) by Month 6 (2027-04-13), choosing either a certification-mark approach or a permissive share-alike license with divergence-disclosure requirements. Publish a clear conformance checklist and versioned certification procedure by Month 14 (2027-12-13). Establish a standing 'Standards Stewardship Committee' within the editorial board (3–5 members, 2–4 hours/month) with authority to review third-party claims to the Clear English name and issue guidance or public statements on non-conforming forks. Draft dispute-resolution procedures and consider low-cost arbitration options for contested conformance claims. Set a policy that substantial divergences (more than 10–15% of rule changes) trigger a requirement to adopt a distinct name.

Risk 10 - Coordination with Existing Controlled Languages

The plan considers alignment with existing controlled-language standards (e.g., ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English) to ease adoption by technical writers. However, coordinating rule changes, vocabulary lists and pronunciation guidance with another standards body's maintenance schedule is operationally complex and constrains the project's independence. If alignment is chosen (Decision 12), changes to the external standard could force Clear English revisions, and conflicts between the two standards could confuse adopters.

Impact: Dependency on an external standards body's revision schedule could delay Clear English v1.0 release by 2–4 months if coordination is required. Unresolved conflicts between Clear English and an external controlled language (e.g., differing ordinal conventions) could make the '100% compatible' alignment claim false, embarrassing both standards. If the external standard is acquired, discontinued or significantly changed, Clear English would need rapid revision, straining the Change-Control and Release Cadence decision.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Medium

Action: If the Controlled-Language Alignment Posture decision (Decision 12) opts for close coordination, formalize a Memorandum of Understanding with the external standards body by Month 4 (2027-02-13), defining scope, change-request procedures, and escalation paths for conflicts. Establish a standing liaison role (0.25–0.5 FTE) to coordinate vocabulary and rule changes. Conduct a detailed compatibility audit at Month 10 (2027-08-13) to identify and resolve conflicts before v1.0 finalization. Include explicit language in the Clear English license and documentation noting any dependency or alignment with external standards. If full compatibility cannot be demonstrated, clearly label the alignment as partial and specify which rules differ.

Risk 11 - Core Lexicon Coverage & Adequacy

The 5,000-word core lexicon is designed to cover ESL and safety-critical use, but its selection basis (Decision 9—frequency-led, domain-led, or incident-driven) determines whether it adequately serves pilots and early adopters. If the lexicon omits high-frequency words needed to read pilot materials or technical glossaries, assessments will suffer from confounding (learners struggle with out-of-lexicon words rather than Clear English effects). An incomplete or misaligned lexicon could undermine pilot credibility and adoption appeal.

Impact: If the core lexicon covers fewer than 85–90% of running text in pilot materials or technical glossaries, comprehension assessments will be confounded and gate metrics unreliable. Discovering inadequate coverage at Month 18 (2028-04-13) would require expansion of the lexicon, adding 4–8 weeks to Phase 2 and inflating pronunciation-recording costs ($20K–$50K per 500 words, estimated). Missing domain-specific terms (e.g., safety jargon) would reduce the appeal of the technical wedge and damage early-adopter credibility.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Finalize the Core Lexicon Selection Basis decision (Decision 9) by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and conduct a pilot lexicon-coverage audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13), analyzing running text from existing ESL curricula and technical glossaries to confirm 85%+ coverage. If coverage falls short, allocate time and budget (estimated $30K–$50K) for targeted lexicon expansion by Month 10 (2027-08-13). Publish the lexicon and its selection methodology openly by Month 12 (2027-10-13), inviting third-party feedback and challenges. Reserve 5–10% of the core-lexicon slots for domain-specific additions identified during Phase 2 pilots before v1.0 lock.

Risk 12 - Timeline Compression & Phase Gate Slippage

The plan specifies three fixed 12-month phases with a hard go/no-go gate at Month 24 (2028-10-13). However, multiple dependencies and unknowns could compress the timeline: rule finalization delays, slow institutional partnerships, audio recording backlogs, psychometric validation setbacks, or pilot recruitment lag. If Phase 1 slips by 4–6 weeks, Phase 2 pilots face a compressed window, reducing data quality. If the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate must be postponed due to incomplete pilot data, Phase 3 outreach and adoption are delayed.

Impact: A 6-week slip in Phase 1 compresses Phase 2 to 10 months, reducing pilot robustness and possibly making the go/no-go gate decision inconclusive, triggering a 6–12 month extension (Month 30–36 = 2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13) that strands Phase 3 funding and delays market entry. Any gate delay beyond Month 24 (2028-10-13) pushes Phase 3 launch to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or later, reducing the project's ability to capitalize on early momentum. Compressed timelines force trade-offs: fewer cohorts, shorter follow-up periods, or weaker assessment instruments.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish monthly project-status reviews with critical-path analysis and rolling forecasts of key milestones (rule finalization, psychometric validation, cohort recruitment, audio completion) from Month 1 (2026-11-13) onward. Build in explicit 2–4 week buffers at key decision points (Month 6 = 2027-04-13 for design freeze, Month 11 = 2027-09-13 for metrics finalization, Month 18 = 2028-04-13 for pilot midpoint) to catch and correct slippage. Identify high-risk dependencies early (e.g., audio recording capacity, partnership commitment letters) and secure contingency plans or backup vendors by Month 3 (2027-01-13). Create a formal escalation path to the editorial board if any critical path item slips >2 weeks, triggering review of timeline and scope.

Risk 13 - Data Privacy & Participant Confidentiality

Phase 2 pilots collect sensitive data: learner literacy levels, pronunciation recordings, test scores, demographic information and 30-day follow-up assessments. Audio recordings of pronunciation are biometric data requiring careful consent, storage and retention protocols. Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics-board approval may be required in the US and UK, depending on whether the pilot is classified as research. Data breaches, unauthorized use of recordings, or privacy violations could expose the project to legal liability and damage participant trust.

Impact: Delays in IRB/ethics approval (2–8 weeks) could compress the Phase 2 pilot window or push recruitment into Month 14–16 (2027-12-13 to 2028-02-13). Privacy violations or data breaches could trigger regulatory investigation (GDPR in UK, state privacy laws in the US) and litigation. Restrictive data-handling requirements (e.g., deletion of audio after transcription, restricted re-use) could limit future analysis and replicability of the go/no-go metrics. Participant concerns about data privacy could reduce cohort recruitment or increase dropout.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Engage an IRB or ethics-review board early (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) to clarify whether the pilot qualifies as research requiring formal review and to draft consent forms and data-handling protocols. Budget $10K–$20K (estimated) for ethics consulting and compliance management. Implement secure audio storage (encrypted, access-controlled, backed up) by Month 6 (2027-04-13) and conduct a data-protection audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13). Publish a clear privacy policy and data-retention schedule on the project website by Month 12 (2027-10-13), explicitly stating how long recordings are kept and who may access them. Offer participants the option to have their audio deleted post-analysis if they request it.

Risk 14 - Reference Accent & Multi-Accent Demand

Choosing a single reference accent (Decision 8) for pronunciation guidance and pilot scoring simplifies measurement but may trigger pressure to add additional accents (British, American, Australian, Indian) to broaden appeal and inclusivity. Multi-accent audio recording (5,000 words × 2–3 accents = 10,000–15,000 audio files) is expensive, complex to manage and complicates the pronunciation consistency score (Which accent is 'correct'?). Scope creep toward multi-accent coverage could inflate audio costs by 2–3× and compress other budget areas.

Impact: Pressure to add accents could emerge at Month 9–12 (2027-07-13 to 2027-10-13) during Phase 1, forcing a decision whether to absorb the cost (estimated $50K–$100K additional, straining Phase 1 budget) or decline and risk criticism from standards bodies and ESL organizations concerned about inclusivity. Multi-accent audio infrastructure (storage, playback, rater training) adds complexity and could delay pronunciation-guidance publication by 4–8 weeks. Scope creep here could cascade to other line items: additional accent guidance in the dictionary, revised pronunciation-consistency scoring procedures, extended pilot timelines.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: Lock the single-accent decision early (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-01-13) with explicit, published justification and a documented commitment to document how other accents map to the anchor by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Set a policy that accent additions are deferred to post-v1.0 (Phase 3 or beyond) and require a formal scope-change proposal with budget impact analysis. Consider recording a small secondary sample (200–300 high-frequency or safety-critical words) in one additional accent as a 'proof-of-concept' for Phase 3, costing $10K–$15K (estimated), rather than committing to full coverage.

Risk 15 - Publisher & Curriculum Vendor Capacity

The plan envisions publishers and ESL material vendors adopting or co-producing Clear English curricula in Phase 3. However, their capacity to invest in new materials, their interest in a non-standard variant, and their willingness to delay publication pending the Phase 2 go/no-go decision are all uncertain. Vendors may be slow to commit resources without market proof, or they may demand guarantees of adoption or a minimum revenue threshold that the project cannot offer. If major publishers decline to participate, Phase 3 adoption will be limited to small providers or open-source projects.

Impact: Low publisher engagement could reduce Phase 3 curriculum diversity, limiting adoption to niche ESL programs or technical contexts. Delayed vendor commitments could push Phase 3 curriculum launch to Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13), missing the window for near-term adoption momentum. Vendor demands for guarantees or revenue sharing could strain the project's governance or budget. Without major publishers, the standard's reach may plateau at 10,000–50,000 learners rather than reaching the 100,000+ needed for credible market presence.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Engage major ESL publishers (Cambridge, Oxford, Pearson, smaller regional publishers) and material-development vendors as advisory partners by Month 3 (2027-01-13), seeking non-binding letters of interest or commitment to pilot or co-develop curricula. Conduct a Phase 3 publisher-readiness assessment at Month 18 (2028-04-13) to gauge commitment levels and identify gaps. Develop a clear, low-friction licensing pathway (Decision 11) and publish it by Month 12 (2027-10-13) to reduce vendor uncertainty. Offer a '30-day rights' window post-publication (Phase 3 start) where early-adopting publishers can claim specific glossaries or grade levels to incentivize rapid adoption.

Risk 16 - Measurement Construct Validity & Outcome Definition

The four gate metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) assume that improvements in these measures indicate that Clear English is superior and worthy of adoption. However, the construct validity of each metric—i.e., whether it actually measures what it claims (e.g., whether ordinal error rate captures ordinal learning or test-taking noise)—is untested. Confounds could inflate or deflate measured effects: e.g., learners might improve ordinal accuracy due to simple repeated exposure rather than Clear English superiority, or pronunciation consistency could be high for both Clear English and standard English if the accent is close to learners' first language.

Impact: Weak construct validity could lead to false-positive or false-negative go/no-go outcomes. A false-positive (gate passes but Clear English provides no real benefit) could launch a standard that fails to deliver on adoption promises, damaging credibility. A false-negative (gate fails but Clear English is actually effective) could kill a viable initiative. Unresolved construct questions at Month 24 (2028-10-13) could force a redo of Phase 2 or a disputed gate decision that stakeholders reject.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Build construct-validity analysis into the Outcome Metric Battery Design (Decision 4) by Month 5 (2027-03-13). Conduct a detailed literature review and expert panel (applied linguists, psychometricians, ESL researchers) to identify potential confounds and design control conditions that isolate Clear English effects from other learning factors. In Phase 2 pilots, include explicit manipulation checks (e.g., explicit instruction on ordinal rules versus implicit learning) to validate that observed effects are due to Clear English comprehensibility and not other factors. Publish a pre-analysis plan documenting the construct-validity framework and all confound-control measures before Phase 2 begins.

Risk 17 - Sustainability & Post-Phase-3 Governance

The plan addresses governance during the three-year project (editorial board, linguistic review, pilot administration) but does not specify how the standard will be maintained, updated and governed after Month 36 (2029-10-13) when external project funding ends. Ongoing tasks—responding to adoption feedback, managing change requests, handling disputes over rule interpretation, updating the lexicon with emerging vocabulary—require sustained funding and staffing. Without a clear post-project governance model and funding plan, the standard could atrophy or become poorly maintained, undermining long-term adoption.

Impact: Lack of post-project governance could degrade the standard within 12–24 months of Phase 3 completion. Ambiguities and errors discovered after v1.0 publication would go unaddressed, reducing credibility and adoption. Emerging vocabulary and cultural shifts would not be incorporated into the lexicon, making the standard feel outdated by Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13). Third-party adopters and educators would face uncertainty about the standard's future, reducing their willingness to invest in long-term adoption.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Define a post-Phase-3 governance and funding model by Month 24 (2028-10-13), before the go/no-go gate decision. Identify potential sustaining organizations (e.g., language education non-profits, standards bodies, academic consortiums) and approach them for funding commitments (estimated $150K–$250K annually for ongoing maintenance, estimated) by Month 30 (2029-04-13). Establish a permanent Standards Stewardship Committee (Decision 7 touches on this) with clear roles, decision authority and term lengths. Publish a 5-year stewardship plan by Month 36 (2029-10-13), outlining how the standard will be updated, how change requests will be prioritized and how conflicts will be resolved.

Risk 18 - Market Saturation & Competing Standards

The English-language standardization space is not empty. Existing initiatives—plain-language standards, controlled-technical languages, reformed spelling movements—compete for attention and adoption. New entrants may emerge during the three-year project timeline. If Clear English is perceived as a marginal variant or a late arrival to a crowded field, adoption may stall. Competitor standards or initiatives endorsed by larger organizations (UNESCO, British Council, ILO) could eclipse Clear English before it gains traction.

Impact: Competition could reduce Phase 3 adoption by 20–40%, capping learner reach at 20,000–50,000 instead of the 100,000+ needed for significant market presence. Competing standards endorsed by larger bodies could crowd out Clear English in institutional procurement decisions (ESL curricula, safety standards). Phase 3 outreach budget would need to be higher to differentiate Clear English and build awareness, straining the $3.5M envelope.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Low

Action: Conduct a competitive landscape analysis by Month 3 (2027-01-13), mapping existing plain-language, controlled-language and spelling-reform initiatives and their adoption rates, funding and organizational backing. Identify Clear English's unique value proposition (e.g., 'ordinal standardization for safety-critical procedures' or 'ESL-optimized pronunciation guidance') and emphasize it in all outreach by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Monitor the field for new entrants during Phase 2 and adjust messaging as needed. Build academic partnerships (universities, research centers) that provide credibility and differentiation from commercial or political initiatives.

Risk 19 - Currency Fluctuation & International Operations

The project operates across multiple currencies (USD primary budget, GBP for UK operations if Location 1 is chosen, EUR for European outreach). Currency fluctuations, particularly if the UK (Location 1) is selected as the operational hub, could inflate costs and compress the budget. A 10–15% depreciation of GBP against USD (as occurred in 2016–2024) could add £50K–£100K in real costs for UK-based office, partnerships and staff without corresponding budget increases.

Impact: A 10% GBP depreciation against USD could reduce UK operational budget purchasing power by £50K–£100K (estimated), forcing cuts in pilot scope, personnel, or outreach. Unhedged currency risk could emerge in Months 12–24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13), when most Phase 2 spending occurs, leaving limited time to adjust. Late discovery of currency pressures could trigger budget-cutting decisions that compromise pilot quality or team capacity.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: Low

Action: Implement the currency strategy outlined in the currency_strategy.md file: denominate all budgeting and reporting in USD; if Location 1 (UK) is chosen, lock GBP exchange rates in contracts by Month 3 (2027-01-13) to avoid variance in office and partner costs; allocate a modest 2–3% contingency within UK-based spending to absorb exchange-rate fluctuation. Monitor currency forecasts quarterly and assess impact on budget; if significant headwinds emerge (>5% adverse movement), propose a budget amendment or deferred spending to leadership by Month 15 (2028-01-13).

Risk 20 - Stakeholder Misalignment on 'Success'

Stakeholders—educators, standards bodies, ESL publishers, learners, safety regulators—may have divergent definitions of what constitutes successful Clear English adoption. Educators may prioritize ease of teaching and learner engagement; regulators may prioritize measurable safety improvements; publishers may prioritize revenue potential; learners may prioritize job prospects or fluency gain. If the project's definition of success (as measured by the four gate metrics) does not align with what stakeholders value, adoption may remain low even if the metrics pass the gate.

Impact: Misaligned stakeholder expectations could lead to post-launch disappointment and reduced adoption (20–40% lower than projected). Educators could resist adoption if they perceive the standard as imposing inconvenient rules rather than delivering classroom benefits they care about. Safety regulators could decline to mandate or incentivize Clear English if they don't see measurable, incident-reduction improvements. This misalignment could be discovered at Month 24 (2028-10-13) (go/no-go) or later, stranding Phase 3 planning.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Conduct stakeholder-expectation interviews and focus groups during Month 1–3 (2026-10 to 2027-01), engaging educators, regulators, publishers and learners to understand their success criteria and concerns. Publish a 'Stakeholder Alignment Charter' by Month 6 (2027-04-13) that documents stakeholder input and explains how the project's metrics and approach address key concerns. Build stakeholder advisory panels (separate from the editorial board) for educators, regulators and publishers, meeting quarterly to surface emerging concerns and expectations. At Month 18 (2028-04-13), conduct a mid-phase stakeholder check-in to assess alignment and adjust Phase 2 or Phase 3 strategy if major gaps are identified.

Risk summary

This three-year, $3.5M language-standardization initiative is ambitious, evidence-gated and operationally complex. The top three critical risks that could jeopardize success are: (1) Regulatory & Standards Adoption (high likelihood, high severity): Educational authorities, standards bodies and ESL publishers may reject Clear English as a non-standard threat or fragmentation risk, blocking institutional adoption and reducing the pilot to voluntary, low-engagement cohorts. This risk requires early engagement with regulatory bodies and a credible licensing framework by Month 12 (2027-10-13). (2) Pilot Recruitment & Retention (high likelihood, high severity): Recruiting sufficient adult ESL and native-speaker cohorts for statistically defensible gate metrics, and retaining them through 30-day follow-up, is operationally challenging and high-cost. Failure to retain 70%+ of recruited learners invalidates the comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency and 30-day retention metrics that trigger the Phase 2 go/no-go decision. This requires early partnership commitments, learner incentives and dedicated cohort management by Month 3 (2027-01-13). (3) Assessment Validity & Rule Ambiguity (medium–high likelihood, high severity): Purpose-built gate metrics must be psychometrically sound and pre-registered by Month 12 (2027-10-13) to be credible; editorial board consensus on morphology, homographs and ordinals must be resolved by Month 11 (2027-09-13) to avoid mid-pilot rule changes. Weak or ambiguous metrics could render the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate scientifically disputable, forcing expensive rework or a failed gate. Secondary risks include Phase 1 timeline slip (compressing Phase 2 pilot window), educator pushback (reducing engagement and public credibility), fragmentation and unofficial variants (undermining standard stability post-launch), and safety-critical liability exposure (if that wedge is chosen). The plan's Pragmatic Foundation path—invariant prefix ordinals, optional pronunciation overlay, ESL-first supplementary wedge, purpose-built validated metrics and even budget spread—substantially mitigates these risks by avoiding aggressive rule choices, protecting compatibility with standard English and ESL pedagogy, and building credible evidence before scaling. However, active risk management (stakeholder engagement, timeline discipline, budget controls, governance clarity) is essential from Month 1 (2026-11-13) onward to prevent slippage and maintain stakeholder confidence through the Phase 2 gate.

Make Assumptions

Question 1 - How should the $3.5M (user constraint) be split across the three phases, and what reserve is held back and who releases it?

Assumptions: Assumption: Roughly even split: Phase 1 $1.1M, Phase 2 $1.2M, Phase 3 $0.85M (proposed), plus a $0.35M (10%, proposed) reserve released by the editorial board only after the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go. Even spreads match the Pragmatic Foundation path and keep rule work and pilots funded.

Assessments: Title: Financial Feasibility Assessment Description: Adequacy of the phased budget and reserve. Details: Largest lines are staff, psychometric validation (estimate $150K-$200K), audio capture and pilot administration. Risk: a $300K overrun (estimate) is 8.6% of budget and would cut pilot scope. Mitigation: monthly tracking, a Month 9 (2027-07-13) spending review, fixed-rate vendor contracts by Month 3 (2027-01-13). Benefit: a no-go at Month 24 (2028-10-13) leaves the reserve and most Phase 3 funds unspent.

Question 2 - Which fixed milestones and buffers govern the gated schedule, including metric pre-registration and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go?

Assumptions: Assumption: Phase 1 runs Months 0-12 (2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13), Phase 2 Months 12-24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13), Phase 3 Months 24-36 (2028-10-13 to 2029-10-13). Rules draft by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with a 30-day comment window, metrics pre-registered by Month 11 (2027-09-13), go/no-go at Month 24 (2028-10-13), with 2-4 week buffers (proposed) at Months 6, 11 and 18 (2027-04-13, 2027-09-13, 2028-04-13).

Assessments: Title: Timeline Feasibility Assessment Description: Credibility of the 36-month gated plan. Details: Critical path: board decisions, lexicon, audio, instrument validation, then recruitment. A 6-week Phase 1 slip compresses pilots to about 10 months. Mitigation: monthly critical-path reviews, escalation for slips over 2 weeks, partner commitments secured by Month 3 (2027-01-13). Opportunity: early pre-registration makes the gate defensible and lets Phase 3 planning begin before Month 24 (2028-10-13).

Question 3 - What core team and external expertise are needed, and how many pilot learners per condition are required?

Assumptions: Assumption: Core team of about 8-10 FTE (proposed): project lead, 2-3 linguists, psychometrician, curriculum designers, Phase 2 cohort manager, educator liaison, developer. Pilot target of at least 50-100 learners per condition (estimate), with 15% over-recruitment for attrition.

Assessments: Title: Resource and Staffing Assessment Description: Capacity to deliver rules, materials and pilots. Details: Psychometric and cohort-management skills are the scarce roles; hire the psychometrician by Month 2 (2026-12-13). Dropout above 30% would weaken statistical power. Mitigation: written enrollment guarantees from 3-4 ESL programs, stipends and certificates, assessments fitted into existing course time. Opportunity: university partners supply raters and graduate assistants cheaply.

Question 4 - What governance structure decides rules, and what licensing and name-stewardship terms apply?

Assumptions: Assumption: Practitioner-leaning editorial board (7-9 members, proposed) with a formal linguist review-and-veto limited to ambiguity and conflict findings. Text and dictionary openly licensed; the 'Clear English' name reserved as a certification mark against a public conformance checklist, decided by Month 6 (2027-04-13).

Assessments: Title: Governance and Regulatory Assessment Description: Decision authority, legitimacy and anti-fragmentation controls. Details: Practitioner weighting serves adoption, while linguist review limits rule ambiguity. Logged decisions and conflict-of-interest rules support legitimacy. Risk: certification may look gatekeeping to publishers; keep checklist light and free. Add ethics review and data-protection compliance (GDPR/US state law) for pilot audio. Post-Month 36 (2029-10-13) stewardship funding is not yet secured.

Question 5 - What safety and liability controls apply to pilots using safety-critical glossaries?

Assumptions: Assumption: Safety-critical pilots are limited to glossary and labeling exercises, not live operational procedures, until after Month 24 (2028-10-13). All materials carry disclaimers and are reviewed by qualified humans; legal counsel retained by Month 2 (2026-12-13), with liability costs capped near $150K-$200K (estimate).

Assessments: Title: Safety and Risk Assessment Description: Liability exposure from misreading in safety contexts. Details: Likelihood is low but severity is high; one incident could end the program. Mitigation: formal safety-case review with partners, incident-reporting protocol, insurance strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13). Because the ESL-first wedge leads, safety exposure is deferred and bounded. Other risks to track: rule ambiguity, educator pushback, fragmentation, all in the register with owners.

Question 6 - What environmental impacts arise from print curriculum, travel and in-person sessions, and how will they be limited?

Assumptions: Assumption: Impact is small. Digital-first materials with limited, on-demand print runs (small pilot batches, proposed) and recycled stock; travel limited to essential partner and board meetings, with virtual meetings as default.

Assessments: Title: Environmental Impact Assessment Description: Footprint of printing, travel and facilities. Details: Main sources are print runs, flights for outreach and pilot-site travel. Benefit: the on-demand pronunciation overlay keeps printed text standard and avoids reprints when rules change. Risk: print materials still need the pronunciation key, so freeze content before printing. Mitigation: shared co-working space, regional pilot sites, track print volume and travel as simple annual indicators.

Question 7 - Which stakeholders must be engaged early and in what roles, and how is their feedback fed into decisions?

Assumptions: Assumption: Advisory roles from Month 1-3 (2026-11-13 to 2027-01-13) for ESL teacher bodies (e.g., TESOL, IATEFL), 3-4 ESL programs, 2-3 technical training organizations, ESL publishers and one standards body. Separate stakeholder advisory panels meet quarterly; a Stakeholder Alignment Charter is published by Month 6 (2027-04-13).

Assessments: Title: Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Description: Buy-in from educators, publishers and standards bodies. Details: Educator pushback and publisher capacity are high-likelihood risks. Mitigation: co-design protocols with teachers, an educator liaison (0.5-1.0 FTE, estimate), stipends or continuing-education credit, non-binding publisher letters of interest by Month 3 (2027-01-13). Positioning as supplementary, never replacement, reduces resistance. A Month 18 (2028-04-13) check-in catches misaligned success definitions before Phase 3.

Question 8 - What operational systems are needed for rule management, the lexicon, audio capture, assessments and the go/no-go?

Assumptions: Assumption: Version-controlled rule repository, lexicon database with pronunciation overlay generator, encrypted audio storage with backups by Month 6 (2027-04-13), an assessment and logging platform, and a pre-registered analysis plan. Single anchor accent chosen by Month 3 (2027-01-13); go/no-go thresholds fixed before pilots (to be set by the board).

Assessments: Title: Operational Systems Assessment Description: Tooling and processes supporting pilots and the gate. Details: Inter-rater reliability target kappa of at least 0.75 (proposed), with extension if below 0.70. Lexicon coverage of at least 85% of pilot text (proposed) to avoid confounds. Risks: audio loss, rule changes mid-pilot invalidating items; mitigate with backups, rule freeze at Month 11 (2027-09-13) and a dry run at Month 10 (2027-08-13). Keep tooling lean to fit budget and post-project maintenance.
