Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Project management and standards development, with specialization in educational language initiatives, evidence-based program design, stakeholder governance, and risk mitigation in multi-phase, fixed-budget public-interest projects.

Domain-specific considerations

  • Gating and go/no-go credibility: The Month 24 (2028-10-13) decision must rest on pre-registered, psychometrically sound metrics that are defensible to educators, standards bodies and regulators; weak instruments render the gate disputable.
  • Stakeholder alignment and adoption bottlenecks: Regulatory approval, educator buy-in and publisher commitment are non-technical risks with high likelihood and high impact; early engagement (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-13 to 2027-01-13) is critical to surface objections.
  • Operational complexity and timeline compression: Multiple sequential dependencies (rules → lexicon → audio → instruments → recruitment) create a single critical path; any 4–6 week slip in Phase 1 compresses Phase 2 pilots, weakening evidence.
  • Budget realism and contingency reserve: The fixed $3.5M envelope must cover rule ambition, audio production, psychometric validation, pilot administration and outreach; overruns in any area (estimated $200K–$500K plausible) force scope cuts that undermine gate credibility.
  • Data integrity and measurement validity: Purpose-built gate metrics must control for confounds (e.g., repeated-exposure effects masking Clear English benefits) and demonstrate construct validity; instrument failure discovered at Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) triggers expensive rework.
  • Post-launch governance and sustainability: The standard's long-term viability depends on unfunded stewardship (maintenance, dispute resolution, version control) after Month 36 (2029-10-13); lack of a funding model invites rapid degradation and loss of adopter confidence.

Issue 1 - Missing Definition of Gate Thresholds and Success Criteria for Four Metrics

The plan names four go/no-go metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) but does not specify the quantitative thresholds (e.g., 'ordinal error rate must drop by at least 25% from baseline') or sample-size targets that trigger a pass. Without pre-registered, numerical pass/fail criteria, the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision becomes subjective and disputable, inviting stakeholders to claim the gate was too lenient or too strict. This ambiguity risks deadlock among editorial board members, regulators and adopters.

Recommendation: By Month 5 (2027-03-13), the editorial board must commission a psychometrician to draft a pre-analysis plan specifying: (1) quantitative pass/fail thresholds for each of the four metrics with explicit justification (e.g., 'ordinal error rate must decline by 20–30% relative to standard-English control; this range reflects literature on instructional effect sizes and educator feedback'); (2) minimum sample sizes per condition (e.g., n≥80 per group to achieve 80% statistical power at α=0.05); (3) primary and secondary outcome definitions; (4) intention-to-treat vs. completer-case analysis rules. This plan must be registered on a public repository (e.g., Open Science Framework) and published by Month 11 (2027-09-13), 30 days before Phase 2 pilots begin. Failure to pre-register triggers an immediate Month 12 (2027-10-13) board decision to delay Phase 2 by 6–12 weeks for instrument finalization.

Sensitivity: If gate thresholds are set too high (e.g., 40% improvement required), a false-negative outcome is likely, potentially killing a viable standard and stranding ~$1.2M–$1.4M (Phase 2–3 budget). If thresholds are too loose (e.g., 5% improvement), a false-positive launches a weak standard, damaging long-term credibility and adoption by 30–50%. A 4-week delay in pre-registration compresses the Phase 2 pilot window from 12 to 11 months, reducing cohort retention by an estimated 5–10 percentage points and inflating measurement error by ~10–15%.

Issue 2 - Absent Contingency Plan for Rule Ambiguity or Editorial Board Deadlock

The plan assumes the editorial board will finalize rules (ordinal marker design, morphology retention threshold, homograph markers) by Month 11 (2027-09-13). However, it does not specify conflict-resolution procedures if linguists, practitioners and learner representatives disagree (e.g., if linguists prefer consistency while teachers prefer simplicity, or if native speakers reject 'oneth'-style ordinals). Without a formal tiebreaker mechanism and decision authority, rule disputes could stall the board for weeks, compressing pilots or forcing ambiguous rules into Phase 2, where mid-pilot clarifications invalidate earlier assessments.

Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), publish an explicit Editorial Board Charter (2–3 pages) specifying: (1) voting rules (e.g., simple majority with a linguist-review veto limited to ambiguity findings, not design preferences); (2) escalation path if voting deadlocks (e.g., a 'neutral arbiter' from an external linguistics or standards body casts a tie-breaking vote); (3) conflict-of-interest disclosure (e.g., publishers on the board recuse themselves from licensing decisions); (4) term limits (e.g., 2-year terms with staggered renewal to preserve institutional memory). For any rule requiring a tiebreaker, the board must document both the majority and minority positions in the published rule rationale, creating transparency. Establish a hard deadline of Month 10 (2027-08-13) for all rule disputes to be resolved, allowing a 1-month buffer for drafting and public comment before the Month 11 (2027-09-13) finalization.

Sensitivity: A 4-week board deadlock compresses Phase 2 pilots by ~3.3% (4 weeks out of ~12 months), reducing effective pilot window to 11 months and inflating measurement error. A forced, ambiguous rule (e.g., 'morphology should be regular except for high-frequency exceptions') could trigger 10–20% rule misapplication during pilots, confounding results. Escalation to an external arbiter adds ~$10K–$20K (estimated) in consulting costs and a 2-week process delay if not pre-negotiated.

Issue 3 - Underspecified Confound Controls and Construct Validity for Gate Metrics

The plan assumes that improvements in comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency and 30-day retention directly indicate Clear English superiority. However, alternative explanations could inflate or deflate observed effects: (a) repeated exposure to ordinals (even in standard form) might improve accuracy without Clear English; (b) learner motivation to participate in a 'new standard' study might boost performance regardless of rule quality; (c) accent proximity to learners' first language might make pronunciation consistency high for both conditions. The plan does not specify control conditions, manipulation checks or confound analyses that rule out these threats. Without explicit construct-validity analysis, the go/no-go decision could rest on noisy or artifactual data.

Recommendation: By Month 5 (2027-03-13), build a construct-validity section into the Outcome Metric Battery Design: (1) identify plausible alternative explanations for each metric (e.g., ordinal accuracy gains due to test familiarity, not Clear English clarity); (2) design explicit control conditions (e.g., standard-English ordinals with explicit rule instruction vs. implicit exposure) to isolate Clear English effects; (3) measure manipulation checks (e.g., ask learners post-test which rule system they learned; confirm mastery of ordinal rules before measuring comprehension); (4) analyze potential confounds (e.g., regress ordinal error rates on learner baseline literacy, first-language phonology, study motivation to isolate Clear English effect). Publish this framework in the pre-analysis plan (Month 11, 2027-09-13). If inter-rater reliability or effect-size analyses at Month 18 (2028-04-13) reveal confounds larger than expected, conduct additional validation by Month 21 (2028-07-13) rather than proceeding to Month 24 (2028-10-13) with questionable data.

Sensitivity: If confounds inflate perceived Clear English effects, a false-positive gate outcome launches a weak standard, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–40% and damaging credibility for 3–5 years. A 1-month delay in construct-validity analysis pushes pre-registration to Month 12 (2027-10-13), eliminating the 30-day public-comment window and risking challenges to instrument validity post-hoc. Failure to measure manipulation checks adds 10–15% measurement error, reducing statistical power to detect true effects by ~15–25%.

Issue 4 - Unaddressed Ecosystem Dependencies: Audio Production Bottlenecks and Multi-Accent Pressure

The plan commits to 5,000-word core lexicon with pronunciation guidance, recorded in a single anchor accent by Month 12 (2027-10-13). However, audio production at scale (5,000 entries × multiple takes/ratings = ~7,500–10,000 files) is bottlenecked by studio availability, rater training and inter-rater reliability calibration (target kappa ≥0.75, proposed). The plan does not estimate studio costs, scheduling lead times or contingency for technical failures (inaudible files, corrupted storage). Additionally, the plan acknowledges pressure to add accents (British, American, Australian, Indian) but defers this as 'post-v1.0', creating scope-creep and coalition risk: if standards bodies or ESL organizations demand multi-accent coverage for credibility, the decision to add accents at Month 12–15 (2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13) could inflate audio budget by $50K–$100K (estimated), straining Phase 1 contingency.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), conduct a detailed audio-production scoping: (1) reserve a studio or recording partner with firm capacity guarantees (lead time, file delivery, backup protocols) for Months 6–11 (2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13); (2) estimate all-in cost per entry (speaker fees, editing, inter-rater scoring) and scale to 5,000 words—if cost exceeds $15–20 per entry (estimate), explore technology-assisted annotation (speech synthesis for baseline, human raters calibrate/correct) to reduce cost; (3) design the inter-rater training and kappa-calibration process (small sample ~100–200 words by Month 9, 2027-07-13, then full production Months 9–11, 2027-07-13 to 2027-09-13); (4) publish a clear, board-approved policy by Month 3 (2027-01-13) that defers accent additions to post-v1.0, with a documented process for considering future requests (prevents scope creep). Identify a contingency provider (secondary studio) by Month 3 (2027-01-13) in case primary partner fails. If, by Month 9 (2027-07-13), costs exceed budget or rater reliability is below target kappa 0.70, pause full production and conduct a 4-week targeted remediation by Month 10 (2027-08-13); if not resolved, flag to editorial board for a potential timeline extension or scope reduction (e.g., record only 3,000–4,000 highest-impact words).

Sensitivity: A 4-week studio delay compresses audio production from 6 months to 5, reducing rater training and inter-rater calibration time by ~17% and increasing kappa-reliability risk (below-target reliability triggers a ~3–6 week remediation). Uncontrolled multi-accent scope creep adds $50K–$100K (1.4–2.9% of Phase 1 budget, straining contingency). A failure to achieve target inter-rater kappa (e.g., kappa 0.65 instead of 0.75) inflates measurement noise by ~20%, reducing statistical power to detect Clear English effects by ~10–15%.

Issue 5 - Incomplete Post-Project Governance and Stewardship Funding Model

The plan extends only to Month 36 (2029-10-13), when external funding and formal project governance end. However, the standard will require ongoing maintenance: responding to adoption feedback, managing version/change requests, updating the lexicon with emerging vocabulary, handling disputes over rule interpretation and conformance. Without a clear stewardship funding model and organizational home, the standard could atrophy within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60, 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), as corrections and updates accumulate and no one is funded to address them. Adopter organizations (ESL programs, publishers, technical writers) would lose confidence in the standard's stability and long-term credibility, reducing Phase 3 adoption and damaging the project's legacy.

Recommendation: By Month 24 (2028-10-13), before the Phase 2 go/no-go decision, define a formal post-project governance and funding model: (1) identify 2–3 potential permanent steward organizations (e.g., language education non-profits, a university consortium, international standards bodies like ISO or ASTM) and approach them by Month 27 (2029-01-13) with a stewardship proposal (estimated annual budget: $150K–$250K for staff, meetings, dispute resolution and lexicon updates); (2) establish a permanent Standards Stewardship Committee (separate from the Phase 1–3 editorial board) with clear decision authority (3–5 permanent members, annual election of rotating seats), term lengths (e.g., 3-year staggered terms) and a published decision calendar; (3) publish a 5-year stewardship roadmap by Month 36 (2029-10-13) specifying how and when the standard will be reviewed, how change requests will be prioritized (e.g., safety-critical updates within 3 months, cosmetic updates in annual releases) and how conflicts will be resolved. Secure written commitment letters from at least one steward organization by Month 33 (2029-07-13); if no commitment is obtained, flag the go/no-go outcome as contingent on stewardship funding, preventing a full Phase 3 public release until stewardship is secured.

Sensitivity: Lack of stewardship funding by Month 36 (2029-10-13) could cause the standard to stagnate, with corrections and updates accumulating unbounded. By Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), perceived instability could reduce Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%, capping learner reach at 15,000–35,000 instead of 100,000+. A 6-month delay in identifying a steward (discovery at Month 30, 2029-04-13 instead of Month 24, 2028-10-13) leaves insufficient time to negotiate and fund stewardship before Phase 3 public release, risking a delayed or conditional go/no-go decision. Annual stewardship costs of $150K–$250K (estimate) over 10 years total $1.5M–$2.5M, dwarfing the one-time $3.5M project budget; failure to secure this funding renders v1.0 undefendable as a public standard.

Review conclusion

This $3.5M, 36-month language-standardization initiative is ambitious and well-scoped for a public-interest program, but it rests on four critical missing or underspecified assumptions: (1) Gate Thresholds: Quantitative pass/fail criteria for the four go/no-go metrics must be pre-registered by Month 11 (2027-09-13) to ensure the Month 24 (2028-10-13) decision is defensible and not disputable. Absent thresholds risk false-positive or false-negative gate outcomes, costing $1.2M–$1.4M (Phase 2–3 budget) or damaging credibility long-term. (2) Rule Deadlock Resolution: An explicit Editorial Board Charter with voting rules, tiebreaker mechanisms and conflict-of-interest protocols must be published by Month 1 (2026-11-13) to prevent rules from remaining ambiguous or contradictory during pilots. (3) Construct Validity and Confounds: The gate metrics must be analyzed for alternative explanations (e.g., repeated exposure, learner motivation) via explicit control conditions and manipulation checks, documented in the pre-analysis plan by Month 5 (2027-03-13). Weak construct validity inflates or deflates observed effects, invalidating the gate outcome. (4) Post-Project Stewardship: A funded, committed organizational home for the standard must be identified and committed to by Month 33 (2029-07-13). Without stewardship, the standard will atrophy post-Phase 3, reducing adoption and long-term credibility. Secondary risks include audio-production bottlenecks (7,500–10,000 files require careful scheduling and inter-rater training), pilot recruitment and retention (targeting 50–100 learners per condition with ≤30% dropout), and timeline compression (a 4–6 week Phase 1 slip compresses pilots by 33–50%, weakening evidence). The Pragmatic Foundation path—invariant prefix ordinals, optional pronunciation overlay, ESL-first supplementary wedge, purpose-built validated metrics and even budget spread—substantially mitigates rule ambition and native-reader rejection risks. However, active management of gate credibility, rule governance, measurement validity and post-launch stewardship is essential from Month 1 (2026-11-13) onward to ensure the initiative delivers on its adoption and evidence-gating promise.

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Conflict of interest in editorial board rule decisions: board members with financial stakes in ESL publishers or standards organizations could steer ordinal, morphology or homograph rules to advantage their employers, compromising rule objectivity and learner benefit.
  • Nepotism in pilot recruitment and cohort management: educators or cohort administrators favoring their own institution's learners for higher incentives or easier assessment conditions, inflating that site's performance metrics and biasing the go/no-go decision.
  • Misuse of pilot audio and learner data: unauthorized retention, sharing or commercial use of pronunciation recordings and learner assessment data beyond stated research scope, exploiting biometric and educational information.
  • Bribery of partner institutions: publishers or standards bodies offering unofficial incentives (early access, licensing fee waivers, board seat offers) to editorial board members or outreach staff in exchange for favorable rule positioning or conformance-checklist leniency.
  • Information asymmetry and insider advantage: project staff with early knowledge of rule finalization (Month 11–12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13) or gate outcomes (Month 24 = 2028-10-13) using that information to guide their own institution's curriculum or publishing decisions before public release.
  • Kickback schemes in vendor contracts: audio studios, curriculum designers or assessment platforms offering undisclosed rebates or revenue-sharing to procurement staff in exchange for inflated contract awards, straining the $3.5M budget.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Budget front-loading and reserve depletion: exhausting Phase 1 funds (budgeted $1.1M) on non-essential rule refinement, lengthy board meetings or duplicate psychometric studies, leaving insufficient buffer ($175K pre-gate cap) to cover audio production overruns or extension costs, forcing Phase 2 pilot cuts.
  • Inefficient audio production and rework: purchasing audio recording without firm studio capacity guarantees, leading to re-records or file loss, doubling the per-entry cost from $15–20 to $30–40 and inflating the audio line item beyond the $80K–$120K budget estimate.
  • Pilot incentive leakage and double-payment: paying learner stipends twice (once through the ESL program partner, again by the project), or reimbursing educator travel separately to both the school and the project, inflating Phase 2 participant costs above the budgeted $208K–$351K.
  • Personnel underutilization and overstaffing: hiring 10 FTE staff (peak proposed) but assigning only 50–60% of their time to the core Phase 1 rule, lexicon and assessment work, with the remainder dispersed across low-value meetings, reporting and internal coordination.
  • Uncontrolled scope creep in the core lexicon: adding domain-specific terms and accent samples beyond the 5,000-word baseline without removing equivalent entries, inflating pronunciation-recording costs by 15–25% ($12K–$30K, estimate) and compressing the Phase 1 timeline.
  • Misreporting progress and contingency release: declaring a rule finalized or a metric pre-registered prematurely (e.g., at Month 10 = 2027-08-13 instead of Month 11 = 2027-09-13) to trigger reserve drawdown or board approval, when the work is incomplete or validity not yet confirmed.

Audit - Procedures

  • Monthly financial tracking and critical-path reviews (Months 1–36 = 2026-11-13 to 2029-10-13): project lead reports actual versus budgeted spend, timeline status against milestones (rule finalization, audio completion, recruitment, metrics pre-registration), and flags slips over 2 weeks for board escalation. Audit trail maintained in shared project repository (version-controlled).
  • Quarterly stakeholder and partner compliance checks (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 = 2027-01-13, 2027-04-13, 2027-07-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-01-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-07-13, 2028-10-13): confirm pilot partner enrollment commitments are met, cohort manager tracks participant attrition and dropouts against the <=30% tolerated rate, and ESL program and technical-training organization compliance with protocol fidelity is sampled (e.g., 10% of sessions observed or audio-recorded for protocol adherence).
  • Pre-gate assessment validity audit at Month 18–22 (2028-04-13 to 2028-08-13): independent external auditor (separate from the psychometrician who designed instruments) reviews pilot data for inter-rater reliability (confirmed kappa >=0.70), construct validity (analysis of confounds and alternative explanations), and data integrity (missing files, outliers, consent violations). Audit report submitted to editorial board by Month 23 (2028-09-13), 1 month before go/no-go, to permit remediation or data extension if validity falls below threshold.
  • Rules and governance audit at Month 11 (2027-09-13): editorial board chair certifies that all rule disputes were resolved per the published Charter, that decision logs document both majority and minority positions on contested rules, and that the pre-analysis plan (metrics, thresholds, sample sizes, primary outcomes) matches the finalized rules and no post-hoc changes have been made. Certification published with the draft standard.
  • Budget and reserve draw audit at Month 24 (2028-10-13, gate decision): finance audit confirms that total Phase 1–2 spending equals planned allocation +/– variance, that all pre-gate draws from the $175K contingency cap are documented and pre-approved, that no unrecorded commitments or purchase orders exist beyond budgeted lines, and that the reserve balance is at least $175K remaining. Auditor reports go/no-go budget fitness to the board.
  • Post-launch conformance audit at Months 30, 36 (2029-04-13, 2029-10-13): spot-check a sample of third-party materials claiming Clear English conformance (e.g., ESL curricula, technical glossaries) against the published conformance checklist; report non-conformances to the Standards Stewardship Committee and recommend corrective action or name-mark revocation within 60 days.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Published Editorial Board Charter and decision log (by Month 1 = 2026-11-13, updated quarterly): governance document specifying board composition, voting rules, conflict-of-interest disclosures, tiebreak procedure and arbiter identity; monthly/quarterly log of all rule decisions, with majority and minority positions and explicit rationale, made available on the project website and updated within 10 days of each board meeting.
  • Monthly financial and timeline dashboard (live from Month 1 = 2026-11-13): public-facing, read-only view of Phase spend versus budget (aggregated by line item: staff, assessment, audio, curriculum, etc.), critical-path milestones (rule completion, lexicon audit, pre-registration, recruitment) with status and variance, and a forward-looking 6-month cash-flow forecast. Updates published within 5 days of month-end.
  • Pre-registered analysis plan and metrics (published Month 11 = 2027-09-13, on OSF or similar public repository): complete specification of the four gate metrics, quantitative pass/fail thresholds, sample-size targets, primary and secondary outcome definitions, control-condition design, confound-control and manipulation-check procedures, and analysis code (R or Python scripts). Any post-registration amendments require written justification and re-publication before gate decision.
  • Draft standard and 30-day public comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13 to Month 12 = 2027-10-13): full text of Clear English Standard v1.0 draft, including rule set, rationale, examples, exceptions, and ordinal/morphology/homograph specifications, published on the project website with a structured comment form. All substantive comments and project responses published by Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • Pilot protocol and informed-consent templates (published by Month 6 = 2027-04-13): study design, inclusion/exclusion criteria, assessment schedules, data-handling and privacy procedures, and a plain-language learner consent form, available on the project website. Any protocol changes require ethics-board approval and publication of an amendment within 10 days.
  • Go/no-go dossier and decision rationale (published within 30 days of Month 24 = 2028-10-13 gate): full analysis of the four gate metrics (tables, plots, effect sizes, statistical tests, confound checks), summary of validity audit findings, enrollment and attrition data, and the editorial board's written decision statement explaining why the standard passed or failed, including any board dissent or conditions on a YES outcome.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Project Steering Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The Clear English program is a 36-month, $3.5M initiative spanning rule specification, pilot design, gate metrics, recruitment and public release across multiple stakeholder groups (educators, publishers, regulators, learners). Strategic decisions on ordinal architecture, G2P depth, adoption wedge, outcome metrics and phase budget allocation directly shape evidence credibility and adoption likelihood. The Steering Committee provides high-level oversight of these critical strategic levers, monitors phase-gate readiness, arbitrates resource conflicts across phases, and ensures alignment with the adoption-first, evidence-gated mandate and no-mandate, no-K12-replacement constraints.

Responsibilities:

  • Approve the five critical strategic levers (Ordinal Architecture, G2P Depth, Adoption Wedge, Outcome Metric Battery, Phase Budget Weighting) and reconcile tensions between rule ambition and adoption
  • Monitor phase-gate readiness (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 rules lock, Month 24 = 2028-10-13 go/no-go metrics): confirm pre-registration of thresholds, validity audit findings, and pilot enrollment/retention targets
  • Authorize draws from the $175K pre-gate contingency reserve for gate-protection needs (psychometric re-validation, Phase 1 timeline extension); recommend to the Editorial Board for post-gate reserve release
  • Escalate unresolved editorial board disputes (rule deadlock, governance conflict) to an external arbiter and make final strategic decision if arbiter is impeded
  • Review quarterly stakeholder alignment assessments and adjust messaging or phase scope if adoption risks (educator pushback, publisher capacity, regulatory delays) exceed mitigation thresholds

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Appoint Steering Committee chair and confirm 5–7 core members (project lead, finance lead, external academic partner, one ESL publisher representative, one standards-body advisor) by Month 1 (2026-11-13)
  • Publish Steering Committee Charter specifying decision authority, voting rules, escalation paths, and meeting schedule by Month 1 (2026-11-13)
  • Confirm the five strategic-lever choices (approved in the 'Pragmatic Foundation' scenario) with explicit written rationale and trade-off documentation by Month 2 (2026-12-13)
  • Establish a Critical Path Dashboard with phase milestones, resource allocation and go/no-go gate conditions; review monthly and escalate slips >2 weeks by Month 1 (2026-11-13)
  • Schedule phase-gate checkpoint meetings: Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-registration review, Month 18 (2028-04-13) midpoint check, Month 23 (2028-09-13) validity audit review, Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision

Membership:

  • Project Lead (internal, full-time)
  • Finance Lead / Budget Controller (internal, 0.5–1.0 FTE)
  • Editorial Board Chair (internal, overlapping role to align rule and resource decisions)
  • External Academic Partner (university applied linguistics or standards program, advisory role, ~4 hours/month)
  • Psychometrician or Assessment Lead (internal, hired Month 2 = 2026-12-13, represents measurement credibility and validity)
  • ESL Publisher Representative (external, non-binding advisory; input on adoption wedge viability)
  • Standards Body Advisor (external, e.g., TESOL, IATEFL representative; input on regulatory and adoption landscape)

Decision Rights: Strategic decisions with financial impact >$50K (equipment, vendor contracts, Phase-wide re-scoping, reserve draws up to $175K pre-gate limit); authorization of phase-gate transitions and go/no-go timing adjustments; approval of escalation paths to external arbiter for rule deadlock. Decisions delegated to the Editorial Board: ordinal marker pronunciation specifics, morphology retention-threshold tuning, homograph-pair list prioritization, individual rule rationale. Budget authority: Steering Committee approves spending within Phase allocations; requests exceeding phase budget or drawing >$50K from reserve require Steering Committee vote.

Decision Mechanism: Steering Committee quorum: 5 of 7 members. Standard decision rule: consensus or simple majority (>50%) with brief documented rationale. Tie-breaker: Project Lead holds a tie-breaking vote. Escalation: if Steering Committee cannot reach consensus on a strategic lever (e.g., adoption wedge sequencing, gate-threshold stringency), the matter is escalated to a neutral External Arbiter (appointed by Month 5 = 2027-03-13, TBD per Editorial Board Charter) for binding recommendation to the Committee within 2 weeks.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly standing meetings (first Tuesday of each month, 2 hours); additional checkpoint meetings at Months 11 (2027-09-13), 18 (2028-04-13), 23 (2028-09-13) (90 minutes each) for gate readiness reviews. Ad-hoc emergency meetings called by the Project Lead if any critical-path item slips >2 weeks or a budget variance >$50K is discovered.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Phase milestone status and critical-path variance (rules finalization, audio completion, recruitment, pre-registration, analysis)
  • Monthly spend report: actual vs. budgeted by line item (staff, assessment, audio, curriculum, partner costs); cumulative variance and forecast; contingency-reserve balance
  • Stakeholder alignment and adoption-risk assessment: educator pushback signals, publisher engagement, regulatory clearance status, pilot partner enrollment progress
  • Governance and rule-decision log: summary of Editorial Board decisions from prior month, any deadlocks escalated, arbiter recommendations
  • Gate readiness: validity audit findings (kappa, construct validity, confounds), pilot data quality, analysis-plan adherence, thresholds locked

Escalation Path: Unresolved strategic disputes (e.g., rule deadlock, adoption-wedge timing, reserve-draw disputes) are escalated to a neutral External Arbiter appointed jointly by the Steering Committee and Editorial Board by Month 5 (2027-03-13). The arbiter's recommendation is binding unless both the Steering Committee and Editorial Board formally object within 5 business days. If both reject the arbiter's recommendation, the matter escalates to the program's Funding Authority (granting body or institutional sponsor) for final decision. Post-Month-36 stewardship funding gaps trigger escalation to a designated Steward-Search Lead appointed by Month 24 (2028-10-13).

2. Editorial Board and Linguistic Review Panel

Rationale for Inclusion: Clear English rules must be specific, defensible, and internally consistent to serve as a credible reference for pilots, third-party adopters and educators. The Editorial Board is responsible for finalizing ordinal marker pronunciation, morphology retention thresholds, homograph-disambiguation policy, core-lexicon selection basis, and rule exceptions. The Board also logs all decisions with explicit rationale, resolves internal conflicts over linguistic priorities (consistency vs. usability), and manages the draft-standard 30-day public comment window. A Linguistic Review Panel (embedded within the Board) provides formal review-and-veto authority on rule ambiguities and contradictions, protecting against drift or oversimplification that would compromise the standard's reference value. This separation of editorial authority from strategic steering ensures that rule quality is not subordinated to adoption or budget pressures.

Responsibilities:

  • Finalize all rule specifications (ordinal marker pronunciation, G2P mapping logic, morphology retention threshold, homograph-pair list, core-lexicon selection basis and exceptions) by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with explicit published rationale for each rule and for any exceptions or boundary cases
  • Manage the Linguistic Review Panel: linguist members conduct formal ambiguity-and-contradiction review of proposed rules; veto authority is limited to findings of logical inconsistency, circularity or lack of publishable justification; no veto on rule choice itself
  • Maintain a Decision Log: document all rule decisions, voting outcomes, dissenting opinions and the rationale for each outcome, updated within 3 business days of each board meeting; publish quarterly (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-13, 2027-04-13, 2027-07-13, 2027-10-13)
  • Conduct conflict resolution and tiebreaker escalation per the published Editorial Board Charter; invite formal linguist review for any deadlocked rule before escalation to the external arbiter
  • Oversee the draft-standard 30-day public comment window (Month 11–12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13): publish the draft, manage comment submissions, respond in writing to all substantive comments, and publish responses with the final v1.0 rule set
  • Commission and review all rule-related studies or evidence (e.g., native-speaker acceptance of ordinal forms, misread rates on homograph pairs during pilots) and integrate findings into rule tuning before v1.0 lock

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Publish Editorial Board Charter by Month 1 (2026-11-13): composition (7–9 members; practitioner-leaning with linguist review-and-veto), voting rules (consensus or simple majority, with explicit tie-breaker), conflict-of-interest disclosure template, and decision-logging protocol
  • Confirm board membership by Month 1 (2026-11-13): recruit 4–5 practitioners (ESL instructors, technical writers, safety trainers), 2–3 linguists (applied linguistics, morphology/phonology specialists), and optionally 1 learner representative; document conflict-of-interest attestations
  • Appoint or confirm the external Arbiter by Month 5 (2027-03-13): independent linguist or standards-design specialist with no financial stake in ESL publishing or standards bodies; agree on fee ($10K–$20K estimate) and availability for 2-week turnaround on escalations
  • Hold the first Editorial Board meeting by Month 2 (2026-12-13) to surface rule-specification tensions and assign workstreams (ordinal, morphology, homograph, lexicon, pronunciation-guidance logic) to subcommittees; set internal deadlines for rule drafts (Month 6 = 2027-04-13)
  • Establish and staff a Linguistic Review Panel: designate 2–3 board linguists to form a standing subcommittee; schedule monthly 90-minute review meetings Months 5–11 (2027-03-13 to 2027-09-13) to examine proposed rules for ambiguity and contradiction before board vote

Membership:

  • Editorial Board Chair (internal, practitioner or linguist with governance experience, 0.5 FTE)
  • Practitioners (4–5 members, internal or closely affiliated): adult ESL instructors (2), technical writer or safety-training specialist (1–2), representing classroom and safety-critical contexts where rules will be applied
  • Linguists (2–3 members, internal or university-affiliated): specialists in morphology, phonology, or applied linguistics; formal veto authority on rule ambiguity and contradiction; at least one with standards-development experience
  • Learner Representative (optional, 1 member): adult ESL learner or recent graduate who can speak to rule comprehensibility and usability from the learner perspective; attends selected meetings and is consulted on rule clarity before public comment
  • Psychometrician or Assessment Specialist (liaison, internal, ~2 hours/month): provides data on rule effects from validity studies and pilot midpoints; informs rule tuning based on evidence (e.g., ordinal error rates, comprehension confounds)

Decision Rights: Full decision authority over all rule specifications, thresholds and exceptions; all rule decisions are final once the Decision Log entry is signed by the Chair and published. The Linguistic Review Panel may veto a rule only if it finds the rule to be internally contradictory, logically circular, or lacking a publishable justification; such vetoes are documented in the Decision Log and escalated to the full board for revision or dispute resolution. The board may not override the Steering Committee's strategic-lever decisions (e.g., the choice of prefix ordinals, optional pronunciation overlay, ESL-first wedge) but may propose refinements or implementation guidance to the Steering Committee if rule-specification work reveals unforeseen conflicts. The board controls the draft-standard comment window process and may integrate substantive public feedback into rule clarification, but core rules cannot be reopened except post-v1.0 via formal Change-Control procedures.

Decision Mechanism: Simple majority voting (>50% of present members); quorum: 5 of 7–9 members. Consensus is sought as the default, but if consensus cannot be reached, a majority vote decides. Linguistic Review Panel veto on ambiguity/contradiction is binding unless the full board overrides it by supermajority (2/3 of present members). If a supermajority override is invoked, the dissenting linguist opinions are documented in the Decision Log and published with the final rule. Tie-breaker: the Board Chair casts the tie-breaking vote if voting is deadlocked; if the Chair is conflicted, an external Arbiter is called to cast the tie-breaker within 2 weeks.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly full Editorial Board meetings (second Thursday of each month, 2 hours); Linguistic Review Panel subcommittee meetings monthly (fourth Thursday, 90 minutes) during Months 5–11 (2027-03-13 to 2027-09-13); additional subcommittee workstreams (ordinal, morphology, homograph, lexicon) meet biweekly (1.5 hours) Months 2–10 (2026-12-13 to 2027-08-13) to draft and refine rules. Emergency Board meetings convened by the Chair if an escalated dispute or public comment requires urgent resolution.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Rule-specification progress reports from subcommittees: ordinal-marker pronunciation logic, morphology retention threshold rationale, homograph-pair selection and enforcement policy, core-lexicon selection basis and coverage audit findings
  • Linguistic Review Panel findings: ambiguities or contradictions identified in proposed rules; revision proposals or escalation requests
  • Conflict resolution and tiebreaker decisions: documented disagreements from prior meetings and the board's resolution
  • Public comment review (Month 11–12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13): summary of substantive comments and project responses; integration of feedback into rule clarifications
  • Integration of pilot data (Month 18 = 2028-04-13 onwards): preliminary ordinal error rates, comprehension speed, pronunciation-consistency findings; implications for rule tuning or exception-list updates before v1.0 lock

Escalation Path: Unresolved rule disputes between practitioners and linguists are escalated to the external Arbiter within 5 business days of a failed board vote; the Arbiter has 2 weeks to make a binding recommendation on how to resolve the conflict (e.g., adopt a minority rule position, refine the rule to address both perspectives, defer the decision to pilot evidence). If the Arbiter's recommendation is rejected by both the Steering Committee and Editorial Board, the matter escalates to the Funding Authority. Disputes over whether a rule is ambiguous/contradictory (triggering Linguistic Review veto) are escalated to the Arbiter if the full board cannot resolve the veto by supermajority override within 2 weeks. Substantive public comments during the Month 11–12 (2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13) comment window that challenge rule validity are triaged by the Editorial Board; if unresolved, a representative comment is escalated to the Arbiter for a recommendation on whether the rule should be revised before v1.0 finalization.

3. Metrics & Validation Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate depends entirely on the credibility of four pre-registered, psychometrically sound outcome metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention). Any weakness in instrument design, inter-rater reliability, construct validity, confound control or data integrity directly undermines the gate decision and risks a false-positive (weak standard launched, damaging long-term credibility) or false-negative (viable standard rejected, stranding Phase 3 and damaging adoption). The Metrics & Validation Committee ensures that instruments are purpose-built and independently validated, that validity assumptions are tested, that measurement procedures are faithfully executed across pilots, and that any validity threats are identified early (Months 18–21 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-07-13) so remediation is possible before Month 24 (2028-10-13). This committee operates at arm's length from the Editorial Board and Steering Committee to maintain measurement impartiality.

Responsibilities:

  • Design the four gate metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) with explicit construct validity analysis; draft the pre-analysis plan specifying quantitative pass/fail thresholds, primary and secondary outcomes, confound-control procedures and manipulation checks by Month 5 (2027-03-13)
  • Commission an independent validity study (N=20–30 learners) in Months 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) to calibrate instruments and confirm that they discriminate between Clear English and standard-English conditions; publish findings in the pre-analysis plan
  • Pre-register the analysis plan (metrics, thresholds, sample sizes, primary outcomes, analysis code) on a public repository (e.g., OSF) by Month 11 (2027-09-13), with explicit documentation of any post-hoc amendments or deviations
  • Establish and monitor inter-rater reliability protocols: target Cohen's kappa ≥0.75 (proposed) for pronunciation consistency and ordinal-error scoring; conduct a calibration study by Month 11 (2027-09-13) and rater-training refreshers at Month 18 (2028-04-13) midpoint if kappa is dropping below 0.70
  • Conduct a mid-phase validity audit at Months 18–22 (2028-04-13 to 2028-08-13) by an external independent auditor: examine pilot data for inter-rater reliability, construct validity (confound analysis, effect-size checks), data integrity (missing files, outliers, consent violations) and compliance with the pre-registered analysis plan; report findings to the Steering Committee by Month 23 (2028-09-13)
  • Monitor measurement compliance during pilots: confirm that all assessments follow protocol, that data is securely stored with backups, that 30-day follow-up is tracked, and that participant dropouts are documented; quarterly data-quality reports to the Steering Committee

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Hire an independent psychometrician (external or internal dedicated role) by Month 2 (2026-12-13); allocate $150K–$200K (estimate) for instrument design, validity study and inter-rater work
  • Draft the Metrics & Validation Committee Charter by Month 2 (2026-12-13) specifying the Committee's authority (independent from Editorial Board and Steering Committee), decision procedures (consensus on technical validity), and escalation paths (validity threats escalate to Steering Committee within 48 hours)
  • Establish the Committee membership by Month 3 (2027-01-13): psychometrician (Chair), 1–2 external applied-linguistics or measurement specialists (e.g., university faculty with publications on ESL assessment), data-integrity specialist or research-compliance officer (internal)
  • Conduct a detailed construct-validity literature review and expert-panel discussion by Month 4 (2027-02-13): identify plausible confounds (repeated exposure, learner motivation, accent proximity, baseline literacy) and design explicit control conditions and manipulation checks to isolate Clear English effects
  • Draft the pre-analysis plan (Months 4–5 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-03-13) and circulate for peer review to external measurement experts; incorporate feedback and finalize by Month 5 (2027-03-13)
  • Design and conduct the validity-study protocol by Month 9–10 (2027-07-13 to 2027-08-13): recruit N=20–30 learners, administer Clear English and standard-English conditions, run preliminary analyses and publish findings in the pre-analysis plan by Month 11 (2027-09-13)

Membership:

  • Psychometrician / Assessment Lead (internal, hired by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, Chair, 0.5–1.0 FTE dedicated to metrics and validation through Month 24 = 2028-10-13)
  • External Measurement Specialist (e.g., university applied-linguistics researcher with ESL assessment publications, ~6 hours/month, advisory role to ensure independence from project bias)
  • Data Integrity & Research Compliance Officer (internal, ~4 hours/month, ensures IRB adherence, data protection, consent and privacy protocols)
  • Pilot Project Manager or Cohort Administrator (internal liaison, ~2 hours/month, provides data-quality updates and flags protocol deviations)

Decision Rights: Full authority over instrument design, validity analysis, data-quality standards and the pre-analysis plan; authority to halt or suspend pilots if data integrity is compromised or inter-rater reliability falls below the 0.70 floor for more than 2 weeks. May recommend changes to pilot protocol (e.g., additional rater training, modified assessment schedule, extended follow-up) to the Steering Committee; the Committee's recommendation is binding on pilot operations. May request extension of Phase 1 by up to 4 weeks (at ~$85K cost, estimate) if the validity study or inter-rater calibration requires additional time; Steering Committee must approve extensions >2 weeks. The Committee cannot override Editorial Board rule decisions but may flag to the Steering Committee if rule changes during Phase 2 pilots would invalidate previously calibrated instruments.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus on technical validity matters (instrument design, confound-control procedures, thresholds, analysis plan). If consensus cannot be reached, the Psychometrician (Chair) makes the final decision with documented rationale. Disagreements between the Psychometrician and external specialist are escalated to the Steering Committee if they affect go/no-go credibility (e.g., conflicting views on minimum sample size, effect-size interpretation). Data-integrity violations or inter-rater reliability below 0.70 trigger an automatic flag to the Steering Committee within 48 hours; remediation steps are determined by consensus of the Committee or, if urgent, by the Psychometrician in consultation with the Steering Committee.

Meeting Cadence: Bi-weekly standing meetings (Mondays, 90 minutes) from Month 2 (2026-12-13) through Month 24 (2028-10-13). Additional meetings at Months 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) (weekly, for validity-study completion) and Months 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) (weekly, for pilot monitoring and midpoint analysis). Emergency meetings convened within 48 hours if data-integrity issues or inter-rater reliability drops are discovered.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Instrument design progress and construct-validity analysis: control-condition design, manipulation-check measures, confound-control procedures
  • Inter-rater reliability: kappa scores and trends, rater calibration and training updates, scoring-procedure adherence
  • Validity-study and pilot data-quality reports: instrument performance, effect sizes, missing data, consent and privacy compliance, participant retention
  • Pre-analysis plan review and finalization: threshold specification, sample-size power analysis, primary and secondary outcomes, analysis code
  • Mid-phase audit findings (Month 18–22 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-08-13): validity threats, remediation recommendations, implications for gate credibility

Escalation Path: Data-integrity violations (missing recordings, unauthorized access, consent breaches) escalate immediately (within 48 hours) to the Steering Committee and the internal Data Integrity Officer; serious breaches (e.g., data loss) trigger suspension of affected pilot arms and immediate notification to IRB/ethics board. Inter-rater reliability below 0.70 for more than 2 weeks escalates to the Steering Committee with a remediation plan (rater retraining, extended inter-rater calibration, or Phase 1 extension); if remediation is not effective by Month 21 (2028-07-13), the Committee recommends to the Steering Committee whether to proceed to gate decision with degraded measurement or extend Phase 2. Construct-validity threats (e.g., evidence that a confound is larger than expected, inflating apparent Clear English effects) escalate to the Steering Committee with a recommendation for additional analysis or a supplementary validity study (costing up to $50K, estimate) by Month 21 (2028-07-13).

4. Compliance & Risk Management Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The Clear English program spans 36 months, operates across multiple jurisdictions (UK, US, possibly EU), manages sensitive biometric data (pronunciation audio), engages vulnerable populations (adult ESL learners), pilots safety-critical documentation, and carries reputational and legal exposure if incidents or violations occur. Key risks include data-privacy breaches (GDPR, US state law violations), ethics-approval delays (2–8 weeks, estimated), safety-critical liability (injury linked to Clear English documentation), educator and standards-body pushback, financial overruns exceeding the $175K pre-gate reserve cap, and fragmentation/unofficial variants post-release. The Compliance & Risk Management Committee provides active, continuous monitoring and mitigation of these risks; escalates emerging threats to the Steering Committee; ensures legal, ethical and regulatory alignment; and maintains a current risk register with ownership and action plans. This committee operates independently from rule development and measurement to maintain impartiality on governance and risk issues.

Responsibilities:

  • Maintain and update a live risk register (20 identified risks from the assumptions document, plus emerging risks) with ownership, mitigation actions, status and escalation criteria; conduct quarterly risk reviews (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36 = 2027-01-13 onwards) and publish a summary risk dashboard to the Steering Committee
  • Secure and monitor ethics-board (IRB) and data-protection compliance: ensure IRB approval of pilot protocol and consent forms by Month 6 (2027-04-13); establish encrypted audio storage with backups by Month 6 (2027-04-13); conduct a data-protection audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13); publish a privacy policy by Month 12 (2027-10-13); ensure GDPR and US state law compliance for all participant data handling
  • Manage legal, liability and safety-critical risk: retain legal counsel specializing in product liability and regulatory compliance by Month 2 (2026-12-13); develop a liability insurance and risk-mitigation strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13) with liability costs capped at $150K–$200K (estimate); establish safety-critical pilot boundaries (glossary and labeling exercises only, no live operational procedures before Month 24 = 2028-10-13) and enforce via protocol review and signed agreements with pilot partners
  • Monitor stakeholder adoption and pushback risks: track educator and publisher engagement metrics (open rates on outreach, meeting attendance, non-binding letters of interest, pilot partner retention) monthly; flag educator-pushback signals (critical social media posts, TESOL/IATEFL concerns, pilot-site withdrawal) within 48 hours to the Steering Committee; trigger corrective outreach (messaging, training, incentives) if engagement drops below thresholds
  • Monitor budget and timeline risks: track monthly spend variance against Phase allocations; flag budget variances >$50K or timeline slips >2 weeks to the Steering Committee; recommend contingency draws (up to $175K pre-gate cap) or scope adjustments; conduct a formal budget-fitness audit at Month 24 (2028-10-13) before go/no-go decision
  • Manage post-release governance and fragmentation risks: by Month 24 (2028-10-13), identify potential steward organizations and approach them for funding commitments; design the licensing and name-stewardship model (certification mark, conformance checklist) and publish by Month 12 (2027-10-13); establish a Standards Stewardship Committee charter and decision procedures by Month 30 (2029-04-13); monitor for unofficial variants and non-conforming uses of the 'Clear English' name post-release and enforce name restrictions via the certification mark

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Appoint Committee Chair and members by Month 1 (2026-11-13): recruit a risk-management or compliance specialist (internal or external advisor, 0.5 FTE), legal counsel or in-house counsel (external retainer, ~4 hours/month), ethics/IRB liaison (internal or academic partner, ~3 hours/month), and a stakeholder-engagement or communications specialist (internal, 0.5 FTE)
  • Publish Compliance & Risk Management Committee Charter by Month 1 (2026-11-13): define committee authority (independent escalation to Steering Committee for risks exceeding tolerances), decision procedures (consensus on risk rating and mitigation ownership), and reporting cadence
  • Develop a comprehensive Risk Register template by Month 2 (2026-12-13): categorize risks by domain (regulatory/standards adoption, pilot recruitment/retention, assessment validity, rule ambiguity, safety-critical liability, budget/timeline, educator pushback, fragmentation, data privacy, stewardship funding); specify likelihood, severity, current mitigation status, owners and escalation thresholds
  • Engage legal counsel by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and develop a liability and insurance strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13), including product liability coverage options, regulatory approval pathways for safety-critical pilots, and disclaimer language for all Clear English materials
  • Initiate ethics-board engagement by Month 1 (2026-11-13); submit IRB protocol for review by Month 2 (2026-12-13); target approval by Month 6 (2027-04-13)
  • Establish data-protection and privacy infrastructure by Month 6 (2027-04-13): contract with a secure audio-storage vendor, implement encryption and access controls, establish backup and disaster-recovery procedures, and conduct a dry-run with a small pilot cohort (N=5–10) by Month 10 (2027-08-13)
  • Schedule the first Committee meeting by Month 1 (2026-11-13) to populate the Risk Register, assign owners and confirm mitigation timelines

Membership:

  • Compliance & Risk Management Committee Chair (internal or external advisor, 0.5 FTE, governance or risk-management background, leads risk reviews and Steering Committee escalations)
  • Legal Counsel / Product Liability Specialist (external retainer, ~4 hours/month, advises on product liability, regulatory pathways for safety-critical use, disclaimer language and insurance options)
  • Ethics & Data-Protection Specialist (internal or external, ~3–4 hours/month, manages IRB/ethics-board approval, data-protection compliance with GDPR and US state law, consent procedures, audit trails)
  • Stakeholder Engagement / Communications Lead (internal, 0.5 FTE, tracks educator and publisher engagement, flags pushback signals, coordinates corrective outreach and messaging)
  • Finance & Budget Lead liaison (internal, ~2 hours/month, provides monthly spend reports, flags budget variances and timeline risks)

Decision Rights: Authority to recommend (but not unilaterally impose) changes to pilot protocol, budget allocation or timeline to mitigate identified risks; recommendations are binding on operations if approved by the Steering Committee. Authority to halt or suspend pilots (in coordination with Steering Committee and Metrics & Validation Committee) if data-privacy breaches, ethics violations or safety-critical incidents occur. Authority to recommend spending from the $175K pre-gate contingency reserve (in coordination with Steering Committee) for legal, ethics, insurance or urgent risk-mitigation costs. Authority to veto or modify any pilot operation that violates IRB approval, data-protection compliance, or safety-critical risk boundaries. Does not control rule specifications (Editorial Board authority) or measurement procedures (Metrics & Validation Committee authority) but may flag to those committees if compliance issues arise from rule or measurement design.

Decision Mechanism: Consensus on risk assessment and mitigation ownership; if consensus cannot be reached on risk severity or mitigation strategy, the Committee Chair makes the final call with documented rationale. Escalation to the Steering Committee is automatic if a risk is rated 'High' likelihood × 'High' severity, or if mitigation is inadequate or delayed. Emergency decisions (e.g., suspension of a pilot site due to ethics violation) can be made by the Committee Chair in consultation with the Steering Committee within 48 hours.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly standing meetings (third Wednesday, 90 minutes) from Month 1 (2026-11-13) through Month 36 (2029-10-13). Quarterly risk reviews (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36 = 2027-01-13 onwards, 120 minutes) with the Steering Committee to present updated Risk Register and escalation summary. Emergency meetings convened within 48 hours if a 'High' risk event occurs (data breach, ethics violation, safety incident, budget overrun exceeding $125K).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Risk Register updates: new risks identified, mitigation progress on existing risks, completion of mitigation actions, status and escalation flags
  • Legal and liability updates: counsel summary of regulatory landscape, product-liability considerations for safety-critical pilots, insurance recommendations and costs
  • Ethics and data-protection compliance: IRB approval status, consent and privacy-audit findings, data-storage security checks, GDPR/US state law compliance summary
  • Stakeholder engagement and pushback monitoring: educator and publisher engagement metrics, critical feedback or resistance signals, corrective outreach plans
  • Budget and timeline variance: monthly spend report, Phase allocation tracking, contingency-reserve balance and recommended draws
  • Stewardship and post-release governance: steward organization identification and funding-commitment status, licensing and name-stewardship model design, fragmentation-control and conformance-checklist planning

Escalation Path: All 'High' likelihood × 'High' severity risks escalate to the Steering Committee within 5 business days of identification or status change, with a documented mitigation plan and timeline. Data-privacy breaches or ethics violations escalate immediately (within 48 hours) to the Steering Committee, IRB/ethics board (if required) and relevant data-protection authorities (e.g., ICO in UK, state regulators in US). Safety-critical incidents linked to Clear English documentation escalate immediately to legal counsel, the Steering Committee, relevant workplace safety regulators (OSHA, HSE) and affected pilot organizations; trigger a formal incident investigation and communication plan. Budget overruns exceeding $125K (half the $250K contingency cap) escalate to the Steering Committee with a scope-adjustment or timeline-extension recommendation. Educator or standards-body pushback signals that could reduce pilot enrollment by >20% or delay regulatory approval by >4 weeks escalate to the Steering Committee with a corrective communication and engagement plan.

Decision Escalation Matrix

Budget Overrun Exceeding Pre-Gate Contingency Cap Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee Approval Process: Steering Committee review of spending variance (>$50K threshold) with Finance Lead presentation; if draw requested exceeds $175K pre-gate cap, escalation to Project Sponsor and Funding Authority for approval of scope reduction, Phase 2 extension costs, or project termination decision. Rationale: The fixed $3.5M budget with only $175K pre-gate contingency (5% of total) is the binding constraint. A $300K overrun (8.6% of budget estimate) would exhaust the pre-gate reserve and force cuts to pilot scope, assessment quality, or curriculum development. This directly threatens gate credibility and adoption feasibility. Negative Consequences: Budget overrun >$175K pre-gate forces either pilot scope cuts (fewer cohorts, smaller assessment battery) that weaken go/no-go evidence, curriculum quality reduction that undermines adoption appeal, or Project Sponsor intervention to extend Phase 1 or Phase 2 at cost to Phase 3 outreach. Uncontrolled spending could strand Phase 3 ($850K) if reserve is depleted mid-pilot.

Inter-Rater Reliability Below Measurement Floor After Calibration Escalation Level: Steering Committee and Metrics & Validation Committee (joint escalation) Approval Process: Metrics & Validation Committee flags kappa <0.70 to Steering Committee within 48 hours; Steering Committee reviews remediation plan (extended rater training, Phase 1 extension by up to 4 weeks at ~$85K estimate) and votes to approve extension or to proceed to Phase 2 with acknowledged measurement degradation. If measurement remains <0.70 by Month 11 (2027-09-13), gate decision is at risk and Steering Committee recommends formal extension or scope reduction. Rationale: Pronunciation consistency and ordinal-error scoring depend on inter-rater reliability (kappa ≥0.75 target, ≥0.70 floor proposed). Scoring below the floor inflates measurement error by 20%+ and reduces statistical power to detect Clear English effects by 10–15%, risking false-negative gate outcome and stranding $1.2M–$1.4M in Phase 2–3 spending. Negative Consequences: Kappa below 0.70 invalidates the pronunciation-consistency metric; gate decision becomes scientifically disputable, potentially triggering partner and standards-body loss of confidence. A false-negative outcome kills a viable standard. A false-positive launches weak standard, damaging credibility by Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13) and reducing Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%.

Editorial Board Deadlock or Ambiguous Rules Unresolved by Month 10 (2027-08-13) Escalation Level: External Arbiter (appointed by Month 5 = 2027-03-13), with final escalation to Project Sponsor if arbiter recommendation is rejected Approval Process: Editorial Board attempts consensus or majority vote by Month 10 (2027-08-13); if deadlocked rule dispute persists, matter escalates to external Arbiter (neutral linguist or standards-design specialist, $10K–$20K cost estimate) for binding recommendation within 2 weeks. If Arbiter's recommendation is rejected by both Steering Committee and Editorial Board, matter escalates to Project Sponsor for final decision by Month 11 (2027-09-13). Rationale: Rules must be finalized by Month 12 (2027-10-13) to allow a 30-day public comment window before v1.0 lock at Phase 2 start. Unresolved disputes (ordinal pronunciation, morphology retention threshold, homograph marker policy) prevent rule publication and delay pilots. Mid-pilot rule changes invalidate earlier assessments and confound results. Negative Consequences: A 4-week board deadlock compresses Phase 2 pilots from 12 to 8–10 months (33–50% reduction in pilot window), weakening statistical power and data quality. Ambiguous rules during pilots cause 10–20% rule misapplication (estimate), confounding results and rendering gate metrics inconclusive. Forced, unclear rules damage educator and publisher confidence in the standard pre-launch.

Pilot Recruitment or Retention Falls Below Minimum Sample Size Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee with Compliance & Risk Management Committee Approval Process: Cohort Manager and Compliance & Risk Management Committee flag enrolment shortfall (<80 completers per arm estimate or dropout >30%) to Steering Committee; Steering Committee reviews retention-incentive options (increased stipends, additional contact hours, partner re-engagement), pilot schedule extension (adding 4–8 weeks to Phase 2, estimated cost $85K–$170K), or scope reduction (reducing to 2 arms or smaller sample). If shortfall cannot be remedied, Steering Committee escalates to Project Sponsor for decision on extension cost or gate delay. Rationale: The go/no-go gate requires ≥80 completers per arm (4 arms × 80 = 320 completers) to achieve 80% statistical power at α=0.05 (proposed). Enrollment <50 per arm or dropout >30% undermines all four gate metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) and renders the Month 24 (2028-10-13) decision scientifically indefensible. Negative Consequences: Insufficient sample size makes gate metrics statistically unreliable; forced gate decision becomes disputable and risks either false-positive (weak standard launched, credibility damaged) or false-negative (viable standard rejected, $1.2M–$1.4M Phase 2–3 spending wasted). High dropout reduces effective n by 15–30%, compounding power loss. Phase 2 extension by 3–6 months ($300K–$600K estimate, unbudgeted) could strain remaining contingency and delay Phase 3 release to Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13).

Safety-Critical Incident or Material Liability Claim Linked to Clear English Escalation Level: Compliance & Risk Management Committee (immediate within 48 hours) to legal counsel, Steering Committee, and relevant safety regulators (OSHA, HSE, workplace safety authority) Approval Process: Incident-reporting protocol triggered: Compliance & Risk Management Committee notifies legal counsel, Project Sponsor, Steering Committee and affected pilot organization within 48 hours. Legal counsel advises on regulatory notification, disclosure obligations and potential liability exposure. Formal incident investigation conducted within 2 weeks; findings and remediation plan reviewed by Steering Committee. If incident is serious (injury, near-miss in safety-critical context), Project Sponsor and Funding Authority make final decision on pilot suspension, materials withdrawal, or project continuation. Rationale: Safety-critical pilots (glossary and labeling exercises, no live operational procedures until Month 24 = 2028-10-13) are bounded by legal disclaimers and human expert review. However, any documented injury, near-miss or serious misreading linked to Clear English documentation triggers liability exposure, regulatory investigation and potential mandate for project pause. Insurance, legal review and risk-approval processes may be costly ($150K–$200K estimate) and slow. Negative Consequences: A serious incident (injury linked to Clear English documentation) could result in litigation, regulatory action (OSHA, EPA, or equivalent investigation), mandatory product recall or withdrawal of the standard, and immediate pause or termination of the initiative. Media scrutiny and credibility loss would follow, reducing Phase 3 adoption to near-zero even if gate is positive. Incident response costs ($100K–$500K estimate) could exceed remaining budget and force Phase 3 cancellation.

Educator Pushback or Standards-Body Regulatory Rejection Blocking Pilot Access or Third-Party Adoption Escalation Level: Project Steering Committee and Stakeholder Engagement Lead, with escalation to Project Sponsor if adoption risk exceeds tolerance Approval Process: Stakeholder Engagement Lead monitors educator and standards-body sentiment (TESOL, IATEFL, national education authorities) and flags critical feedback or rejection signals to Steering Committee within 48 hours if sentiment shifts >20% toward rejection or if a major partner withdraws support. Steering Committee reviews corrective outreach plan (revised messaging, educator training, licensing clarity, partner re-engagement). If regulatory approval is delayed >4 weeks or pilot enrollment declines >20% due to pushback, matter escalates to Project Sponsor for decision on messaging adjustment, timeline extension, or scope reduction. Rationale: Educator and standards-body adoption is essential to pilot recruitment and Phase 3 success. High-likelihood risk: educators may perceive Clear English as a threat to standard English instruction or a non-standard variant imposed from outside. Standards bodies may demand formal approval or alignment with existing curricula. Unmanaged pushback reduces pilot enrollment by 20–50% (estimate) and delays institutional partnerships, compressing Phase 2 timeline and weakening gate credibility. Negative Consequences: Low educator engagement could reduce pilot quality and statistical power, making gate metrics inconclusive or disputable. Public criticism from TESOL, IATEFL or national education authorities could trigger negative media coverage, damaging credibility before go/no-go decision. Regulatory approval delays of 4–8 months (estimate) push pilot timeline into Month 28–32 (2029-02-13 to 2029-06-13), jeopardizing the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate. Even if gate is positive, educator resistance could reduce Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%, capping learner reach at 15,000–35,000 instead of 100,000+.

Monitoring Progress

1. Gate Metrics Credibility and Pre-Registration Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Pre-Analysis Plan Repository (OSF)
  • Metrics & Validation Committee Monthly Report Template
  • Inter-Rater Reliability Tracking Spreadsheet
  • Validity Study Results Dashboard

Frequency: Bi-weekly Metrics & Validation Committee meetings (Months 2-24 = 2026-12-13 to 2028-10-13); monthly reporting to Steering Committee; validity audit mid-phase (Months 18-23 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-09-13)

Responsible Role: Metrics & Validation Committee (Chair: Psychometrician, with external measurement specialist oversight)

Adaptation Process: The Psychometrician and Committee detect measurement validity threats (inter-rater kappa drift below 0.70, effect-size anomalies, confound signals, data integrity issues) via ongoing analysis and the independent mid-phase validity audit. Threats escalate immediately to the Steering Committee with remediation options (rater retraining, extended calibration, supplementary analysis, Phase 1 extension by up to 4 weeks estimated at ~$85K cost). If kappa falls below 0.70 at the Month 10 (2027-08-13) checkpoint and retraining during Month 10-11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) does not restore it to ≥0.70, Phase 1 is extended by 4 weeks with Steering Committee approval.

Adaptation Trigger: Inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) <0.70 for more than 2 weeks; effect sizes falling outside expected range (confound signal); missing pilot data >15% by Month 21 (2028-07-13); validity audit findings (Month 23 = 2028-09-13) that challenge construct validity or reveal data-integrity violations; any deviation from the pre-registered analysis plan discovered during Phase 2 execution.

2. Editorial Board Rule Finalization and Decision Logging

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Editorial Board Decision Log (version-controlled document)
  • Rule Specification Workstream Status Tracker
  • Linguistic Review Panel Monthly Findings Report
  • Dispute Escalation and Arbiter Recommendation Log

Frequency: Monthly Editorial Board meetings (second Thursday, 2 hours) and biweekly rule-workstream subcommittee meetings (ordinal, morphology, homograph, lexicon, pronunciation-guidance) Months 2-10 (2026-12-13 to 2027-08-13); Linguistic Review Panel monthly vetting (Months 5-11 = 2027-03-13 to 2027-09-13); quarterly published Decision Log summaries (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-13, 2027-04-13, 2027-07-13, 2027-10-13)

Responsible Role: Editorial Board Chair (internal, practitioner or linguist with governance experience, 0.5 FTE) with Linguistic Review Panel (2-3 board linguists, monthly 90-minute meetings) and external Arbiter (appointed by Month 5 = 2027-03-13 for tie-breaking if consensus fails)

Adaptation Process: The Editorial Board drafts rule specifications through assigned subcommittees (ordinal marker pronunciation, morphology retention threshold, homograph-pair list, lexicon selection, G2P logic), meeting biweekly through Month 10 (2027-08-13). The Linguistic Review Panel reviews each proposed rule monthly for internal contradiction, ambiguity, or lack of publishable justification; any veto findings are escalated to the full board for resolution. If a rule dispute remains unresolved after board vote and linguist veto, the matter is escalated to the external Arbiter for a binding recommendation within 2 weeks. All decisions are logged within 3 business days with rationale documented. If disputes persist beyond Month 10 (2027-08-13), the escalation to Arbiter triggers immediately; if the Arbiter's recommendation is rejected by both the Steering Committee and Editorial Board, the matter escalates to the Project Sponsor for final decision.

Adaptation Trigger: Any rule remaining ambiguous or internally contradictory at the end of a subcommittee meeting; a Linguistic Review Panel veto on a proposed rule; a board vote that deadlocks (tie) or fails to reach simple majority; a rule-specification workstream milestone missed by >2 weeks; any rule conflict that cannot be resolved by consensus by Month 10 (2027-08-13); Arbiter recommendation issued but rejected by Steering Committee or Editorial Board.

3. Pilot Recruitment, Enrollment and Retention Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Cohort Enrollment and Demographics Tracker (spreadsheet)
  • Pilot Partner Monthly Status Report Template
  • Participant Dropout and Attrition Log
  • 30-Day Follow-Up Completion Dashboard

Frequency: Weekly enrollment updates from Cohort Manager (Months 13-14 = 2027-11-13 to 2027-12-13); monthly partner status reports and retention metrics (Months 15-24 = 2028-01-13 to 2028-10-13); 30-day follow-up tracking from Month 18 (2028-04-13) onwards; mid-phase checkpoint review (Month 18 = 2028-04-13) with Steering Committee

Responsible Role: Cohort Manager (1.0 FTE, hired by Month 6 = 2027-04-13, reports to Project Lead) with Stakeholder Engagement Lead oversight and partner-site liaisons

Adaptation Process: The Cohort Manager monitors enrollment weekly against the target of ≥115 per arm (4 arms, 460 total estimate); flags shortfalls to the Project Lead within 48 hours if enrollment lags >2 weeks behind schedule. Dropout and retention are tracked at each assessment point; if attrition exceeds 30% target by Month 18 (2028-04-13) midpoint, the Project Lead and Compliance & Risk Management Committee review retention-incentive options (increased stipends, additional session scheduling flexibility, partner re-engagement) and recommend either intensified outreach or Phase 2 extension (estimated ~$85K-$300K depending on scope, proposed). The Steering Committee reviews enrollment status at quarterly checkpoints (Months 18, 24 = 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13); if effective sample size at Month 22 (2028-08-13, data lock) falls below 80 completers per arm, the Committee escalates to Project Sponsor and decides whether to extend Phase 2 (3-6 months, estimated cost $300K-$600K unbudgeted) or proceed to a disputed go/no-go decision.

Adaptation Trigger: Enrollment cumulative shortfall >15% of target by end of Week 8 (Month 13.5 = 2027-11-28, estimate); dropout >30% at any checkpoint; 30-day follow-up completion <70% by Month 23 (2028-09-13); any pilot partner withdraws participation or reduces committed enrollment; effective completers <80 per arm by data lock (Month 22 = 2028-08-13); retention patterns diverge significantly between pilot sites or conditions (suggesting confound or delivery failure).

4. Critical Success Factor: Rule Specification Completeness and Clarity

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Rule Finalization Checklist (ordinal, morphology, homograph, lexicon, G2P, pronunciation-guidance specifications)
  • Draft Standard v0.1 Quality Audit Checklist
  • Public Comment and Response Log (Month 11-12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13)
  • Final Clear English Standard v1.0 Completeness Verification Document

Frequency: Monthly rule-workstream progress reviews (Months 2-10 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-08-13); draft-standard preparation and publication (Month 11 = 2027-09-13); public-comment collection and response (Month 11-12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13); rules-lock verification (Month 12 = 2027-10-13); pre-Phase-2 gate checkpoint (Month 12 = 2027-10-13)

Responsible Role: Editorial Board Chair with Project Lead and Compliance & Risk Management Committee support for publication and public-engagement logistics

Adaptation Process: The Editorial Board monitors rule-specification completeness through monthly subcommittee reports: ordinal marker pronunciation (fixed form, spoken reading, legacy-form conversion rules), morphology retention threshold (frequency cutoff, retained list, regularized list with justification), homograph-disambiguation policy (published pair list ≤50 estimate, marker vs. rewrite decision per pair, enforcement in safety-critical docs), core-lexicon specification (5,000 words, selection basis documented, coverage audit ≥85% estimate), and G2P guidance (overlay logic, optional application). Any missing specification or unresolved detail is flagged in monthly Board minutes and assigned to a subcommittee for completion by Month 10 (2027-08-13). The draft standard v0.1 is published Month 11 (2027-09-13) with all core specifications; public comments are collected and responded to within 14 days; substantive comments that clarify rule intent (but do not reopen core rules) are incorporated into v1.0. If substantive public comments challenge rule validity (e.g., a comment that the ordinal marker is ambiguous or the morphology threshold is unjustifiably high), the Editorial Board escalates the comment to the external Arbiter for recommendation on whether rule revision is warranted before v1.0 finalization; if the Arbiter recommends revision, the rule is clarified or refined by Month 12 (2027-10-13).

Adaptation Trigger: Any rule specification incomplete or marked 'TBD' at the end of Month 9 (2027-07-13); Editorial Board unable to reach consensus on a core rule by Month 10 (2027-08-13); draft standard v0.1 missing a major specification (e.g., no ordinal-marker spoken-reading guidance, no morphology-retention list, no homograph-pair list); public-comment window generates substantive challenges to rule logic or clarity that the Editorial Board cannot resolve without revision; Arbiter recommendation issued indicating rule ambiguity that requires pre-v1.0 fix.

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Pilot Partnership Agreement Register (signed commitments, per-partner)
