  • Partner Capacity and Engagement Tracker (monthly contact logs, meeting attendance, materials review)
  • Educator and Standards-Body Advisory Panel Meeting Notes
  • Publisher Letter-of-Interest Log (non-binding commitments)

Frequency: Monthly check-in calls with each of the 5-7 pilot partners (ESL programs and technical/safety-training organizations); quarterly advisory panel meetings with educators, regulators and publishers (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36 = 2027-01-13 onwards); mid-phase stakeholder-alignment review (Month 18 = 2028-04-13); monthly engagement-metric reports to Steering Committee

Responsible Role: Stakeholder Engagement Lead (internal, 0.5 FTE) with Project Lead oversight and Compliance & Risk Management Committee escalation support

Adaptation Process: The Stakeholder Engagement Lead maintains signed partnership agreements with ≥3 adult ESL programs and ≥2 technical/safety-training organizations by Month 3 (2027-01-13), documenting enrollment guarantees, payment terms, educator-training participation, and feedback schedules. Monthly contact logs track partner engagement (meeting attendance, readiness for material delivery, instructor preparation); any partner showing signs of disengagement (missed meetings, enrollment delays, budget constraints) is flagged to the Project Lead within 48 hours for re-engagement outreach. Quarterly advisory panels (educators, regulators, publishers) surface emerging adoption barriers or standards-body concerns; if a panel signals potential rejection or major pushback (e.g., 'Clear English is a threat to standard English instruction'), the Project Lead and Stakeholder Engagement Lead convene an emergency response meeting and recommend corrective messaging or protocol adjustments to the Steering Committee. If a pilot partner withdraws or reduces commitment to <80 committed learners, the Project Lead immediately flags the shortfall and activates a backup partner or expanded recruitment at an existing site.

Adaptation Trigger: A pilot partner misses two consecutive monthly check-ins without explanation; a partner withdraws or reduces enrollment commitment by >20%; educator or standards-body advisory panel reports >20% increase in critical sentiment or adoption concerns; a major ESL publisher or standards body (TESOL, IATEFL, national education authority) signals that Clear English is not aligned with their curricula or standards and declines partnership; educator pushback signals in social media, professional forums or direct feedback reach a threshold of >10% of outreach audience expressing concern or rejection.

6. Risk Management: Budget, Timeline and Contingency Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Spend Report (by Phase, budget line, actual vs. budget variance)
  • Critical Path Dashboard (milestones, resource allocation, variance alerts >2 weeks)
  • Contingency Reserve Balance Tracker
  • Risk Register (quarterly updates, Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, 36 = 2027-01-13 onwards)

Frequency: Monthly financial tracking (cumulative spend, 6-month forecast) and critical-path review; spending-review gate (Month 9 = 2027-07-13) and mid-phase check (Month 18 = 2028-04-13); formal Phase-1 exit review (Month 12 = 2027-10-13); quarterly risk reviews with Steering Committee (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 = 2027-01-13 onwards)

Responsible Role: Finance Lead (0.5-1.0 FTE internal budget controller) with Compliance & Risk Management Committee (Chair) and Project Lead

Adaptation Process: The Finance Lead tracks cumulative monthly spend against Phase allocations ($1.1M Phase 1, $1.2M Phase 2, $0.85M Phase 3) and provides a variance report flagging any line item >10% over or under budget and cumulative Phase variance >$50K. The Critical Path Dashboard is reviewed monthly for slippage >2 weeks on key milestones (rules finalization Month 12 = 2027-10-13, audio completion Month 11 = 2027-09-13, pre-registration Month 11 = 2027-09-13, recruitment/enrollment Month 13 = 2027-11-13, data lock Month 22 = 2028-08-13); any slip triggers immediate escalation to the Steering Committee with impact assessment (does it compress Phase 2 pilot window, risk kappa validation, or push go/no-go decision past Month 24 = 2028-10-13?). The Contingency Reserve Balance ($350K total, capped at $175K draws pre-gate for evidence-protection needs) is tracked monthly; the Finance Lead and Compliance & Risk Management Committee recommend draws for Phase-1 extension (≤$85K estimated) or psychometric re-validation (≤$50K estimated) if gate-protection risks emerge; all draws >$50K require Steering Committee approval. The Compliance & Risk Management Committee reviews the Risk Register quarterly and escalates any High×High risk (e.g., >$50K overrun, pilot recruitment collapse, inter-rater reliability failure, educator pushback >20%, safety incident) to the Steering Committee within 5 business days with mitigation recommendation.

Adaptation Trigger: Any single line-item spend variance >$50K or Phase cumulative variance >$50K; critical-path milestone slip >2 weeks; cumulative spend forecast indicating total project cost will exceed $3.5M by >$125K at any checkpoint; contingency reserve balance falls below $175K pre-gate threshold; identified High×High risk from Risk Register requiring immediate mitigation (e.g., safety incident, data breach, major partner withdrawal); budget variance discovered that cannot be resolved within existing Phase allocations, requiring scope cuts or timeline extension.

7. Risk Management: Safety-Critical Liability and Compliance

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Safety-Critical Pilot Boundary Log (materials type, human-review sign-off)
  • Legal Counsel Regulatory Advice Log
  • Data-Protection Audit Reports (Months 6, 8 = 2027-04-13, 2027-06-13)
  • Ethics/IRB Approval Status and Incident-Reporting Log
  • Disclaimer and Consent-Form Attestation Tracker

Frequency: Monthly review of safety-critical materials and human-expert sign-offs (if any safety pilots are conducted); quarterly legal and compliance check-ins with retained counsel; ethics/IRB communication as needed (ongoing after Month 6 = 2027-04-13 approval); data-protection audit (Month 8 = 2027-06-13) and privacy-policy publication (Month 12 = 2027-10-13); immediate incident-reporting and escalation (within 48 hours if incident occurs)

Responsible Role: Compliance & Risk Management Committee (Chair, risk-management specialist, 0.5 FTE), with external legal counsel (product liability and regulatory compliance specialist, ~4 hours/month retainer), ethics/IRB liaison (internal or external, ~3-4 hours/month), and Data Integrity Officer (internal, ~2 hours/month)

Adaptation Process: The Compliance & Risk Management Committee establishes clear boundaries for safety-critical pilots: glossary and labeling exercises only (no live operational procedures) until after Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision; all materials carry explicit disclaimers ('Clear English is a non-standard variant; use with qualified expert human review') and require sign-off by a qualified human expert (trainer, safety officer) before deployment. Legal counsel advises on regulatory pathways, insurance coverage options ($150K-$200K estimated budget cap), and product liability risk. The Committee ensures ethics/IRB approval is obtained by Month 6 (2027-04-13), covering informed consent, audio-recording protocols, data-protection measures and participant opt-out procedures. A data-protection audit (Month 8 = 2027-06-13) verifies GDPR compliance (UK, if applicable), US state privacy law compliance, encrypted storage setup, backup procedures, and data-retention schedules; any gaps identified are remediated by Month 12 (2027-10-13) with documented attestation. If a safety incident, data breach or ethics violation occurs, the Committee triggers an immediate incident-reporting protocol (within 48 hours): notification to legal counsel, Project Sponsor, Steering Committee, affected pilot organization, and (if required) regulatory authorities; formal investigation within 2 weeks; remediation plan reviewed by Steering Committee; decision on whether to suspend pilots, withdraw materials, or modify protocols.

Adaptation Trigger: Documented safety incident or near-miss in any safety-critical pilot material linking Clear English wording to misunderstanding, wrong action, or injury; data-protection audit finding a gap in encryption, access control, consent documentation or backup procedures; ethics/IRB approval delayed by >2 weeks or conditional on substantive protocol revisions; legal counsel assessment that liability insurance or regulatory approval cost will exceed $200K (estimated cap); incident report from a pilot site or external source alleging that Clear English documentation caused confusion, incorrect action or safety concern; participant complaint regarding data privacy, recording use or consent procedures.

8. Risk Management: Educator Pushback and Adoption Resistance

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Stakeholder Sentiment and Engagement Tracker (quarterly advisory panel feedback)
  • Educator and Standards-Body Pushback Alert Log
  • Corrective Outreach and Messaging Log
  • Stakeholder Alignment Charter and Mid-Phase Review Document

Frequency: Monthly tracking of educator and publisher engagement metrics (open rates on outreach, meeting attendance, sentiment); quarterly advisory panel meetings (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 = 2027-01-13 onwards); real-time monitoring of social media, professional forums (TESOL, IATEFL) and direct feedback for critical signals; mid-phase stakeholder-alignment check-in (Month 18 = 2028-04-13)

Responsible Role: Stakeholder Engagement Lead (internal, 0.5 FTE) with Educator Liaison (0.5-1.0 FTE, hired by Month 6 = 2027-04-13) and Compliance & Risk Management Committee escalation support

Adaptation Process: The Stakeholder Engagement Lead maintains engagement metrics (email open rates, advisory-panel attendance, meeting frequency) and flags declining engagement or critical feedback within 48 hours. Advisory panels (educators, standards bodies, publishers) meet quarterly and provide structured feedback on adoption concerns, messaging clarity and perceived barriers. If educator sentiment shifts negatively (e.g., >20% of panel respondents report concern that Clear English is a threat to standard English instruction) or if a major professional organization (TESOL, IATEFL, national education authority) signals rejection or demands for changes, the Project Lead and Stakeholder Engagement Lead convene an emergency response meeting. Corrective actions may include: revised messaging emphasizing that Clear English is supplementary and optional (not a replacement); expanded educator training and stipends to increase buy-in; modification of pilot protocols to better integrate into existing courses; or escalation to the Steering Committee if institutional approval is jeopardized.

Adaptation Trigger: Any TESOL, IATEFL or major national education-authority public statement indicating concern or rejection of Clear English; educator advisory panel reports >20% increase in critical sentiment about adoption barriers or rule comprehensibility; social media or professional-forum activity critical of Clear English reaches >50 mentions in a month or >10 from respected educators; a pilot partner signals that educator concerns are blocking enrollment or participation commitment; an ESL publisher or major adopter candidate explicitly declines participation citing educator resistance or institutional non-alignment.

9. Critical Success Factor: Pronunciation Consistency Measurement and Reference Accent Anchoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Reference Accent Selection and Justification Document
  • Inter-Rater Reliability Tracking and Rater Training Protocol
  • Pronunciation Audio Storage and Backup Audit Log
  • Pronunciation Consistency Score Preliminary Results (Months 18-24 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13)

Frequency: Accent-selection decision and documentation (Month 3 = 2027-01-13); rater-training completion and inter-rater calibration (Months 10-11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13); monthly audio storage and backup verification (Months 6-24 = 2027-04-13 to 2028-10-13); pronunciation-score reporting and inter-rater reliability checks (Months 15-24 = 2028-01-13 to 2028-10-13, weekly during active pilot scoring)

Responsible Role: Psychometrician (hired by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, 0.5-1.0 FTE) with Metrics & Validation Committee oversight and external measurement specialist consultation; Data Integrity Officer (internal, ~2 hours/month) for audio storage and backup verification

Adaptation Process: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), the Psychometrician and Editorial Board (linguist members) select a single reference accent (e.g., General American, Received Pronunciation, or shared-contrast phonemes across accents) with explicit written justification and documentation of how other accents map to the anchor. Rater training and inter-rater calibration occur in Months 10-11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13): 3-5 raters are trained on pronunciation-consistency scoring rubric using 100-200 sample words from both Clear English and control conditions; Cohen's kappa is computed per rater pair, targeting ≥0.75 (proposed threshold) with a floor of 0.70. If initial kappa falls below 0.70, raters receive targeted retraining and a second calibration round within 2 weeks; if kappa remains <0.70 after retraining, the Phase 1 extension contingency ($85K estimated) is triggered to allow additional rater training by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Audio storage is verified monthly for encryption, access controls, backup functionality and completeness (no missing recordings >1% estimated); a dry-run with a small cohort (N=5-10) occurs at Month 10 (2027-08-13) to test recording quality, file organization and rater workflow. During Phase 2 pilots (Months 15-24 = 2028-01-13 to 2028-10-13), pronunciation scoring occurs weekly; inter-rater reliability is re-checked every 2 weeks (weekly during months 20-24 = 2028-08-13 to 2028-10-13); if kappa drops below 0.70 during active scoring, the Metrics & Validation Committee immediately recommends rater re-calibration or additional training.

Adaptation Trigger: Reference accent choice is not finalized and justified by Month 3 (2027-01-13); initial inter-rater kappa <0.70 after first training in Month 10-11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13); inter-rater kappa remains <0.70 after retraining; audio storage audit identifies >1% missing or corrupted files; rater drift observed (kappa declining >0.05 over a 4-week interval during Phase 2 scoring); pronunciation-consistency preliminary results show no meaningful difference between Clear English and control conditions or effect sizes contradicting pilot expectations (potential confound signal).

10. Risk Management: Post-Project Stewardship Funding and Governance Sustainability

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Steward Organization Identification and Outreach Log
  • Stewardship Funding Commitment Letters
  • Standards Stewardship Committee Charter and 5-Year Roadmap
  • Post-Phase-3 Governance Transition Plan

Frequency: Steward identification and approach (Months 24-27 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-01-13); commitment letters sought (by Month 33 = 2029-07-13); Stewardship Committee and 5-year roadmap finalized (by Month 36 = 2029-10-13); quarterly post-launch governance check-ins (Months 36, 39, 42 = 2029-10-13, 2030-01-13, 2030-04-13, ... as funded)

Responsible Role: Compliance & Risk Management Committee (Chair, risk-management specialist) with Project Lead and Stakeholder Engagement Lead, in collaboration with the Phase 2 go/no-go decision (if GO) Project Sponsor

Adaptation Process: After the Month 24 (2028-10-13) Phase 2 go/no-go decision, if GO, the Project Lead and Compliance & Risk Management Committee begin identifying potential permanent steward organizations (language-education non-profits, university consortiums, international standards bodies such as ISO or academic organizations) with track records in standards maintenance and funding stability. By Month 27 (2029-01-13), outreach is initiated with a stewardship proposal (estimated annual budget $150K-$250K estimate for ongoing maintenance, governance, change-request review, and lexicon updates). Commitment letters from at least one steward organization are sought by Month 33 (2029-07-13); if no commitment is obtained by this date, the Project Lead escalates to the Project Sponsor for a decision: either (a) defer v1.0 public release pending stewardship commitment (delaying release beyond Month 30 = 2029-04-13), (b) release v1.0 with a conditional sunset clause (e.g., 'This standard will be maintained only if stewardship funding is secured by Month X'), or (c) proceed with release and accept the risk that the standard will atrophy if no steward emerges. A Standards Stewardship Committee is formally established by Month 30 (2029-04-13) with 3-5 members (steward-organization representative, Editorial Board continuity, key adopter representatives) and a published charter and 5-year roadmap specifying how the standard will be updated, how change requests will be prioritized and resolved, and how conflicts over rule interpretation will be handled.

Adaptation Trigger: Phase 2 go/no-go is GO (Month 24 = 2028-10-13) and no steward organization has been approached by Month 24 (2028-10-13); steward outreach begins but by Month 30 (2029-04-13) no letter of commitment is in hand; potential steward organizations decline participation (budget constraints, competing priorities); a steward-organization commitment is received but with conditions (e.g., 'only if ESL publisher adoption reaches 50,000+ learners by Month X') that are unrealistic or unverifiable; the Steering Committee or Project Sponsor determines that the standard's post-Phase-3 viability is at risk and recommends either release deferral or conditional-release strategy.

11. Risk Management: Rule Fragmentation and Non-Conforming Variants Post-Release

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Licensing and Name-Stewardship Model Decision Document
  • Conformance Checklist (public, light, free)
  • Third-Party Adoption and Licensing Registry
  • Non-Conforming Fork and Unofficial Variant Alert Log

Frequency: Licensing model finalized (by Month 6 = 2027-04-13) and published (Month 12 = 2027-10-13); conformance checklist published (Month 12 = 2027-10-13); post-release monitoring for unofficial variants and non-conforming uses (quarterly, Months 30, 33, 36, 39 = 2029-04-13, 2029-07-13, 2029-10-13, 2030-01-13, ... post-release, starting Month 30 = 2029-04-13)

Responsible Role: Compliance & Risk Management Committee (Chair) with Standards Stewardship Committee (post-Month 36 = 2029-10-13) and Stakeholder Engagement Lead; external legal counsel if name-stewardship disputes arise

Adaptation Process: By Month 6 (2027-04-13), the Compliance & Risk Management Committee and Project Lead (with external legal counsel input) finalize the Licensing and Name Stewardship model: either (a) text and dictionary openly licensed; 'Clear English' name reserved as a certification mark (requiring conformance against a public checklist) awarded to materials that pass the checklist, or (b) text and dictionary under a permissive share-alike license (permitting derivative works if divergence is disclosed and a distinct name is adopted once >10% of rules diverge, proposed threshold). A public, light, free conformance checklist is published by Month 12 (2027-10-13), specifying the key rules (ordinal marker form, morphology changes, homograph markers, lexicon boundaries) that materials must follow to claim 'Clear English' conformance. Post-release (starting Month 30 = 2029-04-13), the Standards Stewardship Committee (or Project Lead, if Stewardship Committee not yet established) monitors for third-party uses of the 'Clear English' name and for unofficial forks or non-conforming variants. A public registry of licensed adopters is maintained; if an organization uses the name without conformance (detected via social media, publishing announcements, or direct report), the Stewardship Committee issues a public clarification or, if certification model is in force, withholds the mark and may issue a public statement that the variant is non-conforming.

Adaptation Trigger: A third party publicly labels a variant or material as 'Clear English' but the variant incorporates rule changes beyond the 10% divergence threshold (proposed) or omits required core rules; a significant non-conforming fork is discovered (detected via web search, standards-body inquiry, or third-party report) suggesting that the 'Clear English' name is being applied to non-standardized material, creating confusion; the Stewardship Committee receives >3 inquiries or complaints in a quarter about non-conforming use of the name; an offline publisher or organization uses the name in printed material without seeking conformance review and the Stewardship Committee learns of it via partner or standards-body feedback; an open-source project or crowdsourced variant emerges that claims Clear English affiliation but diverges significantly from the published standard.

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness: All core governance components are defined (Editorial Board Charter, Steering Committee Charter, Metrics & Validation Committee Charter, Compliance & Risk Management Committee Charter, escalation matrix, monitoring framework, implementation plan). Governance bodies span rule specification (Editorial Board), strategic oversight (Steering Committee), measurement credibility (Metrics & Validation Committee) and risk/compliance management (Compliance & Risk Management Committee). Decision authority and escalation paths are explicitly mapped. The framework covers all three phases and includes post-Phase-3 stewardship planning (Standards Stewardship Committee, steward identification by Month 33 = 2029-07-13). One core gap: the role and decision authority of the ultimate Project Sponsor (external funding body) is mentioned in Phase 3 implementation but not formally chartered; clarify escalation from Steering Committee to Sponsor for strategic disputes or go/no-go outcome challenges.
  2. Internal Consistency: Rule decisions (Editorial Board) feed into measurement design (Metrics & Validation Committee pre-registers ordinal-error-rate and pronunciation-consistency scoring rubrics tied to finalized rules by Month 11 = 2027-09-13). Pilot recruitment (Compliance & Risk Management Committee and Stakeholder Engagement Lead) is contingent on partner commitments signed by Month 3 (2027-01-13) and ethics approval by Month 6 (2027-04-13), both tracked against timelines. Budget monitoring (Finance Lead, Steering Committee monthly reviews) enforces the $175K pre-gate contingency cap and flags overruns for escalation. Timeline and critical-path tracking (Project Lead, Steering Committee) monitor sequential dependencies (rules Month 12 = 2027-10-13, audio Month 11 = 2027-09-13, pre-registration Month 11 = 2027-09-13, recruitment Month 13 = 2027-11-13, data lock Month 22 = 2028-08-13, gate Month 24 = 2028-10-13). Escalation matrix specifies approval processes and negative consequences for each risk type. No detected logical conflicts; however, the adaptive mechanisms (e.g., how the board proceeds if Arbiter recommendation is rejected, how Phase 1 extension is funded if kappa<0.70) could be more explicit in terms of decision authority and contingency funding draw procedures.
  3. Clarity of Roles and Authority: Editorial Board chair and Steering Committee chair are identified as distinct roles. Editorial Board linguist members hold formal veto authority, limited to rule ambiguity and contradiction findings (not rule substance). Metrics & Validation Committee operates at 'arm's length' from Editorial Board and Steering Committee to maintain measurement independence. Project Sponsor role is mentioned for escalation but is not formally chartered; the Sponsor's approval authority for reserve draws >$175K, Phase extensions, and major scope changes should be explicitly documented in a Sponsor Charter by Month 0 (2026-10-13). Conflict-of-interest disclosure procedures are specified (Editorial Board Charter, attestations collected by Month 1 = 2026-11-13), but no described mechanism for handling conflicts (e.g., if an Editorial Board member's institution benefits from a rule decision). Stakeholder Engagement Lead and Educator Liaison roles are defined with clear responsibilities (partner engagement, corrective outreach), but their authority to modify pilot protocols or messaging without Steering Committee approval is unclear; specify delegation limits.
  4. Process Depth and Operational Clarity: Rule-finalization process is detailed (subcommittees biweekly Months 2-10 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-08-13, Linguistic Review Panel monthly vetting, escalation to Arbiter for deadlock, 30-day public comment Month 11-12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13, v1.0 lock Month 12 = 2027-10-13), with decision-logging discipline. Gate metric design includes construct-validity analysis and pre-registration (Months 4-5 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-03-13 literature review and expert panel, validity study Months 10-11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13, pre-analysis plan finalization Month 11 = 2027-09-13, registration by Month 11.5 = 2027-09-28 proposed). However, three operational processes need more detail: (a) Conflict-of-interest management: no procedure specified for what happens if an Editorial Board member's employer benefits from a rule decision or if a Steering Committee member has financial stake in ESL publishing; (b) Whistleblower or ethics-violation reporting: no designated reporting channel or investigation procedure if misconduct (data manipulation, participant coercion, unauthorized audio use) is alleged; (c) Change-control post-v1.0: the decision specifies 'v1.0 frozen 12 months' but does not detail how errata will be identified, approved and communicated; specify errata-review procedure and timeline.
  5. Process Completeness: Gaps identified in three areas: (1) Quantitative Gate Thresholds: The four metrics (ordinal error rate ≥25% reduction, comprehension speed ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%) are named and loosely specified with proposed thresholds, but the complete pre-analysis plan (including statistical test type, sample-size power analysis calculation, primary vs. secondary outcome hierarchy, intention-to-treat rules, missing-data imputation procedures, effect-size interpretation guidance) must be drafted by Month 5 (2027-03-13), externally peer-reviewed by Month 5.5 (2027-03-28), and locked by Month 11 (2027-09-13) before pre-registration. The canonical facts document specifies the thresholds but does not reference the underlying power analysis or effect-size assumptions; confirm that the $150K-$200K (estimate) psychometrics budget includes power analysis, effect-size justification studies and post-hoc sensitivity analysis. (2) Construct-Validity and Confound Controls: The implementation plan specifies 'detailed construct-validity literature review' (Month 4 = 2027-02-13) and 'expert-panel discussion' (Month 4 = 2027-02-13) but does not describe how confounds (repeated exposure, learner motivation, accent proximity) will be operationalized or measured in the pilot; detail the control-condition design (e.g., standard-English ordinals with explicit rule instruction vs. implicit exposure) and manipulation-check procedures (e.g., post-test questions asking learners which rule system they learned) in the pre-analysis plan. (3) Data Integrity and Consent Escalation: The Compliance & Risk Management Committee monitors data-protection compliance, but the framework does not specify a formal data-privacy incident-response procedure (who investigates, timeline, notification of affected participants, regulatory reporting); draft a written Data-Privacy Incident Response Plan by Month 4 (2027-02-13) and include it in the IRB protocol.
  6. Potential Gaps Requiring Clarification: (a) Project Sponsor Role: The Sponsor (external funding body representative or senior institutional leader) is mentioned as having authority to approve reserve draws >$175K and to make final decisions on Phase extensions or project termination, but is not formally chartered. Draft a Project Sponsor Charter by Month 0 (2026-10-13) specifying escalation thresholds (e.g., Sponsor approval required for budget increases >$300K, timeline extensions >8 weeks, scope reductions >15%), decision timeline (e.g., Sponsor must decide within 10 business days of escalation), and communication protocol (monthly reporting, ad-hoc escalation alerts). (b) Delegation Below Committee Level: The framework grants authority to committee chairs (Editorial Board Chair, Psychometrician as Metrics & Validation Committee Chair, Compliance & Risk Management Committee Chair, Project Lead) but does not specify whether these chairs can make routine operational decisions (e.g., can the Psychometrician hire a research assistant without Steering Committee approval? Can the Project Lead approve a $20K curriculum-design invoice without Finance Lead sign-off?) Define delegation authority thresholds (e.g., <$25K spending, <2-week timeline impact, routine operational decisions delegated to committee chairs; >$50K or strategic decisions require Steering Committee approval). (c) Standards Stewardship Committee Transition: The frame work specifies that a Standards Stewardship Committee will be established by Month 30 (2029-04-13) post-Phase-3, but the relationship between the Phase 1-3 Editorial Board and the post-Phase-3 Stewardship Committee is unclear. Will Editorial Board members serve on the Stewardship Committee? Will there be a formal transition meeting and knowledge-transfer protocol? Will the same decision-logging and conflict-resolution procedures apply post-Phase-3? Specify a Stewardship Committee Charter (to be finalized by Month 30 = 2029-04-13) that documents governance continuity and transition procedures.

Tough Questions

  1. Gate Metrics Credibility: By Month 11 (2027-09-13), can the Psychometrician and Metrics & Validation Committee certify that the four gate metrics (ordinal error rate ≥25% reduction, comprehension speed ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%) are grounded in a defensible power analysis (≥80% power at α=0.05), that the sample size target (≥80 completers per arm) is justified and achievable by data lock (Month 22 = 2028-08-13), and that inter-rater reliability is calibrated to kappa ≥0.70 floor? What assumptions underlie the ≥25% ordinal-error-reduction threshold—is it based on benchmarking against other language-learning interventions, or is it a consensus judgment of the Editorial Board, and if the latter, what is the evidentiary basis?
  2. Rule Finalization and Ambiguity: By Month 11 (2027-09-13), will the Editorial Board publish a complete, non-ambiguous Clear English Standard v0.1 that specifies the ordinal marker symbol, its spoken pronunciation, the morphology retention cutoff with a published list of retained vs. regularized forms, the homograph-pair list with enforcement policy per pair, and the core-lexicon specification with coverage audit showing ≥85% coverage of pilot running text? If the Editorial Board cannot finalize all core rules without escalation to the external Arbiter, what is the timeline for Arbiter resolution, and does it still permit the 30-day public comment window before Month 12 (2027-10-13) v0.1 publication?
  3. Construct Validity of Gate Metrics: What explicit control conditions and manipulation checks will be embedded in the Phase 2 pilots to isolate Clear English effects from alternative explanations (repeated exposure to ordinals, learner motivation to participate in a 'novel standard' study, accent proximity to learners' first language, baseline literacy differences)? By Month 5 (2027-03-13), will the Psychometrician publish a detailed construct-validity section of the pre-analysis plan that documents how each confound is measured and how the primary analysis will control for it (e.g., via regression, matching, or stratified analysis)?
  4. Pilot Recruitment and Retention Evidence: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), what are the signed, written enrollment commitments from 3-4 adult ESL programs and 2-3 technical/safety-training organizations, and what does each commitment document (per-learner guarantee, payment terms, educator training, retention incentives, dropout tolerance)? By Month 13 (2027-11-13), what is the actual enrollment vs. the ≥115 per arm target, and if shortfall is >15%, what is the contingency plan (additional recruitment sites, extended enrollment period, Phase 2 timeline extension) and associated cost within the $175K pre-gate contingency cap?
  5. Budget and Timeline Discipline: At the Month 9 (2027-07-13) Phase 1 spending review, what is the actual cumulative spend vs. the $1.1M Phase 1 budget allocation, and what is the 6-month forecast for Phase 2 spending (Month 9-14 = 2027-07-13 to 2027-12-13)? If Phase 1 spend is >10% over or <10% under budget, what is the root cause and what reallocation is recommended to maintain the $175K pre-gate contingency cap intact? If Phase 2 forecast indicates a $300K overrun (8.6% of total budget), what scope reduction is proposed—fewer pilot cohorts, smaller assessment battery, or Phase 1 extension deferral?
  6. Measurement Inter-Rater Reliability Assurance: By Month 11 (2027-09-13), after rater training and the calibration study (Months 10-11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), will Cohen's kappa for pronunciation-consistency scoring and ordinal-error scoring meet the ≥0.75 (proposed) target and exceed the 0.70 floor across all rater pairs? If any rater pair falls below 0.70 after the initial 2-week retraining window (Month 10-11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), what is the evidence that a 4-week Phase 1 extension (~$85K cost) will remediate the reliability gap, and by what date must kappa be confirmed ≥0.70 (proposed: Month 12 = 2027-10-13) to permit Phase 2 green light?
  7. Educator Engagement and Pushback Signals: By Month 6 (2027-04-13), what baseline metrics establish educator and standards-body sentiment on Clear English (e.g., survey of TESOL members, social-media sentiment analysis, direct interviews with 10-15 curriculum directors)? By Month 18 (2028-04-13), what is the change in sentiment, and what threshold of increase in critical feedback (>20% negative mentions, loss of a major partner commitment, a published TESOL or IATEFL position statement expressing concern) would trigger the 'educator pushback' escalation procedure to the Steering Committee and corrective outreach?

Summary

The Clear English program is a moderately ambitious, evidence-gated, 36-month language-standardization initiative ($3.5M user constraint) spanning rule specification, pilot validation and public release. The governance framework—comprising a practitioner-leaning Editorial Board, an independent Metrics & Validation Committee, a Steering Committee with escalation authority, and a Compliance & Risk Management Committee—is comprehensive and well-structured to manage critical dependencies: rule clarity (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 lock), measurement credibility (pre-registered metrics by Month 11 = 2027-09-13), pilot recruitment and retention (460 learners across 4 arms), and post-launch stewardship (commitment sought by Month 33 = 2029-07-13). The framework prioritizes adoption-first, evidence-based decision-making, with clear escalation paths for rule deadlock, budget overruns, measurement threats and stakeholder pushback. Key strengths include pre-registration discipline, independent validity oversight, and explicit governance charters. Critical remaining gaps are quantitative gate thresholds (must be finalized and pre-registered by Month 11 = 2027-09-13), construct-validity control procedures, stewardship funding security (currently unfunded), and clear contingency procedures if critical path items slip or validity falls short of standards.

Suggestion 1 - ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (Specification maintained by the ASD STE100 Maintenance Group)

A controlled-language standard for technical documentation, originating from aerospace manuals in the 1980s. It comprises about 60 writing rules and a controlled dictionary of approved words with approved meanings. Maintained by the STE Maintenance Group (STEMG) under ASD (AeroSpace and Defence Industries Association of Europe), with periodic numbered issues. Widely used in aerospace, defence, and increasingly other sectors, with certified training and software checkers offered by third parties.

Success Metrics

Sustained use across international aerospace and defence manuals over several decades (documented by ASD) Multiple numbered issues released, showing a working change-control cadence Ecosystem of third-party checkers and training providers (count not verified) Mandated by some aerospace customers' documentation contracts (extent not verified)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Writer resistance to restricted vocabulary: mitigated by an approved-word dictionary with examples and training Specification drift across versions: mitigated by a standing maintenance group and published issues Compliance verification: mitigated by software checkers and certified training offerings Unclear mapping between standard and non-standard text: mitigated by approved-meaning entries and explicit not-allowed alternatives

Where to Find More Information

https://www.asd-ste100.org (official specification site) ASD STE100 Issue documentation, available from the official site on request

Actionable Steps

Contact the ASD-STE100 Maintenance Group via the contact form on the official site to ask how they structure change control and licensing Ask ASD for the current licensing terms for the specification and for guidance on describing partial compatibility Approach STE training providers listed on the official site to learn about writer conversion effort

Rationale for Suggestion

Closest real analogue for the safety-critical glossary track and the one-way mapping table the plan chooses. It shows how a controlled English earns trust among technical writers, how a maintenance group handles versioned releases, and how third-party tool vendors build around an open-but-controlled specification. Geographic proximity is limited (European and US industry), but the sector is the target adopter.

Suggestion 2 - ICAO Language Proficiency Requirements for aviation English

International Civil Aviation Organization standards (Annex 1, Doc 9835) requiring pilots and air traffic controllers on international routes to demonstrate English language proficiency on a six-level scale, with standardized phraseology (ICAO Doc 4444 and Doc 9432). Adopted after language-related accident analyses, with a phased implementation deadline extended by ICAO from 2008 to 2011.

Success Metrics

Adoption by ICAO member states with national test providers (extent varies; not verified) Implementation deadline met only after an extension, showing timeline risk Creation of an ecosystem of aviation English tests and curricula (count not verified)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Accent diversity and rater consistency: mitigated by a holistic rating scale with defined descriptors and rater training Uneven national readiness: mitigated by an extended deadline and guidance manual (Doc 9835) Test quality disputes: mitigated by published guidelines and ICAO-endorsed test-evaluation efforts Liability and safety scrutiny: mitigated by tying language to documented incident analysis

Where to Find More Information

https://www.icao.int (search Doc 9835 Manual on the Implementation of ICAO Language Proficiency Requirements) ICAO Annex 1 and Doc 4444 via the ICAO store

Actionable Steps

Contact ICAO's Air Navigation Bureau or Montreal headquarters through the official contact page Reach out to national civil aviation authorities or aviation English test providers for lessons on rater calibration Ask aviation English researchers at universities with applied linguistics programs about inter-rater reliability experience

Rationale for Suggestion

A real, documented case of rolling out a standardized English subset in safety-critical settings. It demonstrates how a rating scale, test providers, and training materials were built across many accents, and how phased deadlines and extensions were handled. Relevant to accent anchoring, liability, and gate metric design, although it was a mandate (which Clear English avoids).

Suggestion 3 - Basic English (C. K. Ogden, 1930s; later Orthological Institute)

A constructed, limited-vocabulary English of 850 words designed by C. K. Ogden as an international auxiliary and teaching language, promoted in the 1930s-1940s with textbooks, a journal and institutional backing. Interest peaked in the 1940s (including attention from Winston Churchill) and then declined.

Success Metrics

Widespread attention in the 1930s-1940s, including government interest (documented in histories) Published textbooks and a dictionary (counts not verified) Long-term adoption remained limited, informing the plan's modest targets

Risks and Challenges Faced

Learners needed full English anyway: the plan's supplementary positioning addresses this Limited vocabulary led to awkward phrasing: mitigated here by a 5,000-word lexicon Dependence on one founder and institute: mitigated by planned board and steward organization Waning institutional support: mitigated by early stewardship search

Where to Find More Information

Ogden, C. K., Basic English: A General Introduction with Rules and Grammar (1930) Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on Basic English Archives of the Orthological Institute (location not verified)

Actionable Steps

Contact university libraries with Ogden collections (for example McMaster University, which holds Ogden papers; not verified) for archival material Consult applied linguistics historians of language planning for lessons learned Review academic papers on Basic English adoption via Google Scholar

Rationale for Suggestion

A real precedent for a parallel, intelligible English subset aimed at learners, which shows both promotion tactics and why adoption faded. Useful as a cautionary and design reference for lexicon size, supplementary positioning and stewardship. It is geographically British and historical, so operational detail is dated.

Suggestion 4 - Secondary: Simplified Spelling Board (US, 1906) and Shavian alphabet (UK, 1960)

Two real English spelling reform efforts. The Simplified Spelling Board, funded by Andrew Carnegie, proposed respelling about 300 words and gained a presidential endorsement attempt before public and congressional pushback. The Shaw Alphabet competition produced the Shavian alphabet and a published edition of Androcles and the Lion.

Success Metrics

Limited long-term adoption, supporting the no-respelling choice Some forms (for example 'catalog', 'program') persisted in American usage (extent not verified)

Risks and Challenges Faced

Public ridicule and political pushback: avoided here by optional overlay Fragmentation and lack of enforcement: addressed by certification mark and checklist

Where to Find More Information

Encyclopaedia Britannica: Spelling reform Shavian alphabet resources at shavian.info (not verified)

Actionable Steps

Contact the Simplified Spelling Society (UK) via its website for historical material and a view on adoption barriers

Rationale for Suggestion

Secondary suggestion. Both show native-reader rejection of respelling, supporting the plan's decision to keep standard spellings and use an overlay. Details are historical and less operational.

Summary

Clear English is a parallel, ESL-first, evidence-gated standard. The closest real precedents are controlled or simplified language standards and constructed or standardized English variants, plus large-scale ESL pronunciation and assessment projects. Directly matching projects (a parallel English variant with prefix ordinals and a pronunciation overlay) do not exist, so the references below cover separate components: controlled-language governance (ASD-STE100), a limited-vocabulary variant with an adoption history (Basic English), a standardized aviation English with a safety-critical rollout (ICAO English Language Proficiency), and a secondary reference on spelling-reform fragmentation. Figures not verified are labelled as such; contacts are organizations or roles, not named individuals.

1. Gate Metrics Pre-Registration and Psychometric Validation

The go/no-go decision at Month 24 (2028-10-13) is the project's only gate. Weak, un-justified, or post-hoc thresholds render the gate scientifically disputable and risk adopter rejection (20-50% adoption loss). Pre-registration by Month 11 (2027-09-13) locks thresholds before data collection begins, foreclose post-hoc critique and establish external credibility with standards bodies, educators and regulators.

Data to Collect

  • Quantitative pass/fail thresholds for ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, and 30-day retention with empirical justification
  • Power analysis confirming minimum sample size per arm (80+ estimate) achieves 80% statistical power at α=0.05
  • Inter-rater reliability target (Cohen's kappa ≥0.70 floor, ≥0.75 target proposed) with calibration protocol and rater selection criteria
  • Pre-analysis plan with effect-size estimates, intention-to-treat rules, and sensitivity analyses for borderline outcomes
  • Independent psychometrician review of construct validity and confound controls (e.g., repeated-exposure effects, learner motivation artifacts)

Simulation Steps

  • Commission a small validity study (N=20-30 adult ESL and technical learners) Months 10-11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) using draft assessment instruments and order the results by effect size (ordinal error %, comprehension speed %, pronunciation consistency kappa, retention % retention)
  • Conduct inter-rater calibration on a 100-200 word pronunciation pilot sample (Month 9 = 2027-07-13) using at least 3 candidate raters; calculate Cohen's kappa pairwise and consensus; if kappa ≥0.70, proceed to full audio production; if <0.70, retrain raters for 2 weeks and retest by Month 10 (2027-08-13)
  • Run a dry run of the full assessment pipeline (N=5-10 learners, all 4 gate tasks, recording + scoring) Month 10 (2027-08-13); identify logistical, technical, or scoring ambiguities and document time-per-session
  • Model statistical power for each metric under the observed effect sizes and assumed attrition (30-40% dropout estimate); confirm whether 80 per arm or an alternative sample size achieves ≥80% power; document power curve and sensitivity to effect-size assumptions
  • Draft a pre-analysis plan (5-7 pages) specifying numeric thresholds, decision rules (GO/INCONCLUSIVE/NO-GO), and published justification for each threshold; circulate to board for approval

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage an independent psychometrician (external to project team, specialized in ESL or educational measurement) by Month 2 (2026-12-13); commission deliverables: power analysis memo (Month 5 = 2027-03-13), draft pre-analysis plan (Month 10 = 2027-08-13), final registered plan (Month 11 = 2027-09-13)
  • Submit the pre-analysis plan to an independent external reviewer (published applied-linguistics or measurement specialist, no project affiliation) for critique on statistical rigor, effect-size justification, and boundary conditions; publish reviewer summary by Month 12 (2027-10-13)
  • Register the complete pre-analysis plan on Open Science Framework or Aspredicted.org by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with board sign-off; publish registered thresholds on project website immediately for third-party review
  • If inter-rater kappa falls below 0.70 after Month 10 (2027-08-13) retraining, escalate to editorial board by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with recommendation for either (a) hybrid synthetic + verification approach, (b) 4-week Phase 1 extension for additional rater training, or (c) scope reduction (record 3,000-4,000 words instead of 5,000)
  • Convene board vote on final thresholds by Month 12 (2027-10-13); document both majority and any minority positions in the published rule rationale

Responsible Parties

  • Independent psychometrician (hired by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, contract specifying deliverables and timeline)
  • Project lead (coordinate psychometrician engagement, board approvals, and OSF registration)
  • Editorial board (approve thresholds by Month 12 = 2027-10-13 and authorize publication)
  • External independent reviewer (critique pre-analysis plan, publish summary by Month 12 = 2027-10-13)

Assumptions

  • High: Effect sizes for ordinal error (≥25% reduction assumed), comprehension speed (≤10% slower), pronunciation consistency (≥15% above control) and 30-day retention (≥70% assumed) are achievable with 4-8 hours of Clear English exposure over 12 months; benchmark from analogous ESL or literacy interventions supports these targets.
  • High: Inter-rater reliability (kappa ≥0.70 floor, ≥0.75 target) is achievable for pronunciation consistency scoring with 3-4 raters trained on a single reference accent anchor; rater kappa below 0.70 will be detected by Month 10 (2027-08-13) dry run, allowing 1-2 month remediation without compressing Phase 2 start.
  • Medium: Validity study (N=20-30) by Month 11 (2027-09-13 to 2027-09-13) is sufficient to estimate true effect sizes and inform power analysis; pilot-study dropout and completion rates match main-phase projections; ordinal-error task format is discriminative (not at floor or ceiling).
  • Medium: Publication of thresholds and pre-analysis plan by Month 11 (2027-09-13) is sufficient to forestall post-hoc critique; stakeholders accept pre-registered metrics as credible and do not demand alternative thresholds or re-analysis strategies post-gate.
  • Medium: Psychometrician is available for hire by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and can deliver quality work on the compressed timeline (power analysis by Month 5 = 2027-03-13, validity study analysis by Month 10 = 2027-08-13); no hiring delay or psychometric expertise shortage blocks progress.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 11 (2027-09-13), deliver a pre-analysis plan with numeric, empirically justified thresholds for all four gate metrics, registered on Open Science Framework with board sign-off and third-party reviewer attestation. Measurable: plan specifies exact threshold values (e.g., ordinal error ≥25%), sample size with power analysis, and decision rules. Achievable: validity study (N=30) and inter-rater calibration (N=3-4 raters) completed by Month 10 (2027-08-13). Relevant: ensures Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate is defensible and not disputable. Time-bound: registration deadline Month 11 (2027-09-13), 5 weeks before Phase 2 start (Month 13 = 2027-11-13).

Notes

  • Timeline is compressed: validity study must run Months 10-11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) in parallel with Phase 1 rule-locking and audio production. A 2-week psychometric delay cascades into either a 2-week Phase 1 extension (~$42K, estimate) or a Phase 2 start delay.
  • If validity study reveals low effect sizes (e.g., 12% ordinal error reduction instead of 25%), sample-size requirements may increase to 120-150 per arm, raising recruitment risk and cost. Board must decide whether to adjust thresholds downward (risking perception of goalpost-moving) or increase sample size (compressing Phase 2 window).
  • Inter-rater kappa <0.70 at Month 10 (2027-08-13) triggers an automatic 4-week Phase 1 extension or scope reduction (3,000-4,000 word lexicon instead of 5,000), both violating user constraints or budget assumptions.
  • Pre-analysis plan publication is the critical credibility moment. Educators, standards bodies and regulators will scrutinize thresholds; any appearance of post-hoc tuning will reduce Phase 3 adoption by 20-30%.
  • No external benchmark exists for pronunciation consistency kappa in constructed-language contexts; the ≥0.75 target is proposed and may be unachievable for novel ordinal markers. Fallback: document the achieved kappa and note any validity implications for the pronunciation-consistency gate metric.

2. Pilot Partner Commitments and Recruitment Feasibility

Pilot recruitment failure (missing 115 per arm by Month 13 = 2027-11-13 or dropout >30%) reduces final sample to <80 per arm, cutting statistical power by 10-25% and risking false-negative gate outcomes that waste $1.2M Phase 2 spend. Signed partner commitments, baseline-study data, and early cohort-manager engagement reduce recruitment risk and provide early warning signals for course correction (by Month 10 = 2027-08-13, not Month 22 = 2028-08-13 when recovery is impossible).

Data to Collect

  • Written Memoranda of Understanding from ≥3 ESL programs and ≥2 technical/safety-training organizations specifying minimum cohort size (≥50 per partner estimate), enrollment completion date (Month 13 = 2027-11-13), assessment schedule (4 sessions, 60-90 minutes each), penalty for shortfall (e.g., $500-$1K per missing learner estimate)
  • Recruitment baseline study data (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) from pilot sites: eligible learner pool size, recruitment conversion rate (% converting to enrollment), baseline dropout rate by session, demographic retention patterns (age, language background, employment status)
  • Non-binding publisher letters of interest (≥3 ESL publishers) confirming willingness to co-develop Phase 3 curricula contingent on positive Phase 2 gate outcome
  • Interim enrollment milestones (40% enrolled by Month 8 = 2027-06-13, 70% by Month 10 = 2027-08-13, 100% by Month 13 = 2027-11-13) with weekly tracking and dropout-reason documentation
  • Contingency recruitment activation triggers (e.g., if enrollment falls >2 weeks behind schedule by Month 8 = 2027-06-13, activate bonus incentives, weekend sessions, partner marketing campaign; budget $20K-$30K estimate)

Simulation Steps

  • Conduct a small recruitment and retention pilot (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) at 2-3 candidate partner sites with 20-30 learners; measure actual recruitment (phone calls, drop-in rates, enrollment form completion); weekly attendance and dropout patterns; reasons for non-completion (work conflicts, health, moving, lost interest); estimate baseline dropout at 30-40% (vs. the proposed 30% plan assumption)
  • Use pilot baseline data to generate a probabilistic recruitment and retention model (50th, 75th, 90th percentile scenarios) for each partner; document recruitment curve (weeks to reach 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% enrollment) and expected final-cohort size across dropout scenarios
  • Model cash-flow impact if recruitment misses 115-per-arm target: project how many completers survive if enrollment is only 350-400 (vs. target 460); calculate resulting statistical power for each gate metric (expect 15-25% power reduction estimate); document whether the gate remains defensible under low-recruitment scenario
  • Design and pilot-test incentive options ($50 stipend vs. $100 vs. $150; gift cards vs. course credit vs. cash; with/without partner matching funds) with the baseline-study cohort; measure retention under each incentive and calibrate Phase 2 budget (propose $78K-$161K estimate based on 460 enrollees x 4 sessions x incentive level)
  • Use pilot baseline data to draft a Recruitment and Retention Plan (2-3 pages): enrollment timeline, weekly targets, incentive strategy, dropout-response protocol (24-hour contact + one make-up session), partner payment terms (per-learner vs. per-session vs. lump-sum)

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage ≥3 ESL program directors and ≥2 technical/safety-training managers individually by Month 1 (2026-11-13) with a written partnership proposal (1 page) specifying cohort size, schedule, incentives, and partner payment; confirm interest and capability by Month 2 (2026-12-13)
  • By Month 3 (2027-01-13), secure signed Memoranda of Understanding with explicit clauses: guaranteed learner supply, penalty for shortfalls (liquidated damages $500-$1K per missing learner, estimate), 30-day notification requirement if recruitment problems emerge, escalation contact, and indemnification for pilot use
  • Hire a dedicated Phase 2 Cohort Manager (1.0 FTE, $60K-$80K/year estimate) by Month 4 (2027-02-13) (not Month 6 = 2027-04-13) with explicit retention accountability and a 10-15% performance bonus tied to achieving ≥70% completion by Month 22 (2028-08-13); allocate $20K-$40K educator stipends and $30K-$50K contingency buffer for recruitment acceleration if enrollment lags
  • Establish a monthly Retention Dashboard (tracked by cohort manager) visible to the board by Month 4 (2027-02-13): cumulative enrollments, dropout-to-date (with reasons coded), projected final completers, and 95% confidence interval on sample size; flag to board if lower confidence bound falls below 70 per arm by Month 15 (2028-01-13)
  • Conduct a mid-recruitment audit at Month 10 (2027-08-13) with all partner sites: review enrollment progress (actual vs. 70% target), dropout trends, and any emerging retention problems; if recruitment is tracking <450 total by this date, activate contingency plan (increase incentives, launch targeted partner outreach, prepare backup recruitment sites)

Responsible Parties

  • Regulatory and Stakeholder Affairs Manager (identify and approach 4-5 ESL programs and 2-3 technical-training organizations by Month 1 = 2026-11-13; secure signed commitments by Month 3 = 2027-01-13)
  • Phase 2 Cohort Manager (hired by Month 4 = 2027-02-13; manage enrollment tracking, retention, incentives, and contingency activation Months 4-24 = 2027-02-13 to 2028-10-13)
  • Educator Liaison (co-design recruitment protocols with partner teachers, manage educator stipends, conduct quarterly practitioner check-ins)
  • Project Lead (approve partner contracts, monitor cohort-manager performance, escalate enrollment slippage to board)

Assumptions

  • High: ESL program directors and technical-training managers will commit in writing to a minimum cohort size (≥50 per partner) and will prioritize recruitment for the Clear English pilot despite competing operational demands; partners will not reduce or defer enrollment due to institutional budget constraints or competing initiatives during Months 6-13 (2027-04-13 to 2027-11-13).
  • High: Dropout tolerance of 30% is realistic for voluntary adult ESL and technical-training cohorts with incentives ($50-$150 stipends estimate); no dropout spike (e.g., >40%) due to rule complexity, assessment burden, or loss of learner motivation over 12 months; 30-day follow-up completion reaches ≥70% of those completing the main 4 sessions.
  • Medium: Recruitment baseline study (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) with 20-30 learners provides a representative sample of final-cohort characteristics and recruitment/retention patterns; short-term pilot dropout trends (2 weeks) generalize to 12-month pilot retention.
  • Medium: Cohort Manager hired by Month 4 (2027-02-13) has 3+ months to refine enrollment and retention strategies before Phase 2 start (Month 13 = 2027-11-13), sufficient to implement dropout-response protocols and contingency activation tactics without Phase 2 delay.
  • Low: Contingency budget of $30K-$50K (estimate) is sufficient to accelerate recruitment (higher incentives, additional marketing, extended recruitment window) if enrollment falls short; no recruitment scenario requires Phase 2 delay or sample-size reduction below 80 per arm.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 3 (2027-01-13), secure signed Memoranda of Understanding from ≥3 ESL programs and ≥2 technical-training organizations guaranteeing ≥50 learners per partner (≥300 total estimate) with explicit penalty clauses and enrollment deadlines. By Month 13 (2027-11-13), confirm ≥115 per arm (460 total) enrolled across all partners. Measurable: enrollment tracking dashboard shows cumulative enrollments and dropout-to-date by site and cohort. Achievable: recruitment baseline study (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) validates feasibility of 30% dropout tolerance with incentives. Relevant: ensures pilot sample size meets ≥80-per-arm power requirements. Time-bound: baseline study and MOU signing by Month 3 (2027-01-13); interim milestones Month 8, 10 (2027-06-13, 2027-08-13); enrollment completion Month 13 (2027-11-13).

Notes

  • Recruitment timeline is front-loaded: signed commitments by Month 3 (2027-01-13) but enrollment does not begin until Month 12 (2027-10-13)—a 9-month lag during which partner circumstances can change (staffing, budgets, competing initiatives). Risk: partners may withdraw or reduce enrollment targets mid-project. Mitigation: include contract renewal/confirmation clauses (e.g., partner confirms commitment by Month 9 = 2027-07-13) and establish quarterly check-ins.
  • Dropout >30% (realistic estimate is 35-45% for adult voluntary pilots) reduces final sample to <70 per arm, below the 80-per-arm target. A 40% dropout scenario with 460 enrollments yields only 276 completers (69 per arm), invalidating statistical power and forcing a 3-month Phase 2 extension ($300K, estimate) or a NO-GO gate due to insufficient data.
  • Cohort Manager hire at Month 4 (2027-02-13) is tight: 3 months to implement retention strategies before Phase 2 start (Month 13 = 2027-11-13). If this hire is delayed to Month 6 (2027-04-13), only 2 months remain for implementation, reducing effectiveness of dropout-response protocols.
  • Publisher letters of interest (non-binding) at Month 3 (2027-01-13) have no enforcement power. Publishers may withdraw or demand Phase 3 terms (e.g., equity stake, revenue-sharing) if the gate outcome is GO. Phase 3 adoption is not guaranteed by non-binding letters.
  • Contingency recruitment (bonus incentives, marketing campaign, $20K-$30K estimate) may still fall short if partner sites lack capacity. Fallback: scale Phase 2 to fewer sites (e.g., 2 ESL programs, 1 technical-training org) and accept lower total N (≥250-300 completers estimate, ~62-75 per arm), compressing statistical power and increasing gate-decision risk.

3. Editorial Board Governance and Rule Specification Consensus

Rule ambiguity, deadlock or mid-pilot changes invalidate pilot assessment results (learners trained on conflicting rule versions, inter-rater scoring of pronunciation is inconsistent). Explicit governance (voting procedures, arbiter mechanism, decision logging) enables rapid dispute resolution (target <4 weeks per dispute) and locks rules by Month 12 (2027-10-13) so pilots begin with stable, published rules. Public comment and transparent rule rationale build educator and standards-body confidence in legitimacy.

Data to Collect

  • Published Editorial Board Charter (2-3 pages) specifying voting procedures (simple majority, quorum ≥6 of 9 members), tiebreak arbiter mechanism (external neutral, cost cap $10K-$20K estimate, decision timeline 2 weeks), conflict-of-interest disclosure rules, and term limits (recommended 2-year renewable, max 3 consecutive)
  • Signed agreement with external tiebreak arbiter confirming role, fee schedule, conflict-of-interest attestation, and availability Months 1-12 (2026-11-13 to 2027-10-13)
  • Rule-specification drafts and board-approved final rules for: Ordinal Marker Architecture (symbol and spoken form locked by Month 10 = 2027-08-13), Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth (overlay vs. respelling decision with rationale), Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold (frequency cutoff and % of forms changed), Homograph Disambiguation Policy (mandatory marker scope and list), and Reference Accent Anchor (choice and mapping documentation)
  • Published decision log documenting all contested rules, majority and minority positions, arbiter rulings (if any), and rationale for each rule choice; dispute resolution timeline (no dispute >4 weeks unresolved)
  • Draft standard for public 30-day comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) with rule rationale, examples, and response procedure; published comments and project responses by Month 12 (2027-10-13); rule-freeze notice confirming no rule changes after Month 12 (2027-10-13)

Simulation Steps

  • Convene a board kickoff meeting (Month 2 = 2026-12-13) to review the Editorial Board Charter, confirm voting procedures, assign rule-specification workstreams (ordinal, morphology, homograph, accent) to board subcommittees with clear owners (1 lead, 1 support per workstream), and establish monthly subcommittee check-ins
  • Simulate a contested rule decision (e.g., morphology: retain go/went vs. regularize to go/goed) using the voting procedure: draft two rule options with written justification for each, distribute to board 1 week in advance, hold a 90-minute discussion, record voting (3 votes for Option A, 2 votes abstaining, 4 votes for Option B = Option B wins 4-3), and document minority position in decision log
  • Conduct inter-rater reliability check: distribute rule drafts to 2-3 independent applied linguists (external to project) and ask them to score rule clarity (1-5 scale) and ambiguity (any terms needing definition?); average clarity score ≥3.5 (proposed threshold) indicates rule is not internally contradictory; <3.5 triggers revision or board discussion
  • Model timeline pressure: project what happens if a rule dispute (e.g., homograph marker scope: mandatory list of 30 pairs vs. 100 pairs) remains unresolved by Month 9 (2027-07-13) and requires arbiter ruling at Month 10 (2027-08-13), leaving only 2 weeks for rule revision before the public comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13); document the compressed timeline and contingency if the draft standard goes to comment with an unresolved position
  • Prepare a public comment response protocol: identify the expected commenter categories (educators, publishers, standards bodies, ESL learners), draft 3-5 likely objection topics (e.g., 'ordinal markers are unpronounceable', 'morphology regularization confuses learners'), and write model responses documenting how the project addresses each objection while maintaining rule integrity

Expert Validation Steps

  • Publish the Editorial Board Charter on the project website by Month 1 (2026-11-13) and hold the first board meeting by Month 2 (2026-12-13) with all 7-9 members present (in-person or virtual); confirm each member's role, workstream assignment, and understanding of voting procedures
  • Identify and formally approach an external tiebreak arbiter (e.g., senior linguist or standards-development expert from a university or ISO body) by Month 3 (2027-01-13); secure written agreement specifying fee cap ($10K-$20K estimate, estimate), decision timeline (2 weeks from dispute referral), and conflict-of-interest statement by Month 5 (2027-03-13)
  • By Month 10 (2027-08-13), have each rule-specification workstream deliver draft rules with written rationale (1-2 pages per rule) and a list of any contested alternatives; circulate drafts to the full board 1 week before a voting meeting; conduct a 3-hour board session to vote on each rule (record votes and any minority positions)
  • Publish a Decision Log (1-2 pages) by Month 10 (2027-08-13 end) documenting: rule title, voting outcome (e.g., 'Option A 5 votes, Option B 2 votes, abstain 2'), arbiter ruling (if invoked), rationale for chosen rule, and minority position (if any objection >2 votes). Publish this log on the project website by Month 10 (2027-08-13 end)
  • Convene board review of the draft standard by Month 11 (2027-09-13 start); confirm all rules are finalized and rule text is internally consistent (no cross-references to undefined terms); publish draft standard for 30-day comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13 through Month 11.5 ≈ 2027-09-28) with a published schedule for comment response and rule-freeze notification (Month 12 = 2027-10-13)

Responsible Parties

  • Editorial Board Chair (convene meetings, enforce voting procedures, escalate disputes to arbiter)
  • Governance Administrator (document decisions, maintain decision log, publish board charter and minutes)
  • External Tiebreak Arbiter (decide tied votes within 2-week timeline, issue written ruling with rationale)
  • Rule-Specification Workstream Leads (one lead per rule domain: ordinal, morphology, homograph, accent; deliver draft rules by Month 10 = 2027-08-13)

Assumptions

  • Medium: Editorial board members (7-9 appointed by project lead, mix of practitioners and linguists) are available for monthly meetings and can reach consensus on major rules through voting and arbiter escalation; no member resignation or unexpected absence disrupts voting quorum (≥6 of 9) through Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • Medium: A qualified external tiebreak arbiter (linguist or standards-development expert) is available for hire by Month 3 (2027-01-13) at $10K-$20K (estimate) per project and can issue rulings within 2 weeks; no arbiter delays or scheduling conflicts block decision timelines.
  • High: Rule disputes (e.g., morphology threshold, homograph marker scope) can be resolved through voting or arbiter ruling by Month 10 (2027-08-13); no rule is so contentious that neither board consensus nor arbiter ruling is acceptable to stakeholders; disputed rules do not fragment into multiple unofficial variants during pilots.
  • Medium: 30-day public comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) surface any major rule objections (e.g., 'ordinal markers are ambiguous for ESL learners'); project team can address objections through clarification or minor rule adjustment without requiring full re-vote or redesign; no showstopper objection requires pushing rule-freeze past Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • High: Frozen rules at Month 12 (2027-10-13) remain stable through Month 24 (2028-10-13) pilots; no mid-pilot rule change (e.g., due to learner confusion or pilot-site feedback) is approved; all rule clarifications are issued as published errata (not changes) and are applied uniformly across all pilot sites.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 1 (2026-11-13), publish Editorial Board Charter. By Month 2 (2026-12-13), hold first board meeting with all 7-9 members; assign rule-specification workstreams. By Month 10 (2027-08-13), finalize all five rule specifications (ordinal, G2P, morphology, homograph, accent) and publish a decision log documenting voting outcomes and minority positions. By Month 11 (2027-09-13), publish draft standard for 30-day public comment. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), lock all rules, close comment window, and issue rule-freeze notice. Measurable: decision log shows <4-week dispute resolution (voting or arbiter), 100% rule clarity score ≥3.5 from independent linguists. Achievable: board members meet monthly, arbiter available by Month 5 (2027-03-13). Relevant: stable rules by Month 12 (2027-10-13) enable consistent pilot protocol application. Time-bound: rule-freeze Month 12 (2027-10-13), 30 days before Phase 2 start (Month 13 = 2027-11-13).

Notes

  • Rule workstreams are on the critical path. A 4-week rule-specification delay (e.g., morphology threshold takes longer to reach consensus) compresses the public comment window and rule-freeze timeline, forcing either abbreviated comment feedback or a 2-week Phase 1 extension (~$42K estimate).
  • Contested rules (e.g., 'ordinal markers should be silent vs. pronounced') may deadlock the board if arbiter is not selected or empowered early. Failure to lock arbiter by Month 5 (2027-03-13) leaves only 5 months (Month 5-10 = 2027-03-13 to 2027-08-13) to resolve disputes; a 3-week arbiter engagement timeline for a single decision consumes 13% of that window.
  • 30-day public comment period (Month 11 = 2027-09-13 through Month 11.5 ≈ 2027-09-28) is tight: 2 weeks to collect comments, 2 weeks to draft responses and approve rule adjustments. If major objections emerge (e.g., 'homograph markers create ambiguity in safety documents'), rule revision may require board re-vote and slip the Month 12 (2027-10-13) freeze.
  • Public comments may reveal rule ambiguities that internal board review missed. Example: if educators complain that the ordinal marker's spoken form is unclear, the project may need to clarify or revise by Month 12 (2027-10-13), consuming rework budget and time.
  • Rule-freeze at Month 12 (2027-10-13) is absolute: no changes during Phase 2 pilots (Months 13-24 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13). If pilot sites request rule clarifications or learners struggle with a rule, the response must be published errata (clarification only, not rule change) or a scheduled v1.1 (post-Phase 2). Pilot fidelity depends on this commitment.

4. Audio Production, Inter-Rater Calibration, and Pronunciation Consistency Measurement

Pronunciation consistency is a primary gate metric (kappa ≥0.70 floor, ≥0.75 target proposed). Weak inter-rater reliability (kappa <0.70) inflates measurement error by 20-30%, reducing statistical power to detect Clear English effects and risking false-negative gate outcomes that waste Phase 2 investment and kill the project. Audio production bottleneck: if recording is delayed or rater calibration fails, the Phase 1 exit gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-13) is missed and Phase 2 is compressed. Pronunciation guidance (the overlay on print) is a core deliverable: without usable audio, the overlay cannot be taught or assessed.

Data to Collect

  • 5,000-word core lexicon with 2-4 pronunciation recordings per entry (10,000-20,000 audio files, estimate) recorded in the selected reference accent (chosen and justified by Month 3 = 2027-01-13); inter-rater reliability scores (Cohen's kappa, target ≥0.75 proposed, floor ≥0.70 proposed) for each entry based on ≥2 independent raters scoring pronunciation accuracy against anchor
  • Rater-training protocol and manual (2-3 pages) specifying: reference accent anchor phonemic inventory, key vowel and consonant contrasts, diacritical notation (IPA, respelling key, or hybrid), worked examples (20-30 words with correct and incorrect pronunciations), and inter-rater calibration procedure (blind scoring of pilot sample, calculation of pairwise kappa, consensus resolution for disagreements)
  • Inter-rater calibration results (Month 10 = 2027-08-13) from a 100-200 word pilot sample: Cohen's kappa pairwise (3-4 raters rating each word independently, blind to condition and learner ID); if kappa ≥0.70, proceed to full 5,000-word production; if <0.70, document retraining plan and retest timeline (target Month 10.5 ≈ 2027-08-28)
  • Encrypted audio storage infrastructure (on-premises or cloud, AES-256 encryption estimate) with backup protocols, access-control logs, and data-retention schedule (audio retained 3 years post-analysis unless learner requests deletion)
  • Pronunciation-consistency scoring rubric and decision protocol (1-2 pages) used in Phase 2 pilots: how many raters score each learner's audio? How are disagreements resolved? What is the final score (average kappa per learner, or binary match/mismatch count)? Is the score comparable across learner cohorts and pronunciation-consistency gate metric calculation?

Simulation Steps

  • Scope audio production by Month 2 (2026-12-13): solicit firm quotes from 2-3 professional recording studios for 5,000 entries, 2 takes per entry, within 4-week lead time; confirm per-entry cost and total budget ($80K-$120K estimate); if cost exceeds $20 per entry ($100K total), pivot to a hybrid approach: synthesized-speech baseline (TTS) for all 5,000 by Month 7 (2027-05-13) plus human-rater verification of the highest-friction subset (1,000-1,500 words, ~300 entries x 2 takes = 600 files, cost $12K-$20K estimate, by Month 11 = 2027-09-13)
  • Recruit 4-6 candidate raters with ESL or phonetics background (e.g., ESL instructors, speech pathologists, linguists); conduct a 50-word pre-screening by Month 4 (2027-02-13) to identify the top 3-4 candidates; select candidates who score kappa ≥0.75 pairwise on the screening sample
  • Conduct rater training (2-3 sessions, 6-8 hours total estimate, Month 8-9 = 2027-06-13 to 2027-07-13) on the reference accent anchor, scoring rubric, and worked examples; have raters independently score a 100-200 word pilot sample (blind to condition and learner ID) by Month 9 (2027-07-13) end
  • Calculate Cohen's kappa (pairwise, all rater pairs; also multi-rater consensus kappa if using 3+ raters) by Month 10 (2027-08-13 start); if kappa ≥0.70 for all pairwise comparisons, approve full production start; if any pairwise kappa <0.70, identify which rater(s) or which word types (vowels, consonants, schwa) are problematic and conduct targeted retraining by Month 10 (2027-08-13) mid-month; retest kappa by Month 10 (2027-08-13) end
  • Model statistical power of the pronunciation-consistency gate metric under alternative kappa scenarios: if raters achieve kappa 0.75, measurement error is ~12% (estimate); if kappa 0.65, measurement error inflates to ~20% (estimate), reducing power by ~10-15%; document this relationship in the pre-analysis plan (Month 9 = 2027-07-13) so the board understands kappa's impact on gate credibility

Expert Validation Steps

  • Contract with a professional audio recording studio by Month 2 (2026-12-13) with firm pricing, capacity guarantee (5,000 files within 4 weeks from lexicon delivery), backup procedures, and file-format specification (MP3, WAV, metadata tags); identify a contingency studio by Month 3 (2027-01-13) in case primary vendor has capacity shortfall
  • Commission reference-accent anchor documentation (2-3 pages) from a phonetics specialist by Month 2 (2026-12-13), delivered by Month 3 (2027-01-13): phonemic inventory, key vowel (e.g., /ɪ/ vs. /ɛ/, LOT vs. THOUGHT merger status) and consonant contrasts (e.g., /l/ vs. /r/, aspirated vs. unaspirated stops), stress and intonation patterns, and 30-50 exemplar recordings in the chosen accent. Publish this specification on the project website by Month 4 (2027-02-13) for transparency and rater reference
  • By Month 8 (2027-06-13), have raters complete formal training on the reference accent and scoring rubric; issue a rater-training completion certificate and a signed data-use agreement specifying confidentiality and inter-rater reliability targets
  • Conduct the 100-200 word inter-rater calibration pilot (Month 9 = 2027-07-13) with ≥3 of the 4 selected raters; calculate Cohen's kappa for all pairwise combinations (expected: kappa 0.70-0.80 if raters are well-trained and anchor is clear); publish kappa results and rater-pair breakdowns by Month 10 (2027-08-13 start) to identify any outlier raters
  • If kappa ≥0.70 across all raters by Month 10 (2027-08-13 mid), approve full 5,000-word production start by Month 10 (2027-08-13 end) with a completion target of Month 11 (2027-09-13 end); if kappa <0.70, convene an emergency board meeting within 5 days to decide: (a) re-train low-performing raters for 2 weeks with retest by Month 10.5 (2027-08-28), (b) switch to hybrid synthetic + verification model by Month 11 (2027-09-13), or (c) extend Phase 1 by 4 weeks (~$85K, estimate) for additional rater training and kappa recovery

Responsible Parties

  • Audio Production and Technical Infrastructure Manager (contract studio, manage recording schedule and file delivery, oversee encrypted storage; hired by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, contract through Month 11 = 2027-09-13)
