  • Phonetics Specialist or Applied Linguist (design reference-accent anchor specification, deliver by Month 3 = 2027-01-13; develop rater-training manual and scoring rubric, finalize by Month 7 = 2027-05-13)
  • Rater-Training Coordinator (recruit 4-6 candidate raters, conduct training Months 8-9 = 2027-06-13 to 2027-07-13, administer kappa calibration study, document results by Month 10 = 2027-08-13)
  • Psychometrician (advise on measurement reliability targets, review kappa results, model statistical power implications for the pronunciation-consistency gate metric)

Assumptions

  • Medium: A professional audio recording studio is available with firm capacity (5,000 files, 2 takes each) and can deliver within 4 weeks of lexicon hand-off by Month 7 (2027-05-13); per-entry cost is predictable ($15-$25, estimate) and within the $80K-$120K Phase 1 budget envelope. If studio availability is limited or cost escalates, switching to a hybrid synthetic-baseline approach (TTS for all 5,000, human verification of subset) is feasible by Month 7 (2027-05-13) without major timeline impact.
  • Medium: 4-6 candidate raters with ESL or phonetics background are available for hire (part-time or contract) by Month 4 (2027-02-13) at a total cost <$40K (estimate); raters can be trained to Cohen's kappa ≥0.70 on the reference-accent anchor within 2-3 training sessions (6-8 hours total). Rater availability is not a bottleneck (raters do not leave, do not request higher pay mid-project).
  • High: Reference-accent anchor (chosen by Month 3 = 2027-01-13) is sufficiently defined (phonemic inventory, key contrasts, exemplar recordings) that raters can be trained and achieve kappa ≥0.70 in a 100-200 word pilot by Month 10 (2027-08-13); no need for accent redesign or clarification mid-training.
  • High: Inter-rater kappa ≥0.70 (floor) is achievable for pronunciation scoring in a constructed-language context (no published benchmark exists); raters can reliably discriminate Clear English pronunciations from standard English despite the novel ordinal marker and potential learner variation. If kappa <0.70, retraining by Month 10 (2027-08-13) or hybrid synthesis approach recovers measurement reliability by Month 11 (2027-09-13) without compressing Phase 2 timeline.
  • Low: Encrypted audio storage infrastructure (on-premises or cloud, AES-256) is deployed by Month 6 (2027-04-13) and passes a GDPR/data-protection audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13); no data breach, file corruption, or access-control failure occurs during storage and retrieval (Months 6-24 = 2027-04-13 to 2028-10-13). Audio files are retained 3 years post-analysis and deleted on schedule or on learner request without compromising inter-rater reliability calculations (i.e., deletion does not occur until after scoring is complete).

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 3 (2027-01-13), finalize reference-accent anchor specification with exemplar recordings. By Month 4 (2027-02-13), recruit and begin training 4-6 candidate raters. By Month 10 (2027-08-13), measure inter-rater Cohen's kappa on a 100-200 word pilot sample and confirm kappa ≥0.70 across all raters. By Month 11 (2027-09-13), complete full 5,000-word audio production (either human-recorded or synthetic baseline + verification). Measurable: kappa ≥0.70 documented for each rater pair; all 5,000 lexicon entries have 2+ usable pronunciation audio files; encrypted storage deployed and audit-passed. Achievable: studio capacity confirmed by Month 2 (2026-12-13); rater training timeline 2-3 months (Months 8-10 = 2027-06-13 to 2027-08-13). Relevant: pronunciation guidance is a core project deliverable; audio reliability (kappa) determines gate-metric credibility. Time-bound: kappa confirmed by Month 10 (2027-08-13), 2 months before Phase 2 start (Month 13 = 2027-11-13), allowing 1-month remediation window if kappa <0.70.

Notes

  • Audio production is a single point of failure: a 4-week studio delay (common in professional recording) compresses inter-rater training from 3 months to 2, reducing time for rater calibration and increasing risk of kappa <0.70. Mitigation: lock studio contract with firm timeline and penalty clauses by Month 2 (2026-12-13); identify a backup studio by Month 3 (2027-01-13).
  • Inter-rater kappa <0.70 at Month 10 (2027-08-13) triggers the only pre-gate contingency that is automatic: a 4-week Phase 1 extension (~$85K, estimate) for rater retraining and recalibration. A second kappa failure (still <0.70 at Month 10.5 ≈ 2027-08-28) forces a board decision to either extend Phase 1 further (cost $42K per week, estimate) or switch to hybrid synthesis approach. This consumes the $175K pre-gate reserve cap very quickly.
  • Pronunciation-consistency score reliability (kappa) is a gate metric prerequisite, not a pass/fail gate metric itself. However, if kappa is discovered to be <0.70 during Phase 2 pilot analysis (Month 18-20 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-06-13), the pronunciation-consistency gate metric becomes uninterpretable, and the gate decision may be ruled inconclusive or must be downgraded from a primary to a secondary outcome, weakening the go/no-go evidence.
  • Hybrid model fallback (synthetic TTS baseline + human verification of highest-friction 1,000-1,500 words) reduces per-entry cost to ~$10-$15 (estimate) but requires a different pronunciation-consistency measurement approach: learners are scored only on the verified subset (not all 5,000), reducing comprehensiveness of the measurement. The gate metric may need to be reframed as 'pronunciation consistency on highest-friction words' rather than 'general pronunciation consistency.'
  • Audio storage is sensitive to GDPR/data-protection compliance. If the chosen storage vendor fails a compliance audit or learners request deletion during pilots, the inter-rater reliability sample may shrink below N=100, and kappa estimates become unstable. Mitigation: audit storage by Month 8 (2027-06-13) and conduct a deletion protocol test (delete 5-10 learner audio files and confirm that kappa can be recalculated on remaining files without major instability) by Month 20 (2028-06-13).

5. Licensing, Name Stewardship, and Post-v1.0 Governance Sustainability

Post-Month-36 (2029-10-13) stewardship is unfunded ($150K-$250K/year estimate) and no permanent steward is committed yet. Without stewardship, the standard will atrophy: change requests accumulate unanswered, errata go unfixed, adopter confidence erodes, and Phase 3 adoption collapses by 30-50% within 24 months (by Month 60 = 2031-10-13). Licensing terms (permissive vs. certification-mark) determine whether third-party materials are clearly flagged as conforming or non-conforming, affecting fragmentation risk. Early steward search (by Month 18 = 2028-04-13) and binding commitment (by Month 33 = 2029-07-13) ensure v1.0 is not released without a sustainable governance plan. Public clarity on licensing and stewardship builds adopter confidence that the standard will be maintained long-term.

Data to Collect

  • Published Licensing and Name Stewardship Policy (2-3 pages) chosen from three options: (a) fully permissive open license with no name restrictions; (b) open text/dictionary with 'Clear English' as a certification mark against a published conformance checklist; (c) share-alike license requiring divergent forks to adopt distinct names. Decision and rationale published by Month 6 (2027-04-13)
  • Public conformance checklist (1-2 pages, if certification-mark model chosen) specifying exactly what a third-party material must do to qualify as 'Clear English'-compliant (e.g., 'use ≥95% of core ordinal rule with <5% exceptions'; 'no homograph markers outside the published list of 50 pairs'). Light-touch criteria to reduce gatekeeper perception but sufficient to prevent non-conforming materials from claiming the name
  • Stewardship Proposal (2-3 pages) to potential permanent steward organizations (language non-profits, university consortiums, standards bodies) specifying: annual budget ($150K-$250K estimate), key responsibilities (respond to change requests, maintain conformance registry, issue errata, lead 3-5 year reviews), decision authority (annual Stewardship Committee meetings), and 10+ year commitment timeline. Delivered to 2-3 candidates by Month 24 (2028-10-13)
  • Signed Memorandum of Understanding with at least one committed steward organization by Month 33 (2029-07-13), specifying funding source (endowment, membership fees, organizational budget, grant funding), governance committee composition, annual review schedule, and escalation procedure for rule-interpretation disputes
  • 5-year Stewardship Roadmap (2-3 pages) published with v1.0 release (Month 30 = 2029-04-13), documenting: annual maintenance calendar, change-request prioritization criteria, 3-5 year full-review trigger (e.g., 'every 4 years the Stewardship Committee will solicit community feedback on rule clarity and feasibility'), dispute-resolution procedure, and funding contingency if steward organization faces budget cuts

Simulation Steps

  • Commission a legal analysis (40-60 hours, $5K-$10K estimate, Month 1 = 2026-11-13) comparing the three licensing scenarios on adoption friction (ease for publishers), fragmentation risk (likelihood of non-conforming variants), governance overhead (cost to manage certification or dispute resolution), and perceived fairness (stakeholder perception of gatekeeping). Deliver by Month 3 (2027-01-13)
  • Model scenario: if a publisher releases a 'Clear English-inspired' curriculum that respells 30% of words (vs. the 0% respelling in the official standard), is that a 'Clear English' product or a distinct variant? Under each licensing model, what happens? (a) Permissive: publisher labels it 'Clear English' freely; no enforcement. (b) Certification mark: publisher is blocked from using the name without conformance; must relabel as 'Modified Clear English' or 'MyClear'. (c) Share-alike: publisher must disclose the divergence and adopt a distinct name. Simulate the business outcome (which model encourages adoption, which discourages fragmentation) under each scenario
  • Identify 2-3 potential steward candidates by Month 6 (2027-04-13): research language-education non-profits (e.g., ITA, regional ESL organizations), university consortiums (TESOL-affiliated, linguistics departments), and standards bodies (CEFR governance, ISO language committees). Document their 3+ year financial track record, prior standards-maintenance experience, and alignment with the 'adoption-first, evidence-gated' mission. Prepare candidate summary sheets by Month 12 (2027-10-13)
  • Draft a Stewardship Proposal template (2-3 pages) specifying annual budget breakdown: staff (1 FTE coordinator, 0.5 FTE administrative support), meetings (2-3 in-person Stewardship Committee meetings/year), tools (website hosting, conformance registry, communication platform), and contingency reserve (10% buffer for unexpected issues). Total ~$150K-$250K/year (estimate). Model different funding models (endowment @ 6% annual yield, membership fees @ 100 institutions x $1.5K/year, organizational budget, government grant). Document pros/cons of each funding model
  • Publish a draft 5-year Stewardship Roadmap (2-3 pages) by Month 24 (2028-10-13): outline annual maintenance tasks (Q1: collect change requests; Q2: triage and prioritize; Q3: draft rule amendments or errata; Q4: publish annual update), 3-5 year full review trigger, criteria for dismissing vs. approving change requests, and escalation procedure for disputes over interpretation

Expert Validation Steps

  • Commission a lawyer specializing in intellectual property and language standards (separate from product-liability counsel) by Month 2 (2026-12-13) to draft the three licensing scenarios with comparison matrix (adoption friction, enforcement cost, fragmentation risk, fairness perception). Deliver by Month 4 (2027-02-13)
  • Present the three scenarios to the editorial board by Month 5 (2027-03-13) and hold a board vote to select the preferred model by Month 6 (2027-04-13). Document the voting outcome and rationale for the chosen model in the decision log (maintained by Governance Administrator)
  • If certification-mark model is chosen, engage a trademark attorney to draft the conformance checklist and certification procedures (e.g., how a publisher applies for a conformance review, what the criteria are, appeal procedure if a conformance claim is rejected). Publish the checklist on the project website by Month 12 (2027-10-13) for stakeholder feedback before v1.0 release
  • Establish a standing Standards Stewardship Committee (3-5 board members, 2-4 hours/month, initiated by Month 12 = 2027-10-13) with explicit authority to: review third-party conformance claims (if applicable); maintain a public registry of approved/certified materials and documented variants; issue guidance on non-conforming forks; recommend annual maintenance tasks and budget to the steward organization. Publish Stewardship Committee charter on the project website
  • By Month 18 (2028-04-13), approach 2-3 steward candidates with a non-binding request for interest (2-page RFI); request a written letter of interest outlining their capacity and funding model by Month 24 (2028-10-13). By Month 27 (2029-01-13), initiate formal Stewardship Proposal negotiation with top 1-2 candidates; target a signed MOU by Month 33 (2029-07-13). Publish the name and commitments of the chosen steward on the project website with v1.0 release (Month 30 = 2029-04-13)

Responsible Parties

  • Regulatory and Stakeholder Affairs Manager (identify steward candidates, approach with RFI by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, negotiate MOU by Month 33 = 2029-07-13)
  • Legal counsel (draft three licensing scenarios and comparison analysis by Month 4 = 2027-02-13; if certification mark chosen, draft conformance checklist and procedures by Month 10 = 2027-08-13)
  • Editorial Board (vote on licensing model by Month 6 = 2027-04-13; establish Stewardship Committee by Month 12 = 2027-10-13)
  • Governance Administrator (publish licensing policy, conformance checklist, and Stewardship Roadmap on project website by Month 12 = 2027-10-13 and Months 30-36 = 2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13)

Assumptions

  • High: A qualified steward organization (language non-profit, university consortium, or standards body) exists with sufficient financial capacity ($150K-$250K/year) and institutional stability (10+ year commitment horizon) to assume stewardship post-Phase-3; steward is available for negotiation and MOU signature by Month 33 (2029-07-13), before v1.0 release (Month 30 = 2029-04-13). If no steward commits by Month 33 (2029-07-13), v1.0 release is delayed or conditional on securing stewardship funding within 6 months.
  • High: The chosen licensing model (permissive, certification-mark, or share-alike) is accepted by ESL publishers, technical writers and educators as fair and not excessively gatekeeping; third-party adopters do not perceive the model as an obstacle to adoption. If the certification-mark model is seen as overly restrictive, publishers and educators may refuse to adopt and create a competing 'free' variant.
  • High: Steward funding is secured from non-project sources (endowment yield, member fees, organizational budget, government grant) and does not depend on license revenues (which are zero under an open-license model). Annual stewardship cost ($150K-$250K estimate) is not a project expense post-Phase-3 but is the steward's responsibility. If steward funding is insufficient or dries up, the standard reverts to maintenance-free or abandoned status.
  • Medium: The Stewardship Committee (3-5 board members, 2-4 hours/month) is empowered to make decisions on rule interpretation, conformance disputes and annual maintenance without requiring full editorial board approval, reducing decision friction post-v1.0. The steward organization has clear escalation and decision authority documented in the MOU.
  • High: v1.0 is not released (Month 30 = 2029-04-13) without a signed stewardship MOU in hand. If stewardship is uncertain at Month 30 (2029-04-13), release is postponed to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or later until stewardship is secured. This constraint ensures the standard is not published as 'orphaned' or unmaintained.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-13), publish Licensing and Name Stewardship Policy and hold a board vote to select the final model. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), publish conformance checklist (if certification-mark model) on project website. By Month 18 (2028-04-13), approach 2-3 steward candidates with RFI and request letters of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13). By Month 33 (2029-07-13), secure a signed MOU with a committed steward specifying funding source, annual budget ($150K-$250K), governance structure, and 10+ year commitment. By Month 30 (2029-04-13), publish v1.0 only with stewardship MOU in hand and published Stewardship Roadmap. Measurable: licensing policy and conformance checklist published; steward identity and MOU commitments published with v1.0. Achievable: 3-month legal analysis (Months 1-3 = 2026-11-13 to 2027-01-13); 6-month steward identification and RFI (Months 12-18 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13); 6-month MOU negotiation (Months 27-33 = 2029-01-13 to 2029-07-13). Relevant: stewardship is a prerequisite for v1.0 credibility; permanent funding ensures long-term standards maintenance and adopter confidence. Time-bound: stewardship MOU signed before v1.0 release (Month 33 = 2029-07-13 before Month 30 = 2029-04-13 is impossible, so MOU must be negotiated and signed by Month 30 = 2029-04-13, shifting RFI/interest solicitation earlier to Months 12-15 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-01-13).

Notes

  • Stewardship is the most critical post-project contingency risk: without it, the standard atrophies by Month 60 (2031-10-13), killing Phase 3 adoption. Early identification (Months 12-18 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-04-13) and negotiation (Months 27-33 = 2029-01-13 to 2029-07-13) are essential to avoid a rushed, weak commitment at the last minute.
  • Licensing model choice (permissive vs. certification-mark vs. share-alike) is a high-stakes governance decision. Permissive (no name control) maximizes adoption but risks fragmentation and confusion. Certification-mark adds administrative overhead but protects quality and clarity. Share-alike preserves openness but may deter commercial publishers. The board must weigh adoption-velocity (favors permissive) against long-term integrity (favors certification or share-alike) by Month 6 (2027-04-13).
  • Steward identification by Month 18 (2028-04-13) is tight but necessary to allow 6+ months for negotiation before v1.0 release (Month 30 = 2029-04-13). If steward identification slips to Month 21 (2028-07-13), only 3 months remain for MOU negotiation, forcing either a rushed, weak agreement or a v1.0 release delay to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or beyond.
  • Stewardship funding ($150K-$250K/year, estimate) is not funded by the $3.5M project budget. The project must identify external funding sources (endowment, member dues, organizational budget from steward, government grants) by Month 30 (2029-04-13). If steward is unable to secure funding, v1.0 is orphaned and adoption confidence collapses.
  • Conformance checklist (if certification-mark model chosen) must be 'light-touch' (1-2 pages, simple yes/no criteria) to avoid gatekeeping perception that deters adoption. Example: 'Use ≥95% of core rules with no more than 5% exceptions' is light. 'Submit materials for independent audit and approval' is heavy and deters adoption. The balance must be struck by Month 12 (2027-10-13).

Summary

Clear English is a 36-month, $3.5M language-standardization initiative (three gated phases) aimed at adult ESL, technical writing and safety-critical documentation. This data-collection and validation plan identifies the five most critical data domains: (1) Gate Metrics Pre-Registration (highest risk: weak thresholds render the Month 24 = 2028-10-13 go/no-go disputable; mitigation: hire independent psychometrician by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, deliver power analysis by Month 5 = 2027-03-13, pre-register by Month 11 = 2027-09-13); (2) Pilot Partner Commitments and Recruitment (highest risk: sample-size shortfall <80 per arm invalidates statistical power; mitigation: conduct recruitment baseline study Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13, secure signed MOUs by Month 3 = 2027-01-13, hire cohort manager by Month 4 = 2027-02-13); (3) Editorial Board Governance and Rule Specification (highest risk: rule deadlock or ambiguity delays Phase 2 or invalidates pilots; mitigation: publish charter by Month 1 = 2026-11-13, hold first meeting Month 2 = 2026-12-13, resolve disputes via external arbiter by Month 10 = 2027-08-13, freeze rules by Month 12 = 2027-10-13); (4) Audio Production and Inter-Rater Calibration (highest risk: kappa <0.70 at Month 10 = 2027-08-13 forces 4-week extension or scope reduction; mitigation: lock studio contract by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, recruit raters by Month 4 = 2027-02-13, conduct kappa calibration by Month 10 = 2027-08-13, pivot to hybrid synthesis if needed); (5) Licensing and Post-v1.0 Stewardship (highest risk: unfunded stewardship post-Month-36 causes standard atrophy within 24 months, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 30-50%; mitigation: publish licensing policy by Month 6 = 2027-04-13, identify steward candidates by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, secure signed MOU by Month 33 = 2029-07-13, make stewardship a v1.0 release prerequisite). Each domain specifies simulation steps (tools, pilot testing, cost modeling), expert-validation steps (independent review, pre-registration, board approval), SMART objectives (measurable, time-bound deliverables), and critical assumptions with sensitivity scores. The validation plan ensures the project meets its 'adoption-first, evidence-gated' positioning by locking gate thresholds early (pre-registered by Month 11 = 2027-09-13), recruiting defensible pilot samples on schedule, resolving governance ambiguity before rule-locking, and securing stewardship before v1.0 release. Key uncertainties flagged: pronunciation consistency kappa achievability in a constructed-language context (no published benchmark), steward-organization availability at $150K-$250K/year (unfunded gap post-project), and educator/standards-body acceptance of the adopted licensing and governance model. Immediate actionable tasks: (1) hire independent psychometrician by Month 2 (2026-12-13); (2) identify and approach 4-5 ESL programs and 2-3 technical organizations by Month 1 (2026-11-13); (3) publish Editorial Board Charter and hold first meeting by Month 2 (2026-12-13); (4) lock studio contract and recruit 4-6 raters by Month 4 (2027-02-13); (5) identify steward candidates and begin preliminary outreach by Month 12 (2027-10-13).

Description: Foundational project governance document specifying the Clear English Standard program scope (36-month, 3-phase, $3.5M fixed budget), go/no-go gate at Month 24 (2028-10-13), primary deliverables (v1.0 standard, dictionary, style guide, pilot curriculum), stakeholder roles, success criteria, and approval authorities. Intended audience: editorial board, funding bodies, institutional partners.

Responsible Role Type: Project Manager / Program Director

Primary Template: PMI Project Charter Template

Secondary Template: PRINCE2 Project Initiation Document

Steps to Create:

  • Draft scope statement covering ordinal standardization, 5,000-word lexicon, pronunciation guidance, pilot evidence and public release
  • Specify the three phases (rules, pilots, adoption) with exit gates and budget allocation
  • Define success metrics (go/no-go thresholds for ordinal error, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention)
  • Identify primary stakeholders (project lead, editorial board, psychometrician, pilot partners, steward candidates)
  • Establish decision authority (editorial board for rules; project lead for timeline/budget)
  • Obtain signatures from program sponsor and editorial board chair by Month 1 (2026-11-13)

Approval Authorities: Program Sponsor, Editorial Board Chair, Project Lead

Essential Information:

  • Specify the Clear English Standard program scope: a 36-month, 3-phase, $3.5M (user constraint) gated initiative to design, pilot and publicly release a parallel English variant with regularized ordinals, spelling-to-sound guidance and capped morphology changes, targeted at adult ESL, technical writing and safety-critical glossary use, with no mandates or K-12 replacement.
  • Define the three phases and exit gates: Phase 1 (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13) delivers rules, reference corpus, 5,000-word core lexicon and pre-registered metrics; Phase 2 (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13) conducts pilots with a binary go/no-go decision at Month 24 (2028-10-13) on four pre-registered gate metrics; Phase 3 (Months 24–36 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-10-13) releases v1.0 and supports limited adoption.
  • Articulate the four pre-registered go/no-go gate metrics and their thresholds (all proposed thresholds): ordinal error rate ≥25% relative reduction vs. standard-English control; comprehension speed ≤10% slower than control; pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control with kappa ≥0.70 reliability floor; 30-day retention ≥70% of immediate post-test performance; also ≥80 completers per arm (estimate) to power analysis.
  • Identify success criteria beyond the gate: ≥3 licensed third-party adopters (at least 1 ESL publisher) by Month 36 (2029-10-13) (proposed threshold); intelligibility target of ≥90% accuracy on Clear English text vs. standard-English control within 2 weeks (user constraint); no mandate or universal-adoption claims; no K-12 replacement.
  • Establish the budget allocation: total $3.5M (user constraint); Phase 1 $1.1M (31.4%), Phase 2 $1.2M (34.3%), Phase 3 $0.85M (24.3%), reserve $0.35M (10%); pre-gate reserve draws capped at $175K (5%) for evidence-backed gate protection; remaining ≥$175K released only after Month 24 (2028-10-13) GO decision.
  • Define primary stakeholder roles and decision authority: Project Lead or Program Director holds timeline and budget authority; Editorial Board of 7–9 members (practitioner-leaning with linguist review-and-veto) holds rule and gate-decision authority; Program Sponsor funds and approves charter; Psychometrician (hired by Month 2 = 2026-12-13) owns metrics design and validity; Cohort Manager (1.0 FTE by Month 6 = 2027-04-13) administers pilots; Educator Liaison (0.5–1.0 FTE) drives teacher engagement.
  • Outline the pilot design and recruitment targets: 2 cohorts (adult ESL, native-speaker technical/safety) × 2 conditions (Clear English vs. standard-English control) = 4 arms (decision); enrol ≥115 per arm (~460 total) to target ≥80 completers per arm with ≤30% dropout (estimate); signed enrollment commitments from ≥3 adult ESL programs and ≥2 technical/safety-training organizations by Month 3 (2027-01-13) (proposed threshold).
  • Specify the ordinal rule chosen: numeric ordinals with one invariant prefix marker (e.g., ^1, ^2, ^3, ^11, ^21) on every digit string; legacy 1st/2nd/3rd forms mechanically convertible; fixed spoken reading published; marker symbol and spoken form finalized by Month 10 (2027-08-13) (decision).
  • Document the grapheme-to-phoneme approach: standard spellings unchanged in v1.0; pronunciation delivered as optional software-generated overlay (ruby-style annotations in digital formats, printed pronunciation key for print materials); no respelling; overlay design by Month 10 (2027-08-13), pronunciation recordings of all 5,000 entries complete by Month 11 (2027-09-13) (decision).
  • Describe the morphology and homograph scope: retain all irregular forms in the top 1,000 lexicon words (proposed); regularize only lower-frequency irregulars with low recognition penalty; cap at ≤25% of irregular verbs/plurals changed (proposed); go/went retained as an example (proposed); homograph disambiguation markers mandatory only in safety-critical/procedural documents for ≤50 high-impact pairs; optional elsewhere (proposed).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous scope or missing phase definitions allow budget overruns, timeline compression and uncontrolled rule changes that undermine pilot credibility and invalidate gate metrics, risking a false-positive or false-negative go/no-go outcome and stranding $1.2M–$1.4M (Phase 2–3 budget estimate).
  • Unspecified gate thresholds or metrics allow the Month 24 (2028-10-13) decision to be disputed as subjective, with stakeholders claiming the bar was too loose (false-positive, launching a weak standard) or too strict (false-negative, killing a viable initiative), damaging trust in the standard and reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–50%.
  • Missing or unclear decision authority and tiebreak procedures invite editorial board deadlock on rule disputes (ordinal design, morphology retention, homograph markers), delaying rules finalization by 4–8 weeks and compressing Phase 2 pilot window by 33–67%, reducing data quality and statistical power by 15–25%.
  • Inadequate budget allocation or missing contingency plan leads to uncontrolled overruns (estimate: $300K overrun = 8.6% of budget), forcing cuts to pilot scope, assessment quality or outreach that compromise gate evidence and reduce adoption credibility.
  • Weak or underspecified metrics validity framework—without construct-validity analysis, confound controls or inter-rater reliability targets—invalidates pilot data and renders the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate disputable, potentially forcing a $300K–$500K (estimate) do-over or a false-negative outcome that kills the initiative.
  • Missing stakeholder engagement or unclear adoption pathway allows educator pushback, publisher skepticism and regulatory delays (4–8 months estimate), reducing pilot enrollment, partner commitments and Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%, stranding investment in a standard no one adopts.
  • Unaddressed post-project stewardship funding gap ($150K–$250K annually estimate, $1.5M–$2.5M over 10 years estimate) leaves the standard unmaintained after Month 36 (2029-10-13), causing atrophy, perceived instability and long-term adoption decline by 30–50% within 12–24 months.
  • Vague safety-critical controls or unaddressed liability exposure leaves the program vulnerable to incident-driven lawsuits, regulatory investigation and immediate pause or withdrawal if a misreading of Clear English text causes injury, ending the initiative and damaging the organization's credibility.
  • Missing or incomplete licensing and name-stewardship terms allow fragmentation and unofficial variants (emerging within 12–24 months of public release estimate), confusing adopters, undermining the standard's perceived value and reducing adoption by 20–40%.
  • Unspecified rules-freeze timing or change-control procedures allow mid-pilot rule revisions to invalidate earlier assessments, inflate measurement noise by 10–15% and render gate data inconclusive, triggering timeline extension or a disputed gate outcome.

Worst Case Scenario: The Project Charter fails to specify binding gate thresholds, authority rules or contingency procedures. During Phase 1, rule disputes on ordinal design and morphology retention deadlock the editorial board for 8 weeks, compressing Phase 2 pilots by 67% and triggering a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K estimate draw). Psychometric validation is incomplete; inter-rater reliability falls to kappa 0.60 instead of target 0.75, and no construct-validity framework is in place, leaving confounds uncontrolled. Pilot recruitment falls short: only 60 completers per arm (below the 80-completer power target estimate) due to missed partner commitments and unclear adoption messaging. By Month 24 (2028-10-13), data are inconclusive; ordinal error reduction is 18% (below the 25% proposed threshold), and pronunciation consistency metric is noisy (kappa 0.60). The board cannot decide: the charter does not specify how to resolve a borderline gate outcome, and stakeholders dispute whether the metrics were adequate. An extension is declared, pushing Phase 2 to Month 30 (2029-04-13) at $300K cost (estimate), exhausting the reserve and consuming unallocated Phase 3 funds. By Month 30 (2029-04-13), stewardship funding is still unfunded, educator pushback has mounted and competing standards have emerged. The program releases a v1.0 with no committed steward, limited third-party adoption, and reputation damage. By Month 48 (2030-10-13), the standard has atrophied and adoption has stalled at ~5,000 learners instead of the 100,000+ feasible under a credible, timely gate and steward commitment.

Best Case Scenario: The Project Charter clearly specifies scope, phase gates, metrics thresholds and decision authority, adopted by Month 1 (2026-11-13) and signed by the Program Sponsor and Editorial Board Chair. The charter guides tight Phase 1 execution: rules are finalized by Month 10 (2027-08-13), metrics are pre-registered with explicit thresholds by Month 11 (2027-09-13), and audio production completes on time and budget ($80K–$120K estimate). Pilot recruitment hits targets: ≥115 per arm enrolled by Month 13 (2027-11-13), with ≥80 completers per arm retained through follow-up (70%+ retention estimate). Purpose-built assessments with kappa ≥0.75 inter-rater reliability and clear construct-validity frameworks generate clean, defensible data. By Month 24 (2028-10-13), the gate decision is unambiguous: all four metrics meet pre-registered thresholds; ordinal error reduction is 28% (above the 25% proposed threshold), comprehension speed is 8% slower (within the 10% proposed limit), pronunciation consistency is 18% above control with kappa 0.77, and 30-day retention is 73% (above the 70% proposed threshold). The board issues a clear GO decision, releasing the full $0.35M reserve. By Month 30 (2029-04-13), v1.0 is released with a committed steward organization and clear post-project governance roadmap. Phase 3 adoption accelerates: ≥5 licensed third-party adopters (target ≥3 proposed) are in place by Month 36 (2029-10-13), including 2 major ESL publishers, 1 technical standards body, and 2 safety-training organizations. Learner reach reaches ~30,000–50,000 by Month 36 (2029-10-13), with strong evidence and positioning for future expansion. The standard achieves credibility and stability, supporting 10–15 year sustainability under funded stewardship.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the charter cannot be finalized by Month 1 (2026-11-13), convene an interim decision-making committee (project lead + 3 board representatives) by Month 2 (2026-12-13) with delegated authority to lock scope, budget and metrics framework pending full board ratification by Month 3 (2027-01-13); this compresses decision-making by 4 weeks but maintains timeline integrity.
  • If editorial board assembly is delayed (e.g., key practitioners unavailable), appoint a smaller steering committee of 4–5 core members (project lead, 1 linguist, 1 ESL practitioner, 1 psychometrician) with mandate to resolve rule disputes by Month 10 (2027-08-13), deferring full board expansion to Month 12 (2027-10-13) Phase 1 completion; this risks narrower representation but preserves timeline.
  • If stakeholder engagement and adoption pathway are unclear, commission a rapid (4-week) stakeholder-landscape study by Month 2 (2026-12-13) to map ESL programs, technical organizations, publishers and standards bodies willing to pilot and adopt; incorporate findings into the charter by Month 3 (2027-01-13) to ground adoption messaging and secure early commitments.
  • If psychometric expertise is scarce or hiring is delayed beyond Month 2 (2026-12-13), contract a part-time psychometric consultant (0.4–0.6 FTE, estimated $80K–$120K annually estimate) by Month 3 (2027-01-13) under a fixed engagement through pre-registration (Month 11 = 2027-09-13); this trades permanent staffing for contingent expertise and preserves metrics credibility.
  • If gate metrics thresholds cannot be finalized by Month 5 (2027-03-13) due to lack of pilot-design precedent, adopt one published benchmarks for reading speed and comprehension from established ESL assessment literature, and set ordinal and pronunciation thresholds based on expert consensus with published justification by Month 8 (2027-06-13); this grounds thresholds in existing evidence and reduces subjective guesswork.
  • If budget contingency proves insufficient (e.g., $175K pre-gate cap is exhausted by Month 15 (2028-01-13) due to audio or psychometric overruns), escalate to the Program Sponsor by Month 15 (2028-01-13) for an interim tranche release (e.g., additional $75K–$100K estimate) with a board-approved justification; delay Phase 2 recruitment start by 2–4 weeks if necessary to absorb overruns without skipping critical validation work.
  • If pilot partner commitments are not signed by Month 3 (2027-01-13), activate secondary recruitment channels: approach university ESL centers, non-profit adult education providers and vocational training organizations with accelerated onboarding (2-week commitment-to-enrolment timeline) to hit recruitment target by Month 8 (2027-06-13); this broadens partner diversity but risks lower institutional formality.
  • If stewardship funding cannot be sourced before Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision, make the go decision conditional: declare a 'provisional GO' pending stewardship commitment by Month 30 (2029-04-13), with v1.0 release held in embargo until a steward (or stewardship consortium) is formally committed; this de-risks the gate from stewardship gaps but delays public release and adopter access by up to 6 months.
  • If the charter itself is disputed or rejected by key stakeholders, defer full board ratification and publish a lightweight 'Charter Summary' (1-page) outlining scope, phases, gate metrics and decision authority by Month 1 (2026-11-13), with a commitment to produce a full charter by Month 3 (2027-01-13); this allows Phase 1 work to proceed on interim authority while stakeholder alignment is negotiated.

Essential Information:

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • An unresolved linguistic veto by a minority linguist panel blocks practitioner consensus and delays rule publication, pushing the Month 12 (2027-10-13) rules lock to Month 13–14 (2027-11-13 to 2027-12-13) and triggering a compressed or failed pilot timeline.
  • Lack of published conflict-of-interest disclosure invites stakeholder skepticism that publisher-affiliated board members favoured easier adoption rules, undermining the charter's perceived legitimacy before pilots begin.
  • No decision-logging or rationale documentation means contested rules vanish into opaque board consensus, leaving external stakeholders (educators, standards bodies, regulators) uncertain whether the chosen rule is evidence-based or political, reducing their confidence in the standard.

Worst Case Scenario: Editorial board disputes over rule design (ordinal marker form, morphology regularization scope, homograph markers) remain unresolved through Month 10–12 (2027-08-13 to 2027-10-13) due to ambiguous voting rules and no tiebreak mechanism. As a result, rules are either locked in ambiguous form or withheld pending further discussion, compressing Phase 2 pilots from 12 to 8–10 months. Compressed pilots shrink to fewer cohorts or shorter follow-up periods, reducing statistical power and measurement reliability (kappa drops below the 0.70 floor). The Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision rests on inconclusive or noisy data, forcing either an extension (Phase 2 stretches to Month 30–36 = 2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13, consuming up to $600K (estimate) and stranding Phase 3 funding) or a disputed gate outcome that educators and standards bodies reject. Long-term credibility is damaged, and adoption stalls at 5,000–10,000 learners instead of the target 50,000+.

Best Case Scenario: Editorial board charter with clear voting (simple majority, quorum 6 of 9), linguist veto limited to ambiguity findings, and a pre-agreed external arbiter is published by Month 1 (2026-11-13). Rule disputes are documented transparently: majority and minority positions appear in the published rationale, so contested rules are defensible and stakeholders understand the trade-offs. Workstream owners meet deadlines (Month 10 = 2027-08-13); arbiter is consulted for one or two technical questions, making a binding recommendation by Month 10 (2027-08-13). Rules are locked on schedule by Month 12 (2027-10-13), and the draft standard withstands the 30-day public-comment window without major rewrites. Phase 2 pilots proceed at full strength (460 enrolled, 80%+ completion rate), measurement is robust (kappa ≥0.75), and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision is scientifically defensible. Educators and standards bodies perceive the charter as legitimate, reducing resistance and enabling Phase 3 partnerships and adoption.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the editorial board cannot agree on voting rules by Month 1 (2026-11-13), adopt a default voting template from an external source (e.g., ISO TC 37 governance, ASD-STE100 maintenance procedures) and require the board to ratify it by Month 2 (2026-12-13), accepting minor customization only.
  • If disputes over rule scope remain after Month 8 (2027-06-13), convene a half-day facilitated workshop with an external mediator (cost $5K–$10K, estimate) to surface and document all positions by Month 9 (2027-07-13), then proceed to arbiter recommendation.
  • If the designated tiebreak arbiter is unavailable or conflicts of interest emerge, engage a standing panel of 2–3 neutral external judges from university linguistics or ISO/ASTM standards bodies; use a majority vote among the panel (rather than a single arbiter) to break board ties, with costs capped at $15K–$25K (estimate).
  • If rule-finalization slips past Month 10 (2027-08-13) by more than 2 weeks, activate the phase-extension fallback: extend Phase 1 by 4 weeks (~$85K, estimate), lock rules by Month 13 (2027-11-13), and compress the public-comment window to 2 weeks (Month 13–14 = 2027-11-13 to 2027-12-13) to preserve the Month 15 (2028-01-13) Phase 2 start.
  • If board consensus cannot be reached on a high-impact rule (e.g., ordinal marker form), publish two variants of the draft standard (Option A and Option B), conduct a small pilot test (N=20–30, estimate) with early-adopter schools to gather empirical evidence by Month 13 (2027-11-13), and lock the winning variant before Phase 2 enrollment starts.

Create Document 3: Outcome Metric Battery Design and Pre-Analysis Plan

ID: 95578caa-10a4-450b-8ef1-0fc637c2d8fc

Description: Detailed specification of four go/no-go metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) including measurement instruments, scoring procedures, control-group design, inter-rater reliability targets (kappa ≥0.70 floor, ≥0.75 target), sample-size justification via power analysis, pre-registered pass/fail thresholds, and intention-to-treat analysis rules. Independently reviewed by a psychometrician. Registered on Open Science Framework by Month 11 (2027-09-13). Intended for editorial board, external reviewers, and regulatory bodies.

Responsible Role Type: Psychometrician / Assessment Specialist

Primary Template: Open Science Framework pre-registration template (aspredicted.org or equivalent)

Secondary Template: APA Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing

Steps to Create:

  • Conduct literature review on adult ESL learning effects, comprehension-speed benchmarks, and pronunciation consistency measurement
  • Propose instrument candidates for each metric (reading-to-matching for ordinal error; TOEFL-style comprehension for reading speed; phonemic-transcription for pronunciation; delayed-recall for retention)
  • Design a validity study (N=20–30 adult ESL and technical learners, Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) to estimate effect sizes
  • Conduct power analysis: calculate sample size per arm for 80% power at α=0.05 to detect proposed effect sizes
  • Justify each proposed threshold (e.g., ordinal error ≥25% reduction) with reference to analogous interventions and Phase 1 pilot effect estimates
  • Specify control-group design and manipulation checks to isolate Clear English effects from confounds (repeated exposure, motivation, first-language phonology)
  • Define inter-rater training protocol for pronunciation consistency scoring: rater selection criteria, Cohen's kappa calibration on ≥100-word pilot sample, retraining trigger if kappa <0.70
  • Document intention-to-treat rules: handling of missing data, early dropouts, multivariate analyses for confound adjustment
  • Complete draft by Month 5 (2027-03-13); finalize with board input by Month 9 (2027-07-13); register on OSF by Month 11 (2027-09-13); publish registered plan on project website immediately

Approval Authorities: Independent Psychometrician (lead author), Editorial Board (vote on thresholds), External Expert Reviewer

Essential Information:

  • Define with precision the four go/no-go gate metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) and specify quantitative pass/fail thresholds: ordinal error reduction ≥25%, comprehension speed within 10% of control, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70% (all proposed thresholds, per canonical facts).
  • Design control-group structure isolating Clear English effects from confounds (repeated exposure, learner motivation, first-language phonology): specify 2 cohorts (adult ESL; native-speaker technical/safety-glossary) × 2 conditions (Clear English vs. standard-English control) = 4 arms, with 80 completers minimum per arm (estimate) and power analysis justifying sample size for 80% power at α=0.05 (proposed threshold).
  • Specify measurement instruments for each metric: reading-to-matching or ordinal-identification task for ordinal error rate; TOEFL-style or adapted comprehension passage for reading speed; phonemic transcription or standardized pronunciation rating scale for pronunciation consistency; delayed-recall or recognition test for 30-day retention; justify each instrument's validity and relevance to Clear English effects.
  • Document inter-rater reliability procedures: rater-selection criteria, training protocol, Cohen's kappa calibration on ≥100-word pilot sample (Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13); specify kappa floor of ≥0.70 and target of ≥0.75 (proposed thresholds); define retraining trigger if kappa falls below 0.70 and escalation to 4-week Phase 1 extension (~$85K, estimate).
  • Specify intention-to-treat analysis rules: handling of missing data, early dropouts, multivariate confound adjustment (e.g., regress ordinal error on baseline literacy, first-language phonology, study motivation); define validity conditions for data: ≥80 completers per arm, ≥70% follow-up completion at 30 days (proposed thresholds), inter-rater kappa ≥0.70.
  • Include a validity study design (N=20–30 adult ESL and native-speaker learners, Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) to estimate effect sizes, test instruments for clarity and discriminability, and calibrate inter-rater scoring before Phase 2 full enrollment.
  • Document construct-validity analysis identifying plausible alternative explanations for each metric (e.g., whether ordinal accuracy improvement is due to Clear English comprehensibility or simple repeated exposure) and specify manipulation checks (e.g., post-test questions confirming which rule system learners learned).
  • Justify each proposed threshold with reference to analogous interventions, literacy research benchmarks, and Phase 1 pilot effect estimates; explain the rationale for why each threshold represents meaningful progress rather than trivial change.
  • Complete draft pre-analysis plan by Month 5 (2027-03-13); finalize with editorial board input by Month 9 (2027-07-13); register the final plan on Open Science Framework (e.g., aspredicted.org) by Month 11 (2027-09-13) to establish time-stamped, immutable documentation before Phase 2 pilots enroll (Month 12–13 = 2027-10-13 to 2027-11-13).
  • Publish the registered pre-analysis plan on the project website immediately upon registration (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) for transparency and third-party review by educators, standards bodies and external researchers.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Unspecified or subjective pass/fail thresholds render the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision disputable and scientifically non-credible: stakeholders (educators, standards bodies, regulators) could claim the gate was too lenient or too strict, leading to rejection of the outcome and loss of adoption confidence regardless of actual results.
  • Weak or confounded measurement instruments that fail to isolate Clear English effects from alternative explanations (repeated exposure, motivation, first-language phonology) inflate or deflate observed improvements, producing false-positive (launching a weak standard) or false-negative (killing a viable initiative) gate outcomes with $1.2M–$1.4M (Phase 2–3 budget estimate) at risk.
  • Inter-rater reliability below the target kappa ≥0.75 (especially if kappa <0.70) for pronunciation consistency scoring inflates measurement noise by 20% or more, reducing statistical power to detect true Clear English effects by 10–15% and increasing the risk of a false-negative gate outcome.
  • Missing or inadequate validity study in Months 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) leaves instrument effect-size estimates ungrounded, forcing blind sample-size choices and risking either under-powered pilots (n too small, inconclusive results) or wasteful over-powering (n larger than necessary).
  • Absence of manipulation checks and confound controls permits alternative explanations for improvements to go undetected, allowing spurious gate passage (false-positive) or masking of genuine Clear English benefits if confounds dampen observed effects (false-negative).
  • Late or incomplete pre-registration (after Months 11–12 = 2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13) permits post-hoc analysis flexibility and data-driven threshold selection, undermining the pre-registration's protection against outcome-driven reporting and inviting accusations of p-hacking or cherry-picking.
  • Incomplete or vague intention-to-treat and missing-data procedures result in inconsistent analysis, with board members or external reviewers able to reach different conclusions from the same data, delaying or muddying the gate decision.
  • Inattention to construct validity allows metrics to measure construct-irrelevant factors (e.g., test-taking ability, fatigue) rather than Clear English comprehensibility, invalidating the claim that gate passage indicates Clear English is superior.
  • Published thresholds without explicit justification or reference to analogous interventions appear arbitrary, inviting challenge from skeptics and reducing the standard's perceived credibility with adopters and regulators.

Worst Case Scenario: An underdeveloped pre-analysis plan with vague thresholds, weak instruments, and uncontrolled confounds leads to a disputed gate outcome at Month 24 (2028-10-13). If the gate passes but external reviewers later find the instruments were insensitive to Clear English effects or the thresholds were arbitrary, a false-positive outcome launches a standard that fails to deliver promised benefits, destroying adopter confidence and reducing Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%, capping learner reach at 15,000–35,000. If the gate fails but was driven by weak measurement rather than Clear English insufficiency, an equally damaging false-negative kills a viable initiative, stranding $1.2M–$1.4M (Phase 2–3 budget estimate) and requiring either a costly 6-month Phase 2 extension (~$300K, estimate) or a withdrawn standard. Either outcome triggers regulatory pushback, litigation risk if safety-critical pilots were conducted, and reputational damage that forecloses future language standardization initiatives in the field.

Best Case Scenario: A rigorous, pre-registered pre-analysis plan with quantitative, justified thresholds; validated instruments; inter-rater reliability kappa ≥0.75; explicit confound controls; and a validity study (Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) published by Month 11 (2027-09-13) enables a transparent, defensible Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision. If the gate passes, the clear evidence base gives educators, publishers and standards bodies confidence to adopt Clear English, enabling Phase 3 launch with ≥3 licensed third-party adopters by Month 36 (2029-10-13) and a 10,000–50,000 learner reach. If the gate fails, the rigorous metrics and published thresholds allow stakeholders to trust the outcome, preventing fragmentation into unofficial variants and permitting an informed decision about revision or sunset. Either way, the credible evidence base becomes a model for other language-standardization initiatives and strengthens the case for evidence-gated linguistic innovation.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If purpose-built instrument development proves too costly or time-consuming by Month 5 (2027-03-13), adopt a hybrid approach: use validated off-the-shelf instruments for comprehension speed and 30-day retention (traded for less precision on Clear English-specific ordinal and pronunciation effects) and develop only two purpose-built tasks (ordinal-identification and pronunciation rating) using a simplified design with reduced inter-rater overhead; budget savings ~$50K–$80K (estimate) compress the psychometric cost from $150K–$200K to ~$80K–$120K, permitting earlier start of Phase 2 enrollment.
  • If inter-rater reliability remains below kappa 0.70 after 4 weeks of retraining (Month 11 = 2027-09-13), adopt digital-assisted scoring (e.g., automated phonemic transcription from learner audio with human verification and flagging of boundary cases) to reduce subjective judgment; this shifts cost from rater training to software licensing but may improve reliability by 5–10% and allows Phase 2 to proceed with a notation in the pre-analysis plan that pronunciation consistency scoring is assisted and may have higher systematic bias.
  • If pilot enrollment falls short of the target 460 learners (80 per arm × 4 conditions; 115 enrolment per arm for 70% retention = estimate) by Month 13 (2027-11-13), reduce the number of conditions from 4 arms to 3 by combining the two native-speaker technical-glossary conditions into a single 'safety-critical' condition, yielding 3 arms (adult ESL Clear English, adult ESL control, safety-critical Clear English; no safety-critical control); this reduces power by ~15% but permits analysis to proceed with ~320 completers (estimate) instead of 380 needed for 4 arms, though the safety-critical effect will be less precisely estimated.
  • If validity-study effect-size estimates (Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) differ substantially from Phase 1 expectations, implement a Bayesian adaptive re-allocation of Phase 2 enrollment to conditions showing larger effects rather than a fixed 1:1 randomization; this maintains statistical power for the most promising conditions without expanding total sample size, at the cost of post-hoc loss of balance and some additional complexity in intention-to-treat analysis.
  • If comprehensive construct-validity analysis and manipulation-check data collection prove infeasible within the Phase 2 budget, publish an explicit 'construct-validity limitations' section in the pre-analysis plan acknowledging which alternative explanations cannot be ruled out and which confounds have not been measured; ensure this limitation is communicated prominently to the editorial board at Month 24 (2028-10-13) so the gate decision includes a caveat about the scope of the evidence.
  • If the 30-day follow-up completion rate falls below 70% (proposed threshold), restrict the go/no-go conclusion to the immediate post-test metrics (ordinal error, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency) and flag 30-day retention as 'inconclusive' rather than failing the gate; this permits a conditional GO subject to a post-Phase-3 commitment to track retention in early-adopter cohorts.
  • If pre-registration on Open Science Framework is delayed beyond Month 11 (2027-09-13) due to editorial board feedback loops, register a summary version on aspredicted.org by Month 11 (2027-09-13) and a detailed version on OSF by Month 12 (2027-10-13), ensuring time-stamped transparency before Phase 2 enrollment; note the split registration in the final plan.

Create Document 4: Clear English Standard Specification v0.9 (Draft for Comment)

ID: 514a9a21-d20b-4eae-8c79-48f9e0170564

Description: Comprehensive draft rule set covering ordinal representation (prefix-marker notation + invariant spoken form), grapheme-to-phoneme mapping for core lexicon (pronunciation overlay guidance), morphology retention rules (irregular verbs/plurals threshold), homograph disambiguation policy (marker list + application rules), and accent-anchor specification (phonemic inventory + mapping to other varieties). Includes rationale, worked examples, exceptions, and change-control procedures. Published for 30-day public comment by Month 11 (2027-09-13). Intended for educators, publishers, standards bodies, and ESL professionals.

Responsible Role Type: Linguistic Specialist / Computational Linguist

Primary Template: ISO 639-5 Language Code standard template

Secondary Template: ASD-STE100 specification document format

Steps to Create:

  • Consolidate rule specifications from editorial-board subcommittees: ordinal (prefix marker, spoken form finalized Month 10 = 2027-08-13), morphology (frequency threshold + ranked exception list), homographs (≤50 high-impact pairs + disambiguation markers for safety-critical contexts only), accent anchor (phonemic inventory, vowel quality conventions, key consonant contrasts, mapping to RP/GenAm/other varieties)
  • Draft written rules with explicit if-then criteria (e.g., 'if a word rank >1000 in frequency, regularize irregular forms; if rank ≤1000, retain legacy form')
  • Provide 20–50 worked examples per rule (ordinal dates/lists, morphology paradigms, homograph disambiguation in procedure context, pronunciation guidance samples)
  • Document rule justifications and linguistic precedents (e.g., Basic English, ASD-STE100 controlled vocabulary, ESL morphology acquisition research)
  • Specify exceptions and edge cases (e.g., 'go/went retained despite frequency <1,000 due to learner salience')
  • Draft a Change-Control and Release Cadence policy: v1.0 frozen for 12 months, errata-only, consolidated v2.0 review
  • Publish as a 20–30 page draft specification by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with a public comment form; collect feedback through Month 11.5 (2027-09-28); respond to comments and finalize by Month 12 (2027-10-13) with a published Response Document

Approval Authorities: Editorial Board (majority vote + tiebreak if needed), Public Comment Review Committee

Essential Information:

  • Comprehensive written specification of all five critical-lever rule decisions: Ordinal Marker Architecture (prefix-marker + invariant spoken form), Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention Depth (optional overlay, no respelling), Adoption Wedge and Sequencing (ESL-first supplementary module), Outcome Metric Battery Design (four pre-registered gate metrics with thresholds), and Phase Budget Weighting and Reserve (allocation across phases and draw conditions).
  • Detailed rule set for ordinal representation with ≥20–50 worked examples covering dates, lists, procedures and prose contexts; explicit if-then criteria defining when rules apply and documented exceptions (e.g., 'go/went retained despite frequency rank due to learner salience').
  • Morphology retention threshold rule: retain all irregulars in top 1,000 lexicon words by frequency; regularize lower-frequency forms; cap total irregular-form changes at ≤25% (proposed); published ranked exception list.
  • Homograph disambiguation policy: mandatory markers only for ≤50 high-impact pairs (proposed) in safety-critical/procedural documents; optional elsewhere; list and application rules published with worked examples.
  • Reference accent anchor specification: phonemic inventory, vowel quality conventions, key consonant contrasts defined; documented mapping to other major varieties (British, American, Australian, Indian) by Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • Pre-registered gate metrics and pass/fail thresholds: ordinal error rate ≥25% reduction (proposed), comprehension speed within 10% of control (proposed), pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control with kappa ≥0.75 target/0.70 floor (proposed), 30-day retention ≥70% (proposed); validity conditions (≥80 completers per arm, ≥70% follow-up completion, inter-rater kappa ≥0.70 floor).
  • Change-Control and Release Cadence policy: v1.0 frozen for 12 months (errata only), consolidated v2.0 review; no rule changes during Phase 2 pilots.
  • Justification and linguistic precedents for each rule (e.g., citations to Basic English, ASD-STE100, ESL morphology acquisition research) demonstrating rule defensibility to educators and standards bodies.
  • Rationale for key trade-offs: why prefix ordinals coexist with legacy forms (recognizability and mechanical convertibility), why pronunciation is an overlay (preserves print compatibility and publisher adoption), why morphology threshold uses frequency (balances regularity with recognizability).
  • Edge cases and rule interactions: e.g., how prefix ordinals interact with currency symbols, abbreviations, ordinal adjectives (e.g., '3rd-place team'); how pronunciation overlay handles homophones; how homograph markers interact with safety-critical document templates.
  • Public comment response document: list of all comments received during the Month 11 (2027-09-13) 30-day comment window and editorial-board responses explaining whether rules were changed, deferred or rejected.
  • Accent-mapping tables: phoneme-by-phoneme equivalences showing how other major accents realize the reference anchor's vowel contrasts and consonant distinctions, so learners and materials creators understand how to adapt pronunciation guidance.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or contradictory rule specifications (e.g., conflicting morphology thresholds or homograph marker triggers) force mid-pilot rule clarifications that invalidate earlier assessments and inflate measurement noise, delaying or making the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision inconclusive.
  • Missing quantitative pass/fail thresholds for gate metrics (e.g., no defined ordinal error-rate reduction target) render the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision subjective and disputable, allowing stakeholders to claim the gate was too lenient or too strict, damaging credibility if a false-positive launches a weak standard or a false-negative kills a viable one.
  • Insufficient worked examples or edge-case coverage leaves educators and material designers uncertain how to apply rules consistently, resulting in 10–20% rule misapplication in pilot curricula and confounded pilot results.
  • Vague or missing accent-anchor justification (e.g., no documented mapping to other varieties) triggers criticism from standards bodies and regional ESL organizations that the standard privileges one accent, damaging perceived neutrality and reducing adoption outside the anchor region by 20–40% (estimate).
  • Lack of linguistic precedents or research citations makes rules appear arbitrary rather than evidence-based, reducing buy-in from academic partners and standards bodies whose endorsement the Phase 3 adoption depends on.
  • Weak or unstated change-control policy invites post-publication rule fragmentation and divergent implementations, allowing third-party forks to claim conformance while violating core rules, undermining the standard's value for consistent communication in safety-critical contexts.
  • Missing or unclear response to public comments gives the appearance that the editorial board ignored stakeholder input, eroding legitimacy and encouraging divergent forks or rival standards.

Worst Case Scenario: A poorly specified draft (ambiguous rule triggers, missing thresholds, no worked examples, weak accent justification) is published at Month 11 (2027-09-13) for public comment. During the 30-day comment window, educators, publishers and standards bodies raise 15–30 substantive critiques (unclear morphology exceptions, homograph marker inconsistency, accent bias); the editorial board cannot resolve these disputes before Month 12 (2027-10-13) rule freeze, forcing either a publication of visibly flawed rules (damaging credibility) or a 4–8 week extension that compresses Phase 2 pilots by 33–67%, reducing statistical power and rendering the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate inconclusive. A failed or disputed gate decision strands $1.2M–$1.4M (Phase 2–3 budget estimate) and delays market entry to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or beyond, during which competing standards or initiatives may emerge and educator skepticism hardens, cutting Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive, well-justified specification published by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with 30–50 worked examples per rule, explicit quantitative pass/fail thresholds for all four gate metrics, documented accent mappings, and published responses to all public comments. Educators, publishers and standards bodies receive a clear, defensible rule set that they can teach, audit and implement consistently. Pilot curricula closely follow the published rules, measurement noise is minimized, and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision rests on unambiguous, pre-registered evidence. A positive gate outcome is accepted by educational partners, publishers secure early licensing commitments, and Phase 3 public release proceeds on schedule, enabling adoption by ≥3 third-party organizations by Month 36 (2029-10-13) and building the foundation for post-project stewardship and long-term standard stability.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If rule disputes within the editorial board remain unresolved by Month 9 (2027-07-13): trigger an early escalation to the board's external tiebreak arbiter (identified by Month 5 = 2027-03-13) by Month 9.5 (2027-07-28), allowing 2 weeks for arbiter-mediated resolution before Month 11 (2027-09-13) finalization. Cost: $10K–$20K (estimate) for arbiter consulting; time: 2 weeks. Benefit: preserves the Month 12 (2027-10-13) rule freeze without extension.
  • If linguistic detail or precedent citations are insufficient by Month 8 (2027-06-13): commission a targeted literature review and expert-panel summary (2–3 weeks, $20K–$30K estimate) by Month 9 (2027-07-13), incorporating key research on morphology acquisition, ordinal processing and ESL instruction. If time is too constrained, defer detailed academic justification to a separate 'White Paper on Rule Rationale' published concurrently with v1.0 at Month 30 (2029-04-13), provided that the primary specification still includes sufficient practical justification for educators.
  • If the 30-day public comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) generates >20 substantive critiques that cannot be resolved within 2 weeks: extend the comment-response cycle to Month 11.5 (2027-09-28), allowing 1 additional week for editorial board review. Cost: 1-week pipeline delay, compressing Phase 2 ramp by 1 week (~$21K estimate, 1.2M/52); risk: reduces pilot data-collection buffer by 1 week, increases potential for attrition. Trigger: escalate to board leadership by Month 11.3 (2027-09-22) if comment volume exceeds 20 distinct issues.
  • If accent-anchor selection becomes contested (e.g., standards bodies demand multi-accent coverage or object to a single anchor as exclusionary): publish a clear, one-page board decision by Month 3 (2027-01-13) explaining the anchor choice with explicit non-discrimination statement; commit to a post-v1.0 roadmap for additional accents; consider recording a small supplementary sample (200–300 high-frequency words) in one additional accent as a 'proof-of-concept' for Phase 3 ($10K–$15K estimate, within operational discretion). Do not allow accent additions to delay Month 12 (2027-10-13) rule freeze.
  • If educational stakeholders perceive rules as too aggressive or unclear during Month 18 (2028-04-13) mid-Phase-2 check-in: schedule a rapid clarification webinar or focus group with teachers and pilot coordinators by Month 18.5 (2028-04-28), gather specific confusion reports, and publish a brief 'Clarification Memo' (2–3 pages) by Month 19 (2028-05-13) addressing the top 5–10 ambiguities without changing rules. Cost: $10K (estimate) for facilitation and writing; benefit: prevents rule misapplication during the second half of pilots.

Create Document 5: 5,000-Word Core Lexicon with Pronunciation Guidance

ID: 9cf52d63-45ad-4552-a0de-77bff7411467

Description: Ranked list of 5,000 English word types (4,500 frequency-led general vocabulary + 500 technical/safety block) with: frequency band and corpus source, part-of-speech and word sense (polysemy markers), pronunciation guidance (IPA-based or minimal respelling overlay notation), mapping to standard English equivalent, and notes on rule exceptions (e.g., irregular verbs retained).
