  • Deliver pronunciation guidance specification: single anchor-accent specification (IPA-based or minimal respelling overlay notation), notation guide, and mapping of other accents to the anchor. Anchor chosen and justified by Month 3 (2027-01-13); mapping documented by Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • Identify and document rule exceptions: irregular verbs and plurals retained within the frequency cutoff (e.g., go/went retained; proposed), homograph markers required in safety-critical documents only for ≤50 high-impact pairs (proposed cap), and any Clear English-specific regularizations or spelling variants that affect lexicon entries.
  • Produce sortable database format (CSV, Excel, or wiki) with all fields by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Publish summary list and pronunciation key on project website by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Ensure auditability: every entry's source and rule exceptions documented and third-party verifiable.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Lexicon coverage <85% confounds pilot assessments: learners struggle with out-of-list vocabulary rather than Clear English effects, inflating measurement error by 10–15% and reducing statistical power to detect true effects; discovered at Month 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13), a 4–8 week expansion pushes pilots into Month 26–32 (2029-02-13 to 2029-06-13), compressing 30-day follow-up windows.
  • Missing or inconsistent pronunciation guidance (e.g., incomplete IPA mappings, unclear anchor-accent specification) invalidates the pronunciation consistency score (a go/no-go metric): raters cannot score pronunciation against a vague reference, inter-rater reliability kappa drops below 0.70 floor (proposed), inflating measurement noise by 20% and risking a false-negative gate outcome.
  • Unclear or contradictory rule documentation (e.g., conflicting retention thresholds for irregular forms, ambiguous homograph marker scope) causes rule misapplication during curriculum design and pilot administration: 10–20% of pilot materials misapply rules, confounding results and invalidating the gate decision at Month 24 (2028-10-13).
  • Incomplete or poorly organized database structure reduces third-party usability: educators and publishers cannot easily integrate the lexicon into curricula or search tools; adoption friction increases, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 15–30%.
  • Lexicon selection methodology not documented or auditable: standards bodies and educators cannot verify the list's representativeness or objectivity, undermining credibility and regulatory approval; fragmentation risk increases if third parties create competing 'Clear English' lexicons.
  • Pronunciation recordings missing, inaudible or poorly stored by Month 11 (2027-09-13): audio infrastructure failure delays pronunciation-key delivery by 4–8 weeks, compressing pilot rater training and inter-rater calibration (target kappa ≥0.75 proposed), or forces substitution with untested or lower-quality recordings.

Worst Case Scenario: Lexicon is delivered late (Month 15–18 = 2028-01-13 to 2028-04-13) with incomplete pronunciation guidance and <80% coverage. Pilot materials are designed using an out-of-date, partial lexicon. Pronunciation consistency scoring is delayed or unreliable (kappa 0.65), rendering the pronunciation metric non-credible at the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate. Editorial board disputes lexicon selection methodology as unrepresentative, calling the go/no-go outcome into question. Simultaneously, partners discover that key high-frequency words are missing, forcing curriculum designers to rework materials. The gate decision is delayed 6–12 months while the lexicon is revised, stranding $1.2M–$1.4M in Phase 3 funding and damaging stakeholder confidence in the standard's viability. Post-launch, third parties publish competing 'Clear English' lexicons with divergent word selections, fragmenting the standard.

Best Case Scenario: Lexicon is finalized by Month 10 (2027-08-13) with ≥85% coverage, full pronunciation guidance in IPA and overlay notation, and transparent, audited selection methodology published. Pronunciation recordings are complete, inter-rater reliability achieves kappa 0.77 (target ≥0.75 proposed), and pronunciation key is usable for pilot scoring and learner reference. Database is clean, sortable and integrated into curriculum-design tools and pilot assessment platforms, enabling educators and publishers to adopt it immediately. Coverage audit identifies 3–5 missing high-frequency words; targeted additions by Month 10 (2027-08-13) bring coverage to ≥87%, exceeding the ≥85% threshold (proposed). Editorial board approves the lexicon at Month 11 (2027-09-13), and it feeds directly into pilot materials, reducing curriculum-design rework by 40%. The lexicon's transparent methodology and public provenance support regulatory approval and publisher confidence. At Month 24 (2028-10-13), the pronunciation consistency metric is valid and credible, enabling a defensible go/no-go decision and Phase 3 adoption by ≥3 third-party organizations.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If lexicon coverage audit at Month 8 (2027-06-13) reveals coverage <85%, immediately allocate $30K–$50K (estimate) from the pre-gate reserve draw cap to add the highest-frequency missing words by Month 10 (2027-08-13); expand the list to 5,200–5,500 words if necessary, subject to editorial board approval, rather than proceeding with inadequate coverage.
  • If audio production bottlenecks emerge at Month 7 (2027-05-13) and studio capacity cannot deliver 5,000 entries by Month 11 (2027-09-13), switch to a hybrid model: record the 1,500–2,000 highest-frequency and safety-critical words in full production (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13), and deliver pronunciation guidance for the remaining 3,000–3,500 words as IPA-only notation or respelling rules without full audio, subject to editorial board sign-off by Month 8 (2027-06-13). This preserves the 5,000-word user constraint while reducing audio cost by 40–50%.
  • If inter-rater reliability (kappa) falls below the 0.70 floor (proposed) at the Month 10 (2027-08-13) dry-run, pause full-scale recording and conduct a 4-week intensive rater-retraining and calibration protocol (estimate $15K–$25K cost from reserve draw), extending Phase 1 by 4 weeks (cost $85K, estimate). If kappa remains below 0.70 after retraining, reduce the pronunciation-consistency score to a secondary (non-gate) metric and rely on ordinal error rate and comprehension speed as the primary gates, with explicit documentation of the measurement trade-off.
  • If lexicon selection methodology is disputed by the editorial board (Months 4–6 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-04-13), commission an independent external lexicon audit by a second corpus linguist or standards body (cost $20K–$30K, estimate) to validate the frequency counts and coverage claims. Publish both the internal and external audits side-by-side, with documented agreements and disagreements, to build credibility and neutrality.
  • If pronunciation guide notation is deemed unclear by pilot curriculum designers at Month 11 (2027-09-13), publish a brief (1–2 page) Pronunciation Guide Quick-Start supplement with worked examples, inline notation in pilot materials, and a 30-minute educator video tutorial to clarify the overlay system. Allocate $10K–$15K (estimate) for video production and distribute by Month 12 (2027-10-13).
  • If third-party lexicon alternatives emerge during Phase 3 or beyond, publish a Lexicon Comparison Table (2–3 pages) documenting Clear English lexicon scope, selection criteria and coverage data alongside competitors, reinforcing the transparent methodology and post-hoc audit trail that differentiate the official lexicon from forks.

Create Document 6: Pronunciation Guidance System and Rater-Calibration Protocol

ID: 5915ff9b-fbd8-495b-a118-cbffa5cf01d4

Description: Complete specification of the single reference-accent anchor (chosen phoneme inventory, vowel quality conventions, exemplar recordings, mapping to other major English varieties). Includes pronunciation-notation system (IPA-based, minimal respelling, or hybrid) with rater-training manual and inter-rater reliability scoring rubric for the pronunciation-consistency metric. Specifies Cohen's kappa target (≥0.75) and floor (≥0.70), calibration procedure (100–200 word pilot sample), and retraining trigger. Designed so raters can achieve reliable pronunciation-consistency scoring by Month 10 (2027-08-13).

Responsible Role Type: Orthography & Phonetics Designer / Audio Production Manager

Primary Template: IPA Handbook or Pullum & Ladusaw Phonetic Symbol Unicode chart

Secondary Template: ESL pronunciation-teaching manual (e.g., Celce-Murcia, Brinton & Goodwin)

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 3 (2027-01-13), finalize reference-accent anchor: document phonemic inventory, vowel-quality distinctions (e.g., IPA [ɪ] vs [i], [ʌ] vs [ɑ]), key consonant contrasts, syllable stress marking, and intonation conventions; justify choice (learnability for ESL, learner demand, phonological distinctiveness) against 2–3 alternative candidates; provide 20–30 exemplar word recordings in the anchor accent
  • By Month 3 (2027-01-13), decide pronunciation-notation system for the lexicon: IPA transcription (most precise, requires trained eye), minimal respelling (most accessible, less precise), or hybrid (IPA for raters, simplified overlay for learners); document notation conventions with a 1–2 page guide and worked examples for common consonant and vowel patterns
  • Design the Rater Training Manual (3–5 pages): specify rater prerequisites (native or near-native proficiency in reference accent, prior ESL teaching or phonetics training); rater-selection criteria; training sessions (how many hours, what content: anchor pronunciation exposure, practice listening/transcribing on pilot word sample); and certification procedure (raters must achieve kappa ≥0.70 on a 50–100 word training sample before proceeding to full inter-rater calibration)
  • Draft the Pronunciation-Consistency Scoring Rubric (1–2 pages): define the scoring scale (binary match/mismatch vs. 1–5 quality rating), inter-rater procedure (raters score audio files independently, blinded to learner condition and identity), disagreement resolution (if kappa <0.70, identify which phonemes are problematic, retrain, and retest), and edge-case handling (unclear audio, non-native-like but intelligible pronunciations, learner code-switching)
  • By Month 8 (2027-06-13), recruit 3–4 qualified raters and begin training on the anchor accent and notation system
  • By Month 10 (2027-08-13), conduct inter-rater calibration on a 100–200 word pilot sample: each rater independently scores all words, Cohen's kappa is calculated, results reviewed; if kappa ≥0.75, proceed to full lexicon recording; if 0.70–0.74, implement targeted retraining on disagreed phonemes, retest by Month 10.5 (2027-08-28); if <0.70, pivot to hybrid model (speech-synthesis baseline + human verification of highest-friction subset only)
  • Finalize and publish the complete Pronunciation Guidance System (all raters trained, notation documented, rubric tested) by Month 11 (2027-09-13)

Approval Authorities: Audio Production Manager, Independent Psychometrician (kappa validation), Editorial Board

Essential Information:

  • Finalize and document the single reference-accent anchor by Month 3 (2027-01-13): specify the phonemic inventory, vowel-quality distinctions (e.g., IPA [ɪ] vs [i], [ʌ] vs [ɑ]), key consonant contrasts, syllable stress and intonation conventions; justify the choice against 2–3 alternative candidates; provide 20–30 exemplar recordings in the anchor accent
  • Select and document the pronunciation-notation system for the lexicon (IPA transcription, minimal respelling, or hybrid) by Month 3 (2027-01-13), with a 1–2 page conventions guide and worked examples for common consonant and vowel patterns
  • Design the Rater Training Manual (3–5 pages): specify rater prerequisites (native/near-native proficiency in reference accent, prior ESL teaching or phonetics training), selection criteria, training sessions (hours and content: anchor exposure, practice listening/transcribing), and certification procedure (raters must achieve Cohen's kappa ≥0.70 on a 50–100 word training sample before proceeding to full calibration)
  • Draft the Pronunciation-Consistency Scoring Rubric (1–2 pages): define the scoring scale (binary match/mismatch vs. 1–5 quality rating), inter-rater procedure (independent blind scoring), disagreement resolution (retraining if kappa <0.70, identify problematic phonemes), and edge-case handling (unclear audio, non-native but intelligible speech, code-switching)
  • Conduct inter-rater calibration by Month 10 (2027-08-13): recruit 3–4 raters, train on anchor and notation system (Months 8–9 = 2027-06-13 to 2027-07-13), score a 100–200 word pilot sample, calculate Cohen's kappa; if ≥0.75 (target), proceed to full recording; if 0.70–0.74, implement targeted retraining and retest; if <0.70, escalate to editorial board for pivot to hybrid model (speech-synthesis baseline plus human verification) or 4-week Phase 1 extension
  • Finalize and publish complete Pronunciation Guidance System documentation (anchor, notation, training manual, rubric, kappa proof) by Month 11 (2027-09-13) to satisfy the Phase 1 exit gate and enable Phase 2 pilot scoring
  • Secure audio recording infrastructure by Month 6 (2027-04-13): reserve studio with firm capacity guarantees (lead times, file delivery, backup protocols), establish all-in cost estimate per entry (speaker fees, editing, inter-rater scoring); if cost exceeds $20 per entry, design contingency (speech synthesis baseline or subset recording)

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or unspecified anchor-accent choice invites stakeholder disputes over regional bias (British, American, Australian, Indian) at Month 12 (2027-10-13) or later, triggering demands for multi-accent recording that inflate budget by $50K–$100K (estimate) and compress other Phase 1 work
  • Weak rater training or unclear scoring rubric causes inter-rater kappa to fall below 0.70 by the Month 10 (2027-08-13) deadline, triggering a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K estimate) or forced pivot to hybrid model (speech synthesis) that reduces measurement precision
  • Incomplete or inconsistent notation system (IPA vs. respelling vs. hybrid) leads to rater disagreement on how to transcribe and score learner pronunciation, inflating measurement error by 15–25% (estimate) and reducing statistical power to detect Clear English effects
  • Missing or inadequate exemplar recordings (fewer than 20–30 anchor-accent models) force raters to infer pronunciation conventions from the written notation alone, increasing training time and baseline disagreement
  • Failure to pre-test the rater-training procedure and calibration workflow at Month 8–9 (2027-06-13 to 2027-07-13) means real inter-rater reliability issues are discovered only during the Month 10 (2027-08-13) calibration study, leaving insufficient time for remediation before the Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-registration deadline
  • Audio infrastructure failure (studio unavailable, file corruption, storage loss) discovered after recording has begun (Months 6–11 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13) forces costly replacement or deletion, stranding pronunciation-guidance development and delaying lexicon completion
  • Vague or unspecified inter-rater disagreement-resolution procedure leaves raters uncertain whether to retrain, apply strict rules, or flag problematic words, causing inconsistent application and unreliable pronunciation scores during Phase 2 pilots

Worst Case Scenario: The Pronunciation Guidance System remains incomplete or ambiguous through Month 11 (2027-09-13): inter-rater kappa is 0.65 (below the 0.70 floor), the notation system is unclear, exemplars are missing, or the anchor-accent choice is challenged by stakeholders demanding multi-accent coverage. The editorial board cannot pre-register the pronunciation-consistency metric with confidence, forgoing the pre-analysis plan deadline. Phase 2 pilots proceed without reliable pronunciation scoring, inflating measurement noise by 20–30% (estimate) and making the pronunciation-consistency gate metric inconclusive at Month 24 (2028-10-13). The go/no-go decision becomes disputable; stakeholders claim the gate failed due to weak measurement rather than Clear English inadequacy, forcing a costly 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K estimate) to re-collect and re-analyze pronunciation data. If the extension is rejected, a contested no-go outcome strands Phase 3 adoption and damages credibility among ESL publishers and standards bodies.

Best Case Scenario: The Pronunciation Guidance System is finalized by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with clear, documented specifications: a defensible reference-accent anchor (e.g., General American with explicit IPA mappings to other varieties), a hybrid notation system (IPA for raters, simplified overlay for learners), comprehensive rater training and a well-tested scoring rubric. Inter-rater kappa reaches 0.76 (target achieved) by Month 10 (2027-08-13), enabling confident pre-registration of the pronunciation-consistency metric with explicit pass/fail thresholds. Phase 2 pilots proceed with reliable pronunciation scoring, yielding clean, statistically powered results on the pronunciation-consistency gate metric by Month 22 (2028-08-13). The Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision is defensible and not disputed; standards bodies and publishers accept the evidence, enabling Phase 3 public release and adoption by educational partners. The documented accent anchor and notation system become a reusable reference for future dialect or language extensions, multiplying the standard's value.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If inter-rater kappa remains below 0.70 after one round of retraining by Month 10 (2027-08-13), pivot to a hybrid model: use automated speech-synthesis or high-quality commercial pronunciation recordings as a baseline, then have raters verify/correct only the highest-friction phonemes (vowels, diphthongs, consonant clusters) for the core 1,500–2,000 most common or safety-critical lexicon entries. This reduces rater training burden by ~60% (estimate) and lowers per-entry cost, at the cost of reduced precision on lower-frequency words.
  • If the chosen reference accent is challenged at Month 6–9 (2027-04-13 to 2027-07-13) by stakeholders demanding multi-accent coverage, defer comprehensive multi-accent recording to post-v1.0 (Phase 3 or beyond). Document a clear policy (decided and published by Month 3 = 2027-01-13) that reserves 200–300 high-frequency words as a 'proof-of-concept' secondary-accent sample ($10K–$15K estimate) for Phase 3, allowing the project to demonstrate multi-accent feasibility without absorbing full multi-accent cost in Phase 1.
  • If audio-studio capacity is unavailable or costs exceed budget by Month 6 (2027-04-13), negotiate a hybrid production model: recruit native-speaker volunteers (university students, ESL teachers) for recording sessions on a shared schedule, using a low-cost portable microphone and noise-canceling software, rather than renting expensive studio time. Budget $30K–$50K (estimate) for volunteer coordination, file processing and backup infrastructure instead of $80K–$120K studio rental.
  • If the rater-training manual and rubric prove too complex or time-consuming (requiring >20 hours of training per rater), simplify the scoring task: reduce the rubric from a 1–5 quality scale to binary match/no-match against anchor exemplars, or provide raters with computer-assisted tools (waveform comparison software, spectrogram visualization) to support visual discrimination rather than purely auditory judgment. This reduces training time by 30–40% (estimate) and improves consistency.

Create Document 7: Pilot Partner Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs)

ID: 7d530971-4d91-4e4d-8132-fc1488329beb

Description: Legally binding agreements with each pilot partner organization (ESL programs and technical/safety-training sites) specifying: minimum learner enrollment (≥50 per partner by Month 13 = 2027-11-13), assessment schedule (4 in-person/virtual sessions across Months 13–24 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13), data-collection protocols (informed consent, audio recording, test administration), learner incentives ($50–$150 per learner estimate, breakdown by partner), partner payment terms ($30–$50 per session per learner estimate, or lump-sum), and penalty clauses (liquidated damages if recruitment shortfalls, make-up recruitment window by Month 15 = 2028-01-13, escalation contacts). Signed by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

Responsible Role Type: Project Manager / Regulatory Affairs Manager

Primary Template: University-Nonprofit Research Partnership Agreement template

Secondary Template: TESOL Program Partnership MOU template

Steps to Create:

  • Identify 4–5 candidate ESL programs and 3 candidate technical/safety-training organizations; confirm provisional interest and capacity by Month 1 (2026-11-13)
  • Draft a standard MOU template covering: scope (pilot study, experimental materials, 4-month engagement Months 13–24 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13); learner recruitment target (≥50); assessment schedule and on-site requirements (4 sessions, 1–2 hours each); incentive structure (who pays, how much, payment timing); data ownership and confidentiality (Clear English project owns data, partner commits to confidentiality); exit clause (if partner cannot meet enrollment by Month 14 = 2027-12-13, 30-day notice and make-up recruitment window by Month 15 = 2028-01-13); liability and indemnification (materials are experimental, partner assumes risk of use, materials not permitted for operational/life-critical use without explicit written approval)
  • Customize MOU for each partner: specify their committed enrollment (50–75 learners, estimate), partner staff roles (recruitment lead, assessment site coordinator), and partner payment structure (lump-sum vs. per-learner)
  • Include appendices: curriculum outline, informed-consent form, data-collection schedule, learner incentive structure, contact escalation procedures
  • Obtain signed MOUs from ≥3 ESL programs and ≥2 technical/safety-training organizations by Month 3 (2027-01-13); file originals and provide copies to each partner and the project lead

Approval Authorities: Project Manager (legal review), Partner Organization Authorized Representative, Program Sponsor (budget commitment)

Essential Information:

  • Specify the legal structure, authorization requirements and signature authority for each MOU (e.g., which partner official may bind the organization)
  • Define minimum learner enrollment commitment per partner (proposed: ≥50 per partner by Month 13 = 2027-11-13) and escalation procedure if recruitment falls short by Month 14 (2027-12-13)
  • Document the four assessment sessions across Months 13–24 (2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13): dates, location (on-site or virtual), duration, learner preparation and partner staff roles
  • Specify data-collection protocols: informed-consent forms (ethics-approved), audio recording and storage procedures (encrypted, access-controlled, retention policy), test administration standards and confidentiality obligations
  • Itemize learner incentives by partner ($50–$150 per learner estimate): payment schedule, conditions (e.g., paid upon completion of each session or lump-sum post-study), who administers distribution
  • Specify partner payment terms ($30–$50 per session per learner estimate, or alternative lump-sum for the full 4-session engagement across all enrolled learners), invoicing procedure and payment timeline
  • Include liquidated-damages or make-good clauses: if partner recruitment falls below 50 by Month 14 (2027-12-13), partner must recruit additional learners by Month 15 (2028-01-13), or project may recruit replacements and reduce partner payment accordingly
  • Clarify data ownership, use rights and publication: project owns all de-identified data; partner commits to confidentiality; project may publish aggregate results and learner-anonymized case examples
  • State liability and disclaimers: materials are experimental and non-commercial; partner assumes responsibility for safe administration; materials must not be used for operational, life-critical or safety-critical procedures without explicit written project approval and a separate risk-assessment review
  • Define exit and termination conditions: either party may terminate with 30 days' notice if the other materially breaches; termination does not waive confidentiality or data-ownership obligations; learners already enrolled complete the study under existing terms

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous or missing enrollment commitments could result in inadequate pilot cohort size (fewer than 80 completers per arm needed for statistical power), invalidating the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate metrics and forcing a costly 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K estimate)
  • Unclear assessment schedules or data-collection procedures could cause logistics failures (missed sessions, incomplete audio, inconsistent administration), inflating measurement error and reducing inter-rater reliability below the 0.70 floor threshold, forcing psychometric re-validation and a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K estimate)
  • Unspecified or disputed payment terms could trigger partner dissatisfaction, withdrawal mid-study or non-cooperation with assessment protocols, reducing data quality and cohort retention (dropout >30% proposed threshold), invalidating gate metrics
  • Missing or weak liability disclaimers expose the project to legal risk if a partner uses experimental Clear English materials in an operational or safety-critical context without approval, causing harm or regulatory investigation, and damage credibility with safety-critical stakeholders
  • Absent data-ownership and confidentiality clauses invite disputes over publication rights, partner use of learner data, or leaks of sensitive participant information, triggering legal claims and privacy violations (GDPR, US state law), and undermining learner trust and recruitment for future studies
  • Undefined exit conditions and make-good clauses allow partners to withdraw or under-deliver on recruitment without consequences, stranding the project with insufficient data and forcing costly contingency recruitment ($30K–$50K estimate) or timeline extension

Worst Case Scenario: A partner organization signs an MOU without clear enrollment commitments or liability disclaimers, then either enrolls only 25 learners (33% below target) and claims force majeure, or uses Clear English materials in a safety-critical operational procedure without approval, causing a participant injury or near-miss. The project faces simultaneous crises: insufficient pilot data (fewer than 80 completers per arm, invalidating the go/no-go gate), a liability claim or regulatory investigation, partner withdrawal from the study, and reputational damage from the safety incident. The Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate decision is postponed 6+ months while the project remediates and re-recruits, Phase 2 extends into Month 30–36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13), and Phase 3 launch is delayed to Month 42 (2030-04-13) or cancelled, stranding $1.2M–$1.5M in unspent Phase 3 and reserve funds.

Best Case Scenario: All MOUs are signed by Month 3 (2027-01-13) with unambiguous enrollment targets (≥50 per partner, 4–5 partners total = 200–250 learners across ESL and technical cohorts), clear assessment schedules integrated into partner-institution course calendars, and signed liability disclaimers that prevent unauthorized use. Partners and learners comply fully with protocols; dropout stays at or below the 30% proposed threshold; inter-rater reliability and data quality exceed targets (kappa 0.80+). All 4 assessment sessions complete on schedule by Month 24 (2028-10-13), 30-day follow-up data is complete, and all gate metrics meet or exceed thresholds. The Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision is unambiguous and fully defended; Phase 3 launch occurs by Month 30 (2029-04-13) as planned; partner organizations become early adopters and testimonials, credibility with educators and standards bodies is established, and steward organizations express serious interest.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Engage a research-contract firm (e.g., a consulting firm with experience in multi-site educational research) to draft, negotiate and manage all MOUs on the project's behalf by Month 2 (2026-12-13), reducing legal and operational burden on the core team. Cost: $15K–$30K (estimate). This accelerates signature and clarifies roles but introduces vendor dependency.
  • If a partner declines to sign a full MOU, offer a simplified letter of intent (1 page) that commits to enrollment targets and assessment schedules only, deferring payment terms and detailed protocols to a separate vendor invoice agreement. This lowers negotiation friction but risks ambiguity on liability and data use; supplement with a separate data-sharing addendum.
  • For partners with existing research-ethics protocols (e.g., universities with standing IRB agreements), adopt and reference their institutional consent and data-handling templates rather than creating new ones, reducing ethics-review lead time by 2–4 weeks (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13 instead of Month 2–4 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13 instead of 2026-12-13 to 2027-02-13). Verify compliance with the project's data-retention and publication-rights requirements.
  • If partner enrollment commitments cannot be met by Month 3 (2027-01-13), activate a contingency-recruitment clause that allows the project to directly recruit replacement learners from the partner's existing network (with partner's referral support), shifting recruitment responsibility from the partner to the project. Requires explicit MOU language and a $20K–$40K (estimate) contingency budget for direct-recruitment advertising.
  • If a partner withdraws mid-study (breach detected at Month 18–20 = 2028-04-13 to 2028-06-13), invoke the make-good clause requiring the partner to recruit replacement learners by Month 21 (2028-07-13), or allow the project to recruit directly and reduce the partner's final payment by the shortfall amount. Escalate to the project lead and editorial board within 1 week of discovery.
  • If inter-rater reliability or assessment-quality issues emerge at the Phase 1 exit gate (Month 12 = 2027-10-13) or during Phase 2 (Month 18 = 2028-04-13 check), trigger a re-training and re-standardization cycle with partner assessment coordinators: conduct a 1–2 day in-person training at Month 13–14 (2027-11-13 to 2027-12-13) or Month 19–20 (2027-11-13 to 2027-12-13 or 2028-05-13 to 2028-06-13) at project cost ($10K–$15K estimate) to align scoring and procedures.

Create Document 8: Data Protection and Privacy Policy

ID: b3a58520-c73f-4e3b-90b2-ac9c14faa57d

Description: Comprehensive GDPR and US state law-compliant document specifying: data types collected (pronunciation audio, test scores, demographics), collection purpose (pilot measurement for gate metrics), lawful processing grounds (participant consent + research exemption), retention periods (audio 3 years post-analysis; scores 5 years for replication; consent forms 3 years minimum), access controls (authorized team members only, signed data-use agreements), encryption standards (AES-256 or equivalent, FIPS 140-2 validated), backup and disaster-recovery procedures, participant rights (access, correction, deletion within 30 days), breach-notification protocol, and Data Protection Impact Assessment summary (GDPR Article 35). Published alongside informed-consent forms. Audience: research participants, ethics committees, data-protection authorities.

Responsible Role Type: Data Protection Officer / Legal Counsel

Primary Template: GDPR Data Protection Policy template (ICO or national equivalents)

Secondary Template: US University IRB research-participant privacy policy template

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 1 (2026-11-13), commission a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) under GDPR Article 35 or UK Data Protection Act 2018 Schedule 1, documenting: lawful processing ground (explicit consent + research exemption for academic research), data-minimization strategy (inter-rater reliability piloted on 200–300 word subset before full 5,000-word recording), processing necessity, retention schedule, and risk mitigation (encryption, access controls, breach notification)
  • Draft the Privacy Policy (2–3 pages) in plain language: explain what data are collected (pronunciation audio recordings, reading-comprehension test responses, demographic info), why (to measure learning outcomes on Clear English rules), who can access (core research team, auditors, data-protection authorities if breach), how long data are kept (audio 3 years post-analysis unless participant requests longer retention for archival; test scores 5 years for study replication; consent forms 3 years minimum for compliance audit), and participants' rights (see their data, ask for corrections, request deletion within 30 days). Include data-breach notification procedure (internal alert within 24 hours, participant notification within 72 hours if data is material to privacy, regulator notification per GDPR Article 33).
  • Specify encryption and security: audio stored on encrypted servers (AES-256, FIPS 140-2 validated, or equivalent cloud-provider encryption like AWS KMS or Azure Key Vault); access controlled via role-based credentials and audit logs; backups encrypted and geographically separated; encryption keys held in split custody (project team + external escrow service, or cloud-provider key management service)
  • Define participant deletion rights and workflow: if a participant requests deletion, audio file is securely wiped within 30 days; test scores may be anonymized and retained if needed for aggregate analysis; participant receives written confirmation of deletion
  • Draft plain-language Informed Consent Form (1–2 pages in English and ESL learners' home languages if feasible): explain the study, data collection, retention, rights, and risks in accessible language; include signature/digital consent option; provide a copy to each participant
  • Publish Privacy Policy and Informed Consent Form on the project website by Month 8 (2027-06-13); finalize after ethics-board approval (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) for any required language changes

Approval Authorities: Data Protection Officer (lead author), Institutional Review Board (ethics approval), Legal Counsel (GDPR/state law compliance), Project Lead (finalization)

Essential Information:

  • Define data types collected during Phase 2 pilots (pronunciation audio recordings, reading-comprehension test scores, demographic information, consent forms) and specify retention periods for each: audio 3 years post-analysis unless participant requests deletion; test scores 5 years for study replication; consent forms 3 years minimum for compliance audit.
  • Document lawful processing grounds under GDPR Article 6 and US state privacy laws: explicit informed consent + research exemption for academic research; specify any third parties with data access (core research team, ethics auditors, data-protection authorities only in breach scenarios).
  • Specify encryption and access-control standards: AES-256 or equivalent (FIPS 140-2 validated or cloud-provider equivalent); role-based credential access with audit logs; geographic separation of backups; encryption key custody (split or external escrow).
  • Detail breach-notification protocol: internal alert within 24 hours; participant notification within 72 hours if data is material to privacy rights; regulator notification per GDPR Article 33 (UK ICO, US state Attorney General, or equivalent).
  • Define participant rights and deletion workflow: right to access recorded data, request corrections within 30 days, request deletion within 30 days (with written confirmation); anonymization option for test scores if retained for aggregate analysis.
  • Draft plain-language informed-consent form in English and (if feasible) ESL learners' home languages: explain study purpose (pilot measurement for Clear English gate metrics), data collection methods, retention schedule, risks, participant rights, confidentiality protections, and withdrawal option.
  • Conduct and document a Data Protection Impact Assessment (GDPR Article 35) by Month 1 (2026-11-13): identify lawful ground (consent + research exemption), describe data-minimization strategy (inter-rater reliability piloted on 200–300 word subset before full 5,000-word recording), assess processing necessity, enumerate retention rules, and risk-mitigation measures (encryption, access controls, breach response).
  • Identify regulatory approval requirements: IRB (Institutional Review Board) or ethics-board sign-off in the US; UK research ethics committee approval or ICO guidance where applicable; confirmation of approval scope and any conditions by Month 6 (2027-04-13).
  • Publish the Privacy Policy (2–3 pages) and Informed Consent Form (1–2 pages) on the project website by Month 8 (2027-06-13) after ethics-board approval; provide printed or digital copies to all participants at enrolment; update copies annually or upon material changes to data handling.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inadequate encryption or access controls could expose pronunciation audio (biometric data) to unauthorized access, triggering GDPR Article 32 breaches and regulatory investigation by data-protection authorities (ICO, state attorneys general); participants could claim privacy violation and sue for damages or statutory compensation.
  • Missing or unclear data-retention schedules could lead to unlawful data retention past the retention period, violating GDPR Article 5(1)(e) and state data-protection laws; auditors or regulators could demand immediate deletion, disrupting replication studies or post-hoc analysis.
  • Inadequate informed-consent language (too technical, unclear risks, missing withdrawal procedures) could invalidate participant consent and trigger ethics-board rejection of the pilot; studies conducted without valid consent may be deemed unethical and results unusable for the gate decision.
  • Delayed ethics-board or IRB approval (e.g., 8-week delay at Month 2–4 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-02-13 instead of Month 6 = 2027-04-13) compresses the Phase 2 recruitment window by 8 weeks (6.7% of Phase 2 timeline); shortfall in enrolment by ~60 participants (proportional to compressed timeline) could drop effective sample below the n=80 per-arm minimum, reducing statistical power by 15–25%.
  • Missing breach-notification protocol or delayed notification (>72 hours) violates GDPR Article 33 and state breach-notification laws; regulators can impose fines up to €10M or 2% of revenue (GDPR) plus reputational damage and participant distrust; failure to notify affected participants could trigger class-action privacy litigation.
  • Absence of participant deletion rights or unclear deletion workflow could violate GDPR Articles 17 and 21; participants denied deletion could file formal complaints with data-protection authorities, triggering investigation; undeleted data could become evidence of non-compliance, inflating fines.
  • Vague data-minimization or purpose-limitation language could expose the project to regulatory challenge that audio collection is excessive or that data are used beyond the stated research purpose; regulators could require destruction of excess data or prohibit secondary analysis, limiting replication and future improvements.
  • Failure to conduct a DPIA by Month 1 (2026-11-13) leaves high-risk processing (biometric audio recording of vulnerable populations, ESL learners) without documented risk assessment; ethics boards may reject the pilot, and regulators may impose enforcement action if a breach or complaint occurs and no DPIA is available to show reasonable safeguards.

Worst Case Scenario: A privacy breach of pronunciation audio (e.g., server misconfiguration exposing unencrypted files or unauthorized access via compromised credentials) is discovered at Month 16 (2028-02-13) mid-pilot. Notification and investigation delays trigger GDPR Article 33 violations; regulators (ICO, US state AG) launch enforcement action; participants and data-protection advocates publicize the breach; the project's credibility is damaged; ethics boards halt Phase 2 pilots pending remediation (3–6 month delay); liability litigation from affected participants ensues. Concurrently, inadequate informed consent (discovered during ethics-board audit) invalidates pilot data, forcing a Phase 2 restart or no-go at the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate. Combined impact: pilot data unusable, gate decision delayed or failed, Phase 2–3 timeline and budget (estimated $2M–$2.05M) at risk, and public trust in Clear English permanently damaged. Scenario likelihood: low (security and consent breaches are preventable with diligent early planning); impact: extremely high (existential to project credibility).

Best Case Scenario: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), a comprehensive DPIA and ethics-compliant protocols are drafted and approved by the relevant ethics board and data-protection authority by Month 6 (2027-04-13). Encryption, access controls, and breach-notification procedures are implemented and audited by Month 8 (2027-06-13). Clear, multilingual informed-consent forms are published on the project website by Month 8 (2027-06-13) and provided to all 460+ pilot participants at enrolment. Participant deletion requests and withdrawal are processed within 30 days with written confirmation. Phase 2 pilots proceed without ethics or privacy delays, all 460 participants are recruited and retained (70%+ follow-up), and the gate decision at Month 24 (2028-10-13) rests on uncontested, legally defensible data. The Privacy Policy and DPIA become model documentation for ESL and language-education research; regulatory authorities and ethics boards treat Clear English pilots as a benchmark for ethical data handling in education research. Phase 3 adoption is accelerated by demonstrated compliance and participant trust. Public credibility is enhanced; third-party educators and standards bodies view the project as trustworthy stewards of sensitive learner data.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If IRB or ethics-board approval is delayed beyond Month 6 (2027-04-13), pilot start can be deferred to Month 15 (2028-01-13) and Phase 2 compressed to 9 months (ending Month 21 = 2028-07-13), with data analysis and gate decision at Month 23 (2028-09-13). This reduces the 30-day follow-up period or requires overlapping cohorts; statistical power may drop by 10–15%, but the gate decision remains feasible within the Month 24 (2028-10-13) deadline if enrolment and retention targets are met.
  • If encryption or secure-storage infrastructure is unavailable by Month 6 (2027-04-13), audio recording can be deferred and the pronunciation-consistency metric can be scored on a smaller supervised sample (N=50–100) in Month 11–12 (2027-09-13 to 2027-10-13) using live, in-person rater observation rather than recorded playback. This eliminates the need for long-term audio storage but reduces measurement robustness and inter-rater reliability documentation; the pronunciation-consistency gate metric may become weaker or secondary.
  • If participant recruitment is slower than projected (e.g., only 300 enrolments by Month 15 = 2028-01-13 instead of 460 by Month 13 = 2027-11-13), Phase 2 can be extended by 6 weeks (pushing data lock to Month 23 = 2028-09-13, gate decision to Month 24 = 2028-10-13 at final extension). This costs an additional $150K (estimate, 6 weeks of Phase 2 operations, or about $1.2M/12 x 1.15 months) and exhausts the pre-gate reserve draw allowance ($175K cap), leaving no contingency for rework if inter-rater reliability is below target.
  • If informed-consent language is rejected by ethics boards as insufficiently detailed or clear, consent can be re-drafted with ethics-board input (2–4 week cycle) and re-administered to participants with an amended-consent form. This adds 2–4 weeks to the ethics-approval timeline (pushing approval to Month 8–10 = 2027-06-13 to 2027-08-13) but preserves participant buy-in if the new language is simpler or more reassuring. Participants must re-consent; any who decline are withdrawn, reducing enrolment by an estimated 5–10%.
  • If breach-notification procedures are questioned by regulators post-breach (i.e., actual breach occurs and response is audited), an external data-protection consultant can be hired at Month 16–18 (2028-02-13 to 2028-04-13) to conduct a post-incident review and recommend remedial measures (estimated cost $15K–$30K). This does not prevent the original breach but can mitigate regulatory penalties if the response was reasonable; however, damage to project credibility is substantial.

Create Document 9: Pilot Recruitment and Retention Plan

ID: a448d45e-112a-47b5-aea4-39df5b421c54

Description: Operational plan specifying recruitment targets (≥115 enrolled per arm = 460 total by Month 13 = 2027-11-13), recruitment strategy per partner (marketing channels, eligibility criteria, enrollment milestones), learner incentive structure ($50–$150 per learner estimate, breakdown), partner payment terms ($30–$50 per session estimate or lump-sum), dropout-risk mitigation (incentives, flexible scheduling, peer cohorts, make-up sessions within ±1 week), and monthly retention tracking (dashboard showing % enrolled, dropout-to-date, projected completers). Probabilistic enrollment model with 50th/75th/90th percentile scenarios based on pilot baseline study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13). Includes escalation protocol: if enrollment misses interim milestones by >2 weeks, activate acceleration tactics (increased incentives, evening sessions, $20K–$30K budget).

Responsible Role Type: Phase 2 Cohort Manager / Recruitment Specialist

Secondary Template: National Institutes of Health (NIH) recruitment and retention guidance

Steps to Create:

  • By Month 2 (2026-12-13), conduct a Pilot Baseline Study (N=20–30 learners at 1–2 sites, Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13): measure recruitment conversion rate (% of eligible population converting to enrollment), baseline dropout rate (% completing all 4 assessment sessions without active management), and demographic patterns (age, language background, work stability, motivation). Budget $15K–$20K (estimate).
  • Develop a probabilistic recruitment model: use baseline data to estimate enrollment and dropout distributions; forecast completers under 50th, 75th, 90th percentile dropout scenarios (e.g., 75th percentile dropout = 40%, not 30%); use 75th percentile as planning baseline.

  • Specify learner incentives: certificate of completion ($0 cost, high perceived value for ESL learners), course credit (if available through partner), gift cards or stipends ($50–$150 per learner estimate based on assessment burden and regional wage, tiered for full completion vs. 3-of-4 sessions). Total incentive budget: $23K–$69K ($50–$150 × 460 learners, estimate).
  • Specify partner payments: per-session payment ($30–$50 per learner per session, estimate, paid to partner for administrative and facility costs) or lump-sum ($12K–$20K per partner estimate). Total partner payment: $55K–$92K (estimate). Include invoicing and reconciliation procedures.
  • Establish dropout-response protocol: weekly attendance tracking by cohort manager; if a learner misses a session, outreach within 24 hours (phone, email, in-person visit); offer one make-up session within ±1 week; if learner misses 2 consecutive sessions, conduct a brief check-in to assess barriers (work conflict, health, childcare) and offer alternative scheduling or incentive boost ($20–$30 bonus, estimate, if retention is at risk); if learner misses 3 sessions, mark as dropout but maintain contact for 30-day follow-up.

Flag to board if lower confidence bound falls below 70 per arm, triggering Phase 2 delay decision by Month 15 (2028-01-13) rather than Month 22 (2028-08-13) when too late to recover.
  • Establish contingency budget: $20K–$30K (estimate) for recruitment shortfall or dropout exceeding 35% (e.g., bonus payments, evening sessions, transportation reimbursement, partner incentive increases). Activate by Month 8 (2027-06-13) if enrollment tracking suggests shortfall.
  • Publish final Recruitment and Retention Plan by Month 4 (2027-02-13); circulate to all partners and obtain sign-off on enrollment targets and timelines by Month 6 (2027-04-13)

Approval Authorities: Cohort Manager (lead), Project Manager (budget and contingency authority), Pilot Partners (enrollment commitment)

Essential Information:

  • Specify recruitment targets: minimum 115 enrolled per arm (460 total across 4 pilot arms) by Month 13 (2027-11-13), with tolerated dropout ≤30% to reach 80 completers per arm (320 total); document enrollment milestones for each partner (40% by Month 8 = 2027-06-13, 70% by Month 10 = 2027-08-13, 100% by Month 13 = 2027-11-13).
  • Detail recruitment strategy per partner: identify 3–4 adult ESL programs and 2–3 technical/safety-training organizations; specify marketing channels (email, social media, in-class announcement, staff referral), eligibility criteria (age, ESL proficiency, availability), and enrollment window (Months 12–13 = 2027-10-13 to 2027-11-13).
  • Define learner incentive structure: certificate of completion, course credit (if available), and tiered stipends ($50–$150 per learner, estimate, based on assessment burden); total incentive budget $23K–$69K (estimate); bonus structure for high-retention scenarios ($20–$30 additional, estimate).
  • Specify partner payment terms: per-session payment ($30–$50 per learner per session, estimate) or lump-sum arrangement ($12K–$20K per partner, estimate); total partner payment budget $55K–$92K (estimate); include invoicing, reconciliation and sign-off procedures by Month 6 (2027-04-13).
  • Establish dropout-response protocol: weekly attendance tracking; 24-hour outreach (phone, email, visit) if a learner misses a session; one make-up session within ±1 week; barrier assessment at 2 consecutive misses; continuation incentive or alternative scheduling; mark as dropout at 3 consecutive misses but maintain 30-day follow-up contact.
  • Design monthly Retention Dashboard: cumulative enrollments by partner, dropout count and reasons (work conflict, health, family, lost interest, scheduling), dropout rate by session number, projected completers at Month 22 (2028-08-13) with 95% confidence interval; escalation trigger if lower confidence bound drops below 70 per arm, flagging to board by Month 15 (2028-01-13).
  • Conduct Pilot Baseline Study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13, N=20–30 learners at 1–2 sites, budget $15K–$20K, estimate): measure recruitment conversion rate (% of eligible converting to enrollment), baseline dropout rate (% completing all 4 sessions without active management) and demographic patterns (age, language background, work stability, motivation); use results to calibrate probabilistic enrollment model.
  • Build probabilistic recruitment model: forecast completers under 50th, 75th, 90th percentile dropout scenarios (e.g., 75th percentile dropout = 40%, above the 30% tolerated assumption); use 75th percentile as conservative planning baseline.
  • Establish contingency budget: $20K–$30K (estimate) for recruitment shortfall or dropout exceeding 35% (e.g., bonus payments, evening sessions, transportation reimbursement, partner incentive increases); activate by Month 8 (2027-06-13) if tracking suggests shortfall.
  • Publish final Recruitment and Retention Plan by Month 4 (2027-02-13); circulate to all partners and obtain written sign-off on enrollment targets, timelines, payment terms and dropout-response procedures by Month 6 (2027-04-13); create a dashboard template for monthly reporting.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Enrollment shortfall below 80 completers per arm (320 total) or dropout above 30% invalidates the four gate metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) by reducing statistical power; undetectable true effects lead to false-negative go/no-go outcome, potentially killing the standard despite efficacy.
  • Unclear or misaligned enrollment targets across partners causes recruiting confusion, leads to under-commitment by individual sites, and fragments the pilot into weak, non-comparable cohorts; re-recruitment after Month 13 (2027-11-13) consumes 8–12 weeks, compressing the pilot window by 20–25% and forcing reduced assessment quality.
  • Ambiguous or unfunded dropout-mitigation procedures result in inconsistent learner support across sites, elevate attrition above the 30% planning assumption, and degrade the completeness of 30-day follow-up data, rendering the retention gate metric unreliable.
  • Inadequate learner incentives ($<$50 per learner, estimate) or partner payment misalignment trigger recruitment failure and site withdrawal mid-pilot, forcing rapid re-recruitment that consumes $30K–$50K (estimate) contingency and delays Phase 2 by 4–8 weeks.
  • Missing or vague escalation triggers and decision authority allow enrollment shortfalls to persist unaddressed until Month 20–22 (2028-06-13 to 2028-08-13), when remediation is too late to recover; board discovers at data lock that statistical power is insufficient, triggering a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension costing $300K–$600K (estimate).
  • Poorly designed Retention Dashboard or infrequent monitoring (monthly rather than weekly) delays detection of dropout trends by 2–4 weeks, eliminating the window for corrective action; low-performing sites cannot be identified or supported early, and sample heterogeneity increases measurement error by 15–20% (estimate).
  • Incomplete Pilot Baseline Study or failure to calibrate the probabilistic model against empirical dropout data leads to optimistic enrollment assumptions; planning for 30% dropout when actual dropout is 40–50% (estimate) results in undershoot of 25–50 completers per arm, rendering the gate invalid.
  • Unclear participant confidentiality, incentive compliance or data-handling procedures (e.g., unclear how stipends are taxed, withheld, or reported) create administrative friction, erode learner trust, and increase dropout risk by 5–10 percentage points (estimate).

Worst Case Scenario: Enrollment stalls at 60–70% of target by Month 11 (2027-09-13), dropout exceeds 40% across sites despite mitigation efforts, and pilot completion falls to 50–60 learners per arm (200–240 total, below the 320 minimum). The gate metrics become statistically unreliable and inconclusive. The board faces a forced choice at Month 24 (2028-10-13): declare a no-go outcome and strand $1.2M (Phase 3 + reserve), or extend Phase 2 by 3–6 months at a cost of $300K–$600K (estimate), pushing v1.0 release to Month 33–39 (2029-07-13 to 2030-01-13) and killing near-term adoption momentum. If extension is chosen but recruitment barriers persist, a second extension becomes politically and financially unviable, resulting in project termination and reputational damage to the program and partner organizations.

Best Case Scenario: The Pilot Baseline Study identifies high recruitment conversion (60–70%) and baseline dropout (20–25%), enabling confident enrollment by Month 13 (2027-11-13). Partner enrollment and retention tracking proceeds on schedule; incentives and support protocols keep dropout at 25–28%, yielding 115–120 completers per arm (460–480 total, 440–500+ enrolled). The four gate metrics are measured reliably (inter-rater kappa ≥0.75, follow-up completion ≥70%), ordinal error reduction meets the ≥25% threshold, pronunciation consistency exceeds the 15% target, and comprehension speed stays within the 10% tolerance. The Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go outcome is unambiguous, partners and educators accept the gate decision with confidence, Phase 3 public release proceeds on schedule by Month 30 (2029-04-13), and early adopters point to robust pilot evidence when justifying adoption investment.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If enrollment lags at Month 8 (2027-06-13), activate contingency budget ($20K–$30K, estimate) for accelerated incentives (increase stipends by $25–$50 per learner, estimate), evening or weekend sessions at ESL programs, and transportation reimbursement ($10–$20 per session, estimate) to remove practical barriers; increase partner payments temporarily to offset administrative burden of rapid enrollment.
  • If a pilot partner signals dropout risk (>40% attrition projected), immediately implement partner-specific intensive support: weekly check-ins with learners by partner staff, in-session buddy pairings, and a flexible make-up schedule within ±2 weeks instead of ±1 week; allocate an additional $5K–$10K (estimate) per high-risk partner.
  • If statistical power analysis reveals that 80 completers per arm is unachievable given baseline data, reduce the number of arms or measurement time points: e.g., measure comprehension speed and ordinal error rate at two time points (pre/post) instead of three, allowing statistical power to be maintained at 70–75 completers per arm instead of 80; document the trade-off in reduced secondary outcomes.
  • If pilot partner organizational capacity appears strained, recruit a fourth ESL program or a community-college partner by Month 7 (2027-05-13) as a backup, targeting 25–40 learners to distribute load and reduce per-site burden; add this partner to the written commitment framework by Month 6 (2027-04-13) contingent on enrollment tracking results.
  • If learner dropout is driven by assessment burden (compliance costs), redesign the assessment schedule: distribute the four assessment sessions across 6–8 weeks instead of 4 weeks, reducing time per session by 30–40% (estimate); move the 30-day follow-up to an online, self-paced format (5–10 minutes) instead of a supervised in-person session, reducing dropout risk by an estimated 5–10 percentage points.
  • If contingency budget is insufficient ($20K–$30K remaining), seek in-kind contributions from partners (e.g., free facility use, staff time for recruitment and scheduling) to offset cash incentive costs; formalize with a 'match' framework in the partner commitment letter (e.g., 'partner contributes $X in in-kind administrative support').
  • If monthly Retention Dashboard reveals a consistent outlier site (dropout >45%), place that site on a 'corrective action' plan: weekly (not monthly) check-ins with the cohort manager, on-site support visits by the educator liaison, and escalated incentive offers; if dropout remains above 40% by Month 15 (2028-01-13), consider pausing new enrollment at that site and reallocating remaining target to other partners.

Document decision rule: valid data with metric failures = NO-GO; invalid/inconclusive data = board-decided extension

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete risk identification or vague descriptions could allow critical threats (e.g. regulatory rejection, assessment validity) to go unmanaged until they become critical blockers, forcing last-minute scope cuts or timeline extensions that destabilize pilots and invalidate the go/no-go gate decision.
  • Absent or unclear mitigation strategies would leave risk owners without actionable steps, allowing drift and reactive (rather than proactive) problem-solving; lack of specific timeline commits (e.g. 'engage regulators early') makes slippage easier to ignore until it is too late.
  • Missing escalation triggers and contingency budgets would prevent the project manager and editorial board from detecting and responding to emerging risks in time; a $85K Phase 1 extension discovered at Month 10 (2027-08-13) instead of Month 4 (2027-02-13) forces an abrupt replan and undermines timeline confidence.
  • Unassigned risk ownership would diffuse accountability and responsibility; without named risk owners, no one is explicitly accountable for mitigation status, monitoring or escalation, allowing key risks to be deferred or forgotten.
  • Failure to update the register monthly and quarterly would cause the document to become stale; risks identified at Month 3 (2027-01-13) that are not revisited until Month 12 (2027-10-13) could have evolved into critical problems, making the register a historical artifact rather than an active management tool.
  • Lack of contingency budget allocation and reserve-draw rules would make unplanned overruns surprise the project; without clear rules on when and how to tap the $0.35M reserve, ad-hoc draws could deplete reserves before critical needs (e.g. metric revalidation) are funded.
  • Ambiguous decision authority (who decides when to extend Phase 1 or invoke a no-go?) would create governance paralysis; unclear escalation paths could result in contested, delayed or ignored risk decisions at the board level.
  • Disconnection between identified risks and the go/no-go gate criteria would allow risks to be managed in isolation; an ignored educator pushback risk could weaken pilot data quality undetected until Month 24 (2028-10-13), when a marginal gate outcome becomes disputable.

Worst Case Scenario: At Month 18 (2028-04-13), a combination of unmitigated risks converges: (1) regulatory authorities have not responded to outreach, delaying partner approvals by 6 weeks, pushing pilot enrolment into Month 15 (2028-01-13); (2) inter-rater reliability testing at Month 10 (2027-08-13) revealed kappa 0.62 (below the 0.70 floor), but retraining and a second round of calibration were deferred to "resolve later"; (3) an educator focus group (Month 6 = 2027-04-13) flagged resistance to the prefix-ordinal marker, but no mitigation action was documented or board-escalated, leading to 25% non-compliance in pilot materials by Month 18 (2028-04-13); (4) audio production ran 8 weeks over budget and consumed $185K (exceeding the pre-gate draw cap), straining Phase 2 recruitment incentives. By Month 22 (2028-08-13), the data lock reveals: pilot sample is 68 completers per arm (below the 80 minimum), 30-day follow-up completion is 58% (below the 70% gate threshold), ordinal-rule-compliance variance is high, and inter-rater kappa on pronunciation is still 0.68. The editorial board must choose: extend Phase 2 by 3 months (cost ~$300K, exceeding available reserve and forcing Phase 3 cuts) or invoke a no-go decision based on inconclusive data (stranding $1.2M in Phase 2–3 budget and delaying market entry to Month 36 = 2029-10-13 or beyond). Either outcome undermines credibility: an extension signals poor project planning; a no-go on weak data suggests the gate was too ambitious or the measurement was flawed. Post-hoc stakeholder criticism ("the register didn't flag these risks early" and "no one was accountable for mitigation") compounds damage to the editorial board's governance legitimacy and the standard's perceived rigor.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), the risk register is fully operationalized with 20 documented risks, clear ownership, escalation triggers and monthly review discipline. Regulatory outreach (Risk #1 owner: regulatory liaison) identifies approval pathways and secures non-binding advisory letters by Month 4 (2027-02-13), allowing pilot partner recruitment to proceed without delay. Assessment-validity risk (Risk #3 owner: psychometrician) is proactively managed: construct-validity analysis and confound controls are built into the pre-analysis plan draft (Month 5 = 2027-03-13), a small validity study (N=20–30) is completed by Month 11 (2027-09-13) confirming kappa ≥0.75, and metrics are pre-registered on schedule. Editorial-board deadlock (Risk #4) is prevented by an explicit charter (Month 1 = 2026-11-13) and an agreed external arbiter (Month 5 = 2027-03-13), allowing disputed rules to be resolved by Month 10 (2027-08-13) without cascading delays. Audio production (Risk #6 owner: audio production manager) secures a firm studio contract by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and completes all 5,000 entries on schedule by Month 11 (2027-09-13) within budget; rater training is completed by Month 9 (2027-07-13) with kappa validation documented. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), Phase 1 exits cleanly with rules locked, audio complete, metrics pre-registered, lexicon coverage audited at 87%, and ethics approval in hand. Phase 2 enrolment achieves 125 per arm by Month 13 (2027-11-13), providing 10% attrition headroom. A Month 18 (2028-04-13) midpoint check reveals on-track progress with only minor variance (educator compliance at 94%, audio quality spot-checks passing, follow-up completion on target). The Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision is clean: all four metrics meet pre-registered thresholds, sample sizes exceed minimums, inter-rater reliability is robust, and validity conditions hold. The board votes GO with confidence, public release proceeds by Month 30 (2029-04-13) with a written steward commitment in place, and Phase 3 outreach achieves 4+ third-party adopters by Month 36 (2029-10-13). The register becomes a model for other language-standardization initiatives, demonstrating that disciplined risk management enables credible, evidence-gated program decisions.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If comprehensive risk identification and primary risk list are difficult to scope by Month 1 (2026-11-13), use a lightweight rapid-risk workshop (2 days, Months 0.5–1 = 2026-10-27 to 2026-11-13) with the project lead, key workstream owners (linguistics, assessment, operations) and the editorial board chair to brainstorm top 12–15 risks (using the assumptions.md and project-plan.md risk sections as a starting point), assign owners on the spot, and commit to a 30-day review cycle; this produces a Minimum Viable Risk Register by Month 1.5 (2026-11-28) that can be expanded incrementally rather than waiting for a perfect baseline.
  • If monthly risk-owner updates prove burdensome, adopt a biweekly flash-update format (30-minute call, Months 1–12 = 2026-11-13 to 2027-10-13, then monthly thereafter) where owners report only 'on-track', 'variance' or 'escalation needed'; project manager escalates variance/escalation items to the editorial board asynchronously via memo, reducing meeting overhead while maintaining discipline.
  • If detailed contingency-budget allocation is difficult to estimate upfront, allocate contingency reserve ($0.35M) into a flexible fund governed by a simple decision rule: (a) routine mitigation costs <$20K approved by project manager; (b) costs $20K–$50K approved by project manager + budget officer; (c) costs >$50K approved by editorial board with supporting risk narrative; (d) draws are capped at $175K total before Phase 2 go/no-go decision; (e) remaining balance released only post-go/no-go. This defers detailed estimation to the month when the risk is imminent and actual costs can be quoted.
  • If monthly risk reviews drain board time, separate the monthly operational update (project manager and risk owners) from the quarterly strategic risk discussion (editorial board and risk officer); operational updates identify emerging trends; quarterly board meetings make contingency decisions and adjust mitigation strategy if needed.
  • If tracking 20+ risks across the project becomes unwieldy, use a risk-heat matrix (likelihood vs. severity) to define which risks require weekly tracking (high/high), which monthly (med/high or high/med), and which quarterly (med/med or low/high); focus active management on the top 8–10 critical-path risks, with the remainder reviewed for status changes quarterly.
  • If electronic version control and intranet publication of the risk register are not yet in place by Month 1 (2026-11-13), maintain the register as a shared Google Sheet or Excel file with dated versions and a one-page summary memo updated monthly; the key is disciplined updating and visibility, not the platform.
  • If external risk expertise (e.g. applied linguisticsproject-risk specialist) is not available or affordable, engage one focused external advisor (Day rate ~$2,000–$3,000, estimate) for a half-day Month-1 risk-framing workshop and a Month-12 mid-project risk-health check; this provides external credibility and calibration without ongoing consulting cost.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Absence of a detailed itemized budget baseline by Month 1 (2026-11-13) leaves Phase 1 spending undisciplined; funds are drawn ad-hoc without visibility, delaying corrective action. By Month 6 (2027-04-13), cumulative cost overruns may exceed $100K before detection, consuming the pre-gate reserve and narrowing Phase 2 scope.
  • Lack of quantitative variance triggers and escalation procedures means cost overruns are discovered late (Month 9 = 2027-07-13 or later) when corrective options are limited. A $300K overrun (estimate) discovered at Month 9 (2027-07-13) leaves only 3 months to cut scope before Phase 2 begins, forcing either compressed pilots (fewer cohorts, lighter assessments) that weaken gate evidence or unauthorized contingency draws.
  • Unclear contingency-reserve draw rules allow unlimited or uncoordinated draws before Month 24 (2028-10-13), exhausting the $350K reserve by Month 18 (2028-04-13) on non-gate items (office upgrades, staff additions, scope creep). A no-go decision at Month 24 (2028-10-13) then has no unspent funds to return, stranding the project's cost-containment posture.
  • Absence of monthly reconciliation and variance reporting means the project lead and editorial board lack visibility into spending trajectory. A steady 5% monthly overrun (≈$46K/month in Phase 2 estimate) accumulates to $552K by Month 24 (2028-10-13), exhausting both the $175K pre-gate draw cap and the $350K reserve, forcing an undisclosed budget crisis mid-gate.
  • Missing earned-value tracking (SPI and CPI) prevents early detection of schedule and cost misalignment. A Phase 1 slip of 6 weeks (Month 18 = 2028-04-13 effective end) combined with cost overrun compresses Phase 2 pilots and inflates the effective cost per completed assessment, making the gate metrics less reliable and Phase 3 adoption less credible.
  • Lack of a rolling 6-month cash-flow forecast means the project is blind to upcoming liquidity constraints. If Phase 2 audio production is delayed (studio backlog, inter-rater training extension), cash flow could reverse, requiring immediate contingency draws or a pause in payroll/partner commitments mid-project.
  • Unclear responsibility for budget ownership (project lead vs. finance office vs. editorial board) creates accountability gaps. Cost overruns are debated rather than escalated; contingency draws lack clear approvers; variance reports are not timely, and no single owner drives corrective action.
  • Absence of a high-risk line-item watch list means high-cost activities (audio recording, psychometric validation, pilot recruitment incentives, legal consulting) are not proactively managed. A $50K audio overrun (estimate), undetected until Month 11 (2027-09-13), cascades into a late pre-registration and a compressed Phase 2 start.
  • Missing scenario analysis for overrun response leaves the project without pre-decided fallback spending plans. When a $300K overrun is discovered, the board must improvise trade-offs (defer outreach, cut partner payments, extend timeline) without a pre-agreed framework, leading to conflict and slow decision-making.
  • Lack of transparency in spending reduces stakeholder (editorial board, partner organizations, funders) confidence in the program's financial discipline. If actual spending is not visible monthly or if contingency draws occur without explanation, external stakeholders question the project's management and may withdraw commitments (ESL programs, publishers, steward candidates).

Worst Case Scenario: A combination of undetected cost overruns, poor contingency-draw discipline and absent variance reporting leaves the project insolvent mid-Phase 2. Specifically: (1) Phase 1 audio production and psychometric validation overrun by $200K (estimate) by Month 10 (2027-08-13), undetected because no monthly variance reports are issued; (2) the project lead and finance office each assume the other is monitoring, so the overrun is not escalated; (3) by Month 12 (2027-10-13), Phase 2 begins with only $900K remaining in the combined Phase 2 and reserve budget, insufficient to fund 12 months of pilots, assessments and partner payments estimated at $1.2M; (4) contingency draws of $150K–$200K (estimate) are requested ad-hoc in Months 14–18 (2027-12-13 to 2028-04-13) for pilot recruitment shortfalls and rater retraining, exhausting the pre-gate draw cap and the full $350K reserve by Month 18 (2028-04-13); (5) a 3-month Phase 2 extension to complete data collection costs $300K (estimate), but no funds remain, forcing either unauthorized draw requests or cancellation of Phase 2 pilots; (6) the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate is postponed indefinitely, stranding the project and damaging credibility with ESL programs, publishers and standards bodies; (7) a no-go outcome at Month 30–36 (2029-04-13 to 2029-10-13) leaves no unspent Phase 3 or reserve funds to return, negating the cost-containment principle and leaving funders and stakeholders uncertain whether the project was abandoned due to evidence failure or financial mismanagement.

Best Case Scenario: A detailed, disciplined Project Budget and Cash-Flow Forecast document establishes clear financial governance from Month 1 (2026-11-13) forward. Monthly variance reports show spending aligned with plan (±5% actual vs. budget), triggering corrective action promptly when overruns approach 10%. Quarterly earned-value analysis (SPI ≥0.95, CPI ≥1.0) confirms the project stays on schedule and within cost targets. A rolling 6-month cash-flow forecast identifies the peak liquidity need (≈$1.3M cumulative by Month 18 = 2028-04-13, estimate) and confirms adequate reserves to cover Phase 2 extension scenarios up to 3 months. Contingency draws are authorized efficiently: a $50K psychometric re-validation request at Month 10 (2027-08-13) is approved within 2 days, rater training is completed by Month 11 (2027-09-13), and inter-rater kappa reaches 0.75 target, enabling Phase 2 to begin on schedule. By Month 24 (2028-10-13), the go/no-go gate decision is supported by reliable cost and schedule data; if the outcome is GO, Phase 3 launches with full $1.2M ($0.85M Phase 3 + $0.35M released reserve) and no financial distraction; if NO-GO, $1.2M–$1.4M in unspent Phase 3 and contingency funds are returned, demonstrating fiscal responsibility and preserving stakeholder trust for future initiatives. The project is perceived as well-managed, delivers evidence on time and at budget, and achieves credibility with educators, publishers and standards bodies that adopt Clear English in Phase 3.
