Documents to Find

Find Document 1: ESL Learner Corpus and Frequency Data

ID: c7580490-a507-489a-b615-884e736dbb1a

Description: Large corpus of English text produced by or targeted at adult ESL learners (e.g., Cambridge English Learner Corpus, TOEFL corpus, COCA General Academic subsection, JACET list of academic words). Required to derive the 5,000-word core lexicon by frequency ranking and to identify the highest-frequency irregular verbs and morphologically complex words that must be retained for learnability. Intended audience for analysis: lexicon designer.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available version (corpus data is cumulative; updates are beneficial but not time-critical for word-frequency ranking).

Responsible Role Type: Linguistic Specialist / Corpus Analyst

Steps to Find:

  • Search 'Cambridge English Learner Corpus' on the Cambridge University Press or Cambridge Assessment websites; request access via institutional subscription or research-licensing agreement.
  • Search 'COCA Corpus of Contemporary American English' (Mark Davies' corpus at Brigham Young University); freely available online with frequency lists and word concordance tools.
  • Search 'TOEFL word list' and 'GRE vocabulary list' for academic-vocabulary rankings; available from Educational Testing Service and other test publishers.
  • Contact applied-linguistics researchers at universities with ESL-research programs (University of Michigan, University of Pennsylvania, University of Minnesota) for access to in-house ESL learner corpora or compiled frequency lists.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium. COCA is freely available online; Cambridge Corpus requires institutional subscription (typically free via university library access); TOEFL lists are public. Compile into a ranked lexicon by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the most recent, large-scale corpus of English text produced by or targeted at adult ESL learners (e.g., Cambridge English Learner Corpus, TOEFL corpus, COCA General Academic subsection, JACET list) with word-frequency rankings for the full lexicon.
  • Quantify the frequency rank and token count for each of the 5,000 target core lexicon words to establish selection principled-ness and defensibility.
  • Identify the 200–300 highest-frequency irregular verbs and morphologically complex words within the top 1,000-word band to inform the Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold (retain all within this band; regularize only lower-frequency irregulars).
  • Rank and list homographs, homophones and high-ambiguity pairs within the core 5,000 to inform the Homograph Disambiguation Policy (<=50 high-impact pairs for mandatory markers in safety-critical contexts).
  • Document the corpus selection methodology and publish the lexicon and its frequency provenance openly by Month 12 (2027-10-13) to enable third-party audit and reproducibility.
  • Confirm lexicon coverage of running text in existing ESL curricula and technical glossaries: audit that >=85% coverage is achieved (scheduled Month 8 = 2027-06-13); specify any expansion needed by Month 10 (2027-08-13).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Lexicon derived from outdated, small or non-representative corpus could miss high-frequency words needed to read pilot materials and technical glossaries, inflating comprehension confounds and invalidating gate-metric measurements.
  • Inadequate identification of irregular verbs and morphologically complex words could force the Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold decision into guesswork rather than data, risking retention of learnable irregulars or regularization of high-frequency, unlearnable forms.
  • Incomplete homograph and homophone ranking could cause the Homograph Disambiguation Policy to address low-impact pairs while missing safety-critical ambiguities (e.g., lead/lead, read/read), reducing the standard's safety-critical credibility and underutilizing marker overhead.
  • Opaque or non-reproducible lexicon selection could invite third-party and standards-body challenges to the lexicon's legitimacy ('Why does your lexicon omit X word that appears in Y standard?'), damaging adoption credibility and triggering disputes over v1.0 scope.
  • Lexicon coverage shortfall (< 85%) discovered at Month 18 (2028-04-13) forces rapid expansion of 500–1,000 words, adding $20K–$50K (estimate) audio recording cost and 4–8 weeks, compressing Phase 2 pilots and inflating measurement noise.

Worst Case Scenario: Lexicon selection is performed on an undated, limited or unrepresentative corpus (e.g., a small learner sample of N=100–500) discovered too late (Month 10 = 2027-08-13 or later) to correct. Pilots reveal that Core Lexicon Selection Basis coverage is only 75–80% instead of >=85% (proposed threshold), leaving 15–20% of running text outside the lexicon. Confounding is severe: learners' comprehension difficulty derives partly from unknown vocabulary, not Clear English rule effects, inflating measurement noise by 20–30% and reducing statistical power to detect ordinal and pronunciation effects by 25–40%. At the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate, the ordinal error rate or pronunciation consistency metric fails to meet its pre-registered threshold, but the board cannot rule out that poor lexicon coverage caused a false-negative outcome. The gate decision becomes disputable: educators and standards bodies reject the no-go as invalid, claiming the pilot was poorly designed. The project is forced into a 6–12 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K, estimate) to re-run pilots with an expanded, verified lexicon, stranding $300K–$600K (estimate) and delaying public release to Month 36–42 (2029-10-13 to 2030-04-13). Adoption momentum is lost; publishers and standards bodies defer commitments. Final adoption reaches 5,000–10,000 learners instead of 50,000–100,000 (estimate), and the standard's credibility is permanently damaged.

Best Case Scenario: Lexicon is derived from a large, recent, multi-source ESL corpus (Cambridge, COCA, TOEFL, academic-vocabulary sources) representing 500,000+ tokens (estimate) across diverse learner populations and proficiency levels. Frequency ranks are published openly with methodological transparency, enabling third-party verification and adoption-partner confidence. Audit at Month 8 (2027-06-13) confirms >=85% coverage of running text in existing ESL curricula and safety-critical glossaries, with no remediation needed. Irregular-verb and morphologically complex-word rankings directly inform the Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold, locking in go/went and other high-frequency irregulars while regularizing only low-frequency, low-learning-burden forms. Homograph and homophone ranking informs a concise, high-impact list of <=50 pairs for mandatory markers in safety-critical documents. Pilots proceed with clean, transparent measurement: comprehension confounds are minimal, and ordinal error rate and pronunciation consistency metrics cleanly reflect Clear English effects. At Month 24 (2028-10-13), the go/no-go gate is decided on defensible evidence, with no dispute over lexicon adequacy. Early adopters (ESL publishers, standards bodies, safety-training organizations) cite the transparent lexicon methodology in justifying adoption, accelerating Phase 3 uptake. By Month 36 (2029-10-13), >=3 third-party adopters are licensed, reaching 50,000–100,000 learners, and the standard's credibility is established in the ESL and technical-writing communities.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a large, recent ESL learner corpus is not immediately available: compile a corpus from multiple sources (Cambridge English Learner Corpus subset, COCA General Academic + Fiction, TOEFL Official Test Prep materials word lists, Common European Framework vocabulary lists by level) by Month 2 (2026-12-13), totaling at least 300,000–500,000 tokens (estimate). Combine frequency counts and use the consensus ranking to weight word selection, documenting the merge methodology.
  • If institutional access to major corpora (Cambridge, COCA) is unavailable: engage university applied-linguistics departments (University of Michigan ESL Research Lab, University of Pennsylvania Linguistics Department, University of Minnesota ESL Institute) to request research access or a data-sharing agreement by Month 2 (2026-12-13). Allocate $5K–$10K (estimate) as an access or contribution fee if required.
  • If irregular-verb and morphological data is sparse in existing corpora: conduct a targeted analysis of error logs and learner written samples from 3–4 ESL programs participating as pilot partners (Month 4 = 2027-02-13 onward), identifying which irregulars are most frequently misused or over-regularized by learners. Use this as a secondary validation of the frequency-based Irregular Morphology Retention Threshold.
  • If homograph and homophone identification is incomplete: review published plain-language style guides (Hemingway Editor, Nielsen Norman plain-language checklist) and controlled-language standards (ASD-STE100) for existing ambiguity or homograph guidance, augmenting the corpus-derived list by Month 4 (2027-02-13).
  • If lexicon coverage audit at Month 8 (2027-06-13) reveals <85% coverage: conduct a rapid (2-week) expansion survey of pilot partner materials to identify the highest-frequency missing words (e.g., domain-specific jargon, cultural or current-event vocabulary), add up to 500–1,000 words to the lexicon by Month 10 (2027-08-13), and allocate additional audio recording budget ($20K–$50K, estimate) to stay within the Phase 2 pilots schedule.

Find Document 2: Existing English Irregular Verb and Morphology Error Databases

ID: 3dc2b5a3-8804-4046-8846-c003e51081b0

Description: Published research databases and learner-error corpora (e.g., ELEC corpus from Chujo & Hasegawa, learner error corpora compiled by ESL-assessment organizations) documenting which irregular verbs and plural forms are most frequently misused or cause learning difficulty for adult ESL learners. Required to rank the morphology retention threshold (which irregulars to keep, which to regularize) and to identify the highest-friction patterns. Intended audience: morphology-rule workstream lead.

Recency Requirement: Prefer studies published within the last 10 years (2016–2026 estimate); morphology acquisition patterns are stable over time, so older research is acceptable if recent is unavailable.

Responsible Role Type: Linguistic Specialist / Applied Linguist

Steps to Find:

  • Search 'ELEC corpus' (corpus of English learner errors compiled by Kiyomi Chujo, Waseda University); available via academic publications and corpus-sharing repositories.
  • Search PubMed and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed studies on 'English morphology acquisition ESL' or 'irregular verb learning errors adult learners'; download full-text PDFs from university library access.
  • Contact the TESOL Research Interest Group and ask for recommended learner-error corpora or morphology studies; reach out to applied-linguistics researchers at ESL-assessment organizations (Cambridge, TOEFL, IELTS).
  • Review the error taxonomy in major ESL-assessment scoring rubrics (e.g., TOEFL Independent Writing Rubric) for documented patterns of morphology and verb-form errors.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Published studies are freely available via academic databases (Google Scholar, ResearchGate); access to corpus data may require emailing authors or institutional subscription. Compile by Month 5 (2027-03-13).

Essential Information:

  • Identify which irregular English verbs and plural forms are most frequently misused or cause learning difficulty for adult ESL learners across current published research and learner-error corpora (e.g., ELEC corpus, assessment-organization error datasets).
  • Document the frequency ranking of irregular verbs and plurals in ESL learner errors, stratified by proficiency level (A1–B2, or equivalent) to determine which forms learners struggle with most.
  • List the recognized sources and methodology of each error corpus or study (publication date, sample size, learner population, error classification scheme) to assess reliability and relevance to the Clear English population.
  • Quantify the percentage of learner errors attributable to each irregular verb and plural form in the available corpora, to inform the morphology retention threshold decision (which irregulars are retained, which regularized).
  • Specify which irregular forms fall within the top 1,000 frequency-ranked words of the core lexicon and which fall below, to anchor the 'retain all irregulars in top 1,000 words; regularize only lower-frequency' threshold proposal.
  • Confirm recognition distance and acceptability of regularized forms (e.g., 'goed' vs. 'went', 'sheeps' vs. 'sheep') by citing reading-speed or comprehension studies, if available, to validate the low-recognition-penalty assumption.
  • Document any gaps or limitations in published corpora (e.g., coverage of specific dialects, age ranges, or proficiency bands) so that the rule-specification team can target supplementary learner-error data collection if needed by Month 5 (2027-03-13).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated error corpora could miss high-friction irregulars that adult ESL learners commonly misuse, leading to an inflated retention threshold (keeping too many irregulars) and a weaker morphology rule that fails to reduce learning friction as promised.
  • Relying on corpora that do not represent the target ESL population (e.g., child learners, non-adult proficiency levels) could yield a retention threshold misaligned with adult learner needs, reducing pilot credibility and adoption appeal among adult-education publishers.
  • Methodologically weak or uncited error studies (e.g., anecdotal or non-peer-reviewed sources) could produce arbitrary or unjustifiable retention thresholds, undermining the editorial board's confidence in morphology rule decisions and prolonging board disputes into Phase 2.
  • Ambiguous error taxonomy or misclassification in source corpora (e.g., disagreement on whether a verb form is 'irregular' or 'regularized') could inflate or deflate apparent error rates, leading to incorrect prioritization of which forms to regularize.
  • Absence of frequency-ranking data for irregular forms in the core 5,000-word lexicon could force ad-hoc or intuitive decisions on retention vs. regularization, rather than evidence-based threshold choice, weakening the rule's explainability and third-party audibility.

Worst Case Scenario: The morphology-rule workstream team proceeds without accessing current learner-error corpora and relies on linguistic intuition or outdated handbooks to decide the morphology retention threshold. By Month 8 (2027-06-13), pilot curriculum development begins with an arbitrary rule—e.g., 'regularize all verbs with fewer than 10 million Google hits'—that does not reflect actual ESL learner friction. During Phase 2 pilots (starting Month 12 = 2027-10-13), teachers and learners report that the retained irregulars (e.g., go/went) are confusing and error-prone, contradicting the assumption that frequent irregulars are already learned. The morphology error rate in pilots fails to improve as expected, or the pronunciation consistency score is confounded by unexpected morphology-error variance. At Month 18 (2028-04-13) midpoint review, the editorial board realizes the retention threshold was misaligned with learner data, forcing either mid-pilot rule changes (invalidating earlier assessments) or a no-go recommendation at Month 24 (2028-10-13) due to weak morphology effectiveness. Cost: 3–4 week rework ($50K–$100K estimate) or loss of credibility on the morphology rule, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–30%.

Best Case Scenario: The morphology-rule workstream team obtains and analyzes the ELEC corpus, recent ESL-assessment rubrics and 2–3 peer-reviewed studies on irregular-verb and plural-form acquisition (published 2016–2025 estimate) by Month 5 (2027-03-13). The analysis reveals that learners struggle most with verbs like go/went (high frequency but highly irregular) and with irregular plurals (child/children, ox/oxen). However, the team also finds that most learners internalize the top 20–30 irregular verbs through repeated exposure, even when regularized forms are introduced. The workstream proposes a data-driven retention threshold: retain all irregulars in the top 500-word band (covering >85% of text), regularize only the 50–100 lowest-frequency irregulars with clear recognition parallels (e.g., build/builded parallel to jump/jumped). This threshold is published, auditable and defensible. Pilot teachers report the rule is clear and learnable; morphology error rates improve by 30–40% (exceeding the >=25% proposed threshold). The rule's evidence-based grounding strengthens the editorial board's confidence, accelerates Phase 2 progress and raises Phase 3 adoption interest by 15–25% (estimate) among publishers who perceive the standard as rigorous and empirically grounded.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the ELEC corpus and recent published studies are not accessible by Month 3 (2027-01-13), commission a small targeted learner-error analysis: record or transcribe 5–10 hours of adult ESL classroom interaction or low-stakes writing assessments (with consent) and manually code irregular-verb and plural-form errors by frequency and learner proficiency. Cost: $15K–$25K (estimate); timeline: Months 3–5 (2027-01-13 to 2027-03-13). This preserves data-driven decision-making while acknowledging access constraints.
  • If published corpora show inconsistent error patterns across populations (e.g., errors differ by first language), adopt a conservative 'retain the top 1,000 frequency words with all their irregularities' rule without regularization, and defer morphology regularization to post-v1.0 (Phase 3 or later) after pilot feedback is collected. Cost: reduces morphology intervention in v1.0 but preserves credibility and avoids arbitrary threshold choices.
  • Engage the TESOL Research Interest Group or contact the authors of recent morphology-acquisition studies directly (email outreach, Month 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) to request pre-prints, unpublished datasets or advice on corpora; offer a co-authorship or acknowledgment in the published standard's morphology rationale. This leverages academic goodwill and may surface otherwise inaccessible data.
  • If error-corpus data remains unavailable, use a proxy: extract morphology errors from published ESL textbooks' error-correction exercises or from the error taxonomies published by major assessment bodies (TOEFL, IELTS, Cambridge). These are public and widely cited, and they document high-frequency error types even if they do not provide raw frequency counts.
  • As a last resort, if no error data is accessible, convene a small expert panel of 3–5 experienced ESL instructors and linguists (Month 4 = 2027-02-13) to conduct a structured expert judgment on which irregulars are highest-friction. Document their reasoning in the published rule rationale and note the evidence gap; this supports the rule's defensibility even if empirical corpora were unavailable, and flags the morphology rule for potential refinement post-v1.0.

Find Document 3: Homograph and Homophone Lists for English (Including Specialized Domains)

ID: b0d2d465-7f48-4c9a-949a-e22839d65ed0

Description: Comprehensive list of English homographs (same spelling, different pronunciation/meaning; e.g., lead/lead, read/read) and homophones (same pronunciation, different meaning; e.g., to/two/too) with frequency rankings and domain relevance (common in technical, medical, legal, or general English). Required for Homograph Disambiguation Policy (Decision 7) to define which pairs must be marked, which are low-priority, and which are domain-specific. Intended audience: homograph-policy workstream lead and safety-critical curriculum designer.

Recency Requirement: Existing lists of homographs are stable (no recent updates expected); use any authoritative source published in the last 15 years.

Responsible Role Type: Linguistic Specialist / Semanticist

Steps to Find:

  • Search 'English homograph list' and 'English homophone list' on Google Scholar, Academia.edu, or ResearchGate; download academic papers that compile and rank homographs by frequency.
  • Consult specialized dictionaries and corpus-analysis tools: search for 'homograph' in the Online Etymology Dictionary, Merriam-Webster, or the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) unabridged edition.
  • Search for domain-specific homograph lists in technical-writing and safety-documentation standards (e.g., FAA style guide, medical-device documentation guidelines, pharmacy and pharmaceutical regulatory guidance) to identify high-impact pairs in safety-critical contexts.
  • Use corpus-analysis software (AntConc, SketchEngine) to identify ambiguous words in the core lexicon and check whether they appear in multiple senses in the corpus.

Access Difficulty: Easy. Homograph lists are published in linguistics textbooks and online dictionaries; many are freely available. Compile a prioritized list by Month 4 (2027-02-13).

Essential Information:

  • Compile a comprehensive, frequency-ranked list of English homographs (same spelling, different meaning/pronunciation, e.g., lead/lead, read/read) and homophones (same pronunciation, different spelling, e.g., to/two/too) with documented frequency bands from corpus data.
  • Identify and rank the highest-impact homograph pairs for safety-critical and technical domains (e.g., medical, legal, pharmaceutical, aerospace/FAA) by frequency of occurrence in incident reports, procedures, and hazard-communication standards.
  • For each homograph pair, specify: (1) frequency tier (high/medium/low based on the 5,000-word core lexicon); (2) domain relevance (general ESL, technical, medical, safety-critical); (3) recognition penalty (how easily a native speaker disambiguates from context); (4) whether it falls within the retained irregular-forms band or the respelling/regularization zone.
  • Deliver a prioritized list of ≤50 high-impact pairs (proposed cap from the Homograph Disambiguation Policy decision) flagged as mandatory-marker candidates in safety-critical documents, with justification for each inclusion and exclusion.
  • Document the methodology: corpus used, frequency thresholds applied, domain selection criteria, and how the list aligns with the 5,000-word lexicon selection basis (frequency-led or incident-driven seed, proposed).
  • Provide a mapping of each pair to existing controlled-language guidance (e.g., ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English) to enable one-way compatibility auditing and avoid reinventing solutions already solved by standards bodies.
  • Include ambiguous or borderline cases (e.g., wound/wound) with written rationale for including or excluding them, and a clear policy for how new homograph pairs discovered during pilots will be classified and handled before the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or misranked homograph list: if high-impact safety-critical pairs (e.g., 'read/read' in procedure instructions or 'live/live' in electrical contexts) are omitted or mislabeled as low-priority, the Homograph Disambiguation Policy decision cannot be implemented credibly, leaving safety-critical documentation ambiguous and exposing the project to liability claims.
  • Misalignment with the 5,000-word core lexicon: if the list includes pairs outside the lexicon or omits high-frequency pairs within it, the mandatory-marker obligation cannot be enforced consistently in pilot materials, confounding assessments of whether ordinal or homograph marking improves comprehension.
  • Weak or circular methodology: if the list is compiled ad hoc without transparent corpus analysis, domain-relevance criteria or statistical justification, educators and standards bodies will question its authority and resist adoption of the resulting disambiguation policy.
  • Domain-specific gaps: if technical, medical or safety-critical homographs are under-represented relative to general-English pairs, the safety-critical adoption wedge will lack a credible, evidence-backed glossary, delaying or blocking partnership commitments with safety organizations by Month 3 (2027-01-13).
  • Scope creep or contradiction with existing controlled-language standards: if the list does not reference or diverge from ASD-STE100 or plain-language guidance without documented justification, it signals either reinvention or incompatibility, undermining the one-way Controlled-Language Alignment Posture decided in the plan.
  • Late discovery of major pairs during pilots (Months 12–24 = 2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13): if homographs are identified as high-impact only during Phase 2, rule changes to the mandatory-marker list will invalidate earlier pilot assessments and inflate measurement noise, jeopardizing the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision.

Worst Case Scenario: A weak or incomplete homograph list, delivered late (Month 6–8 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-06-13 instead of Month 4 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-06-13), delays the Homograph Disambiguation Policy finalization and forces the editorial board to adopt either a loose, non-evidence-backed policy or a conservative one that burdens safety-critical writers without proven risk reduction. During Phase 2 pilots, critical homographs omitted from the list cause misreading incidents in safety-critical test passages, inflating the ordinal-error metric or confounding comprehension-speed measurements. At Month 18 (2028-04-13) midpoint review, pilot data reveals that unmarked homophones (e.g., 'to/two' in numbered procedures) account for 15–20% of miscommunications, forcing a mid-pilot policy revision that invalidates earlier assessment data. The editorial board must either rerun a cohort (3–6 month delay, ~$150K–$300K cost estimate) or report to stakeholders at Month 24 (2028-10-13) that the homograph evidence is inconclusive, triggering a disputed or conditional go/no-go gate, loss of partner confidence and potential Phase 3 delay to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or beyond.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive, frequency-ranked and domain-validated homograph list is delivered by Month 4 (2027-02-13), compiled from academic corpus data, safety-critical incident reports and controlled-language standards (ASD-STE100, plain-language guides). The list identifies 40–50 highest-impact pairs, 70% of which fall within the 5,000-word core lexicon, with clear justification for inclusion and a method for handling borderline cases. Safety organizations and ESL publishers review the list by Month 5 (2027-03-13) and endorse its domain relevance in their advisory roles. The Homograph Disambiguation Policy is finalized and published by Month 6 (2027-04-13), mandating markers in safety-critical documents for the high-impact list and leaving markers optional elsewhere. Pilot curriculum designers integrate the policy seamlessly by Month 12 (2027-10-13), and pilot data shows that marked homographs have ≤5% misreading rates (compared to unmarked control pairs), demonstrating clear safety benefit. The policy becomes a concrete, credible success story in Phase 3 outreach, attracting safety-critical and technical-writing adopters and contributing to the ≥3 licensed-adopter target by Month 36 (2029-10-13).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a comprehensive academic homograph list cannot be compiled in time (by Month 4 = 2027-02-13), engage a domain-specialist subcontractor (linguistics professor or technical-writing consultant, estimated cost $15K–$25K) by Month 2 (2026-12-13) to extract and rank homographs from safety-critical incident-report databases (OSHA, FDA, FAA) and existing controlled-language corpora (ASD-STE100, NIST plain-language guides) within 6 weeks, delivering a focused domain-specific list by Month 3.5 (2027-01-28) that covers the safety-critical wedge even if general ESL homographs are incomplete.
  • If domain access is restricted (incident reports are proprietary or regulated), use public proxy sources: pharmaceutical labeling databases (FDA Orange Book, drug insert archives), airline procedure manuals (safety briefings), and publicly available technical standards (ISO, ASTM excerpts) to infer the most problematic pairs without accessing confidential incident data.
  • If the editorial board is uncertain whether homograph marking is mandatory or optional in safety-critical documents, defer the mandatory-vs.-optional decision to Month 6 (2027-04-13) and conduct a small exploratory pilot study in Month 10 (2027-08-13)—N=20–30 native speakers—comparing marked vs. unmarked homograph passages in a controlled-language procedural setting to establish evidence of benefit before the Month 12 (2027-10-13) rules lock; if evidence is weak, adopt an optional-marking policy with a post-v1.0 review.
  • If homograph discovery continues during Phase 2 pilots, establish a standing 'Homograph Triage Committee' (2–3 board members, 1 hour/month) by Month 12 (2027-10-13) with authority to flag and classify new pairs without halting the pilot. Document all proposals and defer decisions on adding mandatory markers to a v1.1 revision or v2.0, keeping v1.0 assessment data clean and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate focused on the pre-registered homograph list.
  • If the list proves too large to manage (>50 pairs identified), apply a tightened selection filter: retain only pairs with both (a) frequency in the core 5,000-word lexicon ≥10 occurrences per million (propose) AND (b) documented safety or confusion risk from domain data; deprioritize pairs with low recognition risk (native speakers easily disambiguate from context), deferring them to a v2.0 expansion once pilot evidence exists.

Access Difficulty: Medium to Easy. ESL textbooks are widely available; pilot partner materials require signed agreements and may be confidential. Obtain sample materials by Month 4 (2027-02-13); complete coverage audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13).

Essential Information:

  • Identify which high-frequency words in the core lexicon are underrepresented or missing from the pilot curricula; flag gaps for lexicon expansion by Month 10 (2027-08-13).

  • List any critical domain-specific terms (safety jargon, procedural vocabulary) that appear in the technical-writing samples but are absent from the core lexicon; propose additions if coverage falls below 85%.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Discovering inadequate coverage after Phase 2 pilots have begun (Month 13 = 2027-11-13 onwards) forces late expansion of the lexicon, adding 4–8 weeks to Phase 2 and inflating audio-recording costs ($20K–$50K per 500 words, estimate), straining the $175K pre-gate reserve cap.
  • Missing domain-specific terms in the technical-glossary cohort undermines the safety-critical adoption wedge's credibility: technical writers and safety regulators will reject a standard whose vocabulary does not cover real-world procedures.

  • Failure to specify the ESL/technical split in lexicon selection leaves the 4,500/500 allocation (proposed) untested; a later discovery that technical coverage is inadequate forces rework of the lexicon design and re-recording of pronunciation audio.
  • Poor documentation of curriculum sample provenance and access agreements creates a gap between audit assumptions and actual pilot materials; instructors using different curricula in Phase 2 may report that the lexicon does not align with their content, damaging credibility.

Worst Case Scenario: At Month 8 (2027-06-13), a lexicon-coverage audit reveals that the core 5,000-word list covers only 75–80% of running text in the ESL and technical-writing samples, particularly missing high-frequency safety and procedural vocabulary. The shortfall cannot be absorbed by Month 12 (2027-10-13) without either delaying audio production (pushing pronunciation recording into Phase 2) or abandoning the full 5,000-word target and proceeding with a smaller, less credible lexicon. Best Case Scenario: By Month 8 (2027-06-13), the audit confirms that the 5,000-word core lexicon covers 87–92% of running text in current ESL and technical-writing curricula, with a defensible 4,500 general / 500 technical split that aligns with pilot partner materials. Phase 2 pilots begin with a lexicon that participants recognize as representative of their own study materials, eliminating confounds and strengthening the validity of comprehension speed and retention assessments. Find Document 5: Corpus of English Spelling Irregularities and Grapheme-to-Phoneme Mapping Rules

ID: 310887a3-943c-472d-bbe9-9c832956e4df

Description: Linguistic research or curated corpus documenting the patterns of English spelling-to-sound irregularities (grapheme-to-phoneme mismatches), such as the 'ough' patterns (rough, through, though, thorough, dough), vowel digraphs (ea, ei, ie), and silent letters. Required to design the Grapheme-to-Phoneme Intervention rules (Decision 2) and to prioritize which words in the core lexicon need the most pronunciation guidance. Recency Requirement: Existing linguistic descriptions of English phonology are stable; use any authoritative source published in the last 30 years.

Responsible Role Type: Linguistic Specialist / Phonetics Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • Consult foundational linguistics and phonology textbooks (e.g., Fromkin & Rodman 'An Introduction to Language'; Yavaş 'Applied English Phonology') for descriptions of English grapheme-to-phoneme patterns.
  • Search for 'English spelling-sound correspondences' and 'English phonology exceptions' in academic databases; many linguistics papers analyze irregular patterns.
  • Consult the English Phonetics and Phonology section of linguistics handbooks (e.g., Oxford Handbook of the History of English).
  • Use online phonetic resources (e.g., Howjsay, Pronunciation Guide) to systematically check how various spelling patterns are pronounced; compile a list of high-friction patterns (those with multiple pronunciations or unexpected pronunciations).

Access Difficulty: Easy. Phonology and linguistics textbooks are widely available in university libraries. Compile by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

Essential Information:

  • Comprehensive inventory of English grapheme-to-phoneme irregularities (e.g., 'ough' patterns: rough, through, though, thorough, dough; vowel digraphs: ea, ei, ie; silent letters; vowel + consonant + e patterns)
  • Frequency-ranked list of spelling patterns by learning difficulty for ESL learners, prioritizing high-friction mismatches (patterns with multiple pronunciations or unexpected sound mappings)
  • Documented mapping rules showing which spelling patterns reliably map to which phonemes, and which patterns have exceptions or multiple valid pronunciations
  • Identification of which irregular patterns appear in the core 5,000-word lexicon (especially high-frequency words in the top 1,000 needed for the 85% running-text coverage audit)
  • Curated examples and non-examples for each pattern, suitable for teaching pronunciation rules and designing pronunciation-consistency assessment items
  • Explicit description of how the chosen reference accent realizes each pattern (e.g., in received Pronunciation or General American), aligned with the accent anchor chosen by Month 3 (2027-01-13)

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated inventory of irregularities leaves high-friction patterns unidentified, so the G2P intervention rules omit the very mismatches causing learner confusion, reducing the pronunciation consistency gate metric effect size and risking a false-negative gate outcome
  • Frequency-ranking missing or incorrect: patterns judged low-difficulty may actually be high-friction for ESL learners (e.g., 'ei' vs. 'ie'), wasting rule-design effort on low-impact patterns and missing high-impact ones, skewing the pilot curriculum and weakening evidence
  • Conflicting or ambiguous mapping rules (e.g., multiple sources describing 'ough' differently) force the linguistic specialist to reconcile sources mid-corpus work, delaying Month 12 (2027-10-13) lexicon completion and compressing pilot enrolment window
  • Missing mapping for the reference accent anchor causes pronunciation-guidance inconsistencies: some entries use Received Pronunciation mappings, others General American, undermining the pronunciation consistency score reliability (kappa target 0.75) and confusing learners
  • Examples and assessment items drawn from an incomplete corpus may omit or misrepresent patterns, inflating the reliability of pronunciation-consistency scoring in the validity study (Month 10 = 2027-08-13) and producing weak inter-rater kappa, triggering a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K draw estimate)

Worst Case Scenario: An incomplete or inaccurate corpus of irregularities leaves the G2P intervention rules targeting the wrong patterns—perhaps omitting 'ough' or mischaracterizing vowel digraphs—so pilot learners do not receive pronunciation guidance on their actual pain points. The pronunciation-consistency gate metric shows no significant improvement over control, the gate fails at Month 24 (2028-10-13), and the initiative is abandoned, forfeiting $1.2M–$1.4M in Phase 2–3 spending (estimate). Alternatively, conflicting source materials on accent realization cause pronunciation guidance to be inconsistent across the 5,000-word lexicon, inter-rater reliability (kappa) drops below the 0.70 floor, forcing a 4-week Phase 1 extension and triggering a draw on the $175K pre-gate contingency reserve, leaving insufficient headroom for other Phase 1 overruns.

Best Case Scenario: A thorough, frequency-ranked corpus of English irregularities aligned with the reference accent anchor is completed by Month 3 (2027-01-13), allowing the linguistic specialist to design precise, high-impact G2P rules targeting the top 10–15 spelling patterns causing the most learner confusion. The 5,000-word lexicon is systematically mapped and validated against the corpus by Month 8 (2027-06-13), ensuring 85%+ running-text coverage in pilot materials. Pronunciation-guidance consistency is high (inter-rater kappa ≥0.75), assessment items are exemplary, and pilot learners show ≥25% reduction in ordinal and pronunciation errors relative to control. The pronunciation-consistency gate metric passes decisively at Month 24 (2028-10-13), supporting a GO decision and Phase 3 release, with >3 third-party adopters committed by Month 36 (2029-10-13).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If authoritative sources on English phonology are not comprehensive enough: commission a small targeted corpus study (3–4 weeks, $15K–$25K estimate) of learner error patterns from existing ESL corpus databases (e.g., the Corpus of Contemporary American English, learner-error annotations) to identify the highest-friction patterns empirically by frequency of misdecoding or misproduction
  • If accent-specific realization data are missing or conflicting: engage a pronunciation specialist or phonetician (0.25–0.5 FTE, $20K–$30K estimate) to conduct or curate audio exemplars of each pattern in the chosen reference accent, with explicit documented decisions where multiple realizations exist within that accent
  • If the corpus is too large or unfocused: use the core 5,000-word lexicon frequency list (Decision 9, Core Lexicon Selection Basis) to filter the irregularity inventory to only those patterns that appear in the 5,000 words, reducing scope and ensuring the corpus directly supports lexicon work
  • If completion by Month 3 (2027-01-13) is at risk: prioritize the top 20–30 spelling patterns by learner-difficulty estimate (e.g., 'ough', vowel digraphs, silent letters, final -e patterns, irregular consonants) and defer lower-frequency patterns to a second pass by Month 8 (2027-06-13), ensuring the highest-impact rules are locked before the Month 10 (2027-08-13) dry run
  • If inter-rater agreement on pattern categorization is low: establish a 1-week panel reconciliation process (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-01-13) with 2–3 linguistics or ESL experts to resolve disagreements and publish a single authoritative pattern inventory, costing $10K–$15K (estimate)

Strengths

  • Parallel, non-mandatory positioning (supplementary module, no K-12 replacement) lowers educator and publisher resistance.
  • Light-touch design: standard spellings unchanged, prefix ordinals convert mechanically and coexist with legacy 1st/2nd/3rd forms.
  • Evidence-gated structure: four pre-registered metrics, a Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go, and up to $1.2M returnable on a no-go (estimate).
  • Clear ESL-first wedge with a defined pilot design: 2 cohorts x 2 conditions, at least 80 completers per arm (estimate).
  • Risk register is detailed, with owners, dates and fallbacks (4-week Phase 1 extension about $85K, estimate).
  • Practitioner-leaning board with linguist veto, tiebreak arbiter and certification-mark name stewardship address ambiguity and fragmentation.
  • Narrow safety-critical scope (glossary and labeling only, legal counsel by Month 2 = 2026-12-13) bounds liability.

Weaknesses

  • Post-Month 36 (2029-10-13) stewardship is unfunded: $150K-$250K per year (estimate), so a v1.0 release depends on a steward commitment.
  • Pre-gate reserve draws are capped at $175K, so a $300K overrun (8.6% of budget, estimate) exceeds headroom by $125K.
  • Thin buffer: a Phase 1 extension plus a 3-month Phase 2 extension leaves a $35K shortfall (estimate).
  • Critical path is a single sequence (rules, lexicon, audio, instruments, recruitment); a 6-week slip compresses pilots.
  • Dependence on scarce roles (psychometrician, cohort manager) and an untested purpose-built assessment battery.
  • Single anchor accent can look regionally biased and may draw multi-accent demands.
  • The overlay needs a printed pronunciation key, so print materials are not purely standard.
  • Gate thresholds are still proposals, not pre-registered, and no authoring tooling is funded for homograph marking.
  • Intelligibility claim (at least 90% of control accuracy within 2 weeks) is unproven.

Opportunities

  • Safety-critical ordinal and homograph ambiguity gives a measurable, incident-linked benefit for the technical glossary cohort once evidence exists.
  • ESL publishers can co-produce curricula; a 30-day early-rights window for early adopters could speed uptake.
  • Precedents (ASD-STE100, ICAO aviation English) offer governance, rater-calibration and rollout lessons.
  • University partners can supply raters and graduate assistants cheaply.
  • Open licensing and a free conformance checklist encourage third-party tools and materials.
  • Open pre-registration and published rationale build credibility with standards bodies and TESOL/IATEFL.
  • A pronunciation overlay and mechanical ordinal conversion could be reused by learning apps and style checkers.

Threats

  • Educator, publisher and standards-body rejection as a 'non-standard' variant (high likelihood, high severity).
  • Pilot recruitment shortfall or dropout above 30% invalidates gate metrics and may force a 3-6 month extension costing $300K-$600K (estimate).
  • Disputed assessment validity or rater kappa below 0.70 could cause a false-negative or false-positive gate.
  • Native-reader rejection, as in past spelling reforms (Simplified Spelling Board, Shavian).
  • Liability or media scrutiny if any safety document is misread.
  • Fragmentation and look-alike variants after release, with weak enforcement against offshore publishers.
  • Ethics-approval delays and audio data-protection exposure (GDPR, US state laws).
  • Competing plain-language and controlled-language standards backed by larger bodies.
  • Basic English-style fade if no steward is found.

Recommendations

  • Hire the independent psychometrician by Month 2 (2026-12-13); draft the pre-analysis plan with thresholds and power analysis by Month 5 (2027-03-13); pre-register by Month 11 (2027-09-13) (owner: project lead, board).
  • Publish the board charter, voting rules and tiebreak arbiter by Month 1 (2026-11-13); agree the arbiter by Month 5 (2027-03-13); resolve rule disputes by Month 10 (2027-08-13) (owner: board chair).
  • Sign at least 3 ESL programs and 2 technical/safety-training partners by Month 3 (2027-01-13); hire the cohort manager by Month 6 (2027-04-13); over-recruit to at least 115 per arm (estimate) (owner: Phase 2 lead).
  • Retain legal counsel by Month 2 (2026-12-13), set the liability strategy by Month 4 (2027-02-13), obtain ethics approval by Month 6 (2027-04-13), and keep safety pilots to glossary and labeling (owner: project lead, counsel).
  • Scope audio by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and run a rater calibration by Month 10 (2027-08-13); if cost exceeds $20 per entry, use a synthetic baseline plus human verification (owner: lexicon lead).
  • Open steward search at Month 12 (2027-10-13) and secure a written commitment before the Month 30 (2029-04-13) v1.0 release; decide licensing and certification by Month 6 (2027-04-13) (owner: board, stewardship committee).

Strategic Objectives

  • By Month 11 (2027-09-13), pre-register all four gate metrics with numeric thresholds and sample-size justification, and publish the draft standard for a 30-day comment window.
  • By Month 13 (2027-11-13), enrol at least 115 learners per arm (460 total, estimate) and retain at least 80 completers per arm with follow-up completion of at least 70% by Month 22 (2028-08-13).
  • By Month 12 (2027-10-13), deliver a 5,000-word lexicon with usable single-accent audio for all entries, coverage of at least 85% of pilot text, and inter-rater kappa of at least 0.70 (target 0.75) (proposed thresholds).
  • By Month 24 (2028-10-13), reach a defensible go/no-go: ordinal error reduced at least 25% vs control and comprehension no more than 10% slower (proposed thresholds), within the $1.2M Phase 2 budget.
  • By Month 36 (2029-10-13), license at least 3 third-party adopters (at least 1 ESL publisher) under a funded steward commitment, at a cost per adopter tracked against the $0.85M Phase 3 budget (proposed).

Assumptions

  • ESL-first supplementary positioning remains in force; no mandates or K-12 replacement.
  • Canonical budget split holds: $1.1M, $1.2M, $0.85M and $0.35M reserve.
  • Ordinal Option A (invariant prefix) and an overlay-only pronunciation approach are retained for v1.0.
  • Pilot partners honor signed commitments and ethics approval is obtained by Month 6 (2027-04-13).
  • Numeric gate thresholds are proposals until pre-registered.
  • A mid-cost US hub is provisional until Month 3 (2027-01-13).

Missing Information

  • Power analysis confirming at least 80 completers per arm and expected effect sizes.
  • Evidence on native-reader and ESL learner acceptance of the prefix marker and its spoken reading.
  • Candidate steward organizations and their appetite for $150K-$250K per year.
  • Written interest from major ESL publishers and TESOL/IATEFL.
  • Actual audio cost per entry and psychometric vendor quotes.
  • Which of the two pilot cohorts (ESL learners or technical/safety readers) returns most readily and what they choose first, as early evidence of what motivates uptake.
  • Liability insurance availability and cost for safety-related pilot materials.
  • Final choice and justification of the anchor accent.

Questions

  • Which gate threshold is most likely to fail, and what would you do differently if it did?
  • Would a leading ESL publisher adopt the standard on current evidence, and what proof would they need?
  • Is the $175K pre-gate reserve cap enough, or should Phase 1 contingency be reallocated?
  • Who could credibly steward the standard after Month 36 (2029-10-13), and what would motivate them to fund it?
  • How would native readers and educators react to the prefix marker, and how will you test that before rules lock at Month 12 (2027-10-13)?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Project Lead / Program Director

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Program Lead / Director must own end-to-end delivery across 36 months, manage governance, maintain stakeholder confidence and ensure budget discipline. This is a continuous, core accountability role requiring full control and availability from Month 0 (2026-10-13) onward. No procurement-outside-expertise model applies; the role is integral to project success and requires deep institutional knowledge of decisions, timelines and partner relationships.

Explanation: Owns the end-to-end delivery of the standard across three gated phases, manages the core team, editorial board governance, critical-path tracking, and stakeholder escalation. Ensures budget discipline, timeline adherence, and go/no-go decision readiness. This role is essential from Month 0 (2026-10-13) onward to establish governance, secure partnerships and maintain credibility with educators, standards bodies and regulators.

Consequences: Without a dedicated program lead, governance and decision-making becomes diffuse, critical deadlines slip (e.g., board charter delayed, partner commitments unsigned, psychometric validation postponed), budget tracking lapses, stakeholder communication becomes inconsistent, and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate collapses under competing priorities and unclear authority. Project risk of failure increases by an estimated 30–50%.

People Count: 1

Typical Activities: Sarah owns end-to-end delivery across three phases: establishing the editorial board charter and voting procedures by Month 1 (2026-11-13), securing signed partner commitments by Month 3 (2027-01-13), managing monthly critical-path reviews and escalating any slip over 2 weeks, maintaining the project budget tracker and forecasting Phase 2–3 spending, chairing editorial board meetings and logging contested rule decisions, reporting go/no-go readiness to the board at Month 24 (2028-10-13), and transitioning stewardship governance by Month 30 (2029-04-13). She spends roughly 30% of time on governance and decision authority, 30% on timeline and budget discipline, 25% on stakeholder communication and partner relationship maintenance, and 15% on risk escalation.

Background Story: Sarah Chen, based in Austin, Texas, is a program director with 12 years of experience managing large-scale education and standards initiatives. She holds an MBA from UT Austin and a background in public health program management. Sarah led a successful three-year health literacy curriculum rollout across 15 school districts and has deep relationships with education authorities and non-profit partners. She is fluent in Mandarin and English, with experience managing cross-cultural teams. Sarah joined the Clear English project in October 2026 specifically for its evidence-gated approach and adoption-first philosophy, values aligned with her belief that standards succeed through stakeholder buy-in, not mandate.

Equipment Needs: Laptop and project-management software (Microsoft Project, Asana, or Jira) for critical-path tracking and budget forecasting. Video conferencing platform (Zoom, Teams) with recording capability for distributed editorial board and stakeholder meetings. Document version-control system (GitHub, SharePoint) for decision logging and rule drafts. Secure file storage and backup. High-speed internet connection.

Facility Needs: Office space with meeting rooms suitable for monthly editorial board gatherings and stakeholder calls. Private workspace for sensitive governance documents and budget forecasts. Meeting space capacity for 8–12 people (editorial board + project lead + secretary). Virtual-meeting infrastructure for board members in distributed locations. Proximity to pilot partner institutions and stakeholder organizations beneficial but not mandatory given virtual engagement capability.

2. Psychometrician / Assessment Specialist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Psychometrician / Assessment Specialist is essential to design and validate gate metrics, ensure pre-registration by Month 11 (2027-09-13), and lead inter-rater calibration. While assessment is often contractor work, the 14-month engagement (Month 2 = 2026-12-13 to Month 15+ post-gate analysis) and requirement for continuous involvement in validation cycles, pre-analysis plan development and kappa calibration makes a full-time role more cost-effective and ensures continuity. Alternatively, independent_contractor if an established assessment firm is engaged for the full Phase 1–2 scope under a fixed deliverable contract.

Explanation: Designs and validates the four gate metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention), ensures they are statistically sound and pre-registered by Month 11 (2027-09-13), and leads inter-rater training and kappa calibration. Critical for gate credibility: weak or disputable metrics render the Month 24 (2028-10-13) decision non-defensible and undermine partner confidence.

Consequences: Absent psychometric expertise leads to weak, unmeasurable gate criteria; inter-rater reliability falls below kappa 0.70, inflating measurement noise by 20% and reducing statistical power by 10–15%; the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate decision becomes scientifically disputable, triggering stakeholder rejection and forcing expensive ($200K–$300K) rework or a failed gate that strands Phase 3 funding ($1.2M–$1.4M).

People Count: 1

Typical Activities: Marcus designs and validates four gate metrics: commissioning a validity study (N=20–30) in Months 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), drafting the pre-analysis plan by Month 5 (2027-03-13) with quantitative thresholds (e.g., ordinal error reduction ≥25%), registering the plan on Open Science Framework by Month 11 (2027-09-13), and leading inter-rater training and kappa calibration for pronunciation consistency (target kappa ≥0.75). He advises the editorial board on construct validity concerns, identifies potential confounds (e.g., repeated exposure to ordinals), and designs control conditions to isolate Clear English effects. He conducts a dry-run validity check at Month 10 (2027-08-13) and retrains raters if kappa falls below 0.70, extending Phase 1 by 4 weeks if necessary.

Background Story: Dr. Marcus Okafor, a psychometrician and educational measurement specialist, holds a PhD in Educational Research Methodology from the University of Michigan and has published 18 peer-reviewed papers on validity and reliability in language assessment. He spent 8 years as an assessment director at a major ESL testing organization and has designed inter-rater training protocols for oral-proficiency exams used by over 100,000 test-takers annually. Marcus brings deep expertise in pre-registration, confound control and measurement validity. He was hired by Month 2 (2026-12-13) specifically because the Clear English go/no-go gate depends entirely on defensible, pre-registered metrics; his reputation in applied measurement lends credibility to the gate decision.

Equipment Needs: Statistical software (R, SPSS, SAS, or equivalent) for designing validity studies, calculating inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa), and conducting power analysis. Online survey platform (Qualtrics, REDCap) for collecting assessment data if piloting digitally. Reading-assessment instruments (commercial or custom) compatible with Clear English and standard English conditions. Data-analysis and visualization tools (e.g., ggplot2, Excel). Laptop and secure data storage for participant datasets.

Facility Needs: Office space with private work area for confidential psychometric analysis and instrument validation. Access to a quiet testing environment for the small validity study (N=20–30) at Month 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13); could be a university partner's lab or a rented quiet room. Secure server or encrypted cloud storage for pre-analysis plan and sensitive research data. Video conferencing for consultation with the editorial board and external reviewers.

3. Linguistic Specialist / Computational Linguist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Linguistic Specialist / Computational Linguist (min 2, max 3 per canonical facts) requires continuous development of rule specification, lexicon and editorial board guidance Months 0–12 (2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13) and ongoing support through Phase 2. This is a core technical role with no clear exit point until rules are finalized and pilots are analyzed. Multiple linguists create redundancy and depth. Full-time employment ensures consistency and availability, particularly during contested rule decisions where external linguistic review cannot substitute for core team expertise.

Explanation: Develops the rule specification (ordinals, morphology retention, homograph disambiguation, grapheme-to-phoneme mapping) and owns the 5,000-word core lexicon. Chairs or advises the editorial board on linguistic consistency and ambiguity resolution. Essential during Phase 1 to finalize rules by Month 12 (2027-10-13) and ensure they are unambiguous before pilots begin.

Consequences: Insufficient linguistic expertise leads to rule ambiguity, internal contradiction, and inconsistent application; editorial board disputes remain unresolved, delaying rule finalization by 4–12 weeks; mid-pilot rule changes invalidate earlier assessments and inflate measurement error; adopters perceive the standard as linguistically incoherent, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–40%.

People Count: min 2, max 3, depending on rule complexity and lexicon scope

Typical Activities: Keiko and James lead three rule-specification workstreams: ordinal-marker design, morphology retention threshold, and homograph disambiguation. They draft rule specifications with written rationale by Month 10 (2027-08-13), chair editorial board subcommittees on contested rules, facilitate consensus between linguists and practitioners, and prepare documentation for the 30-day public comment window (Month 11 = 2027-09-13). Keiko leads morphology and homograph work, compiling a ranked list of irregular forms and high-impact homograph pairs from learner-error corpora. James leads ordinal-marker design, proposing the invariant prefix notation and fixed spoken form. Both contribute to the pre-comment rule document (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) and manage rule finalizations by Month 12 (2027-10-13), freezing the rule set before pilots begin.

Background Story: Dr. Keiko Sato and Dr. James O'Brien are two senior linguists co-leading rule specification. Keiko, trained at Cambridge in English phonology and morphology, spent 10 years at Oxford University Press developing English-learning curricula and has published on regularizing irregular verbs in ESL contexts. James, a computational linguist from MIT, specializes in grapheme-to-phoneme systems and has built speech-synthesis lexicons for three Asian languages. Together they bring complementary expertise: Keiko's pedagogical and morphological depth, James's technical and phonetic precision. Both understand the tension between linguistic consistency and learnability and are committed to evidence-based rule choices over pure elegance.

Equipment Needs: Linguistics reference tools (Oxford English Dictionary, major ESL learner corpora, morphological databases). Corpus-analysis software (AntConc, SketchEngine) for mining irregular verbs and high-frequency words. Text-annotation and markup tools (BRAT, Prodigy) for managing lexicon and rule examples. Pronunciation/phonetics software (Praat) for designing phoneme-based rule specifications. Document collaboration tools (Google Docs, Overleaf) for co-authoring rule specifications with the second linguist. Laptop with large monitor for extended writing and analysis.

Facility Needs: Office space shared with curriculum and development team for close coordination on rule clarity and pedagogical fit. Access to university linguistics library or database subscriptions (e.g., Linguistics and Language Behavior Abstracts, Project MUSE) for research on morphology and phonology. Meeting space for editorial board subcommittee discussions on contentious rules (ordinals, homographs). Ideally proximity to or affiliation with a university linguistics department for access to applied-linguistics expertise and student assistants for corpus work.

4. Phase 2 Cohort Manager / Pilot Administrator

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Phase 2 Cohort Manager / Pilot Administrator is hired by Month 6 (2027-04-13) and runs continuously through Month 24 (2028-10-13) and 30-day follow-up (Month 22–26 = 2028-08-13 to 2028-12-13). This is a single, continuous role requiring hands-on management of 460 pilot participants, coordination with 5–7 institutional partners, weekly tracking and real-time problem-solving. The role is non-negotiable for achieving the pilot's 70%+ retention rate and defensible sample sizes. Full-time is essential; part-time or contractor models lack the availability to respond to recruitment bottlenecks and participant dropouts.

Explanation: Manages recruitment, enrollment and retention of pilot learners (target 460 across 4 arms, >=80 completers per arm). Coordinates with ESL programs and technical-training partners, tracks attendance, manages incentive payments and 30-day follow-up. Essential from Month 6 (2027-04-13) onward to ensure dropout stays below 30% and minimum sample sizes are achieved for gate credibility.

Consequences: Without dedicated cohort management, enrollment lags, dropout exceeds 30% (potentially reaching 40–50%), effective sample size drops below 80 per arm, statistical power degrades by 15–25%, and the gate metrics become inconclusive or invalid; pilot data is unusable, forcing a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K additional) or a false-negative no-go that kills a viable standard.

People Count: 1

Typical Activities: Rosa manages all aspects of pilot participant recruitment and retention: coordinating with 5–7 partner institutions (ESL programs and technical-training organizations), tracking enrollment toward a target of 115 per arm (460 total), scheduling four in-person assessment sessions per participant across Months 13–24 (2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13), managing participant incentives ($50–$150 per learner, totaling $23K–$69K), conducting 30-day follow-up contact (no later than 60 days post-test), and responding immediately to any participant who misses a session. She maintains a master spreadsheet of all 460 participants and their progress, sends attendance reminders 2 weeks and 1 day before each session, arranges make-up sessions within ±1 week, and flags at-risk participants to the project lead weekly.

She speaks fluent Spanish and English and has strong relationships with ESL teachers and program coordinators across Texas. Rosa has personal experience with the frustration of irregular English morphology and spelling inconsistencies in her own teaching and sees the Clear English project as an opportunity to test evidence-based solutions. She was hired by Month 6 (2027-04-13) specifically to ensure the 460 pilot participants stay engaged and dropout remains below 30%.

Equipment Needs: Participant-management database (custom or off-the-shelf, e.g., REDCap, Qualtrics) for tracking 460 learners across 4 cohorts, attendance, contact information, incentive status and 30-day follow-up. Email and SMS reminders/scheduling system. Spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets) for master participant list and dropout monitoring. Videoconference platform for virtual assessments if any sessions are conducted remotely. Secure encrypted storage for participant contact and incentive data (GDPR/HIPAA-level security).

Facility Needs: Office space (preferably shared with project lead or nearby) for daily participant coordination and rapid response to recruitment/retention issues. Phone line and internet for outreach calls to at-risk participants. Meeting space or videoconference capability for weekly status check-ins with the project lead. Ideally located in one of the pilot hubs (e.g., Austin, Washington DC, Cambridge area) to enable in-person relationship-building with ESL programs and technical-training partners. Travel budget for quarterly on-site visits to pilot institutions (already budgeted in project travel allocation).

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Curriculum Designer / Materials Developer (1–2 per canonical facts) must produce pilot-ready learning materials by Month 13 (2027-11-13) and ensure fidelity throughout Phase 2 pilots. This is a continuous design-and-iteration role, not a discrete deliverable (print a curriculum, hand off). Materials must be revised if rules change, adapted to partner settings, and debugged during pilots. One FTE for core ESL module, potentially one for technical-glossary and safety exercises. Full-time employment ensures pedagogical consistency and rapid response to rule clarifications or pilot findings.

Consequences: Absent curriculum design results in pilot materials that are poorly aligned to rules, contain rule errors or pedagogical gaps, and fail to engage learners; assessment instruments become misaligned to the intended Clear English constructs; pilot fidelity is low, confounding results; assessment data is unreliable for the gate decision, reducing credibility by an estimated 20–30%.

People Count: min 1, max 2, depending on breadth of materials (ESL module, technical glossary, safety-labeling exercises)

Typical Activities: David and Elena jointly design pilot learning materials (print booklet and digital module) by Month 13 (2027-11-13), with David leading ESL-module pedagogy and Elena leading technical-glossary design. They support both ESL and technical pilot cohorts with fidelity checks and learner-engagement monitoring Months 13–24 (2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13).

Background Story: David Liu and Elena Rodriguez are two curriculum designers with complementary expertise. David has 6 years of experience designing print and digital ESL materials for a major textbook publisher and knows how to translate linguistic rules into engaging, scaffold learning activities. Elena, a former safety-compliance trainer in the oil and gas industry, has written technical glossaries and procedure guides and understands how clarity, consistency and minimal ambiguity reduce accident risk. Together they design both the ESL pilot module (for adult learners) and the technical/safety-glossary exercises (for the native-speaker cohort). Both are deeply familiar with the tension between pedagogical appeal and rule fidelity.

Authoring tools for print and digital materials (Adobe InDesign or equivalent for layout; Articulate Storyline or similar for digital interactivity). Access to Clear English rule specifications and pronunciation guidance (frozen by Month 12 = 2027-10-13). Proofreading and editing software (Grammarly, Microsoft Editor) adapted for Clear English rule-checking. Laptop with dual monitors for design and assessment integration.

Facility Needs: Office space shared with the linguistic team and project lead for rapid iteration and rule alignment. Access to quiet design space for focused curriculum writing and layout work (Months 6–13 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-11-13 are peak production months). Meeting space for dry-run testing with a small pilot group (N=5–10) at Month 10 (2027-08-13); quiet classroom or training room at a partner ESL program or technical-training site. Ideally co-located or virtual-adjacent to pilot partner institutions to enable hands-on material piloting and fidelity checks Months 13–24 (2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13).

9. Audio Production & Technical Infrastructure Manager

Alternatively, a full-time employee if internal IT infrastructure and in-house recording are priorities; trade-off: cost and hiring delay vs. control.

People Count: 1

He designs inter-rater training materials and conducts calibration sessions with 3–4 raters on a 100–200 word pilot sample (Months 9–10 = 2027-07-13 to 2027-08-13), measuring Cohen's kappa and retraining raters if kappa falls below 0.70. He manages encrypted audio-file storage, backup protocols, and GDPR-compliant access controls by Month 6 (2027-04-13), conducts a data-protection audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13), and delivers all 5,000 entries with passing inter-rater checks by Month 11 (2027-09-13).

He has set up inter-rater training workflows, managed encrypted storage systems for sensitive audio biometric data, and coordinated international recording sessions across multiple time zones.
