Secure on-premises or cloud-hosted server infrastructure for encrypted audio storage, backup and GDPR-compliant access control (location-agnostic; cloud or dedicated server).

Omissions

1. Absence of Quantitative Gate Thresholds and Pre-Registration Plan

The plan names four go/no-go metrics (ordinal error rate, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) but does not specify quantitative pass/fail criteria (e.g., 'ordinal error must drop by ≥25%') or sample-size targets. Without pre-registered thresholds fixed before Month 11 (2027-09-13), the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision becomes subjective and disputable, undermining partner confidence and gate credibility.

Recommendation: By Month 5 (2027-03-13), commission the psychometrician to draft a pre-analysis plan specifying: (1) quantitative thresholds for each metric with explicit justification (e.g., ordinal error reduction ≥25% proposed, comprehension speed ≤10% slower than control proposed, pronunciation consistency kappa ≥0.75 proposed, 30-day retention ≥70% proposed); (2) minimum sample sizes per arm (≥80 completers proposed for 80% statistical power); (3) primary outcomes and intention-to-treat rules. Register this plan on Open Science Framework by Month 11 (2027-09-13) and publish publicly 30 days before Phase 2 begins. If pre-registration is not complete by Month 11 (2027-09-13), delay Phase 2 start and gate decision by 6–12 weeks to ensure thresholds are defensible.

2. Missing Construct Validity and Confound-Control Framework for Gate Metrics

The plan does not specify how to control for alternative explanations of measured effects. Repeated exposure to ordinals (even in standard form) might improve accuracy independent of Clear English; learner motivation to participate in a novel standard could inflate performance; accent proximity to learners' first language might make pronunciation scores high in both conditions. Without explicit control conditions and confound analyses, the gate metrics become scientifically disputable.

Recommendation: By Month 5 (2027-03-13), build a construct-validity section into the Outcome Metric Battery Design decision: (1) identify plausible alternative explanations for each metric (e.g., repeated exposure, motivation, accent proximity); (2) design explicit control conditions (e.g., standard-English ordinals with rule instruction vs. implicit exposure) to isolate Clear English effects; (3) measure manipulation checks (ask learners post-test which rule system they learned); (4) pre-register confound-analysis plan (e.g., regress ordinal error on baseline literacy, first-language phonology, study motivation). Publish this framework in the Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-analysis plan. If effect sizes or inter-rater reliability at Month 18 (2028-04-13) reveal confounds larger than expected, conduct additional validity work by Month 21 (2028-07-13) rather than proceeding to the gate with weak data.

3. Unspecified Fallback if Inter-Rater Reliability Falls Below Target Kappa

The plan targets Cohen's kappa ≥0.75 (proposed) for pronunciation-consistency scoring, with a floor of 0.70 (proposed). However, no explicit action plan specifies what happens if rater calibration achieves only kappa 0.65–0.70. A weak inter-rater reliability inflates measurement noise by 20%, reducing statistical power to detect Clear English effects by 10–15%, risking a false-negative gate outcome that kills a viable standard or forces expensive rework.

Recommendation: Include in the Phase 1 schedule (by Month 8 = 2027-06-13): design inter-rater training and calibration protocol; recruit ≥3–4 raters with ESL/phonetics background; conduct training on the anchor accent (chosen by Month 3 = 2027-01-13) on a pilot sample of 100–200 words by Month 9 (2027-07-13); measure Cohen's kappa by Month 10 (2027-08-13) and require kappa ≥0.70 (floor) to proceed to full production. If kappa falls below 0.70 at Month 10 (2027-08-13), halt full production, conduct additional rater retraining and calibration (2–4 weeks, extending to Month 10.5 = 2027-08-28 = ~2027-08-28), and retest kappa by Month 11 (2027-09-13). If kappa remains below 0.70, flag to the editorial board for either a 4-week Phase 1 extension (new deadline Month 15 = 2028-01-13) or scope reduction (record only 3,000–4,000 highest-impact words). This ensures pronunciation-consistency scoring meets measurement-reliability standards before pilots begin.

4. Undefined Post-Project Stewardship Funding Model and Governance

The plan extends only to Month 36 (2029-10-13), when external funding and formal project governance end. However, the standard will require ongoing maintenance: responding to adoption feedback, managing version/change requests, updating the lexicon, and handling disputes over rule interpretation. Without a clear stewardship funding model and organizational home identified by Month 33 (2029-07-13), the standard could atrophy within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13). Adopter organizations will lose confidence in stability, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%.

Recommendation: By Month 24 (2028-10-13) (coinciding with the Phase 2 go/no-go decision), identify ≥2–3 potential permanent steward organizations (language-education non-profits, university consortiums, standards bodies such as ISO or TESOL) and document their capacity and mission alignment. By Month 27 (2029-01-13), approach the top candidates with a formal Stewardship Proposal specifying annual budget ($150K–$250K estimate), key responsibilities (responding to change requests, managing conformance claims, issuing errata, leading full review every 3–5 years) and decision authority. By Month 30 (2029-04-13), negotiate a formal Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with at least one steward organization committing to assume stewardship for ≥10 years; have it signed and published by Month 33 (2029-07-13). Publish a public 5-year Stewardship Roadmap by Month 36 (2029-10-13) documenting review cycles, change-request prioritization, governance-committee composition and dispute-resolution procedures. If no steward commitment is secured by Month 33 (2029-07-13), flag to the editorial board that v1.0 public release is contingent on stewardship being in place, preventing a launch without long-term maintenance capacity.

5. Audio Production Bottleneck and Multi-Accent Scope Creep Risk

The plan commits to 5,000-word core lexicon with single-accent pronunciation guidance by Month 12 (2027-10-13). Audio production at scale (5,000 entries × ≥2 takes estimate = 10,000+ files) is bottlenecked by studio availability, rater training and inter-rater reliability calibration (target kappa ≥0.75 proposed). The plan does not estimate studio costs, scheduling lead times or contingency for technical failures. Additionally, pressure to add accents (British, American, Australian, Indian) could emerge at Month 9–12 (2027-07-13 to 2027-10-13), inflating audio budget by $50K–$100K (estimate) and straining Phase 1 contingency.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), conduct detailed audio-production scoping: (1) reserve a professional recording studio or language-recording service with firm capacity guarantees for Months 6–11 (2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13); document lead times, file specifications and backup protocols in a signed contract; identify a contingency provider by Month 3 (2027-01-13); (2) estimate all-in cost per entry (speaker fees, editing, inter-rater scoring): if cost exceeds $20 per entry (estimate), pivot to hybrid approach—speech-synthesis baseline for all 5,000 words by Month 7 (2027-05-13), then human rater verification on the highest-friction 1,000–1,500 words by Month 11 (2027-09-13); (3) by Month 3 (2027-01-13), publish a board-approved policy deferring accent additions to post-v1.0, with a documented process for future requests; cap scope-creep risk by specifying that accent additions require a formal scope-change proposal with budget impact. (4) By Month 9 (2027-07-13), assess production progress and kappa-reliability status; if kappa falls below 0.70 (floor proposed) or costs exceed budget, halt and conduct 2–4 weeks targeted remediation by Month 10 (2027-08-13); if not resolved, flag to board for Phase 1 extension or scope reduction (record 3,000–4,000 words only, violating the 5,000-word constraint and requiring board waiver).

6. Insufficient Contingency Reserve and Pre-Gate Draw Procedure

The plan allocates a $0.35M reserve (10% of budget), with only $175K (5% of budget) available for pre-gate draws. A $300K overrun (8.6% of budget estimate) would exhaust the pre-gate draw cap by $125K, leaving no further contingency before the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision. If Phase 1 extends 4 weeks (~$85K estimate) and Phase 2 encounters unexpected psychometric validation costs or recruitment delays, the remaining headroom ($90K estimate) is inadequate for typical project contingencies.

Recommendation: Establish a clear pre-gate draw procedure by Month 1 (2026-11-13): (1) cap pre-gate draws at $175K (5% of budget, half the reserve), available only for pre-approved, evidence-backed gate-protection needs (e.g., psychometric re-validation, rater retraining, recruitment incentive increases); (2) require the project lead to request draws with written justification to the editorial board, specifying why the expense protects gate credibility and why it could not be anticipated; (3) maintain a running forecast of spending by Month 9 (2027-07-13) and assess whether Phase 2 can proceed on schedule; if remaining pre-gate headroom falls below $90K (estimate) or cumulative overrun exceeds $100K, convene the editorial board at Month 9 (2027-07-13) to decide whether to extend Phase 1 (costing ~$85K per month estimate), reduce Phase 2 scope (fewer cohorts, shorter follow-up) or release additional reserve funds with a board-documented decision. (4) Implement monthly project-status reviews and rolling 6-month spending forecasts from Month 1 (2026-11-13) onward, with escalation to the program lead if any line item tracks >10% over budget.

Potential Improvements

1. Clarify Editorial Board Tiebreaker Mechanism and Timeline

The plan specifies an external tiebreaker arbiter for rule disputes but does not detail how to engage the arbiter, timeline for tiebreaker decisions, cost ceiling or how minority-position documentation will be handled. Vague escalation procedures could delay rule finalization, compressing Phase 2 pilots by 4–12 weeks. A formal, pre-negotiated tiebreaker process with clear decision timelines (e.g., arbiter must rule within 2 weeks) ensures rule disputes do not stall the project.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), the editorial board must identify and secure a written agreement with an external neutral arbiter (e.g., a senior linguist or standards-development expert from an external institution such as a university or ISO body). Document in the Editorial Board Charter: (1) arbiter's decision authority (e.g., 'arbiter is called if voting deadlocks 4–5 after two discussion rounds'); (2) decision timeline (e.g., 'arbiter must render a written ruling within 2 weeks of referral'); (3) arbiter cost (cap at $10K–$20K estimate per project, or $5K per decision estimate); (4) publication protocol ('both majority and arbiter-preferred positions published in rule rationale'). By Month 5 (2027-03-13), have the arbiter's signed agreement on file and publish a one-page summary on the project website explaining the tiebreaker process. If a rule dispute is referred to the arbiter, the project lead tracks the timeline and escalates if the arbiter's decision takes >2 weeks.

2. Establish Clear Partner Enrollment Guarantees and Make-Up Protocols

The plan requires ≥3–4 ESL programs and ≥2–3 technical-training organizations to provide ≥115 learners per arm (460 total estimate) and achieve a dropout rate ≤30% (estimate). However, the team-members document does not specify what happens if a partner fails to meet enrollment targets or if a learner misses a session. Vague make-up and escalation procedures could lead to unplanned sample-size reductions and statistical power loss.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), finalize written partner Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) that specify: (1) minimum guaranteed enrollment (e.g., 'Partner A commits to enroll ≥75 ESL learners by Month 13 = 2027-11-13'); (2) assessment schedule (e.g., 'four in-person sessions of 60–90 minutes each across Months 13–24 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13'); (3) make-up session protocol ('any learner missing a scheduled session has the option for a make-up within ±1 week'); (4) escalation ('if enrollment falls >10% short of guarantee by Month 14 = 2027-12-13, partner notifies project lead within 2 days and project lead activates backup recruitment'); (5) incentive and payment terms (e.g., '$75 per learner for completion incentive; partner receives $40 per learner-session to cover costs'). By Month 13 (2027-11-13), the Cohort Manager confirms that enrollment meets targets and begins tracking attendance. Document all make-up sessions and attendance deviations in the master participant log to assess dropout trends early.

3. Specify Pronunciation Consistency Scoring Procedure and Rater Independence

The plan designates pronunciation consistency as a gate metric requiring Cohen's kappa ≥0.75 (proposed target) inter-rater reliability. However, it does not detail: (1) how raters will be selected and trained; (2) whether raters must be independent of the project team; (3) how audio files will be presented to raters (randomized, blinded to condition); (4) how disagreements will be resolved. Without these procedural details, pronunciation scoring could be biased or inconsistently applied, inflating kappa or introducing rater drift.

Recommendation: By Month 4 (2027-02-13), the psychometrician and audio-production manager must draft a detailed Pronunciation Scoring Protocol specifying: (1) rater recruitment and training (e.g., 'at least 3–4 raters with ESL teaching or speech-pathology background; independent of Clear English development team; trained on reference-accent anchor by Month 9 = 2027-07-13 using a 100–200 word calibration sample'); (2) scoring procedure ('raters score audio files in randomized order, blinded to condition and learner identity; each file scored by ≥2 independent raters; scoring on a validated scale, e.g., 1–5 rating or binary match/mismatch'); (3) inter-rater reliability check (Cohen's kappa calculated on calibration sample by Month 10 = 2027-08-13; target ≥0.75 proposed, floor 0.70 proposed); (4) disagreement resolution ('if raters disagree, a third independent rater breaks the tie; if tie-breaker also disagrees, entry marked as 'unclear' and excluded from scoring'); (5) rater-training documentation ('all raters sign confidentiality agreements and a statement confirming they received training on the scoring protocol'). Publish this protocol in the pre-analysis plan (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) to ensure scoring is transparent and auditable.

4. Define Lexicon Coverage Audit Procedure and Expansion Trigger

The plan specifies that the 5,000-word core lexicon must cover ≥85% of pilot running text (proposed threshold) and commits to a coverage audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13), with fixes by Month 10 (2027-08-13). However, it does not specify: (1) which text corpus will be analyzed (pilot ESL curriculum? technical glossaries? both?); (2) how coverage will be calculated (types vs. tokens?); (3) what constitutes an 'expansion' (adding words to the core 5,000, or creating a secondary 500-word block?); (4) cost and timeline if expansion is needed.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), specify the lexicon-audit scope: (1) coverage will be calculated on the actual pilot curriculum and technical-glossary documents planned for use in Phase 2, plus running text from at least 2–3 existing ESL textbooks; (2) coverage metric is word type coverage ('how many distinct word forms in pilot text are in the 5,000-word list') calculated on the first 10,000 running words (or entire curriculum if <10,000 words) to approximate early-learning engagement; (3) coverage target ≥85% (proposed); (4) if coverage falls short, the 5,000-word list may be expanded by drawing from a pre-compiled secondary candidate list (e.g., the next 500 highest-frequency words from the same corpus used to build the base 5,000). By Month 8 (2027-06-13), conduct the audit and identify any shortfalls. If expansion is needed, allocate $20K–$50K (estimate) for pronunciation recording of new entries and revise recording timeline: record new entries by Month 11 (2027-09-13) (compressing other work or extending Phase 1 by 1–2 weeks). Document the final lexicon and its coverage in the published v1.0 standard.

5. Clarify Data Privacy and Participant Consent Workflow

The plan notes that ethics/IRB approval and GDPR compliance are required by Month 6 (2027-04-13) but does not specify the consent workflow or data-retention schedule. Ambiguity could delay ethics approval or create compliance gaps, jeopardizing pilot recruitment or exposing the project to regulatory investigation.

Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), the project lead and regulatory affairs manager must engage an ethics review committee (IRB, research ethics committee) and draft a study protocol specifying: (1) research classification (is the pilot human-subjects research requiring IRB review? Likely yes; confirm with the IRB); (2) informed-consent process (in writing, in multiple languages if ESL learners speak different home languages, using plain language; electronic or paper consent; right to withdraw and data deletion); (3) data types collected and retention schedule ('audio recordings: 3 years post-analysis or until learner requests deletion; test scores and demographics: 5 years for replication studies; consent forms: 3 years minimum for compliance audit'); (4) access controls ('authorized research team members only; all team members sign data-use agreements'); (5) storage and security ('encrypted on-premises or cloud server, GDPR-compliant, with backup and audit logs'). Obtain written ethics approval by Month 6 (2027-04-13). By Month 10 (2027-08-13), publish standard informed-consent forms and a Data Protection and Privacy Policy on the project website, clearly stating how long data is retained and participants' rights. Provide all participants a copy of the consent form and privacy policy at enrollment.

6. Document Phase 2 Pilot Timeline and Contingency Windows

The plan specifies Phase 2 occurs Months 12–24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13) with enrollment complete by Month 13 (2027-11-13) and data lock by Month 22 (2028-08-13), leaving only 2 months for analysis and gate-decision dossier preparation (Months 22–24 = 2028-08-13 to 2028-10-13). This timeline is compressed and leaves little room for data-quality issues or analysis surprises. Clarifying the pilot schedule with explicit checkpoints and contingency windows improves timeline discipline and reduces gate-decision risk.

Recommendation: Establish a formal Phase 2 schedule and contingency plan by Month 9 (2027-07-13): (1) Enrollment Phase: all recruitment complete by Month 13 (2027-11-13); 1-week buffer for stragglers (to Month 14 = 2027-12-13); (2) Assessment Phase: four sessions per participant across Months 13–24 (2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13); Session 1 by Month 14 (2027-12-13); Session 2 by Month 17 (2028-03-13); Session 3 by Month 20 (2028-06-13); Session 4 by Month 23 (2028-09-13); (3) 30-day follow-up: completed by Month 22 (2028-08-13) (last session Month 23 = 2028-09-13 + 30 days ~Month 24 = 2028-10-13 or slightly later; data collection extended 1–2 weeks if needed); (4) Data lock and quality check: Month 22 (2028-08-13); (5) Analysis and dossier preparation: Months 22–24 (2028-08-13 to 2028-10-13); gate decision Months 24 (2028-10-13). If data quality issues are identified (e.g., >10 files corrupted, dropout exceeds 35%, inter-rater kappa <0.70 in preliminary checks), flag to the editorial board by Month 21 (2028-07-13) with options: (a) extend Phase 2 by 3–6 months for remediation or additional data collection; (b) proceed with inconclusive data and conditional gate decision; (c) conduct targeted re-assessment on a subset of participants. Document all contingency triggers and board-decision authority in the Phase 2 Project Plan by Month 12 (2027-10-13).

7. Specify Licensing Model Decision Criteria and Timeline

The plan states that a Licensing and Name Stewardship decision will be made by Month 6 (2027-04-13), choosing between three options: (a) permissive open license with no name restrictions; (b) name-as-certification-mark with a published conformance checklist; (c) share-alike license requiring divergent works to adopt a distinct name. However, it does not specify which decision criteria (ease of adoption, protection against fragmentation, governance overhead) will weigh most heavily or who decides in case the editorial board is divided.

Recommendation: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), the regulatory affairs manager must commission a legal analysis (estimated $10K–$20K) comparing the three licensing scenarios on: (1) adoption friction (ease for publishers to adopt); (2) fragmentation risk (likelihood of non-conforming variants); (3) governance overhead ($cost and staff time for certification/dispute resolution); (4) perceived fairness/openness (stakeholder perception of gatekeeping). By Month 4 (2027-02-13), present the analysis to the editorial board with a recommendation. Establish a board vote by Month 5 (2027-03-13) with clear voting rules (e.g., simple majority; if tied, program lead + external arbiter decide). The chosen model must be published with explicit rationale by Month 6 (2027-04-13). If the board selects certification mark (option b), publish a free, light conformance checklist by Month 12 (2027-10-13) specifying exactly what materials must do to qualify as Clear English, with a goal of reducing gatekeeping perception and enabling fast approval for most straightforward adaptations.

8. Establish Monthly Budget Tracking and Spending Forecast Protocol

The plan mentions budget controls and a Month 9 (2027-07-13) spending review but does not specify: (1) who tracks spending monthly (project lead? dedicated finance person?); (2) what spending forecast tool is used; (3) what variance thresholds trigger escalation (e.g., >10% over budget on a line item?); (4) escalation procedure. Without clear financial discipline, budget overruns can accumulate silently, consuming contingency reserves without board awareness.

Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), establish a monthly budget-tracking system: (1) project lead or a part-time finance administrator maintains a detailed spending log in a shared spreadsheet or accounting system, tracking actual spend vs. budget for each major line item (staff, psychometrics, audio production, pilot incentives, travel, etc.) monthly; (2) by the 5th business day of each month, produce a summary dashboard showing year-to-date actuals, forecast-to-completion, and variance (actual spend % of monthly budget allocation); (3) variance threshold: escalate to the editorial board if any line item is >10% over budget or if cumulative overrun exceeds $50K in a single month (estimate); (4) at Month 9 (2027-07-13), conduct a formal Phase 1 spending review: assess whether Phase 1 is on budget; if overrun >$100K, convene the board to decide whether to extend Phase 1, reduce Phase 2 scope or release additional reserve funds; (5) establish rolling 6-month spending forecasts at Months 9 (2027-07-13), 15 (2028-01-13), 21 (2028-07-13) and 27 (2029-01-13) to identify future budget gaps early and allow mid-course corrections. Document all budget decisions and board actions in the decision log maintained by the governance administrator.

9. Define Pilot Fidelity Monitoring and Rule-Compliance Checkpoints

The plan specifies that curriculum designers will conduct dry runs and support fidelity checks during pilots (Months 13–24 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13), but does not detail: (1) what 'fidelity' means (consistent rule application? all rules taught? rules taught in the specified order?); (2) how fidelity will be measured (classroom observations? curriculum deliverable reviews? learner quiz on rule accuracy?); (3) how rule violations will be corrected. Poor fidelity could introduce confounds (learners in one site receive incomplete rule instruction), inflating measurement noise and weakening gate evidence.

Recommendation: By Month 12 (2027-10-13), the curriculum design team must document a Fidelity Monitoring Protocol specifying: (1) definition of fidelity: ('Clear English' cohorts are taught all core rules (ordinals, morphology, homographs, pronunciation guidance) in the prescribed order and frequency; control cohorts receive standard-English instruction); (2) fidelity measures: (a) instructor compliance checklist (curriculum designers or an independent observer confirm that each of the 4–6 core rules was taught in the prescribed sessions); (b) learner comprehension check (brief 5–10 minute quiz after each rule unit, scored to confirm learners understood the rule); (c) delivery logs (instructors record which rules were taught each session and any deviations); (3) fidelity monitoring schedule: Month 14 (2027-12-13) initial site visit to all partners; Month 17 (2028-03-13) midpoint fidelity audit (review delivery logs and conduct random classroom observations); Month 23 (2028-09-13) final audit; (4) corrective action: if fidelity is <80% (estimated) at any site by Month 17 (2028-03-13), the curriculum team contacts the instructor, reviews the lesson materials, and provides coaching; if fidelity remains <80% by Month 20 (2028-06-13), flag to the project lead for consideration of excluding that site's data or requiring re-teaching. Document all fidelity findings in the gate-decision dossier (Months 22–24 = 2028-08-13 to 2028-10-13) to contextualize any low ordinal-accuracy or pronunciation-consistency scores.

1.4.A Issue - Pre-Registration and Psychometric Validation Are Dangerously Underspecified

The project plan specifies four gate metrics (ordinal error ≥25% reduction, comprehension speed ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%) as 'proposed thresholds,' not pre-registered. The psychometrician hire is scheduled for Month 2 (2026-12-13), but the pre-analysis plan (PAP) is not due until Month 9 (2027-07-13), with pre-registration by Month 11 (2027-09-13)—only 30 days before Phase 2 pilots begin. This compressed timeline creates three failures: (1) no pilot validity study (N=20–30) to calibrate thresholds before they are locked; (2) no time to correct instrument ambiguity if the dry run at Month 10 (2027-08-13) exposes flawed items; (3) post-hoc claims by educators and regulators that thresholds were rigged or arbitrary, undermining the gate decision credibility that is the entire epistemic foundation of the project.

1.4.B Tags

  • psychometrics-timeline-compression
  • pre-registration-delay
  • validity-study-absent
  • gate-credibility-risk
  • threshold-not-empirically-justified

1.4.C Mitigation

Hire the psychometrician by Month 1 (2026-11-13) (not Month 2 = 2026-12-13) and commission a phased deliverable: (1) By Month 3 (2027-01-13), submit a draft instrument specification, item pool and effect-size justification. (2) By Month 5 (2027-03-13), conduct and complete a small pilot validity study (N=20–30 adult ESL learners and native speakers, 2–3 assessment sessions) to estimate effect sizes and refine items. (3) By Month 8 (2027-06-13), deliver the final pre-analysis plan with numeric thresholds backed by observed effect sizes, not proposals. (4) Pre-register by Month 10 (2027-08-13) (not Month 11 = 2027-09-13), allowing 6 weeks for editorial board review and early third-party comment. If a validity study is not feasible by Month 5 (2027-03-13), defer Phase 2 pilots and extend Phase 1 by 8–12 weeks (cost ~$170K–$255K, estimate) to establish credible baselines.

1.4.D Consequence

Without pre-registered, empirically justified thresholds, the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision will be scientifically disputable. Educators and standards bodies will claim the thresholds were set to produce a predetermined outcome, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–50% and triggering public criticism. A false-positive gate (passing weak evidence) could launch a flawed standard; a false-negative (rejecting real effects) wastes $1.2M on inconclusive pilots and forfeits 12 months' credibility building.

1.4.E Root Cause

The project plan prioritizes timeline compression over epistemic rigor. Hiring the psychometrician 1 month after project start, then compressing the validity study, instrument refinement and pre-registration into 9 months, reflects an assumption that thresholds can be proposals until Month 11 (2027-09-13). This assumption is false: standards bodies, funders and educators demand empirically grounded thresholds locked before evidence collection begins. The root cause is insufficient allocation of Phase 1 time and budget to psychometrics.

1.5.A Issue - Pilot Recruitment and Retention Strategy Lacks Contingency Depth and Early Verification

The plan specifies signed commitments from ≥3 ESL programs and ≥2 technical organizations by Month 3 (2027-01-13), with enrolment beginning Month 12 (2027-10-13) (9 months later) and completion by Month 13 (2027-11-13). This 9-month lag creates three risks: (1) signed letters are non-binding or evaporate if institutional circumstances change; (2) no early verification of learner eligibility, willingness or capacity until Month 12 (2027-10-13), when reversal costs are maximal; (3) no pilot recruitment trial run (mini-pilot, N=20–30) to test assessment logistics, dropout drivers and incentive adequacy before full-scale enrolment. The plan budgets for a 30% dropout tolerance but provides no data-driven dropout prediction, contingency learner pools, or escalation triggers (e.g., 'if dropout exceeds 20% by Month 15 = 2028-01-13, recruit an additional cohort of 40–50').

1.5.B Tags

  • recruitment-timeline-lag
  • non-binding-commitments
  • no-mini-pilot
  • dropout-contingency-absent
  • retention-strategy-reactive

1.5.C Mitigation

(1) By Month 2 (2026-12-13), recruit and run a mini-pilot (N=20–30 adult learners and native-speaker technical trainees, at 1–2 partner sites) through at least 2 full assessment cycles (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-13 to 2027-02-13). Document actual dropout, reasons for attrition, dropout timing, incentive sufficiency and assessment burden. (2) By Month 4 (2027-02-13), use mini-pilot data to calibrate a dropout-prediction model and revise enrolment and retention protocols. (3) By Month 3 (2027-01-13), obtain signed Memoranda of Understanding (not just letters) with explicit clauses: guaranteed learner supply with liquidated damages ($500–$1K per missing learner, estimate) if recruitment targets are missed; institution's escalation contact and 30-day notification of shortfalls. (4) By Month 6 (2027-04-13), conduct a recruitment triage: identify learners at high dropout risk (e.g., attendance history, work instability) and apply differentiated retention tactics (higher incentives, flexible scheduling, peer cohorts). (5) Establish an escalation trigger: if dropout exceeds 20% by Month 15 (2028-01-13), immediately recruit a standby cohort of 40–50 learners (cost ~$30K–$50K, estimate) to reach the minimum 80 per-arm threshold.

1.5.D Consequence

If pilot recruitment falls short or dropout exceeds 30%, effective sample size drops below 80 per condition, reducing statistical power to ~60% (estimate). This inflates the Type II error (false-negative) risk: real Clear English effects are not detected, triggering a false-negative gate outcome and a no-go decision despite potential efficacy. Alternatively, retention shortfalls compress the data-collection window and force rushed, incomplete 30-day follow-up assessments, invalidating the retention metric. Either path wastes Phase 2 budget (~$1.2M) and forces a 6-month extension (cost ~$300K–$600K, estimate) or project termination.

1.5.E Root Cause

The recruitment strategy treats pilot partners as static commitments rather than active collaborators with changing capacity. The 9-month lag between signed commitments and actual enrolment reflects an assumption that letters of intent guarantee delivery without ongoing relationship management. The plan lacks early verification (mini-pilot) and contingency learner pools, indicating insufficient budgeting for recruitment risk and retention management. The cohort manager is hired at Month 6 (2027-04-13), after recruitment design should be finalized, creating a downstream, reactive posture.

1.6.A Issue - Inter-Rater Reliability and Audio Production Timeline Creates a Critical Single-Point Failure

The plan specifies audio recording of 5,000 lexicon entries (≈10,000 files at 2 takes) during Months 6–11 (2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13), with inter-rater training and calibration during Months 8–10 (2027-06-13 to 2027-08-13). If inter-rater Cohen's kappa falls below 0.70 at Month 10 (2027-08-13), the fallback is '2–4 weeks additional retraining.' This assumes retraining succeeds, but provides no contingency if kappa remains ≤0.70 after retraining. The plan proposes a 4-week Phase 1 extension (~$85K cost, estimate) as the only fallback, but this single extension does not address the core failure modes: (1) selected raters may be unsuitable for pronunciation judgement (accent, ear training, language background); (2) audio quality or speaker training may be poor, inflating noise; (3) the reference accent anchor may not be sufficiently defined for consistent scoring. Without alternative rater sources, pre-screening, or a synthetic-audio fallback, any kappa failure at Month 10 (2027-08-13) blocks full Phase 2 launch.

1.6.B Tags

  • inter-rater-reliability-single-point-failure
  • audio-production-timeline-critical-path
  • kappa-floor-0.70-brittle
  • accent-anchor-undefined
  • rater-prerequisites-not-validated

1.6.C Mitigation

(1) By Month 2 (2026-12-13), establish rater pre-screening criteria: phonetics or applied-linguistics background (MA or equivalent), native or native-like proficiency in the reference accent, and prior rater-training experience. Pre-screen at least 6–8 candidate raters by Month 4 (2027-02-13), testing each on a 50-word calibration sample to identify the 3–4 most reliable. (2) By Month 3 (2027-01-13), finalize and document the reference accent anchor in a 2–3 page specification: vowel inventory, key consonant contrasts, stress and intonation patterns, and recordings of example words. Provide raters with this spec and 20–30 anchor exemplars by Month 7 (2027-05-13). (3) By Month 5 (2027-03-13), conduct a micro-pilot recording session (100–200 entries) with the top rater candidates; measure inter-rater kappa on this sample by Month 6 (2027-04-13). If kappa ≥0.75, proceed to full production by Month 7 (2027-05-13). If 0.70–0.74, implement targeted retraining (focused on misaligned phoneme categories) and retest by Month 7.5 (2027-05-28). If <0.70, pivot immediately to a hybrid model: (a) Synthetic speech (TTS) baseline for all 5,000 entries by Month 8.5 (2027-06-28) (cost $15K–$25K, estimate); (b) human rater verification only on the top 1,500–2,000 highest-friction words (irregular, diphthongs, schwa words) by Month 11 (2027-09-13). (4) By Month 9 (2027-07-13), if human recording is still in progress, secure a backup studio and a secondary rater by Month 8 (2027-06-13) to parallelise sessions and reduce single-vendor risk.

1.6.D Consequence

If inter-rater kappa falls below 0.70 and retraining fails, the project faces a hard stop at Month 10.5 (2027-08-28). Proceeding to Phase 2 with kappa <0.70 inflates the pronunciation-consistency metric's measurement error by 20–30%, reducing statistical power to detect true Clear English effects by 10–15% (estimate). The gate outcome becomes unreliable: pronunciation consistency could falsely pass (Type I error, false positive) or falsely fail (Type II error), invalidating the go/no-go decision. A 4-week Phase 1 extension addresses timeline slippage but not the underlying validity crisis. Without a pre-planned hybrid (synthetic + verification) fallback, kappa failure forces a 12-week extension (~$170K–$255K cost, estimate) or scope reduction (recording only 3,000 words, violating the 5,000-word user constraint).

1.6.E Root Cause

The audio production timeline is on the critical path, compressed into 6 months (Months 6–11 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13) with only a 4-week contingency buffer. The project assumes raters can be trained to kappa ≥0.70 by Month 10 (2027-08-13), but provides no pre-screening, no rater-selection validation and no synthetic-audio fallback plan. The reference accent anchor is not finalized until Month 3 (2027-01-13) (or later), leaving only 3–4 months for raters to internalize the standard before calibration testing. The single-point failure is the absence of a hybrid recording strategy (synthetic baseline + verification subset) that would allow Phase 2 launch even if human rater kappa is delayed or subthreshold.

Audio cost overruns or late rater-training discovery compress the Phase 1 rules-lock deadline, forcing either a 6-week extension (cost $125K-$150K estimated) or a scope reduction that violates the 5,000-word user constraint. Past precedent (ICAO aviation-English pilot studies 2010-2015) shows that under-resourced recruitment and late assessment readiness are the top reasons pilots fail to generate defensible evidence; the cost of remediation is typically 2-3 months and $200K-$400K, not the projected 4 weeks and $85K.

This mirrors the risk register's flag: 'Weak or disputable assessment validity and rater reliability (kappa below 0.70)' is a key risk, yet mitigation says only 'extend Phase 1 by 4 weeks if kappa stays below 0.70,' implying a reactive, not proactive, approach.

(3) cross-border transfer—if the US-based hub stores encrypted audio on cloud servers (AWS, Azure), GDPR requires data-processing agreements (DPAs) with the cloud vendor, which add 2–4 weeks of legal negotiation. (4) data-minimization principle—can inter-rater reliability be assessed on a 200-word subset instead of 5,000 entries, or is the full-corpus recording non-negotiable? The plan mentions 'encrypted storage by Month 6 (2027-04-13) and audit by Month 8 (2027-06-13)' but does not specify which encryption standard (AES-256?), key-management protocol (who holds the decryption key?), or cloud-vendor DPA status.

4.6.D Consequence

Without a detailed Liability Strategy and confirmed insurance by Month 4 (2027-02-13), the project risks uninsured exposure: if a pilot partner uses Clear English materials in a live setting and an injury or near-miss occurs, the project team could face product-liability claims (estimated $100K–$1M+ defense costs, settlement or judgment), regulatory investigation (OSHA recordkeeping, HSE prosecution, state board review), and reputational damage that blocks Phase 3 adoption by all technical and safety-critical partners (estimated 30–50% of adoption target). Additionally, if the IRB discovers that liability exposure has not been quantified or mitigated, it may withdraw ethics approval or downgrade the pilot to 'non-operational use only,' narrowing the scope and reducing the credibility of the safety-critical evidence at the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate. Conversely, over-conservative disclaimers that position the standard as 'not suitable for any operational use' will deter safety-critical partners from participation, eliminating the technical-glossary cohort from pilots and reducing the overall adoption case.

4.6.E Root Cause

The plan treats safety-critical liability as a secondary concern ('limit pilots to glossary and labeling') and assigns it a single line item ('legal strategy by Month 4 = 2027-02-13'), without distinguishing between research liability (covered by IRB approval and institutional indemnity) and product liability (exposure to third-party injury claims, regulatory prosecution, and reputational harm). The root causes are: (a) no clarity on what 'glossary and labeling exercises' means operationally—are learners labeling pharmaceutical bottles with Clear English ordinals in a supervised classroom, or are pilot partners introducing labeled materials into actual workplace settings?; (b) no differentiation between US and UK liability frameworks (US relies on product-liability tort law; UK relies on Consumer Protection from Unfair Trading Regulations and Health & Safety at Work etc. Act 1974); (c) no assessment of whether a 'research study' exemption applies if the materials are not released commercially; (d) no insurance-market research to confirm whether liability coverage is available or affordable at $150K–$200K (estimate) for a novel, unproven standard.

7.4.A Issue - Pre-Registration Thresholds Remain Proposals, Not Locked Commitments; Gate Credibility Is at Risk

The pre-analysis plan and gate thresholds (ordinal error ≥25%, comprehension speed ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%) are labelled 'proposed' throughout the canonical facts and risk assessments. No signed commitment from the independent psychometrician exists; no power analysis confirming that 80 completers per arm achieves 80% statistical power for these effect sizes; no threshold for inter-rater kappa reliability is pre-locked. At Month 11 (2027-09-13), three documents require simultaneous publication: a pre-analysis plan, thresholds and a 30-day public comment window. Without locked thresholds by Month 9 (2027-07-13), stakeholders can dispute the gate outcome as post-hoc tuning, and educators/standards bodies will reject the result as scientifically undefensible. This is a critical path item with zero schedule buffer.

By Month 2 (2026-12-13), have a signed contract. By Month 5 (2027-03-13), receive the draft pre-analysis plan including justification for each threshold. By Month 9 (2027-07-13), finalize thresholds and deposit on Open Science Framework. Month 11 (2027-09-13) comment window then proceeds with a defensible, auditable baseline. Allocate $200K (within the $150K-$200K psychometrics budget) for this work and bump the critical path.

7.4.D Consequence

Without locked, pre-registered thresholds, the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision is disputable. Educators, standards bodies (TESOL, Ofqual) and publishers will claim the gate was tuned to produce a GO. A false-positive GO launches a weak standard with low Phase 3 adoption (risk: 20-50% uptake reduction). A false-negative NO-GO on inconclusive data triggers a $300K-$600K Phase 2 extension that exhausts the $175K pre-gate reserve and produces a shortfall. Either outcome erodes stakeholder confidence and undermines the 'adoption-first, evidence-gated' positioning that is the project's core legitimacy claim.

7.4.E Root Cause

No psychometrician hired; thresholds chosen by example rather than pre-registered; power analysis deferred. The pre-project assessment identifies this as the top priority action, but the canonical facts do not confirm a hire or a signed contract. Threshold proposals derive from the initial plan document, not from validated research design.

7.5.A Issue - Pilot Recruitment and Retention Risks Are Underestimated; Fallback Capacity Is Weak

The plan requires ≥80 completers per arm (320 total across 4 arms) by Month 22 (2028-08-13), with enrolment ≥115 per arm (460 total) by Month 13 (2027-11-13) and dropout ≤30%. Pilot partner commitments are due Month 3 (2027-01-13), and a cohort manager is not hired until Month 6 (2027-04-13)—a 3-month gap where recruitment momentum is lost. The 30% dropout tolerance (80 / 0.70 ≈ 114) is high for adult learners in month-long assessments; typical ESL pilot dropout is 30-50%. No fallback is budgeted if enrolment misses 115 per arm; the partner commitments specify 'minimum guaranteed cohort size' but no penalty or recovery plan if they miss. Safety-critical cohort is secondary and unproven in terms of recruitment speed or incentive effectiveness. A single cohort manager with no assistant creates a bottleneck for 460 participants across 5-7 sites.

The plan assumes dropout <=30%, but typical adult-education and technical-training pilot dropout is 35-45% without active incentive management. No cohort manager is hired until Month 6 (2027-04-13), leaving 3 months of recruitment unmanaged. If recruitment lags (only 70-80 enrolments per arm by Month 10 = 2027-08-13) and dropout reaches 40% (realistic without manager), only 48-60 completers per arm survive, dropping below the 80-per-arm minimum by >25%, invalidating statistical power for the four gate metrics.

8.5.B Tags

  • pilot-sample-size-risk
  • recruitment-timeline-compressed
  • retention-management-delayed
  • statistical-power-threatened

8.5.C Mitigation

Establish a Pilot Recruitment and Retention Plan (2-3 pages) by Month 2 (2026-12-13): conduct a pilot baseline study with 2-3 candidate ESL programs and 1 technical-training organization (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13, budget $15K-$20K, estimate) to measure realistic recruitment (% of eligible population converting to enrolment), baseline dropout (% completing all 4 sessions without intensive management), and demographic retention patterns (age, language background, motivation). From this, generate a probabilistic recruitment model with 50th, 75th and 90th percentile scenarios, and a retention curve month-by-month. Use the 75th percentile dropout rate (not 30%) as your planning baseline. By Month 3 (2027-01-13), require each partner to submit a written recruitment plan specifying: list of all eligible learners (N), weekly recruitment calls/emails, in-person enrollment sessions (dates, venues), and partner staff time allocated. Establish interim enrollment milestones (40% enrolled by Month 8 = 2027-06-13, 70% by Month 10 = 2027-08-13, 100% by Month 13 = 2027-11-13) with automatic escalation if missed by >2 weeks: if a partner falls behind, the cohort manager (hired early, by Month 4 = 2027-02-13, not Month 6 = 2027-04-13) activates acceleration tactics (increased incentives, evening/weekend sessions, partner marketing campaign, $20K-$30K budget, estimate). Hire the cohort manager by Month 4 (2027-02-13) (not Month 6 = 2027-04-13) and allocate 30% of their time Months 4-12 (2027-02-13 to 2027-10-13) to pre-Phase-2 recruitment support and contingency planning. Establish a monthly retention-tracking dashboard visible to the board: enrollments to date, dropout-to-date (with reasons), projected completers, and a 95% confidence interval on final sample size; flag to the board if the lower confidence bound falls below 70 per arm, triggering an automatic Phase 2 delay decision by Month 15 (2028-01-13) (before data collection starts) rather than Month 22 (2028-08-13) when it is too late to recover.

8.5.D Consequence

If recruitment achieves only 350-400 enrolments by Month 12 (2027-10-13) (a 20-25% miss, within historical range for voluntary adult pilots) and dropout averages 35% (not 30%), only 227-260 completers survive across 4 arms, leaving 57-65 per arm, cutting sample size by 30-40% below the 80-per-arm target. Statistical power drops from 80% to ~60%, raising the Type II error (false-negative) rate from 20% to 40% and making it 40% likely the gate will fail to detect a true, clinically meaningful effect on ordinal error or pronunciation consistency. A weakened gate forces either an inconclusive outcome and a 3-month Phase 2 extension ($300K, estimate), or a false-negative gate that kills the project despite potentially real effects masked by sample-size underpowering.

8.5.E Root Cause

The plan separates recruitment (signed by Month 3 = 2027-01-13) from retention management (cohort manager hired Month 6 = 2027-04-13), creating a 3-month gap where enrolment ramps without active support. Dropout tolerance (30%) is policy-level rather than based on external benchmarking or partner experience. No intermediate enrollment targets (e.g., 50% enrolled by Month 9 = 2027-07-13) trigger early course correction. The 460-enrolment target is treated as a firm commitment risk rather than a probabilistic forecast with sensitivity analysis.

8.6.A Issue - Gate Metrics Pre-Registration and Threshold Justification Incomplete; Defensibility at Risk

The plan proposes four gate thresholds (ordinal error ≥25% reduction, comprehension ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%), but none are pre-registered. Pre-registration is scheduled for Month 11 (2027-09-13), just 5 weeks before pilots begin. No power analysis has been conducted to justify why 80 completers per arm is sufficient to detect these effect sizes with 80% power, and no published benchmarks exist for 'pronunciation consistency' kappa targets in a novel constructed-language context. The plan lacks justification for why ≥15% above control is meaningful, or whether ordinal-only error reduction (the single rule tested most) is likely to yield ≥25% improvement when pilot participants see only 4-8 hours of Clear English exposure across 12 months. Without pre-registered, justified thresholds, the board faces pressure post-hoc to adjust thresholds to match observed data (goalpost-moving), inviting stakeholder claims that the gate was rigged.

8.6.B Tags

  • pre-registration-delayed
  • power-analysis-absent
  • threshold-justification-weak
  • gate-defensibility-compromised

8.6.C Mitigation

Immediately commission a Power Analysis Memo (2-3 pages) from the independent psychometrician by Month 2 (2026-12-13), with delivery by Month 5 (2027-03-13). The memo must: (1) specify the assumed effect sizes for each of the four gate metrics (ordinal error reduction, comprehension speed, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention), justified by reference to analogous interventions (e.g., citation to adult ESL learning studies for retention benchmarks, dyslexia or speech-therapy research for pronunciation consistency effect sizes); (2) conduct a power analysis for each metric, showing the sample size (per arm) required to achieve 80% power at α=0.05 (two-tailed) for each effect size; (3) justify why 80 per arm (or the revised number) is feasible and cost-effective given the partner commitment and dropout assumptions; (4) propose a decision rule for the four metrics (e.g., GO if ≥3 of 4 metrics meet thresholds and all are valid, INCONCLUSIVE if 1-2 metrics fail but data quality is high, NO-GO if ≥2 metrics fail or data quality is compromised). Circulate this memo to the board by Month 6 (2027-04-13) for approval and comment. By Month 10 (2027-08-13), the psychometrician must deliver the finalized pre-analysis plan (5-7 pages) specifying: exact thresholds for each metric (with effect sizes and sample sizes cited), minimum sample size per arm (with sensitivity analysis: power under 70, 80, 100 per arm scenarios), primary outcomes (ordinal error and comprehension speed) and secondary outcomes (pronunciation consistency, retention), the justification for any thresholds that differ from Month 5 (2027-03-13) proposals, and the specific decision rule for the board gate vote. Register this plan on Open Science Framework or equivalent by Month 11 (2027-09-13 at 14:00) with board sign-off, and publish it on the project website immediately. By Month 12 (2027-10-13), commission an independent external expert (not the project's psychometrician) to review the pre-analysis plan for statistical rigor and boundary conditions (e.g., 'what happens if comprehension time is highly skewed or outlier-laden?'), and publish their review summary on the website. This sequence ensures thresholds are justified, pre-committed and defensible by Month 11 (2027-09-13), 5 weeks before pilots begin, and establishes external credibility for the gate.

8.6.D Consequence

At Month 11 (2027-09-13), when the board convenes to pre-register thresholds, if the psychometrician's power analysis reveals that 80 per arm is underpowered (true power 65-70%) to detect a 25% ordinal error reduction, the board faces three bad choices: (1) freeze thresholds at pre-registered but underpowered levels, risking inconclusive gate findings; (2) adjust thresholds downward post-hoc (e.g., 20% reduction instead of 25%), inviting the appearance of goalpost-moving and stakeholder skepticism ('the bar was lowered to get a GO'); (3) delay pilots by 4-6 weeks to recruit additional participants, compressing the assessment window and reducing data quality. Any of these outcomes weakens the gate's credibility as a defensible, pre-committed decision rule. If a NO-GO is reached on the ordinal-error metric (e.g., 18% reduction, below the 25% threshold), stakeholders can claim the threshold was arbitrary because it was never justified against external evidence or similar standards.

8.6.E Root Cause

The plan treats pre-registration as a procedural checklist item (Month 11 = 2027-09-13) rather than as foundational evidence work that must precede protocol sign-off. No power analysis or effect-size literature review has been conducted to anchor the 80-per-arm sample-size estimate or the proposed thresholds. The pronunciation consistency metric is novel (no published kappa benchmarks in this domain) and its meaningfulness is asserted rather than validated. The plan assumes a psychometrician will be hired by Month 2 (2026-12-13) but does not require them to deliver a power-analysis memo by Month 5 (2027-03-13) before rule-locking, so threshold design is decoupled from the rule-specification timeline.
