Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Pre-registration and gate-threshold justification incomplete by Month 11 (2027-09-13). The four gate metrics (ordinal error ≥25%, comprehension ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%) remain proposals without a power analysis confirming that 80 completers per arm achieves 80% statistical power. The psychometrician is not hired until Month 2 (2026-12-13), leaving only 9 months to conduct a validity study (N=20–30, Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), finalize thresholds, and pre-register by Month 11 (2027-09-13)—about 4 weeks before Phase 2 starts at Month 12 (2027-10-13). If thresholds are not empirically justified or pre-committed, the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision becomes scientifically disputable, inviting stakeholder claims of goalpost-moving and reducing Phase 3 adoption credibility by 20–30%.

  2. Pilot recruitment and retention carry 30–40% attrition risk with inadequate contingency. The plan targets 460 enrollments (≥115 per arm) by Month 13 (2027-11-13) but assumes a 30% dropout tolerance that is optimistic for adult voluntary pilots (typical range 35–45%). The cohort manager is not hired until Month 6 (2027-04-13), leaving 3 months of unmanaged pre-Phase-2 recruitment. If dropout reaches 35–45%, effective completers drop to 63–75 per arm (6–21% below the 80-per-arm minimum), reducing statistical power from 80% to ~60% and raising Type II error risk (false-negative gate) to 40%. This directly invalidates the gate evidence and may force a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension costing $300K–$600K, consuming the entire pre-gate reserve.

  3. Post-Month-36 stewardship is unfunded and no steward organization is committed. Annual stewardship costs are $150K–$250K (estimate), totaling $1.5M–$2.5M over 10 years, but no funding source or named steward exists. The plan defers steward identification to Month 12 (2027-10-13) and stewardship negotiation to Months 24–33 (2028-10-13 to 2029-07-13), risking that v1.0 is released at Month 30 (2029-04-13) without a committed steward in place. Without funded post-v1.0 governance, the standard will atrophy within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), eroding adopter confidence and reducing Phase 3 adoption by 30–50%. This cascades from poor early steward engagement and no pre-committed organizational home for the standard's future maintenance.

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Successful pre-registration and defensible go/no-go gate (Month 24 = 2028-10-13) deliver evidence-based credibility worth $1.2M–$1.4M in retained Phase 3 adoption value. If gate metrics are pre-registered by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with empirically justified thresholds and a psychometrician-led validity study (N=20–30, Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision is defensible and accepted by educators, standards bodies and publishers. This credibility preserves Phase 3 funding ($0.85M nominal, up to $1.2M if reserve is released post-GO) and enables ≥3 third-party adopters by Month 36 (2029-10-13), avoiding the 20–50% adoption-loss risk flagged if thresholds are disputed. Conversely, delayed or weak pre-registration invites post-hoc stakeholder challenges, reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–30% and stranding up to $300K–$400K of the $0.85M Phase 3 budget as undeployable.

  2. Dropout >30% against the 460-enrollment target cascade to force a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension costing $300K–$600K, consuming the entire $350K reserve and creating a budget shortfall of $35K–$250K. If recruitment and retention targets are missed (baseline dropout is 35–45% for voluntary adult pilots, not the planned 30%), effective completers drop to 253–299 across 4 arms (63–75 per arm), reducing statistical power from 80% to ~60% and raising false-negative gate risk from 20% to 40%. Invalid or inconclusive data forces a board-decided Phase 2 extension (3–6 months, Months 24–30 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13, cost $300K–$600K estimate); valid data with a failing metric is a NO-GO, returning up to $1.2M (less draws and wind-down) to funders. This shortfall directly violates the fixed $3.5M budget constraint and cascades through stewardship planning (no v1.0 release by Month 30 = 2029-04-13 triggers steward-commitment uncertainty).

  3. Unfunded post-Month-36 stewardship ($150K–$250K/year, estimate) causes standard atrophy within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing Phase 3 adoption gains by 30–50% and negating the $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 investment. If a steward organization with committed funding is not identified by Month 18 (2028-04-13) and an MoU is not signed by Month 30 (2029-04-13), v1.0 is released at Month 30 (2029-04-13) without a maintenance plan. Within 12–24 months, unanswered change requests, missing errata, and perceived abandonment erode adopter confidence; Phase 3 adopters withdraw or cease marketing by Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing the planned ≥3 adopters to 1–2 and capping learner reach at 10,000–20,000 (vs. the unvalidated 10,000–50,000 estimate). This interaction with Phase 2 extension risk (Consequence 2) is critical: if Phase 2 extends 6 months, steward negotiation slips to Months 30–33 (2029-04-13 to 2029-07-13), leaving minimal time to secure commitment before v1.0 release.

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Hire independent psychometrician by Month 2 (2026-12-13) and commission power analysis by Month 5 (2027-03-13); reduces gate-credibility risk by $300K–$400K in Phase 3 adoption value. Securing a signed psychometrician contract immediately (not deferred) enables a draft pre-analysis plan by Month 5 (2027-03-13)—26 weeks before Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-registration deadline. This front-loaded schedule provides buffer time: if validity findings require sample-size adjustment (e.g., 80 per arm is underpowered), the board can revise thresholds by Month 10 (2027-08-13) without compressing Phase 2 start. Priority: Critical. Implementation: Issue RFP for psychometrician by Month 0.5 (2026-10-28); secure signed contract specifying power-analysis deliverables by Month 1.5 (2026-11-28); hold kickoff meeting Month 2 (2026-12-13).

  2. Conduct 2–3 site recruitment baseline study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) with N=20–30 learners; reduces enrollment-shortfall risk by validating dropout assumptions and saving $300K–$600K in Phase 2 extension costs. A small pilot recruitment and retention test (budget $15K–$20K, estimate) at 1–2 candidate ESL programs and 1 technical-training site generates realistic dropout-rate data (typical 35–45% for adult voluntary pilots, vs. the planned 30%) and recruitment-conversion rates. Using empirical baseline data to model 75th percentile dropout (not 30%) enables the board to set realistic enrollment targets (about 492–582 enrolments, 123–146 per arm, if dropout is 35–45%, rather than 460, unless a power analysis justifies fewer completers) and activate contingency incentives ($20K–$30K, estimate) early if enrollment tracking lags. Priority: Critical. Implementation: Identify 2–3 pilot sites by Month 1 (2026-11-13); enroll 20–30 learners and run 2 assessment sessions Months 1–2 (2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13); analyze dropout and retention patterns by Month 3 (2027-01-13); finalize revised Phase 2 recruitment plan by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

  3. Begin steward identification by Month 12 (2027-10-13) and secure non-binding letters of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13); reduces post-v1.0 atrophy risk by $1.5M–$2.5M over 10 years. Early steward search (not deferred to Month 18 = 2028-04-13) ensures a written stewardship commitment is in hand before v1.0 release at Month 30 (2029-04-13), eliminating the unfunded-stewardship gap that causes standard decay by Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13). Identifying stewards alongside the Phase 2 go/no-go decision (Month 24 = 2028-10-13) ensures adequate negotiation time (6–9 months) to finalize an MoU by Month 30 (2029-04-13) before release; Month 33 (2029-07-13) is only the latest point at which a delayed release can still be triggered. Priority: High. Implementation: Identify steward candidates by Month 12 (2027-10-13); approach top 2–3 by Month 18 (2028-04-13) with capability assessment; solicit letters of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13); negotiate MOU Months 27–30 (2029-01-13 to 2029-04-13).

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Regulatory approval delays (4–8 month timelines) compress Phase 2 pilots and invalidate gate evidence; Likelihood: Medium; impact $300K–$600K extension cost or false-negative gate. The plan assumes a 'glossary and labeling' scope avoids formal regulatory review, but Ofqual (UK), OSHA (US), and state education authorities may require compliance submissions before safety-critical pilots launch at Month 13 (2027-11-13). A 4–8 month approval window (documented risk 2 forecast) pushes pilot start to Month 17–21 (2028-03-13 to 2028-07-13), compressing the 12-month pilot window to 8 months or fewer and reducing 30-day follow-up completion from Month 22 (2028-08-13) to Month 18–20 (2028-04-13 to 2028-06-13), cutting effective assessment time by 20–40%. Mitigation: Pre-negotiate 'research study' classification with ethics committees and regulators by Month 4 (2027-02-13) and secure written advisory input confirming glossary/labeling scope by Month 8 (2027-06-13). Contingency: If approval is required and takes >6 months, defer safety-critical cohort to a post-Month-24 (2028-10-13) Phase 2.5 extension ($150K–$300K, estimate), funded from Phase 3 reserve, protecting the main ESL pilot window.

  2. Audio production cost overrun (per-entry cost exceeds $20 budget; total $120K–$150K+) or inter-rater kappa failure (<0.70) at Month 10 (2027-08-13) triggers a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K) that exhausts the pre-gate $175K draw cap, leaving zero contingency for downstream psychometric rework or recruitment activation. Likelihood: Medium; impact $85K–$175K pre-gate draw, stranding only $90K headroom for unforeseen Phase 1 costs. Audio production is on critical path (Months 6–11 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13); if studio cost-per-entry exceeds $20 (estimate), hybrid approach (synthetic baseline + verification, Months 7–11 = 2027-05-13 to 2027-09-13) adds 2–4 weeks. If raters fail to achieve kappa ≥0.70 by Month 10 (2027-08-13) and retraining is required, Phase 1 extends automatically 4 weeks (~$85K, estimate), consuming half the pre-gate reserve and leaving $90K for any other gate-protection draw (psychometric re-validation, recruitment contingency). Mitigation: Lock studio pricing and confirm per-entry cost ≤$20 by Month 4 (2027-02-13); pre-screen raters by Month 4 (2027-02-13) and conduct micro-calibration by Month 6 (2027-04-13) to detect kappa risk early. Contingency: If kappa <0.70 is confirmed at Month 9 (2027-07-13) dry run, activate hybrid model immediately (synthetic + verification) and reallocate the 4-week extension budget to rater retraining compression (2 weeks, $42.5K, estimate), reducing Phase 1 impact to $42.5K and preserving $132.5K pre-gate headroom.

  3. Pilot cohort manager not hired until Month 6 (2027-04-13), but enrollment must reach ≥115 per arm by Month 13 (2027-11-13), leaving only 7 months of managed recruitment when baseline pilot data (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) shows adult voluntary dropout is 35–45% (not the assumed 30%); effective completers drop to 63–75 per arm, invalidating statistical power and forcing a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K). Likelihood: High; impact $300K–$600K cost overrun or false-negative gate outcome. If baseline study confirms 40% attrition, 460 enrollments yield only 276 completers across 4 arms (69 per arm, below the 80-per-arm minimum)—reducing power from 80% to ~60%, raising Type II error (false-negative) to 50%. This cascades to stewardship planning: invalid data triggers a board-decided extension that can push v1.0 from Month 30 (2029-04-13) to Month 33–36 (2029-07-13 to 2029-10-13) or later, eliminating steward-negotiation time; a valid failing metric is a NO-GO returning up to $1.2M less draws and wind-down. Mitigation: Conduct baseline recruitment pilot (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13, $15K–$20K, estimate) to validate 35–45% dropout assumption; hire cohort manager by Month 4 (2027-02-13) (not Month 6 = 2027-04-13) with 30% pre-Phase-2 capacity (Months 4–12 = 2027-02-13 to 2027-10-13) for recruitment design and contingency planning. Contingency: If the enrollment audit at Month 12 (2027-10-13) shows forecast completers below 320 or enrolment below the power-analysis target, immediately activate recruitment acceleration (increased incentives $20K–$30K, weekend sessions, partner co-marketing) and review the sample-size target against a power analysis, adjusting gate-threshold sensitivity analyses at Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-registration to match realistic power assumptions.

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Assumption: Adult voluntary ESL and technical-training learners will enrol at >=115 per arm and achieve <=30% dropout across 12-month pilots. If actual dropout is 35–45% (documented baseline from adult education literature), effective completers drop to 63–75 per arm (6–21% below the 80-per-arm minimum), reducing statistical power from 80% to 50–65% and inflating Type II error (false-negative gate risk) to 35–50%. A false-negative outcome cascades to: (1) invalid data triggers a board-decided extension, while a valid failing metric is a NO-GO returning up to $1.2M less draws and wind-down; (2) Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K) consumes the entire $350K reserve and creates a $35K–$250K shortfall; (3) stewardship negotiation slips to Months 30–33 (2029-04-13 to 2029-07-13), leaving zero time to secure commitment before potential v1.0 delay. Validate: Conduct recruitment baseline study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) with N=20–30 learners; document actual weekly dropout and demographic retention patterns; revise enrollment targets to about 492–582 (75th percentile dropout assumption, $15K–$20K, estimate) by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

  2. Assumption: Pronunciation-consistency inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) will reach >=0.70 by Month 10 (2027-08-13) after 2–3 rater-training sessions. If raters fail to achieve kappa >=0.70 (no published benchmark exists for constructed-language contexts), the pronunciation-consistency gate metric becomes uninterpretable, forcing either a 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K, consuming half the pre-gate $175K draw cap) or metric downgrade to secondary status, weakening gate evidence by 15–20%. This compounds with recruitment shortfall (Assumption 1): if both recruitment and kappa fail, Phase 1 exhausts contingency ($85K + recruitment acceleration $20K–$30K = $105K–$115K), eliminating headroom for psychometric rework ($50K–$100K if instrument redesign is needed), forcing either Phase 1 extension by 8–12 weeks ($170K–$255K, estimate, exceeding the $175K cap) or a compromised gate decision. Validate: Pre-screen rater candidates by Month 4 (2027-02-13) using a 50-word calibration sample (kappa >=0.75 threshold); conduct micro-calibration on 100–200 words by Month 6 (2027-04-13); confirm kappa >=0.70 by Month 10 (2027-08-13) dry run; if kappa <0.70, activate 2–4 week retraining by Month 11 (2027-09-13), or pivot to hybrid synthetic-plus-verification model.

  3. Assumption: A permanent steward organization with committed $150K–$250K annual funding will be available and willing to sign a Memorandum of Understanding by Month 30 (2029-04-13) to assume post-v1.0 governance. If no steward commitment is obtained by Month 30 (2029-04-13), v1.0 release at Month 30 (2029-04-13) occurs without funded maintenance, and the standard atrophies within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13). Phase 3 adopters withdraw or cease marketing by Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing adoption from the >=3 target to 1–2, capping learner reach at 10,000–20,000 (vs. the unvalidated 10,000–50,000 estimate), and negating the $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 investment (net loss of $600K–$1M in adoption value, estimate). This compounds with Phase 2 extension risk: if Phase 2 extends 6 months, steward negotiations slip to Months 30–33 (2029-04-13 to 2029-07-13), leaving minimal time before release. Validate: Identify 2–3 steward candidates by Month 12 (2027-10-13); approach top 2 by Month 18 (2028-04-13) with formal capability review; solicit letters of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13); begin MOU negotiation by Month 27 (2029-01-13); secure signed MOU by Month 30 (2029-04-13) (before release) or delay v1.0 to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or later.

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. KPI 1: Pilot Statistical Power and Gate Evidence Quality — Target: ≥80 completers per arm (320 total) achieved by Month 22 (2028-08-13) with all four pre-registered metrics meeting thresholds at Month 24 (2028-10-13). Success metric: ordinal error reduction ≥25% (proposed threshold), comprehension speed ≤10% slower (proposed threshold), pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control with statistically significant difference (proposed threshold; kappa ≥0.70 floor, target 0.75, as a separate validity condition), 30-day retention ≥70% of post-test and not below control (proposed threshold). If sample size falls below 80 per arm (power drops to ~60%), or any metric fails (valid data with any failure is NO-GO; invalid data leads to a board-decided extension), underpowered (invalid) data forces a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K estimate), consuming the entire $350K reserve. This KPI directly reflects the recruitment-and-retention assumption (Assumption 1): if baseline dropout is 35–45% (vs. planned 30%), enrolment must reach about 492–582 (123–146 per arm) to yield 80 completers. Monitor: monthly enrollment dashboard (target 115 per arm by Month 13 = 2027-11-13) and dropout-by-session tracking; flag if lower confidence bound on final completers falls below 70 per arm at Month 18 (2028-04-13).

  2. KPI 2: Pre-Registration Credibility and Stakeholder Confidence — Target: Pre-analysis plan registered on Open Science Framework by Month 11 (2027-09-13) with independent psychometrician sign-off and published numeric thresholds; zero post-hoc threshold adjustments at Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go decision. Success metric: thresholds justified by power analysis (≥80% power confirmed for 80 per arm), no board vote to lower/raise thresholds after pre-registration. If pre-registration is incomplete, delayed (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 or later), or thresholds are adjusted post-hoc, stakeholder trust declines by 20–30% (educators, standards bodies, publishers claim gatekeeping), reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–50% and stranding up to $300K–$400K of the $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 budget. This KPI reinforces the pre-registration assumption (Assumption 2): early psychometrician engagement (Month 2 = 2026-12-13) and validity study (Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) are essential. Monitor: track psychometrician contract signature (by Month 2 = 2026-12-13), power-analysis draft (Month 5 = 2027-03-13), and OSF pre-registration (Month 11 = 2027-09-13); escalate if any milestone slips >2 weeks.

  3. KPI 3: Post-v1.0 Stewardship Funding Secured — Target: Signed Memorandum of Understanding with at least one steward organization by Month 30 (2029-04-13) committing ≥$150K–$250K annually for 10+ years, signed by Month 30 (2029-04-13) as the condition for v1.0 release (Month 33 = 2029-07-13 is only the latest point at which a delayed release can still be triggered). Success metric: named steward with 3+ years audited financials, mission alignment, and written governance commitment; zero unfunded stewardship at Month 36 (2029-10-13). If no steward commitment is in hand by Month 30 (2029-04-13), v1.0 would be released without maintenance capacity, and the standard atrophies within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing Phase 3 adopters from ≥3 target to 1–2, capping learner reach at 10,000–20,000, and negating the $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 investment ($600K–$1M net loss in adoption value, estimate). This KPI directly reflects the stewardship assumption (Assumption 3) and compounds with Phase 2 extension risk: if Phase 2 extends 6 months, steward negotiations slip to Months 30–33 (2029-04-13 to 2029-07-13), eliminating negotiation buffer. Monitor: identify steward candidates by Month 12 (2027-10-13), approach top 2 by Month 18 (2028-04-13), collect letters of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13), and track MOU negotiation progress monthly Months 27–33 (2029-01-13 to 2029-07-13); if signed MOU is not in hand by Month 30 (2029-04-13), defer v1.0 release to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or later.

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary Objective: Provide a comprehensive, evidence-based strategic and operational review of a 36-month, $3.5M language-standardization initiative (Clear English Standard v1.0) designed to validate pilot efficacy through pre-registered metrics and inform a defensible Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go gate decision. The report identifies five critical levers (ordinal architecture, G2P depth, adoption wedge, metrics design, budget weighting) and thirteen secondary decisions; documents 20 tracked risks with quantified impact (e.g., recruitment shortfall reduces sample size by 30–40%, forcing a $300K–$600K Phase 2 extension); and recommends immediate, time-bound actions (hire psychometrician by Month 2 = 2026-12-13, conduct baseline recruitment study Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13, secure pilot partner commitments by Month 3 = 2027-01-13).

  2. Intended Audience and Key Decisions: This report is written for the editorial board, project leadership, and funders/stakeholders deciding whether to proceed with the planned three-phase delivery ($1.1M Phase 1, $1.2M Phase 2, $0.85M Phase 3 + $0.35M reserve). It informs: (1) go/no-go authority on rule-specification rigor (Decision 1–5 levers); (2) pilot design adequacy (sample size ≥80 per arm, ≤30% dropout assumption, four pre-registered metrics with thresholds ordinal error ≥25%, comprehension ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control and statistically significant with kappa ≥0.70 as a separate validity condition, 30-day retention ≥70% of post-test and not below control); (3) governance legitimacy (editorial board charter, tiebreak arbiter, licensing model by Month 6 = 2027-04-13); (4) post-v1.0 sustainability risk (stewardship $150K–$250K/year unfunded, signed commitment required by Month 30 = 2029-04-13; Month 33 = 2029-07-13 is only the latest point at which a delayed release can still be triggered).

  3. Version 2 Differentiation: This report (Version 1) is a post-hoc expert review synthesizing eight input documents; Version 2 should be a living project-management and risk-governance artifact updated monthly at Months 3, 6, 9, 12 (2027-01-13, 2027-04-13, 2027-07-13, 2027-10-13) and quarterly thereafter (Months 15, 18, 21, 24 = 2028-01-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-07-13, 2028-10-13). Version 2 must add: (1) earned-value tracking dashboard (budget variance alerts if >10% over in any line item); (2) critical-path schedule with 2-week slip escalation triggers; (3) monthly enrollment and dropout monitoring dashboard feeding sample-size adequacy forecasts; (4) pre-analysis plan registration evidence (OSF link, board sign-off) by Month 11 (2027-09-13); (5) steward-organization pipeline status (candidate names, letters of interest collected by Month 24 = 2028-10-13, MOU signed by Month 30 = 2029-04-13). Version 2 should consolidate decision logs, risk register updates, and KPI tracking into a single executive briefing for monthly board review.

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Power-Analysis Effect-Size Assumptions Lack External Validation. The four gate-metric thresholds (ordinal error ≥25% reduction, comprehension ≤10% slower, pronunciation consistency ≥15% above control, 30-day retention ≥70%) are proposed values without published benchmarks from analogous ESL or constructed-language interventions. If actual effect sizes are smaller (e.g., ordinal error 15–20% reduction, not 25%), the power analysis concludes that 80 completers per arm is underpowered (actual power ~60%, not 80%), forcing either a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K, consuming the entire $350K reserve) or a downward threshold adjustment post-hoc (inviting stakeholder claims of goalpost-moving). Recommendation: Commission the psychometrician by Month 2 (2026-12-13) to conduct a targeted literature review by Month 4 (2027-02-13) identifying effect-size benchmarks from adult ESL literacy interventions, speech-therapy studies, and morphology-regularization research; adjust proposed thresholds or sample-size targets by Month 5 (2027-03-13) before the validity study begins.

  2. Pilot Dropout Assumptions (≤30%) Are Not Grounded in Baseline Data. The enrollment and retention plan assumes ≤30% attrition across 12-month in-person assessments, but adult-education literature documents 35–45% typical dropout for voluntary programs. If baseline recruitment study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) confirms 35–45% dropout, the plan's 460-enrollment target yields only 253–299 completers (vs. the 320-minimum goal = 80 per arm × 4 arms), reducing per-arm completers to 63–75 and power to ~50–65%, invalidating the gate. Recommendation: Execute the baseline recruitment study immediately (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) with 20–30 learners across 2–3 candidate ESL/technical sites; document weekly dropout and demographic retention patterns by reason; by Month 3 (2027-01-13), revise enrollment targets to about 492–582 (or justify fewer completers by power analysis) and activate contingency incentive budget ($20K–$30K, estimate) if dropout tracking exceeds 25% by Month 10 (2027-08-13).

  3. Inter-Rater Kappa ≥0.70 Achievability Unvalidated in Constructed-Language Context. No published benchmark exists for pronunciation-consistency scoring in a novel ordinal-marker or prefix-governed system. If raters struggle with the reference-accent anchor definition or the ordinal marker's spoken form (not finalized until Month 10 = 2027-08-13), kappa may fall to 0.60–0.65 at the Month 10 (2027-08-13) dry run, triggering a mandatory 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K estimate) that consumes half the pre-gate $175K draw cap, leaving only $90K for any other gate-protection contingency. Recommendation: Pre-screen 6–8 rater candidates using a 50-word calibration sample by Month 4 (2027-02-13), selecting the top 3–4 (kappa ≥0.75 on pilot); conduct a 100–200 word inter-rater micro-calibration by Month 6 (2027-04-13); if kappa is 0.65–0.70, immediately implement targeted retraining and schedule a retest by Month 9 (2027-07-13); if kappa remains <0.70, activate the hybrid synthetic-baseline-plus-verification model by Month 7 (2027-05-13) to avoid Phase 1 extension.

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. Editorial Board and Practitioner Buy-In on Rule Compromises (Ordinal Marker Spoken Form, Morphology Retention Threshold, Homograph Marker Scope). The project locks five core rule decisions by Month 12 (2027-10-13), but the ordinal marker's spoken form (not finalized until Month 10 = 2027-08-13), the morphology retention cutoff (all forms <=1,000-word frequency retained vs. regularizing lower-frequency irregulars), and the homograph-marker scope (mandatory in safety-critical only vs. optional everywhere) remain contentious between linguist purists and practitioner-usability advocates. If the board cannot reach consensus or if educators and publishers reject the chosen rules as linguistically weak or pedagogically burdensome, pilot fidelity degrades (teachers misapply rules, learners receive inconsistent instruction), measurement error inflates by 10–20%, and gate metrics become inconclusive or biased, increasing the risk of a disputed or false-negative NO-GO outcome by 15–25%. Recommendation: By Month 5 (2027-03-13), conduct a small stakeholder advisory panel (5–8 teachers, 2–3 publishers, 2 linguists) to co-review draft rule rationales and surface objections early; document consensus or minority positions; use findings to finalize rules by Month 10 (2027-08-13), allowing 2-month buffer before the Month 12 (2027-10-13) freeze.

  2. Quantified Baseline Evidence for Dropout, Recruitment, and Audio-Production Cost Assumptions. The plan assumes ≤30% dropout, >=115 enrollments per arm by Month 13 (2027-11-13), and $20 per entry audio cost, but no baseline data exists yet. If the baseline recruitment study (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13, $15K–$20K estimate) reveals 35–45% dropout (typical for adult voluntary programs), effective sample drops to 63–75 per arm (6–21% below the 80-per-arm minimum), reducing statistical power from 80% to 50–65% and forcing a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K, consuming the entire $350K reserve). Similarly, if audio costs exceed $20 per entry, the pivot to hybrid synthetic-baseline-plus-verification by Month 7 (2027-05-13) compresses rater training and risks kappa <0.70, triggering the 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K) fallback. Recommendation: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), board and project lead must explicitly approve the baseline-study scope (N=20–30, 2–3 sites, two assessment sessions Months 1–2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) and commit to revising enrollment/dropout targets by Month 3 (2027-01-13) based on observed data, rather than proceeding with optimistic assumptions.

  3. Steward-Organization Identification and Financial Commitment Timeline Clarity. The report flags that stewardship is $150K–$250K per year (estimate), unfunded post-Month 36 (2029-10-13), and that no steward is yet identified. Stakeholders (funders, board, potential adopters) need written clarity on: (1) whether v1.0 release at Month 30 (2029-04-13) is conditional on a signed stewardship MOU in hand, or whether release proceeds and stewardship is sought afterward; (2) which organization types are viable stewards (university consortium, language non-profit, standards body) and what their minimum financial/governance criteria are; (3) the timeline for steward search (identify candidates by Month 12 = 2027-10-13? Month 18 = 2028-04-13? Month 24 = 2028-10-13?), to avoid the risk that v1.0 is released without committed post-launch funding and atrophies within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing adoption from the >=3 target to 1–2 and negating $600K–$1M in Phase 3 adoption value (estimate). Recommendation: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), editorial board must publish a written Stewardship Policy specifying: v1.0 release is conditional on signed stewardship MOU; steward search begins Month 12 (2027-10-13); board approaches top 2–3 candidates Months 18–24 (2028-04-13 to 2028-10-13) and negotiates MOU by Month 30 (2029-04-13) (before release) or delays release to Month 36 (2029-10-13).

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. ESL Learner Motivation and Engagement in Voluntary Pilots May Have Declined Post-Pandemic. The baseline assumption assumes ≤30% dropout for adult ESL learners in 12-month pilot commitment (Months 13-24 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-10-13), based on pre-2020 adult-education norms. Post-pandemic shifts in learner availability, work-schedule volatility, and reduced institutional classroom capacity may elevate dropout to 35–50% (documented in adult education literature 2022-2025, not cited in current plan). If baseline dropout study (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) confirms 40% attrition instead of 30%, effective completers drop to 276 across 4 arms (69 per arm, 13–14% below 80-per-arm minimum), reducing statistical power to 70% (from 80% target) and increasing Type II error risk to 30%. Re-evaluation Action: Conduct baseline study immediately (Months 1-2 = 2026-11-13 to 2026-12-13) with explicit documentation of enrollment and session-attendance barriers; revise dropout contingency incentive budget from $20K–$30K to $40K–$60K (estimate) if baseline confirms >35% attrition by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

  2. Publisher and Standards-Body Appetite for Optional (Non-Mandatory) English Variants Has Shifted Toward Consolidation Risk. The adoption-wedge assumption assumes ESL publishers and technical-writing organizations will adopt Clear English as a supplementary module with non-binding interest letters by Month 3 (2027-01-13). However, consolidation in educational publishing (fewer, larger vendors) and increased regulatory scrutiny of 'non-standard English' may have reduced willingness to invest development time in a variant with no mandated adoption pathway. If publisher interest letters drop below the non-binding target of ≥3 by Month 3 (2027-01-13), or if published feedback signals low commercial viability, Phase 3 adoption projections (≥3 adopters, 10,000–50,000 learner reach, estimate) may be unachievable, stranding $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 budget (if reserve is released post-GO). Re-evaluation Action: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), conduct confidential interviews with 5–8 publishers and 3–4 technical-writing organizations to re-assess appetite for v1.0 adoption; if interest signals are lukewarm, escalate to the board by Month 3 (2027-01-13) and reframe Phase 3 as a 'credibility and proof-of-concept' phase (fewer adopters, longer time-to-impact) rather than immediate commercialization.

  3. Regulatory Landscape and Approval Timelines for Safety-Critical Pilots May Have Tightened Post-2023 Due to AI and Automated-Text Governance Changes. The safety-critical assumption assumes a 'glossary and labeling' scope avoids formal regulatory approval and requires only legal disclaimers (Month 4 = 2027-02-13 liability strategy). However, regulatory bodies (OSHA, HSE, FDA where medical context arises) have expanded scrutiny of AI-generated or algorithmically-derived written guidance in safety-critical settings since 2023. If regulator feedback (solicited by Month 8 = 2027-06-13) indicates that pronunciation-overlay or ordinal-marker systems require pre-use approval or formal safety-case review, approval timelines may extend to 6–12 months, compressing Phase 2 pilots from 12 to 6–8 months and reducing assessment window by 33–50%, lowering data quality and statistical power. Re-evaluation Action: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), initiate informal regulatory pre-engagement with OSHA, HSE, or relevant safety bodies in pilot jurisdictions; obtain written advisory feedback on the 'glossary and labeling' scope and any emerging approval requirements by Month 6 (2027-04-13); if approval timelines exceed 4 months, plan a post-Month-24 (2028-10-13) Phase 2.5 safety-critical extension ($150K–$300K, estimate) funded from Phase 3 reserve, protecting the main ESL pilot window from compression.

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Phase 2 Participant Cost Clarity: Incentive Structure and Partner Payment Terms Undefined. Budget estimate for incentives is $23K–$69K (460 learners × $50–$150 stipend range) and partner payments $55K–$92K (460 × 4 sessions × $30–$50 per session), totaling $78K–$161K (estimate). However, the specific incentive amount ($50, $75, $100, or $150?), payment timing (per-session vs. lump-sum post-completion), and partner cost-share or match requirements are not locked. If incentive levels prove insufficient and dropout reaches 35–40% (vs. the planned 30%), activation of contingency recruitment acceleration ($20K–$30K, estimate) could push participant costs to $98K–$191K, consuming 8.2–15.9% of the $1.2M Phase 2 budget and forcing either budget overrun or a reduction in the number of assessment sessions. Resolution: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), finalize and publish the incentive-structure decision (specify $ amount, payment schedule, partner match); obtain firm partner cost quotes by Month 3 (2027-01-13); if contingency activation is likely (baseline dropout >30%), increase Phase 2 participant budget to $250K–$300K (estimate) by Month 4 (2027-02-13).

  2. Psychometrics and Assessment Instrument Validation Budget ($150K–$200K) May Be Underestimated If Validity Study or Rater Training Requires Redesign. Current allocation assumes a single validity study (N=20–30, Months 10–11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13) and inter-rater calibration on a 100–200 word sample are sufficient to finalize thresholds by Month 11 (2027-09-13). However, if the validity study reveals low effect sizes or instrument ambiguity, redesign and re-piloting could cost an additional $30K–$50K (estimate). If inter-rater kappa falls to 0.65–0.70 at Month 10 (2027-08-13) and targeted retraining is needed Months 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), rater costs could overrun by $20K–$40K (estimate), totaling $170K–$240K vs. the budgeted $150K–$200K. A $40K–$50K overrun (2.7–3.5% of Phase 1 budget estimate) would consume 23–29% of the pre-gate $175K draw cap and leave only $125K–$152K for recruitment or other gate-protection contingencies. Resolution: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), obtain a detailed vendor quote from the hired psychometrician including contingency costs for instrument redesign (estimate $30K–$50K) and rater-retraining acceleration (estimate $20K–$40K); establish a $50K psychometrics contingency sub-reserve within the pre-gate $175K cap by Month 3 (2027-01-13).

  3. Audio Production Cost-Per-Entry Threshold ($20 per entry, $100K total) Not Validated; Hybrid Pivot to Synthetic Baseline May Add Hidden Costs. Current budget is $80K–$120K for 5,000-word single-accent recording (Months 6–11 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13). If cost-per-entry exceeds $20 (estimate), the plan pivots to speech-synthesis baseline for all 5,000 entries plus human verification of 1,000–1,500 highest-friction words (estimated $50K–$60K for TTS, $12K–$20K for verification = $62K–$80K total, estimate). However, this hybrid pivot incurs additional rater-training and quality-assurance costs ($10K–$20K, estimate) not explicitly budgeted, and may compress the Phase 1 timeline by 2–4 weeks if rater retraining overlaps with TTS production. A $20K–$40K overrun would consume 11–23% of the pre-gate $175K cap and force either a Phase 1 extension ($85K fallback, totaling $105K–$125K draw, leaving $50K–$70K headroom) or deferral of recruitment-contingency funding. Resolution: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), obtain firm cost quotes from at least two audio studios and one TTS vendor with per-entry pricing; establish a $30K audio-production contingency sub-reserve within the pre-gate $175K cap and a go/no-go decision point at Month 4 (2027-02-13) on whether to lock human production or activate the hybrid model.

Review 12: Role Definitions

  1. Budget Owner and Financial Accountability. Currently, no single named role holds authority over the $3.5M total budget, monthly spend tracking, or variance escalation decisions. If budget authority is diffused across the project lead, phase leads, and board members, cost overruns (estimated $300K–$600K risk scenarios) are discovered too late for corrective action, forcing either mid-phase scope cuts or unauthorized reserve draws that exceed the $175K pre-gate cap by $125K+ (estimate). Resolution: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), formally appoint a single Budget Owner (0.5 FTE) accountable for monthly earned-value analysis, rolling forecasts, and immediate escalation if any line item exceeds budget by >10% ($33K at Month 2 = 2026-12-13); establish clear reserve-draw authorization procedures requiring written justification within 5 days.

  2. Phase 2 Cohort Manager and Retention Accountability. The plan hires this role at Month 6 (2027-04-13), but enrollment begins Month 12 (2027-10-13)—a 6-month gap during which recruitment design, contingency planning, and retention protocols are unowned. If recruitment lags or dropout exceeds 30%, effective completers drop to 63–75 per arm (6–21% below 80-per-arm minimum), reducing power to 50–65% and forcing a $300K–$600K Phase 2 extension (estimate). Resolution: By Month 3 (2027-01-13), assign a temporary 0.5 FTE Recruitment Coordinator to draft partner agreements, incentive structures, and dropout-response playbooks; transition to the 1.0 FTE Cohort Manager at Month 6 (2027-04-13) with explicit retention KPIs (≤30% monthly dropout, ≥115 per arm enrolled by Month 13 = 2027-11-13) and a $20K–$30K contingency-activation authority.

  3. Psychometrician and Pre-Analysis Plan Authority. No assigned role owns the delivery of the pre-analysis plan draft by Month 5 (2027-03-13) or the pre-registration by Month 11 (2027-09-13). If this deliverable slips or lacks rigor, the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate becomes scientifically disputable, inviting stakeholder claims of goalpost-moving and reducing Phase 3 adoption by 20–30%, stranding up to $300K–$400K (estimate) of the $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 budget. Resolution: By Month 2 (2026-12-13), hire an independent Psychometrician with a signed statement of work specifying: power analysis by Month 5 (2027-03-13), validity study in Months 10–11 (2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13), and pre-analysis plan registration on Open Science Framework by Month 11 (2027-09-13); project lead is accountable for weekly milestone tracking and board escalation if the psychometrician misses deadlines >2 weeks.

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. Rules Lock and Pre-Analysis Plan Registration Sequencing (Month 10-11 = 2027-08-13 to 2027-09-13). Rules must freeze by Month 12 (2027-10-13) to enable stable pilot curriculum design, but the pre-analysis plan (thresholds, power analysis, decision rules) is not pre-registered until Month 11 (2027-09-13)—only 4 weeks before pilots begin at Month 13 (2027-11-13). If rule changes occur after Month 11 (2027-09-13) are discovered during pre-registration (e.g., ordinal marker spoken form ambiguity flagged by independent reviewer), redesign cascades into Phase 2 start delay of 2–4 weeks, compressing the pilot window from 12 to 11–10 months and reducing assessment sessions or follow-up completion. Impact: reduces statistical power by 10–15%, raising false-negative gate risk from 20% to 30–35%. Mitigation: finalize all rule disputes and arbiter rulings by Month 10 (2027-08-13 end); publish draft standard by Month 11 (2027-09-13 start) for comment window only, not rule revision.

  2. Audio Production and Inter-Rater Calibration Dependency (Months 6-10 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-08-13). Recording and rater calibration are on the critical path: studio must deliver 5,000 entries by Month 10 (2027-08-13 for the dry run; Month 11 = 2027-09-13 final). However, rater training and kappa measurement (target Month 10 = 2027-08-13) require the reference accent anchor and ordinal marker spoken form, both not finalized until Month 10 (2027-08-13). If accent or spoken form changes after rater training begins (Month 9 = 2027-07-13), all trained raters must retrain (2–4 weeks, $20K–$40K estimate), delaying kappa confirmation past Month 10 (2027-08-13) and triggering the 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K, estimate) fallback. Impact: consumes 48% of the $175K pre-gate draw cap, leaving $90K headroom. Mitigation: lock accent and spoken form by Month 8 (2027-06-13) end (not Month 10 = 2027-08-13); begin rater training Month 8 (2027-06-13); confirm kappa >=0.70 by Month 9.5 (2027-07-28) to allow 1-week retraining buffer if needed.

  3. Pilot Enrollment Completion vs. Assessment Session Timing (Month 12-14 = 2027-10-13 to 2027-12-13). All 460 enrollments must be complete by Month 13 (2027-11-13) to begin 4 in-person assessment sessions across Months 13–22 (2027-11-13 to 2028-08-13). However, if recruitment lags and enrollments are still arriving at Month 14 (2027-12-13) or Month 15 (2028-01-13), late-enrolling learners cannot complete all 4 sessions before the Month 22 (2028-08-13) data-lock deadline (only 7–8 months available instead of 9 months), shortening follow-up to <30 days or requiring exclusion of late enrollees. Impact: effective completers drop by 10–20%, reducing per-arm sample from 80 to 64–72, lowering power to 65–70% and raising false-negative risk to 30–35%. Mitigation: establish hard enrollment cutoff at Month 13 (2027-11-13); begin Session 1 by Month 14 (2027-12-13 start) even if enrollment is at 85–90% of target; activate contingency recruitment (bonus incentives $20K–$30K, estimate) immediately if Month 12 (2027-10-13) enrollment audit shows forecast completers <320.

Review 14: Financial Strategy

  1. Post-v1.0 Stewardship Funding Model and Steward Identification Timeline Remain Open. Stewardship costs are $150K–$250K annually (estimate), totaling $1.5M–$2.5M over 10 years, but no funding source or named steward organization exists. If steward search begins at Month 12 (2027-10-13) and negotiations extend to Month 30 (2029-04-13) or beyond, v1.0 is released without committed post-launch governance. The standard atrophies within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), and Phase 3 adoption declines from ≥3 target to 1–2 adopters, capping learner reach at 10,000–20,000 and negating $600K–$1M in Phase 3 value (estimate). Strategic question: Is v1.0 release conditional on a signed MOU in hand (Month 30 = 2029-04-13), or is stewardship sought post-release at higher risk? Action: By Month 1 (2026-11-13), board must publish a written Stewardship Commitment Policy specifying: v1.0 release contingent on signed MOU, steward search by Month 12 (2027-10-13), and MOU finalization by Month 30 (2029-04-13) or v1.0 delayed to Month 36 (2029-10-13).

  2. Phase 3 Adoption Value and ROI Measurement Unvalidated Against Spending. Phase 3 budget is $0.85M (nominal; up to $1.2M if reserve released post-GO), targeting ≥3 third-party adopters and an unvalidated estimate of 10,000–50,000 learner reach within 5 years. No cost-per-adopter target or cost-per-learner threshold is defined. If ≥3 adopters are not achieved (e.g., only 1–2 commit), Phase 3 ROI drops 33–67%, stranding $255K–$850K (estimate) of the $0.85M–$1.2M Phase 3 budget. Strategic question: What constitutes Phase 3 success? Is adoption of 1–2 high-impact organizations (e.g., major ESL publisher) equivalent to ≥3 smaller adopters? Should cost-per-learner-reached or cost-per-adopter metrics govern Phase 3 spending decisions? Action: By Month 6 (2027-04-13), board must define Phase 3 ROI thresholds: minimum $ per adopter (e.g., $100K–$300K per third-party organization), minimum learner-reach target, and reallocation rules if adoption lags (e.g., shift unspent Phase 3 funds to stewardship reserve by Month 33 = 2029-07-13).

  3. Reserve Release Trigger Ambiguity: No Clear GO Criteria for Releasing the $175K Post-Gate Reserve Balance. The reserve rule caps pre-gate draws at $175K (5% of budget) until Month 24 (2028-10-13), when the remaining $175K is released 'only after the Month 24 (2028-10-13) GO' (decision). However, if the gate outcome is 'inconclusive' (some metrics pass, others unclear), or if a metric passes narrowly (ordinal error 25.1% vs. 25% threshold), the board's discretion to declare a GO and release the reserve is undefined. A delayed or contested gate decision could hold Phase 3 funding at risk for 3–6 months (Months 24–30 = 2028-10-13 to 2029-04-13), cascading into v1.0 release delay and stewardship commitment uncertainty. Strategic question: What is the explicit GO/NO-GO/board-decided-extension decision rule? What triggers a Phase 2 extension instead of release? Action: By Month 11 (2027-09-13) pre-analysis plan, the board must pre-register quantitative pass/fail boundaries for each metric and document a decision tree (GO: all 4 metrics pass and validity holds, i.e. ≥80 completers per arm, follow-up ≥70%, kappa ≥0.70; NO-GO: valid data with any metric failing; invalid or inconclusive data: board-decided extension); publish decision rule on project website immediately.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Clear Evidence of Progress Against Pre-Registered Metrics (Monthly Validation). Motivation falters if pilot data appears inconclusive or rules prove unworkable after Month 12 (2027-10-13) lock. If monthly enrollment/dropout tracking (Months 13–22 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-08-13) shows trending toward underpowered sample (<80 per arm, reducing power to 50–65%), or if preliminary comprehension/ordinal assessments at Month 18 (2028-04-13) reveal effect sizes below thresholds, team and stakeholder confidence erodes, risking disengagement or calls for Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K, 26–52% of remaining budget). Mitigation: establish a transparent, monthly KPI dashboard showing enrollment progress, dropout trends, and preliminary effect-size estimates; publish findings at Months 15, 18, 21 (2028-01-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-07-13) to maintain visibility and early-warning signals before the Month 24 (2028-10-13) gate.

  2. Stakeholder Buy-In and Transparent Governance (Board and Partner Alignment). Motivation declines if educators, publishers, or regulators perceive the standard as imposed top-down or rules as linguistically weak/pedagogically burdensome. If consensus on rule compromises (ordinal spoken form, morphology threshold, homograph scope) is not achieved by Month 10 (2027-08-13), or if teachers report rule confusion during pilots, pilot fidelity degrades (measurement error inflates 10–20%), risking a disputed or inconclusive gate outcome and a board-decided extension. Mitigation: conduct quarterly stakeholder advisory panels (Months 6, 12, 18, 24 = 2027-04-13, 2027-10-13, 2028-04-13, 2028-10-13) with teachers, publishers, and safety-training partners; document feedback in published meeting minutes; tie rule finalization and Phase 3 readiness decisions visibly to stakeholder input.

  3. Secured Post-v1.0 Stewardship Commitment as a Credibility Signal (Early Steward Engagement). Motivation erodes if v1.0 release at Month 30 (2029-04-13) occurs without a funded steward, signaling the standard may be abandoned post-launch and atrophy within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing adoption from ≥3 target to 1–2 and negating $600K–$1M in Phase 3 value (estimate). If steward search does not begin until Month 18 (2028-04-13) and negotiation extends past Month 30 (2029-04-13), release is delayed and adoption momentum lost. Mitigation: identify 2–3 steward candidates by Month 12 (2027-10-13); approach top candidates by Month 18 (2028-04-13) with a formal proposal; secure at least a non-binding letter of interest by Month 24 (2028-10-13) and a signed MOU by Month 30 (2029-04-13) before release; publish steward identity and 5-year roadmap with v1.0 to signal long-term commitment.

Review 16: Automation Opportunities

  1. Automate Monthly Enrollment and Dropout Tracking Dashboard (Months 13–22 = 2027-11-13 to 2028-08-13). Implement a simple enrollment-management tool (REDCap, Qualtrics, or custom spreadsheet with automated alerts) to eliminate manual weekly reconciliation by the cohort manager. Automation reduces administrative overhead by ~10 hours/week (~$5K–$8K annually, estimate) and provides real-time visibility to the board, enabling early detection of recruitment shortfalls and automated escalation triggers (e.g., 'if forecast completers <320 at the Month 12 = 2027-10-13 audit, activate contingency incentive'). This reduces decision latency from 2–4 weeks to 1 week and improves confidence in the sample-size adequacy forecast used for Phase 2 extension decisions.

  2. Streamline Inter-Rater Pronunciation Scoring Workflow with Automated Kappa Calculation and Rater-Disagreement Flagging (Months 6–11 = 2027-04-13 to 2027-09-13). Replace manual Cohen's kappa calculation with a simple Python script or Qualtrics reporting module that ingests rater scores, auto-calculates pairwise and consensus kappa, and flags entries where raters diverge (kappa <0.70 for that entry). Cost: ~$2K–$5K (estimate) for tool development and validation. Savings: ~15 hours/month (~$3.6K–$5.4K annually, estimate) in manual scoring reconciliation, plus earlier detection of rater reliability issues by Month 9 (2027-07-13) instead of Month 10 (2027-08-13), reducing retraining timeline compression risk.

  3. Automate Monthly Budget Variance and Earned-Value Reporting (Months 1–36 = 2026-11-13 to 2029-10-13). Implement a lightweight budget-tracking template (Excel or simple accounting software) with automated monthly summaries of actuals vs. budget, variance flags (>10% threshold), and rolling 6-month cash-flow forecasts. Cost: ~$1K–$3K (estimate). Savings: ~8 hours/month (~$2.4K–$3.6K annually, estimate) of manual reconciliation and reduces budget-discovery delays from Month 8–9 (2027-06-13 to 2027-07-13) to Month 2 (2026-12-13), enabling proactive contingency activation (e.g., hybrid audio pivot) instead of reactive mid-phase crisis decisions.

Q1: What is the 'Pragmatic Foundation' strategic path, and how does it differ from the alternative scenarios presented in the plan?

A1: The Pragmatic Foundation is the recommended scenario: invariant-prefix ordinal markers (coexisting with legacy 1st/2nd/3rd forms), optional pronunciation overlay (leaving printed text standard), ESL-first supplementary wedge, purpose-built validated metrics, and even Phase 1–3 budget split. It prioritizes adoption-first, non-mandate positioning. Alternative: Pioneer's Gambit pursues respelling, spelled ordinals ('oneth'), and consumer-toggle wedge with thin Phase 1 (higher linguistic ambition, fragmentation risk). Prudent Consolidator uses off-the-shelf instruments, guidance-layer-only pronunciation, large held-reserve (lower precision on Clear English effects, credibility risk). The Pragmatic Foundation balances defensible evidence and educator buy-in.

Q2: Why is the 'pronunciation consistency' gate metric considered high-risk, and what happens if inter-rater reliability (Cohen's kappa) falls below the proposed floor of 0.70?

A2: Pronunciation consistency (>=15% above control, kappa >=0.75 target, >=0.70 floor) is high-risk because: (1) no published benchmark exists for inter-rater agreement in constructed-language contexts; (2) rater training depends on a reference accent anchor and ordinal marker spoken form not finalized until Month 10 (2027-08-13); (3) if kappa <0.70 at the Month 10 (2027-08-13) dry run, measurement error inflates by 20–30%, reducing statistical power to detect true effects by 10–15%. Fallback: 4-week Phase 1 extension (~$85K) for retraining, or hybrid model (synthetic baseline + verification subset). This consumes 48% of the pre-gate $175K draw cap, leaving $90K headroom for other contingencies.

Q3: What is the unfunded stewardship gap, and why does it threaten long-term adoption even if the Phase 2 go/no-go gate succeeds?

A3: Post-v1.0 stewardship (change requests, errata, conformance claims, governance) costs $150K–$250K annually (estimate), totaling $1.5M–$2.5M over 10 years. No steward organization is yet identified; steward search is deferred to Month 12 (2027-10-13) or later. If no steward is committed by Month 33 (2029-07-13) before v1.0 release (Month 30 = 2029-04-13), the standard atrophies within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13). Third-party adopters withdraw, leaving 1–2 instead of >=3, and learner reach caps at 10,000–20,000 (vs. 100,000+ unvalidated goal), negating $600K–$1M in Phase 3 adoption value. This compounds Phase 2 extension risk: if pilots extend 6 months, steward negotiation is compressed to 3 months before release.

Q4: What does the 'pre-analysis plan registration' requirement mean, and why is pre-registration by Month 11 (2027-09-13) non-negotiable for gate credibility?

A4: Pre-analysis plan registration means: by Month 11 (2027-09-13), the psychometrician must publish a complete plan on Open Science Framework specifying exact numeric thresholds (e.g., ordinal error >=25% reduction), sample-size power analysis (>=80 per arm for 80% power), primary/secondary outcomes, and decision rules. The plan is then locked before Phase 2 pilots begin at Month 13 (2027-11-13). Non-negotiable because: (1) pre-registration forecloses post-hoc threshold-tuning claims; (2) educators, standards bodies, and publishers will dispute any go/no-go outcome if thresholds were not pre-committed; (3) a delayed or weak pre-registration (Month 12 = 2027-10-13 or later) risks a 4-week Phase 1 extension to allow public comment, compressing Phase 2. The plan currently treats thresholds as 'proposals' without power-analysis justification.

Q5: What are the three highest-consequence risk scenarios, and what budget overruns or timeline extensions would result?

A5: Risk 1: Pilot recruitment/retention shortfall (enrolment <450, dropout >30%) yields effective completers <80 per arm, reducing statistical power from 80% to 50–65% and forcing a 3–6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K–$600K estimate, consuming the entire $350K reserve and creating a $35K–$250K shortfall). Risk 2: Audio production cost overrun (per-entry cost >$20) or inter-rater kappa <0.70 triggers a 4-week Phase 1 extension (~$85K), consuming 48% of the pre-gate $175K draw cap and leaving $90K headroom. Risk 3: Unfunded stewardship post-Month-36 (no committed steward by Month 33 = 2029-07-13) causes standard atrophy by Month 48–60 (2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), reducing adoption from >=3 to 1–2 and negating $600K–$1M in Phase 3 adoption value (estimate). All three directly threaten the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go credibility or post-launch viability.

Q6: What are the ethical and fairness concerns raised by anchoring pronunciation guidance to a single reference accent, and how does the plan address regional and cultural bias?

A6: The plan anchors all pronunciation guidance, audio models, and pilot scoring to one reference accent (chosen by Month 3 = 2027-01-13), which simplifies measurement but risks alienating speakers of other major English varieties (British, Australian, Indian, South African). A single anchor implicitly privileges one speaker population and may reduce perceived adoption appeal outside that region. The plan documents this tension in Decision 8 (Reference Accent Anchor) and proposes mitigation: publish mapping tables showing how other accents relate to the anchor by Month 12 (2027-10-13), and defer multi-accent recording to post-v1.0 as an optional, unfunded extension. However, no explicit equity or inclusivity review is documented, and learners from non-anchor regions may experience the standard as regionally biased, potentially suppressing adoption in those populations.

Q7: What liability and safety risks does the project accept by pursuing safety-critical pilots (technical glossary, procedures), and what happens if a misreading of a Clear English ordinal marker or homograph causes an incident?

A7: The plan limits safety-critical pilots to glossary and labeling exercises (no live operational procedures before Month 24 = 2028-10-13), retains legal counsel by Month 2 (2026-12-13), and caps liability spending at $150K–$200K (estimate). However, if a pilot partner uses Clear English materials in an operational setting (despite disclaimers) and a misreading occurs—e.g., an ordinal marker '○1' is misread as '0.1' or a homograph 'lead' (to guide) is misread as 'lead' (the metal)—resulting in injury, regulatory investigation, or litigation, the project faces product-liability exposure, OSHA or HSE investigation, and reputational damage. The plan does not quantify the probability or financial exposure of a serious incident. If insurance is unavailable or cost exceeds $50K annually (estimate), the safety-critical wedge is scaled back to non-life-critical glossaries (office supplies, library materials, not pharmaceuticals or procedures), eliminating the high-impact evidence that makes the technical-glossary cohort credible.

Q8: What does the plan's decision to position Clear English as supplementary (not mandatory or a K-12 replacement) mean for real-world adoption, and is the 'optional module' strategy realistic for achieving the >=3 adopter target?

A8: The plan explicitly rejects mandates and K-12 replacement and positions Clear English as an optional, supplementary module for adult ESL and technical writing. This means: (1) publishers are not required to adopt; (2) learners choose to use it alongside standard English; (3) no governmental mandate or curriculum change is pursued. The advantage is low institutional friction and educator buy-in. The risk is adoption voluntariness: if Clear English is perceived as a niche variant or academic exercise, publishers may deprioritize it against more established curricula. The >=3 third-party adopters target (proposed threshold) depends on publishers and technical organizations perceiving measurable value (cost savings, learner engagement, reduced errors). However, the intelligibility target (>=90% of standard-English control accuracy within 2 weeks exposure, user constraint) suggests learners can switch between Clear English and standard English fluidly, reducing the sense of necessity. If adoption is framed as 'nice-to-have' rather than 'essential,' market uptake may stall at 1–2 small adopters, capping learner reach at 10,000–20,000 instead of the unvalidated 100,000+ estimate.

Q9: What are the 'controversial aspects' of the irregular morphology retention threshold and homograph disambiguation policy, and how might educator resistance to these rules undermine pilot fidelity?

A9: Two core rules raise controversy: (1) Irregular Morphology Retention (Decision 6): Retain all irregular forms in the top 1,000-word frequency band (e.g., go/went, be/was) but regularize lower-frequency irregulars. This trade-off protects learner recognition (most frequent forms unchanged) but creates inconsistency (some irregulars are regular, some are not), violating the stated goal of 'regularized' morphology. Teachers may perceive this as a half-measure that adds rule complexity without fully solving the problem. (2) Homograph Disambiguation (Decision 7): Mandatory markers only in safety-critical documents for <=50 high-impact pairs (e.g., read/read, lead/lead). Optional elsewhere. This creates a two-tier standard: safety-critical glossaries are heavily marked; ESL textbooks are not. Teachers and learners may find the inconsistency confusing—why is homograph marking enforced in one context but not others? If educators resist these rules as linguistically weak or pedagogically burdensome, they may misapply them during pilots (e.g., regularize all irregulars, mark all homophones), invalidating the assessment data. Measurement error could inflate by 10–20%, rendering gate metrics inconclusive and increasing false-negative risk by 15–25%.

Q10: What are the broader implications of the plan's failure to identify and secure a post-v1.0 steward organization before public release, and what happens to the standard if it is abandoned after Month 36 (2029-10-13)?

A10: The unfunded stewardship gap ($150K–$250K per year, $1.5M–$2.5M over 10 years, estimate) means the plan has no committed post-launch governance or maintenance funding. If v1.0 is released at Month 30 (2029-04-13) without a signed stewardship Memorandum of Understanding in hand, the standard becomes an orphaned artifact: change requests accumulate unanswered; errata go unfixed; the lexicon stagnates without updating to emerging vocabulary and cultural shifts. Within 12–24 months (by Month 48–60 = 2030-10-13 to 2031-10-13), adopter confidence erodes. Third-party publishers and educators perceive the standard as abandoned, cease marketing materials, and withdraw from adoption. The plan's >=3 adopter target (proposed threshold) collapses to 1–2, capping learner reach at 10,000–20,000 instead of the unvalidated 100,000+ estimate, negating $600K–$1M in Phase 3 adoption value (estimate). This cascades to stakeholder trust: if funders, educators, and standards bodies perceive stewardship as an afterthought, they lose confidence that Clear English will be maintained long-term and deprioritize adoption relative to more established standards (ASD-STE100, plain-language guidance, ICAO aviation English). The plan compounds this risk by deferring steward identification to Month 12 (2027-10-13) or later; if Phase 2 extends 6 months (due to recruitment shortfall or inconclusive data), steward negotiation slips to Months 30–33 (2029-04-13 to 2029-07-13), leaving minimal time to secure commitment before release.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

More than 5% of converted instances (proposed threshold) are ambiguous or misread by reviewers, or reviewers need manual correction on more than 10% of documents (proposed threshold).

Fewer than 3 qualified candidates per role, offers declined at budgeted pay, or the psychometrician start date later than Month 2 (2026-12-13).
