Consistency: first pass found 3 high / 3 medium / 1 low contradictions. Repair: round 1: 42 edits → 1 high / 4 medium; round 2: 42 edits → 0 high / 3 medium. Published: round 2 (fewest high-severity issues). Shown below: the final check of the repaired documents (0 high / 3 medium / 3 low).

1. Reserve cannot fund the extensions and top-ups charged to it (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • canonical reserve_draw_rule; Review 14 #3: Reserve: pre-gate draws capped at $175K; the remaining balance is released only after the Month 24 GO.
  • Review 2 #2, Review 5 #1, Review 1 #2, Review 4 #1, Review 10 #3: A 3-6 month Phase 2 extension ($300K-$600K) is 'consuming the entire $350K reserve'; Phase 2.5 safety extension is 'funded from Phase 3 reserve'; 'consuming the entire pre-gate reserve'.
  • Why it conflicts: An extension follows invalid or inconclusive data, which has no GO, so the post-gate half of the reserve is not releasable. Pre-gate draws are capped at $175K, and even the full $350K is below a 6-month extension ($600K). The same reserve is also claimed for Phase 3 top-up, Phase 2.5 and pre-gate protection, with no ranking.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide and document one waterfall for the $0.35M: pre-gate gate-protection (cap $175K), extension after inconclusive data, Phase 3 top-up, any Phase 2.5. Options: (a) let the board release a defined part of the post-gate balance for a validated extension without a GO; (b) cap the extension at what the pre-gate cap and Phase 3 underspend can cover; (c) treat an extension as unfunded and require descoping. Replace 'entire reserve' wording with the chosen rule, and correct the $35K-$250K shortfall figures accordingly.

2. Steward receives the $0.35M reserve vs stewardship unfunded (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Pitch, Collaboration Opportunities (post-v1.0 steward): Steward 'receive[s] $0.35M reserve release post-gate plus pro-rata Phase 3 funding if a written commitment is signed by Month 30'.
  • Executive Summary Risk 3; Review 14 #1; canonical stewardship_funding_gap: Post-Month-36 stewardship ($150K-$250K per year) is unfunded and no steward or funding source exists; Risk 3 'stewardship unfunded'.
  • Why it conflicts: The pitch states a transfer to the steward as fact, while every other document treats steward funding as an open gap. The same $0.35M is also the pre-gate protection pool, the Phase 3 top-up and the extension source, so it cannot be given away as well.
  • Suggested resolution: Remove the transfer from the pitch until decided. Decision options: (a) the steward receives nothing from the project budget; (b) a fixed, capped seed from unspent Phase 3 or reserve funds, ranked after pre-gate protection and any extension; (c) steward funding is entirely external. State the choice in the project plan and the pitch.

3. Safety-critical cohort deferral vs 4-arm, 320-completer gate and conflicting triggers (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • canonical pilot_design, phase2_go_no_go_rule; Pitch Stakeholder Benefits; Executive Summary: Pilot design is 2 cohorts x 2 conditions = 4 arms; gate validity needs at least 80 completers per arm (320 total); pitch promises validated technical-glossary benefits.
  • Review 4 #1, Review 10 #3, Self-audit 2 and 14, Premortem A5: If approval takes more than 6 months, defer the safety-critical cohort to a post-Month-24 Phase 2.5 (Review 4); more than 4 months (Review 10, Self-audit 14, Self-audit 2). Written regulator advice is due Month 4 (premortem A5), Month 6 (Review 10), Month 8 (Review 4, Self-audit 14).
  • Why it conflicts: Removing two arms before Month 24 changes the gate population and the 320-completer validity condition, yet the gate rule and pitch assume four arms. The deferral threshold (4 vs 6 months) and the advice date differ, and the liability strategy at Month 4 would precede advice not due until Month 8.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide the fallback: ESL-only 2-arm gate with re-registered validity conditions (160 completers) and technical cohort as non-gating, or a deferred cohort. Use one trigger (4 months is the more defensible, since the pilot window is only 12 months) and one date for written advice (Month 4, matching the liability strategy). Qualify the pitch's technical-glossary claims as conditional.

4. Steward fallback: cancel v1.0 at Month 33 vs defer to Month 36 or later (🔴 High) — needs a project decision

  • Premortem FM4 stop rule; Review 6 KPI 3 (first clause): No signed commitment by Month 30: release not triggered; Month 33 is the latest point at which a delayed release can be triggered; if none by then, v1.0 is cancelled and the project closes.
  • Review 5 #3, Review 6 KPI 3, Review 9 #3, Review 14 #1, Self-audit 20: If no signed MOU by Month 30, 'defer v1.0 release to Month 36 (2029-10-13) or later'; 'delays release to Month 36'; 'defer v1.0 release from Month 30 to Month 36'.
  • Why it conflicts: Cancellation at Month 33 and deferral to Month 36 or later are different outcomes. A release at or after Month 36 falls outside the funded 36-month program, leaves no time for the at least 3 licensed adopters by Month 36, and no funded team exists to carry it.
  • Suggested resolution: Choose one rule. If a deferral beyond Month 33 is wanted, decide who funds the team after Month 36 and re-date the adopter target; otherwise adopt the FM4 rule (release by Month 33 or cancel and archive) everywhere. Never state 'Month 36 or later' as a release option unless funded.

5. Underpowered/inconclusive pilot treated as NO-GO or 'false-negative gate' (🟡 Medium)

  • canonical phase2_go_no_go_rule; Executive Summary: Fewer than 80 completers per arm makes data invalid; invalid or inconclusive data leads to a board-decided extension; NO-GO applies only to valid data with a failing metric and returns up to $1.2M.
  • Self-audit 5; Review 2 #1-#2, Review 4 #3, Review 5 #1; Review 2 #1: 'a false-negative gate (no-go on inconclusive data, stranding $1.2M Phase 2 spend)'; power 'from 80% to ~60% ... raising false-negative gate risk'; 'Type II error ... to 50%' at 60% power; 'credibility worth $1.2M-$1.4M'.
  • Why it conflicts: Under the canonical rule an underpowered pilot is invalid and leads to an extension, not NO-GO. A NO-GO returns funds rather than stranding them. Phase 2 spend is not 'stranded' by the gate, and funds at risk are $1.2M (Phase 3 + reserve), not $1.2M-$1.4M. At 60% power the Type II error is 40%, not 50%.
  • Suggested resolution: Reword: sample below 80 per arm = invalid = extension; false-negative language applies only to valid, adequately powered data. Replace '$1.2M-$1.4M' with '$1.2M (Phase 3 $0.85M + reserve $0.35M)'. Make power/Type II pairs consistent (60% power = 40% Type II).

6. Baseline recruitment study precedes ethics, consent and partner commitments (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • Project Plan Compliance Actions and Dependencies; canonical pilot_partner_commitments: Ethics approval by Month 6; signed partner commitments by Month 3; consent forms and privacy policy by Month 12.
  • Executive Summary Risk 1 and Feedback #2; Review 3 #2; Review 8 #2; Premortem A3: Baseline study with 20-30 learners and 2 assessment sessions in Months 1-2, to validate the 35-45% dropout assumption and set enrolment targets.
  • Why it conflicts: A human-subject study with assessments and attrition tracking would start before IRB approval, before consent forms exist and before partners are signed. Two months also cannot observe 30-day follow-up or the up-to-12-month attrition it is meant to validate.
  • Suggested resolution: Decide the form: (a) obtain an ethics exemption/approval before Months 1-2 and secure consent and partner agreement first; (b) re-scope to a non-participant evidence review (partner historical attrition and literature) in Months 1-3; or (c) move the study after Month 6 and drop the claim that it validates 30-day or 12-month dropout. Update the Month 3 retargeting deadline accordingly.

7. Ordinal spoken form locked in the same month as the kappa check that depends on it (🟡 Medium) — needs a project decision

  • canonical ordinal_rule, phase1_extension_fallback; Premortem FM2 and FM8 tripwires; Review 8 #3; Review 9 #1: Marker symbol and spoken form fixed by Month 10; kappa check and dry run at Month 10; ordinal spoken form 'not finalized until Month 10'.
  • Review 13 #2; Premortem FM2 early warning: Lock accent and spoken form by Month 8; begin rater training Month 8; confirm kappa by Month 9.5; FM2 early warning 'spoken form unresolved at Month 8'.
  • Why it conflicts: Raters cannot be calibrated on a reading fixed only in the month of the check. A Month 10 lock leaves no buffer before the 4-week extension fallback, and ordinal audio recorded in Months 6-11 would precede the fixed reading.
  • Suggested resolution: Adopt Month 8 as the lock date across documents (Month 10 stays the backstop and kappa-check date). Align FM2/FM8 tripwires and Reviews 8 and 9 to Month 8, and have the kappa check follow at least 4-6 weeks after the lock.

8. Enrolment audit month, tripwires and dropout units (🟡 Medium)

  • canonical pilot_enrolment_and_dropout; Review 4 #3; Review 13 #3; Self-audit 4 and 20: Enrol at least 115 per arm (460 total), dropout at most 30%, enrolment complete Month 13; audit shows forecast completers at least 320 (Month 12 in Reviews 4, 13, Self-audits).
  • Premortem FM3; Review 8 #2; Review 6 KPI 1; Review 12 #2: Audit at Month 13 'one month after enrolment opens' (FM3); 'activate contingency if dropout tracking exceeds 25% by Month 10' (Review 8); flag if completers below 70 per arm at Month 18 (KPI 1); 'at most 30% monthly dropout' (Review 12).
  • Why it conflicts: The audit month differs (12 vs 13). A Month 10 dropout check precedes any Phase 2 enrolment (starts Month 12). A 70-per-arm warning is below the 80-per-arm validity minimum, so the alarm fires after validity is lost. A 30% monthly dropout is a different quantity from the 30% tolerated total dropout.
  • Suggested resolution: Use one audit at Month 12 (enrolment opens) with a forecast completers at least 320 test, a follow-up check at Month 13 (enrolment close), and an 80-per-arm warning bound at Month 18. Replace the Month 10 dropout check with the baseline/partner-history evidence. Express the retention KPI as at most 30% cumulative dropout.

9. Psychometrics timeline: lead-time arithmetic and what is 'due' when (🟡 Medium)

  • canonical psychometrics_cost, rules_freeze_preregistration; Executive Summary; Self-audit 20: Power analysis and pre-analysis plan draft by Month 5; pre-registered Month 11; rules locked and Phase 2 starts Month 12; enrolment complete Month 13.
  • Review 13 #1; Self-audit 3; Review 1 #1: 'pre-registered until Month 11 - only 4 weeks before pilots begin at Month 13'; 'Pre-analysis plan and power analysis are not due until Month 11'; validity study Months 10-11 feeds thresholds registered at Month 11.
  • Why it conflicts: Month 11 to Month 12 is about 4 weeks and to Month 13 about 8-9, so the lead time and pilot start are mixed. Self-audit 3 says the power analysis is due at Month 11 while its own mitigation and Self-audit 20 say Month 5. A validity study ending in Month 11 cannot inform thresholds registered at the same date without a stated sequence.
  • Suggested resolution: State: power analysis Month 5; validity study Months 10-11 ends before registration (e.g., results by Month 10.5 or registration at end of Month 11); about 4 weeks to Phase 2 start (Month 12) and about 8-9 weeks to enrolment close (Month 13). Correct Self-audit 3.

10. Pre-gate headroom and percentage arithmetic (⚪ Low)

  • canonical free_reserve_after_fallbacks, overrun_exposure (recomputed): $85K is about 49% of the $175K cap, leaving $90K headroom; $85K + $20K-$30K leaves $60K-$70K; $40K-$50K is 3.6-4.5% of $1.1M; $35K is a shortfall on the whole reserve after $85K + $300K.
  • Executive Summary Feedback #3; Review 11 #2; Review 5 #2: '$35K-$90K headroom estimate' under the cap; '$40K-$50K overrun (2.7-3.5% of Phase 1)' leaving '$125K-$152K'; '$105K-$115K' 'exhausts contingency'.
  • Why it conflicts: $35K is not headroom under the cap. $40K-$50K is 3.6-4.5% of $1.1M and leaves $125K-$135K. $105K-$115K leaves $60K-$70K, which is not an exhausted cap.
  • Suggested resolution: Correct to: headroom $90K after a 4-week extension; $60K-$70K after adding recruitment contingency; 3.6-4.5% of Phase 1; $125K-$135K remaining.

11. Cohort manager timing and ownership gap (⚪ Low)

  • canonical staffing; Executive Summary; Project Plan: 1.0 FTE cohort manager hired by Month 6.
  • Review 4 #3; Review 12 #2; Review 1 #2: 'hire cohort manager by Month 4 (not Month 6)'; add a 0.5 FTE Recruitment Coordinator by Month 3; 'hires at Month 6, but enrollment begins Month 12 - a 6-month gap during which recruitment design ... unowned'.
  • Why it conflicts: The Month 4 hire and the extra coordinator are stated as mitigations while the Executive Summary treats Month 4 only as a proposal with cost to be assessed. The 'gap' argument is illogical: a Month 6 hire covers Months 6-12; the unowned period is Months 0-6.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep Month 6 as the plan value; list a Month 4 hire or interim coordinator as a costed option only. Rewrite the gap as Months 3-6, before the hire.

12. Stewardship roadmap horizon: 5-year vs 10-year (⚪ Low)

  • Executive Summary Key Deliverables; Review (Issue 5 recommendation): A 5-year roadmap is published by Month 36.
  • Pitch, Long-term Vision: Steward receives 'a published 10-year governance roadmap, change-control calendar and annual budget'.
  • Why it conflicts: The deliverable's horizon differs between documents. The 10-year figure is the funding-gap horizon, not the planned roadmap.
  • Suggested resolution: Keep the 5-year roadmap as the Month 36 deliverable and refer to the 10-year funding gap separately.

Summary

The plan is largely consistent on its core structure: budget split, 4-arm design, gate rule, Month 30 release conditional on a steward commitment, and the 10% morphology/accent/ordinal design choices. Most earlier fixes have held. The remaining problems are concentrated in funding and fallback logic: the $0.35M reserve is claimed by several competing uses, safety-cohort and steward fallbacks are unresolved, and an extension after invalid data has no stated source of funds. Several lower-level timing and arithmetic slips (enrolment audit month, ordinal lock vs kappa check, headroom percentages) are fixable by editing to the canonical values. The user's intelligibility constraint (at least 90% of control accuracy within 2 weeks) is not operationalized as a gate metric in any document.

How the canonical facts were reconciled

The budget split ($1.1M + $1.2M + $0.85M + $0.35M = $3.5M) and the 8.6%, 86%, 115-per-arm and 460-learner figures recompute correctly and were kept. Corrected: participant costs summed only two of five listed lines ($78K-$161K) and now total $208K-$351K; the Phase 1 staff envelope was overstated ($0.7M-$0.8M) and is now about $0.5M-$0.7M after non-staff lines; the Phase 1 exit kappa (0.75) was aligned with the 0.70 floor used by the fallback and Phase 2 validity rule; the pre-gate draw cap leaves at least half (not 'most') of the reserve returnable; a garbled date/text fragment in the stewardship basis was repaired. Added a free-reserve fact because the same $350K reserve was implicitly counted against both the 4-week Phase 1 extension ($85K) and the 3-month Phase 2 extension ($300K), which together exceed it by $35K; the separate lexicon-reduction fallback was merged into the audio fact to stay within the fact limit, and the $20/entry trigger vs. $24/entry upper budget, partner-capacity sizing and the freeze running past Month 36 (2029-10-13) were flagged in basis fields.

Initial Prompt

Plan:
Design and launch a new standardized variant of English (“Clear English”) that fixes high‑friction inconsistencies across ordinals, spelling‑to‑sound, irregular morphology, and ambiguous homographs, while remaining intelligible to current English speakers. The goal is a parallel standard for education, ESL, technical writing, and safety‑critical documentation—not a wholesale replacement of English.

Define a three‑year program with gated phases. Phase 1 (12 months) specifies the rules and produces a reference corpus; Phase 2 (12 months) pilots learning materials and tests usability; Phase 3 (12 months) publishes a public standard and launches limited‑scope adoption.

Scope and constraints:
- Intelligibility: average adult comprehension within 2 weeks of exposure.
- Ordinals: remove special cases (11th/12th/13th; 1st/2nd/3rd; 21st/31st patterns). Choose one approach: (A) numeric + invariant ordinal marker, or (B) fully spelled ordinals with regularized endings; justify.
- Spelling‑to‑sound: define a minimal, consistent grapheme‑to‑phoneme mapping; keep Latin alphabet; diacritics optional but must be minimal and justified.
- Morphology: regularize a defined subset of irregular verbs and plurals (e.g., go/went, mouse/mice), but cap changes to preserve recognizability. Specify a threshold for when irregular forms are retained.
- Homographs and homophones: introduce disambiguation rules or optional markers for a limited list of high‑impact pairs (e.g., lead/lead, read/read), with a clear policy for when disambiguation is required.
- Core lexicon: 5,000 words with regularized pronunciation guidance and a mapping from standard English.
- Avoid aggressive scenarios: no mandates, no immediate K‑12 replacement, no universal adoption claims.
- Pilot cohorts: adult ESL learners and native speakers using a safety‑critical or technical glossary.
- Budget: $3.5M total across three years (propose a realistic split).

Deliverables:
- “Clear English Standard v1.0” with formal rule set and rationale.
- Reference dictionary (word list + pronunciation guidance + mappings).
- Style guide covering ordinals, disambiguation markers, and regularized morphology.
- Pilot curriculum (print + digital) with assessments.
- Public licensing policy enabling third‑party adoption.

Define governance (editorial board + linguistic review), risk register (educator pushback, rule ambiguity, fragmentation), and outreach plan (academic partners, ESL publishers, standards orgs). Include a clear go/no‑go decision point after Phase 2 based on pilot data (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency score, learner retention after 30 days).

Optimize for user adoption. Don't optimize for linguistic purity.
Don't pick the most aggressive scenario.

Today's date:
2026-Oct-13

Project start ASAP

Prompt Screening

Verdict: 🟢 USABLE

Rationale: The prompt describes a concrete, detailed three-year program to design and launch a standardized English variant, with phases, scope constraints, a $3.5M budget, deliverables, governance, and decision gates. It is ambitious but specific and plannable.

Redline Gate

Verdict: 🟢 ALLOW

Rationale: The prompt requests a benign project plan for a standardized, optional English variant for education and technical writing; it carries no harm potential or operational risk.

Violation Details

Detail Value
Capability Uplift No

Premise Attack

Why this fails.

Premise Attack 1 — Integrity

Forensic audit of foundational soundness across axes.

[STRATEGIC] A third, invented English variant that must stay readable to current speakers yet re-spell, re-pronounce and re-inflect 5,000 words has no buyer: the one niche where a controlled English works already has a governed standard, and everywhere else learners need the English that people actually speak.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A parallel 'Clear English' for ESL and safety-critical writing duplicates an established standard in the only niche that needs it and asks learners to master a variant that nobody else uses.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The safety-critical and technical-writing niche is already served by ASD-STE100, a maintained, industry-backed controlled English, so a $3.5M newcomer must displace an incumbent that regulators, manufacturers and translators already use.
  • The brief demands both that adults comprehend the variant within 2 weeks of exposure and that it regularize spelling-to-sound, irregular verbs and plurals, but each regularization lowers recognizability, so the two requirements pull against each other and cannot both be met.
  • Adult ESL pilot cohorts would be taught a 5,000-word 'Clear English' that no employer, examiner, colleague or native speaker uses, so every learner pays twice: once to learn it and again to unlearn it for exams and real conversation.
  • A single grapheme-to-phoneme mapping forces the project to choose whose English sounds 'correct' among competing national and regional accents, which invites rejection from the educators and ESL publishers it is supposed to recruit.
  • The problems targeted are minor in practice: ordinal oddities (1st/2nd/3rd, 11th-13th) are already handled by writing numerals, and lead/read-type homograph pairs are resolved by context, so a 36-month, three-phase program with a go/no-go gate is aimed at friction that does not justify a new standard.
  • An openly licensed standard with no mandate and no K-12 route has no mechanism for convergence, so the likeliest outcome is competing forks and house dialects rather than one adopted standard, which is the opposite of the 'standard' the program promises.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: Rule drafting and early public announcement draw criticism from linguists, plain-language practitioners and technical-writing bodies who point to ASD-STE100 and Basic English, and the project is cast as another spelling-reform stunt before any pilot data exists.
  • 1–3 years: Pilot results come from a self-selected, small adult cohort that is poorly matched to the real target population, so the go/no-go metrics (30-day retention, ordinal error rate) are ambiguous, and safety-critical firms decline to run a trial that would double their document-review burden.
  • 5–10 years: The published standard sits as a niche artifact with a few enthusiast forks, while any safety-critical use leaves legacy documents in two variants and creates a misreading and liability exposure that no regulator asked for.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — Simplified Spelling Board (1906): Carnegie-funded effort with a 300-word list and a Roosevelt order was reversed when the House voted 142-25 to bar the spellings from federal documents, and the Board's spellings never caught on.
  • Case/Incident — ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (first released 1986 as an AECMA document): a governed, industry-backed controlled English for aircraft maintenance documentation, now at Issue 9 (2025) with roughly 900 approved words, which already fills the safety-critical niche this plan targets.
  • Case/Incident — Basic English, C.K. Ogden (1930): a deliberately simplified 850-word English promoted for international use that did not become a widely adopted standard.

Premise Attack 2 — Accountability

Rights, oversight, jurisdiction-shopping, enforceability.

[STRATEGIC] — Fork In The Cockpit: a new spelling, ordinal and verb-form variant aimed at safety-critical documentation adds a second reading standard to the one place where a reader cannot afford to wonder which standard a page is written in, and it attacks the spelling layer when the controlled-language layer that already serves technical writing is what matters.

Bottom Line: REJECT: Fork In The Cockpit puts a second, unrecognised spelling standard into the documents where only one can be trusted, and past English-reform efforts suggest it would end up as a stranded dialect with a small user base. The need for clearer technical English is real, but this premise does not meet it.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Adult ESL learners and technical staff would spend scarce study hours on a variant that no employer, exam board or regulator recognises, and a worker told to read a manual in a made-up dialect has no real choice about it.
  • The editorial board, the pilot and the go/no-go decision all sit with the people who built the standard, with no regulator, aviation or industrial authority obliged to accept it, so nobody outside the project is accountable when a reader misreads a page.
  • An openly licensed variant can be copied and altered by anyone, and once a maintenance manual or label is printed in it, mixed Clear English and standard English will circulate in the same workplaces for as long as the documents live.
  • The premise misallocates $3.5M (user constraint) to re-spelling 5,000 words (user constraint), while the real problem in technical English is ambiguous sentences and uncontrolled vocabulary, which an existing standard already targets, and a 2-week average comprehension target is far too loose for safety-critical reading.

Second-Order Effects

  • Months 0-12 (2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13) — The Cracks Appear: Linguists, ESL publishers and standards bodies split over which irregular verbs and homographs to regularise, and the rule set reopens at every meeting because no outside authority can close it.
  • Months 12-36 (2027-10-13 to 2029-10-13) — Pilot Theatre: Pilot cohorts of motivated volunteers produce flattering comprehension numbers that say nothing about stressed, tired workers reading a warning label, and the go/no-go gate is decided on the wrong evidence.
  • Months 36-60 (2029-10-13 to 2031-10-13) — Copycats Arrive: Rival variants appear under the open licence, each claiming to be the real Clear English, and a handful of companies print mixed-standard documents that readers must now decode twice.
  • Months 60-120 (2031-10-13 to 2036-10-13) — The Reckoning: Learners who invested in the variant are stranded with a skill no exam or employer recognises, and archives of dual-standard technical documents become a permanent source of avoidable misreading.

Evidence

  • Law/Standard — ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: a maintained controlled-language standard for aerospace and defence maintenance documentation, whose current edition (January 2025) is reported as having 53 writing rules and roughly 900 approved words, and which already serves non-native readers without changing English spelling.
  • Case/Report — Simplified Spelling Society (founded 1908) and the Carnegie-funded Progressive Era simplified-spelling campaign in the United States: both pushed spelling reform for decades, and the American effort was undermined in part by schoolteachers' quiet resistance.
  • Case/Report — Shavian alphabet: commissioned under George Bernard Shaw's will, selected in a 1958 competition from 467 entries, and never seriously adopted as an alternative way to write English.
  • Case/Report — Basic English (C. K. Ogden, 850 words, 1930s): even with a 1943 Churchill-era cabinet committee behind it, it did not become an international language, and what survives is its word list as a beginner vocabulary.

Premise Attack 3 — Spectrum

Enforced breadth: distinct reasons across ethical/feasibility/governance/societal axes.

[STRATEGIC] A voluntary English variant must out-compete both standard English and an incumbent technical-writing standard, yet offers learners a dead-end dialect and safety documents a fresh misreading hazard.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A voluntary, unmandated English variant with $3.5M and three years cannot displace standard English or the established technical-English standard, and its only certain product is one more convention that safety-critical readers must tell apart from the original.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Adoption has no engine: with no mandates, no K-12 entry and no universal-adoption claim, nothing compels a single publisher, employer or regulator to switch, and $3.5M cannot buy the network effect that every language standard lives or dies on.
  • Safety-critical text is the worst place to introduce a second reading convention: a technician trained on invariant ordinal markers instead of 11th/12th/13th, or on optional lead/lead disambiguation tags, will misread a standard-English manual the day the two meet.
  • The niche is already occupied: controlled English for safety-critical and technical documentation exists as an industry-governed standard, so a pilot on a 'safety-critical or technical glossary' duplicates a rival with decades of installed manuals and audit acceptance.
  • ESL learners are the intended beneficiaries yet are the ones harmed: a 5,000-word regularized lexicon is a second system on top of the standard English they must still master for jobs, exams and street signs, so every hour spent is a toll paid twice.
  • The intelligibility target contradicts the ambition: if adults must understand it within 2 weeks of exposure the changes must be trivial and fix little, and if they fix go/went, mouse/mice and spelling-to-sound at scale the text stops being intelligible to current speakers.

Second-Order Effects

  • 0–6 months: The editorial board cannot agree on ordinal option A versus B or on the threshold for retaining irregular forms, so Phase 1 rule-writing becomes a public quarrel and educators and standards bodies hear 'another spelling reform' before they hear any data.
  • 1–3 years: Pilot results from self-selected adult ESL volunteers and technical staff show decent 30-day retention inside the course and nothing outside it; publishers see no paying market, and the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go becomes a contested reading of flattering numbers.
  • 5–10 years: The open licence yields a handful of divergent forks and a scatter of documents in mutually unreadable rule sets, leaving the standard as one more orphaned variant that adds ambiguity to the very safety documentation it was meant to clarify.

Evidence

  • Case/Incident — Simplified Spelling Board and Roosevelt order (1906): Roosevelt ordered the Government Printing Office to use 300 simplified spellings, the House voted in December 1906 to keep dictionary spellings, and he rescinded the order; this program asks for a lexicon more than sixteen times larger (recomputed: 5,000 / 300).
  • Report/Guidance — ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, Issue 9 (2025): an existing controlled-language standard for technical documentation, widely used in aerospace and defence, already occupies the safety-critical clarity niche this plan targets.
  • Case/Incident — Initial Teaching Alphabet, Sir James Pitman (1960s): a regularized sound-to-symbol system adopted in UK and US classrooms and largely abandoned by the late 1970s, with learners still having to transition to standard spelling.

Premise Attack 4 — Cascade

Tracks second/third-order effects and copycat propagation.

This is a strategic flaw: a fourth, privately authored orthography is proposed as a "parallel standard" to a language whose entire value is that everyone else already uses the incumbent form. Every learner and safety-critical reader would have to master Clear English and still be fluent in Standard English, so the product has negative marginal value for exactly the audiences it targets, and the "optimize for adoption" goal is contradicted by the design itself.

Bottom Line: Abandon the premise: do not create a new variant of English with new spellings, because a second system that users must learn on top of the first has negative adoption value regardless of how well the rules are written. If the real aim is clarity in ESL and safety-critical documents, the premise of re-spelling English is the source of the failure, not the governance, budget or phasing.

Reasons for Rejection

  • The Double-Tax Learner: an adult ESL learner who studies Clear English still has to read street signs, prescription labels, contracts, exam papers and employer documents in Standard English. Clear English is therefore an additional cost, never a substitute, and a plan that must be learned on top of the thing it improves cannot win adoption from rational buyers. The 2-week intelligibility target (user constraint) quantifies the cost of entry but nothing in the plan quantifies a payoff.
  • The Occupied Niche: safety-critical and technical writing already has a controlled-language incumbent, ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (about 900 approved words and 53 writing rules in the January 2025 edition, originating in 1980s aerospace). It cuts ambiguity without re-spelling anything. A 5,000-word re-spelled lexicon enters that niche as a harder, riskier, less-established rival with no regulator, airline or OEM asking for it.
  • The Recognizability-Regularity Vise: the plan demands rules regular enough to fix spelling-to-sound and irregular morphology, yet capped so that current speakers understand it within two weeks. Each regularization (went→goed, mice→mouses) either breaks recognizability or is capped so heavily that the irregulars that cause the real friction remain. Any threshold for 'retain irregular forms' is arbitrary and will be attacked by both reformers (too timid) and users (too strange) at once.
  • The Accent Hostage Problem: a 'minimal, consistent grapheme-to-phoneme mapping' must pick a reference pronunciation, but English has no single one (rhotic vs non-rhotic, cot/caught, trap/bath, Indian, Nigerian, Singaporean and American norms). Whatever accent anchors the mapping makes the standard 'wrong' for a majority of the intended ESL audience, and the 5,000-word pronunciation guidance becomes a dialect-politics dispute instead of a teaching tool.
  • The Self-Graded Gate: the Month 24 (2028-10-13) go/no-go metrics (comprehension speed, ordinal error rate, pronunciation consistency, 30-day retention) measure how well people learn the new system on the project's own materials, with volunteer cohorts. None of them measures transfer back to Standard English, interference errors (mixing the two systems), or error rates in real safety-critical tasks, which are the only outcomes that decide adoption. A gate that cannot return a meaningful 'no' is theater.

Second-Order Effects

  • Months 0-12 (2026-10-13 to 2027-10-13): the editorial board spends its credibility on decisions with no empirical anchor (ordinals option A vs B, which accent, which 'high-impact' homographs). Linguists outside the project publish critiques of the rule set before the reference corpus exists, and fragmentation arrives early as forks of the draft rules circulate.
  • Months 12-24 (2027-10-13 to 2028-10-13): pilot recruitment skews to motivated volunteers, producing flattering 2-week comprehension and 30-day retention numbers. Pilot ESL teachers report the interference problem informally (students mixing Clear and Standard forms on tests such as those they actually need), but these reports are not captured by the four gate metrics.
  • Months 24-36 (2028-10-13 to 2029-10-13): a 'go' on weak data triggers publication of Standard v1.0 and an open licence. Third parties immediately fork it, and the stated risk of fragmentation is realized by design: an open licence for a standard with no enforcement body yields multiple incompatible 'Clear English' variants.
  • Months 36-60 (2029-10-13 to 2031-10-13): the budget ($3.5M, user constraint) is spent with no sustaining revenue or institutional owner. ESL publishers decline to license because certification bodies and exams do not recognise the variant. Technical-writing teams stay on ASD-STE100 or their house style guides, and the project survives as a hobbyist community.
  • Months 60-120 (2031-10-13 to 2036-10-13): the best case is a documentation archive and a small online user group. The worst case is that a few safety documents are issued in Clear English and a mix-up with Standard English ordinals or spellings contributes to a reportable error, which discredits the whole concept of controlled-language variants in regulated industries.

Evidence

  • Simplified Spelling Board (1906): funded by Andrew Carnegie at $25,000 per year, with members including Mark Twain and Melvil Dewey, it proposed 300 simplified spellings. On Aug 27, 1906 President Theodore Roosevelt ordered the Government Printing Office to use them in executive-department documents. On Dec 13, 1906 the House of Representatives resolved, unanimously, that the printer should follow the standard in generally accepted dictionaries, and Roosevelt rescinded his order. Presidential backing and money still lost to the dictionary incumbent within months.
  • Initial Teaching Alphabet (i.t.a.): devised by Sir James Pitman in the early 1960s as an easier route into English reading, it saw considerable uptake in that decade and then fell out of use from the 1970s. A principal reason cited is that children struggled to transfer i.t.a. reading skills to standard orthography and were confused by juggling two writing systems. This is the Double-Tax Learner in a real classroom experiment, and the plan has no metric for transfer.
  • ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: a controlled-language standard created in the 1980s at the request of the European airline industry, maintained by the ASD and now at about 900 approved words and 53 rules (January 2025 edition). It is the direct incumbent in the 'safety-critical documentation' niche that Clear English claims, and it works without changing spelling, so there is no gap that a re-spelled variant fills.
  • The plan has no direct precedent as a voluntary, non-mandated, parallel orthography that was adopted at scale by regulated industries; the adopted analogues (STE, plain-language guidelines) change vocabulary and sentence structure, not spelling. This specific combination is unprecedented in its folly.

Premise Attack 5 — Escalation

Narrative of worsening failure from cracks → amplification → reckoning.

[STRATEGIC] — Orphan Dialect Trap: A voluntary, mandate-free English variant that is close enough to standard English to be 'intelligible in two weeks' yet different enough to need teaching is born with no installed base, no regulator, and no employer, so the more it fixes, the less anyone can use it.

Bottom Line: REJECT: A voluntary, near-English variant with no authority, no installed base and no customer demanding it cannot be both easy enough to adopt and different enough to matter, and it would turn learners and safety documentation into the unwilling test population for that contradiction. The gate is closed.

Reasons for Rejection

  • Adult ESL learners are a time-poor, status-vulnerable population who need the English that employers, exam boards, immigration offices and colleagues actually use, and spending their scarce hours on a variant that none of those institutions recognise treats their ambition as raw material for an experiment.
  • No body with legal or professional authority sits behind the standard: a self-appointed editorial board and a linguistic review panel would issue rules for safety-critical documents with no certification regime, no liability owner and no route for anyone to answer for a regularised ordinal or disambiguation marker that is misread in the field.
  • Introducing a parallel written standard into safety-critical and technical documentation creates a new translation boundary between 'Clear English' and standard English, and every boundary, every mixed-form document and every partial adopter is a fresh point where meaning can be silently corrupted.
  • The value proposition contradicts itself: a variant that current speakers grasp within two weeks without real study has changed too little to fix spelling-to-sound or morphology, while one that changes enough to help must be taught, which the plan's own cap on changes, ban on mandates and 'don't optimise for purity' constraint forbid it from achieving.

Second-Order Effects

  • T+0–6 months (Months 0-6 = 2026-10-13 to 2027-04-13) — The Cracks Appear: The board cannot choose whose pronunciation the grapheme-to-phoneme mapping encodes, and whichever accent it picks alienates the others; arguments over the first ordinal choice and the first 'retain or regularise' cases consume the schedule before a single learner sees material.
  • T+1–3 years (Months 12-36 = 2027-10-13 to 2029-10-13) — Copycats Arrive: Small, self-selected pilot cohorts produce flattering comprehension numbers that get quoted far beyond their validity, while rival groups publish competing 'clearer' variants and publishers bolt on their own markers, so fragmentation arrives before adoption does.
  • T+5–10 years (Months 60-120 = 2031-10-13 to 2036-10-13) — Norms Degrade: Technical documents appear in unlabelled mixtures of Clear English, standard English and house variants, reviewers can no longer tell which rule set a sentence obeys, and learners trained on the variant are quietly marked down by mainstream tests and hiring managers.
  • T+10+ years (Month 120 = 2036-10-13 onward) — The Reckoning: The standard survives as a dormant specification and a cohort of graduates holding a literacy that no institution recognises, while the first documented safety-relevant misreading of a variant marker converts a language experiment into a liability story.

Evidence

  • Case/Report — Initial Teaching Alphabet (i.t.a.): Sir James Pitman's 44-character reform was taken up by 140 of 158 UK education authorities in at least one school by 1966, then largely abandoned by the late 1970s because moving pupils back to standard spelling proved harder than expected (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_Teaching_Alphabet).
  • Standard/Case — ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: it exists because the European airline industry asked for it in the 1980s, and its current edition (January 2025) has 53 writing rules and about 900 approved words (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Technical_English); it succeeded through demand-pull and narrow scope, which a supply-push variant with a 5,000-word lexicon and no mandate does not have.
  • Principle/Analogue — Economics of Standards: the value of a standard rises with the number of users (network effects), so a variant that begins at zero users, has no mandate and explicitly forbids replacing anything has no mechanism for passing the tipping point.
  • Principle/Analogue — Second-Language Acquisition: negative transfer (interference) predicts that two systems which are similar but conflict in detail produce more learner errors than two clearly distinct ones, so a near-English variant risks degrading the standard English the learner still needs.
